name: Skill Builder Set 2: Hard Questions
source: Original LR and RC questions written for LSAT Trainer to give the mastery path and mixed sets more fresh hard questions, difficulty 3–5, in the style of PrepTests 150–159. Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

questions.stimulus: Retail consultant: Every store in the Garrick chain that missed its sales target last quarter has had its advertising budget cut, and no Garrick store whose advertising budget has been cut will open a second location this year. The chain's Elm Street store missed its sales target last quarter. So the Elm Street store will not open a second location this year.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Every supplier that delivers late is fined by the Garrick chain, and no supplier that has been fined receives a year-end bonus. The Harbor Bakery received no year-end bonus this year, so it must have delivered late.

Most clinics that hire a second nurse shorten their waiting times, and most clinics that shorten their waiting times attract new patients. The Pell Street clinic hired a second nurse, so it will probably attract new patients.
The Rennick Library will not lend out its atlas of shipping routes, since the atlas is printed on brittle paper, every brittle book is kept in the archive room, and no archive-room book is lent out.

Every store that renovates its entrance draws more shoppers, and every store that draws more shoppers raises its sales. The Dale Road store did not renovate its entrance, so its sales will not rise this year.

Every orchard in the valley that was hit by the spring frost lost part of its crop, and some orchards that lost part of their crop will close this year. The Ames orchard was hit by the frost, so it will close this year.
questions.explanation: The consultant's argument is a valid chain: the Elm Street store is in group A, every A is B, no B is C, so the store is not C. (C) has exactly that shape, with the conclusion stated first: the atlas is brittle (A), every brittle book is in the archive room (B), no archive book is lent (not C), so the atlas won't be lent. (D) is the trap for readers matching the store topic; it denies the first condition and concludes the outcome won't happen, which is invalid. (A) reverses the chain, (B) chains two 'most' claims into a 'probably', and (E) relies on 'some'.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Elm Street store will not open a second location this year.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Elm Street missed its target; every store that missed its target had its ad budget cut; no store with a cut budget will open a second location.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: X is A; every A is B; no B is C; so X is not C.

breakdown.analysis: Ignore the stores. Map the logic: missed target → budget cut → no second location. Elm Street missed its target, so it rides the chain all the way to "no second location." That's valid. We need an answer with a specific case, an "every" link, a "no" link, and a definite negative conclusion. Watch for answers that run the chain backward, deny the first link, or swap "every" for "some" or "most." Also remember the conclusion can come first: "since" tells you the premises follow.

choices.note: Tempting because it keeps the Garrick chain and the fines-and-bonuses feel. But it starts from the end (no bonus) and works back to the beginning (delivered late). Not getting a bonus could have many causes. That's a reversal, not the original's forward chain.
Two "most" links and a "probably" conclusion. The original uses "every" and "no" and concludes with certainty. Different strength, different structure.

CORRECT. Reorder it: the atlas is brittle (X is A); every brittle book is in the archive room (A → B); no archive-room book is lent out (B → not C); so the atlas won't be lent out (X is not C). Same chain; the conclusion just comes first.

Tempting, because it's about stores and uses two "every" links. But it denies the first condition: no renovation, so no rise in sales. Sales could rise for other reasons. The original affirms the first condition; this negates it, which is invalid.
The second link is "some," not "no" or "every." Knowing some frost-damaged orchards will close tells you nothing about Ames in particular. The chain breaks.

questions.stimulus: Most of the shoppers who used the self-service checkout lanes at Penhallow Market last month were regular customers. No regular customer at Penhallow has ever been asked to fill out the store's satisfaction survey. It follows that most of the shoppers who used the self-service lanes last month have never been asked to fill out that survey.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Most of the members of the Alder Valley hiking club joined before 2015, and most members who joined before 2015 have never led a club hike. So most of the club's members have never led a club hike.

Every tenant in the Pryor building has lived there for over ten years, and no tenant who has lived there that long pays the current market rent. It follows that none of the tenants in the Pryor building pays the current market rent.

Most of the volunteers at the county food bank are retirees, and no retiree who volunteers at the food bank works the overnight shift. It follows that none of the food bank's volunteers works the overnight shift.

None of the paintings in the museum's east gallery has been restored, and most of the museum's restored paintings are portraits. It follows that most of the paintings in the east gallery are not portraits.

Most of the trucks in the Larsen Freight fleet were bought after 2020, and none of the trucks bought after 2020 runs on diesel fuel. It follows that most of the trucks in the Larsen Freight fleet do not run on diesel.
questions.explanation: The argument is valid: most A are B, no B is C, so most A are not C. (E) matches it term for term with trucks, purchase dates and diesel. (A) is the wording-copy trap: its sentences track the original, but its second premise is 'most' rather than 'no', which makes it invalid. (B) is valid but runs on 'every' and concludes 'none', (C) inflates a 'most' into 'none', and (D) puts the quantifiers in different places.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most self-service shoppers last month have never been asked to fill out the survey.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most of those shoppers were regulars; no regular has ever been asked.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Most A are B; no B is C; so most A are not C.

breakdown.analysis: Check the quantifiers in order: "most," then "no," then "most ... not." The majority of shoppers who were regulars all escape the survey, so most shoppers escape it. Valid. The right answer needs the same three slots. Two easy ways to go wrong: change the "no" premise to "most" (that chain breaks), or change the "most" conclusion to "none" (too strong).

choices.note: Tempting, because its wording tracks the original almost word for word. But the second premise says "most," not "no": most + most doesn't chain. The club's members could all be among the early joiners who have led hikes. The wording matches; the logic doesn't.
Valid, but it's "every" then "no" then "none." The original starts with "most" and can only conclude "most." Same feel, stronger quantifiers.
Too strong. From "most volunteers are retirees" and "no retiree works overnight," you get "most volunteers don't work overnight," not "none do." The non-retiree minority might.

Different shape. It says nothing about the east gallery's paintings being in the restored group; it says they aren't. Knowing which restored paintings are portraits tells you nothing about the unrestored ones.
CORRECT. Most trucks were bought after 2020 (most A are B); none bought after 2020 runs on diesel (no B is C); so most trucks don't run on diesel (most A are not C). Exact match.

questions.stimulus: Hospital administrator: Haldane Hospital will open a pediatric wing next year only if it recruits a second pediatric surgeon, and it can recruit such a surgeon only if the state approves the salary increase the hospital has requested. But the state has rejected that request. Therefore, Haldane Hospital will not open a pediatric wing next year.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
choices: The Corwin Orchestra will not tour abroad next season, since it will tour only if it finds a sponsor, it will find a sponsor only if it records an album, and it will not record one.

If the state approves the requested salary increase, Haldane Hospital will recruit a second pediatric surgeon, and if it recruits one, it will open a pediatric wing. Since the state has rejected the increase, the wing will not open.

The city museum will build a sculpture garden only if it secures a major donor, and it will secure a major donor only if its attendance rises this year. So it will build the garden only if its attendance rises this year.

A bakery will add a night shift only if demand for its bread rises, and demand for its bread will rise only if a supermarket opens nearby. A supermarket is opening nearby, so the bakery will add a night shift.

If a pharmacy chain raises its prices, it will probably lose customers, and if it loses customers, it will probably close stores. The Dorrit pharmacy chain is raising its prices, so it will probably close some of its stores.
questions.explanation: The administrator's chain is: pediatric wing → second surgeon → salary increase approved; the increase was rejected, so no wing. (A) has the same chain of necessary conditions and the same denial of the last one, with its conclusion placed first. (B) is the trap that copies the topic: it rewrites the 'only if' claims as 'if' claims and then denies the first condition, which is invalid. (C) is valid but concludes a conditional rather than a definite prediction, (D) affirms a necessary condition, and (E) is a probabilistic forward chain.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Haldane Hospital will not open a pediatric wing next year.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Pediatric wing → second pediatric surgeon → state approves salary increase; the state rejected it.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: A only if B; B only if C; not C; so not A.

breakdown.analysis: Translate "only if": what follows it is necessary. Wing → surgeon → salary approval. Kill the last link (no approval) and everything before it dies too. That's a valid contrapositive chain. The match needs two "only if" links, a denial of the final requirement, and a definite "won't happen" conclusion. Watch the hospital answer: same words, but the arrows point the other way.

choices.note: CORRECT. Tour → sponsor → album; no album; so no tour. The conclusion comes first ("will not tour abroad ..., since ..."), but the structure is identical.

Tempting, since it's Haldane Hospital again. But "if the state approves, it recruits" is not "it recruits only if the state approves." Here approval is sufficient, and denying a sufficient condition proves nothing. The hospital might find the money elsewhere.
Valid, and it has the same two links. But it stops at a conditional conclusion (garden only if attendance rises) instead of denying the last requirement and concluding the event won't happen.

This affirms the last requirement (a supermarket is opening) and concludes the first event will happen. A necessary condition being met doesn't guarantee anything. Invalid, and different from the original.
A forward chain of "probably" claims, ending in a probable prediction. The original denies a requirement and reaches a certain negative conclusion.

questions.stimulus: Every brand of sunscreen that Ostrum Pharmacy stocks has been tested by an independent laboratory. Some of the sunscreens that dermatologists in Sefton County recommend to their patients are brands that Ostrum stocks. Hence, some of the sunscreens that Sefton County dermatologists recommend to their patients have been tested by an independent laboratory.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Every bicycle helmet that has passed the Corran safety test is sold at Vey Sports, and some helmets sold at Vey Sports are recommended by cycling coaches. Hence, some helmets that passed the test are recommended by cycling coaches.

Some of the novels on this year's prize shortlist were written by first-time authors, and some first-time authors have been published by Moreau Press. Hence, some of the shortlisted novels were published by Moreau Press.

Every bus on the Route 9 line has a wheelchair lift, and every bus with a wheelchair lift was inspected by the transit authority this spring. Hence, every bus on the Route 9 line was inspected this spring.
Every bicycle sold at Larkin Cycles has a two-year warranty. Some bicycles in this year's Coastal Classic race came from Larkin Cycles. Hence, some bicycles in the race have a two-year warranty.

Every restaurant on Canal Street passed its most recent health inspection, and some restaurants that passed their most recent inspection serve seafood. Hence, some of the restaurants on Canal Street serve seafood.
questions.explanation: The argument is valid: all A (Ostrum brands) are B (lab-tested); some C (recommended sunscreens) are A; so some C are B. (D) matches: every Larkin bicycle has a warranty, some race bicycles are Larkin bicycles, so some race bicycles have a warranty. (A) looks closest but reverses the 'every' statement, so its conclusion doesn't follow. (E) is the subtler near miss: its 'some' link attaches to B rather than to A, which breaks the chain. (B) chains two 'some' claims, and (C) is an all-all chain with an 'every' conclusion.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Some sunscreens recommended by Sefton dermatologists have been lab-tested.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Every brand Ostrum stocks is lab-tested; some recommended sunscreens are Ostrum brands.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: All A are B; some C are A; so some C are B.

breakdown.analysis: The overlap is what matters: some recommended sunscreens fall inside the Ostrum group, and everything in that group is tested. So those overlapping sunscreens are tested. Valid. The match needs the "some" premise to connect to the group the "every" premise covers. If the "some" attaches to the wrong group, the chain breaks.

choices.note: Tempting, because its premises look like the original's. But the "every" runs backward: all tested helmets are sold at Vey, not all Vey helmets are tested. The Vey helmets the coaches recommend might be untested ones. Invalid.
Two "some" premises can't be chained. The first-time authors on the shortlist and the ones Moreau published could be entirely different people.
Valid, but all + all → all. The original has a "some" premise and a "some" conclusion.
CORRECT. All Larkin bicycles have a warranty (all A are B); some race bicycles are Larkin bicycles (some C are A); so some race bicycles have a warranty (some C are B). Exact match.

Tempting, because it has "every" and "some" in the same order. But the "some" is about restaurants that passed inspection (B), not about Canal Street restaurants (A). The seafood places that passed could all be on other streets.

questions.stimulus: Pharmacy manager: More than half of the pharmacists who work at Lomax Drug's stores have been trained to give flu shots, and more than half of Lomax's pharmacists work at stores that are open around the clock. So at least one Lomax pharmacist who works at an around-the-clock store has been trained to give flu shots.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
choices: More than half of the members of the Fenwick choir sing in the church services, and more than half of its members travel with the choir on tour. So more than half of the members who travel on tour sing in the church services.

At least one Gorsley Theater subscriber who attends weekday matinees holds a student discount card, since more than half of the theater's subscribers attend weekday matinees and more than half of its subscribers hold such cards.

Exactly half of the members of the Kell rowing club compete in regattas, and exactly half of the club's members coach junior rowers. So at least one member of the club who competes in regattas also coaches junior rowers.

More than half of the city's hospitals have expanded their emergency rooms, and more than half of the hospitals that expanded their emergency rooms have hired more nurses. So more than half of the city's hospitals have hired more nurses.

More than half of the vendors at the Sunday market sell produce, and every vendor at the market who sells produce accepts credit cards. So more than half of the vendors at the Sunday market accept credit cards.
questions.explanation: Two majorities of the same group must overlap in at least one member, so the manager's argument is valid. (B) makes exactly that move, conclusion first: a majority of subscribers attend matinees and a majority hold student cards, so at least one does both. (A) is the trap with the same two majorities that inflates the conclusion from 'at least one' to 'more than half'. (C) uses exact halves, which need not overlap, (D) chains two majorities, and (E) is a valid most-plus-all chain, a different pattern.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: At least one Lomax pharmacist at an around-the-clock store is trained to give flu shots.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: More than half of Lomax pharmacists are flu-shot trained; more than half work at around-the-clock stores.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: More than half of G are A; more than half of G are B; so at least one G is both A and B.

breakdown.analysis: Picture 10 pharmacists. At least 6 are trained and at least 6 work around the clock. You can't fit 6 + 6 into 10 without someone in both groups. So the overlap is guaranteed, but only "at least one," not a majority. The match needs two majorities of the same group and a modest "at least one" conclusion.

choices.note: Tempting, because it has the same two majorities. But it inflates the conclusion from "at least one" to "more than half." Six service singers and six travelers out of ten could overlap in just two people. Right premises, wrong conclusion.
CORRECT. More than half of subscribers attend matinees and more than half hold student cards; so at least one matinee subscriber holds a card. Same pattern, conclusion stated first.
Close, but exact halves can split cleanly: 5 compete, the other 5 coach, no overlap. The original needs "more than half" twice. This one is invalid.
This chains: more than half of hospitals expanded, and more than half of those hired. That's a majority of a majority, which can be less than half the total. Different structure, and invalid.
Valid, but it's a different pattern: most + every → most. The original has two separate majorities of one group and concludes overlap.

questions.stimulus: In 2023, garden supplies accounted for 18 percent of the Brenning hardware chain's total revenue. In 2024 they accounted for 24 percent, even though the chain's total revenue was 10 percent lower in 2024 than in 2023. Brenning sold the same range of products in both years and closed none of its stores.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?
choices: Brenning sold a greater number of garden-supply items in 2024 than it had sold in 2023.
Brenning's revenue from products other than garden supplies fell by a larger percentage from 2023 to 2024 than its total revenue did.
The decline in Brenning's total revenue in 2024 was caused mainly by falling sales of power tools and building materials.
Garden supplies were the single largest source of revenue for the Brenning chain in 2024.
Customers who bought garden supplies at Brenning in 2024 spent more per visit, on average, than such customers had in 2023.
questions.explanation: Garden supplies were 18 percent of 100 in 2023 and 24 percent of 90 (21.6) in 2024, so everything else went from 82 to 68.4, a drop of about 17 percent, which is more than the 10 percent drop in the total. (B) states that from the other side, by talking about the non-garden products. (A) is the dominant trap: garden revenue did rise, but revenue is not the number of items sold, since prices or the mix of items could have changed. (C) names specific products and a cause the facts never mention, (D) needs a comparison with each other category, and (E) is about spending per visit.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Garden supplies: 18% of total revenue in 2023, 24% in 2024; 2. Total revenue fell 10% from 2023 to 2024; 3. Same products, same stores.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase, so run numbers. Say 2023 revenue was 100. Garden: 18; everything else: 82. In 2024 the total is 90. Garden: 24% of 90 = 21.6; everything else: 68.4. So garden revenue rose about 20%, and everything else fell from 82 to 68.4, about 17%, which is steeper than the total's 10% drop. Most students pick (A) because garden revenue went up, so "they sold more garden stuff." It fails because revenue is dollars, not items: a few pricey patio heaters could beat a pile of cheap seed packets.

choices.note: Tempting. Garden revenue did rise (18 → 21.6). But dollars aren't units. Brenning could have sold fewer, more expensive garden items. The facts never mention item counts.

CORRECT. Non-garden revenue went from 82 to 68.4 (out of a 100 → 90 total), a drop of about 17%, versus the total's 10%. It has to be: the garden share grew while the total shrank, so the rest fell faster than the total.
We don't know the chain sells power tools or building materials, and nothing tells us what caused the decline. New information plus a causal claim.
24% might be the biggest slice, or another category might be 30%. We have no other category's share.
Spending per visit needs visit counts, which we don't have. A different measure entirely.

questions.stimulus: All of the physicians at the Rookwood clinic who prescribe the new cholesterol drug Velatrin have attended the manufacturer's information session about it. Some of the clinic's physicians who attended that session have since stopped prescribing older cholesterol drugs altogether. No Rookwood physician who has stopped prescribing the older drugs is a cardiologist.
questions.stem: Which one of the following can be properly inferred from the statements above?
choices: Not all of the Rookwood physicians who attended the manufacturer's session are cardiologists.
Some of the physicians at the Rookwood clinic who prescribe Velatrin are not cardiologists.
Some of the Rookwood physicians who prescribe Velatrin have stopped prescribing the older cholesterol drugs altogether.
None of the cardiologists at the Rookwood clinic prescribes Velatrin to any of the patients they treat.
Every Rookwood physician who has stopped prescribing older cholesterol drugs attended the manufacturer's session.
questions.explanation: Some session attendees stopped prescribing the older drugs, and no one who stopped is a cardiologist, so some attendees are not cardiologists. (A) says exactly this in negated form ('not all'). (B) is the dominant trap: it assumes the attendees who stopped are Velatrin prescribers, but prescribers are only a subset of attendees, and the attendees who stopped could all be non-prescribers. (C) makes the same unwarranted overlap, (D) and (E) are possible but never established.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Prescribes Velatrin → attended the session; 2. Some attendees stopped prescribing older drugs; 3. Stopped older drugs → not a cardiologist.

breakdown.analysis: Chain what you can. Fact 2 gives you some people who are attendees and stoppers. Fact 3 says stoppers aren't cardiologists. So: some attendees are not cardiologists. That's it. Fact 1 points the wrong way to help: it says prescribers are inside the attendee group, not that attendees are prescribers. Most students pick (B) because Velatrin is the star of the stimulus and it feels like the attendees "are" the prescribers. It fails because the attendees who stopped could be people who went to the session and never prescribe Velatrin.

choices.note: CORRECT. Some attendees stopped the older drugs; stoppers are never cardiologists; so at least one attendee isn't a cardiologist. "Not all are cardiologists" is just that, stated in reverse.

Tempting. It links the attendee-stoppers to Velatrin prescribers. But fact 1 is one-way: prescriber → attendee, not attendee → prescriber. The non-cardiologist attendees might prescribe no Velatrin at all.
Same bad overlap. We know some attendees stopped; we don't know any of them prescribe Velatrin.
Could be true, but nothing rules out a cardiologist who attended and prescribes Velatrin while still using older drugs.
Reverses the "some": some attendees stopped, but there might be stoppers who never attended. Not established.

questions.stimulus: Last year, the average annual bonus that Ellery Logistics paid to its warehouse employees was $2,400, and the average bonus it paid to its office employees was $1,900. Every warehouse employee received a bonus of at least $1,000. Each Ellery employee works in exactly one of these two groups, and the company has more office employees than warehouse employees.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: The total amount Ellery paid in bonuses to its office employees last year was greater than the total it paid to its warehouse employees.
Most of Ellery's warehouse employees received larger bonuses last year than most of its office employees received.
At least one of Ellery's office employees received a bonus of less than $1,000 last year.
Last year the average bonus Ellery paid across all of its employees was less than $2,150.
The largest single bonus that Ellery paid last year went to one of its warehouse employees.
questions.explanation: With equal numbers in the two groups, the company-wide average would be exactly the midpoint, $2,150; because office employees, who average less, outnumber warehouse employees, the overall average is pulled below $2,150, which is (D). (A) is the dominant trap: it treats 'more office employees' as 'more office bonus money', but 11 office employees at $1,900 receive less in total than 10 warehouse employees at $2,400. (B) reads averages as 'most', and (C) and (E) are possible but not required.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Warehouse average bonus $2,400; 2. Office average bonus $1,900; 3. Every warehouse bonus ≥ $1,000; 4. More office employees than warehouse employees; everyone is in one group.

breakdown.analysis: What happens when you combine two averages? The overall average lands between them, closer to the bigger group. Equal groups would give the midpoint, $2,150. Office (the lower average) is the bigger group, so the overall average sits below $2,150. Most students pick (A) because more office people sounds like more office money. It fails on the numbers: 11 office workers × $1,900 = $20,900, and 10 warehouse workers × $2,400 = $24,000. More people doesn't mean more dollars when each gets less.

choices.note: Tempting. It turns a headcount fact into a dollar fact. But office employees get $500 less on average. With 11 office and 10 warehouse, the warehouse total is bigger. Only a large headcount gap would flip it, and we don't know the gap.
Averages don't tell you about "most." A handful of huge warehouse bonuses could lift that average while most warehouse employees got less than most office employees.
The $1,000 floor applies to warehouse employees. Office bonuses might all sit near $1,900. We don't know any office bonus was under $1,000.
CORRECT. The overall average is a weighted average of $2,400 and $1,900. With office (the lower one) as the bigger group, the weight tilts toward $1,900, so the result is below the $2,150 midpoint.
One office employee could have received a huge bonus while the rest got little. Averages say nothing about the single largest bonus.

questions.stimulus: Every store in the Wyncote grocery chain that offers curbside pickup also offers home delivery, and most Wyncote stores offer curbside pickup. None of the Wyncote stores that offer home delivery stays open past 10 p.m. Some Wyncote stores that do stay open past 10 p.m. have in-store pharmacies.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Some of the Wyncote stores that offer home delivery do not offer curbside pickup.
Most of the Wyncote stores that have in-store pharmacies stay open past 10 p.m.
Fewer Wyncote stores stay open past 10 p.m. than offer home delivery.
None of the Wyncote stores that offer curbside pickup has an in-store pharmacy.
Most of the Wyncote stores that do not offer curbside pickup stay open past 10 p.m.
questions.explanation: Curbside stores are a majority and all offer delivery, so delivery stores are a majority; late-night stores never offer delivery, so they are drawn from the minority that doesn't, and must be fewer than the delivery stores, as (C) says. (A) is the dominant trap: it reads 'most offer curbside' as 'not all', but the stores offering delivery could be exactly the stores offering curbside. (B), (D) and (E) each assert a proportion or exclusion the facts never fix.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Curbside → home delivery; 2. Most stores offer curbside; 3. Home delivery → not open past 10 p.m.; 4. Some late-night stores have pharmacies.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it: curbside → delivery → not open late. Most stores offer curbside, so most offer delivery, so most close by 10. The late-night stores all come from the non-delivery side, which is a minority. So late-night stores are outnumbered by delivery stores. Most students pick (A) because "every curbside store offers delivery" seems to leave room for delivery-only stores. Room isn't proof. Every delivery store could also offer curbside. "Most" (and "every A is B") never forces a leftover.

choices.note: Tempting. It assumes the delivery group is bigger than the curbside group. But the two groups could be identical. Nothing says any store offers delivery without curbside.
We know some pharmacy stores stay open late, not most. Lots of early-closing stores could have pharmacies too.

CORRECT. Delivery stores are a majority (they include the curbside majority). Late-night stores can't offer delivery, so they're within the minority left over. A minority group is smaller than a majority group.
The pharmacy stores we know about stay open late, but other stores could have pharmacies too, including curbside ones. Not required.
Stores without curbside could mostly close early; we only know that late-night stores are among them, not that they make up most of them.

questions.stimulus: Public health official: In the city of Vantor, the number of reported cases of foodborne illness was higher in 2024 than in 2019. Yet the number of reported cases per 100,000 residents was lower in 2024 than in 2019. Throughout that period, Vantor's health department used the same procedures for collecting reports of foodborne illness.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Restaurants and food vendors in Vantor followed safe food-handling practices more consistently in 2024 than they had in 2019.
Residents who moved to Vantor after 2019 were less likely to report a case of foodborne illness than residents who already lived there.
The number of reported cases of foodborne illness in Vantor rose in each year from 2019 through 2024.
In every age group of Vantor's residents, foodborne illness was less common in 2024 than it was in 2019.
Vantor's population grew by a larger percentage from 2019 to 2024 than its number of reported cases of foodborne illness did.
questions.explanation: A count that rises while the rate per resident falls means the number of residents rose by a larger proportion than the count did; (E) states this. (A) is the dominant trap: a falling rate invites a causal story about safer food handling, but nothing in the facts supports any particular cause. (B) is one possible explanation among many, (C) claims a year-by-year pattern the two endpoints can't show, and (D) extends a citywide figure to every age group.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. More reported cases in 2024 than 2019; 2. Fewer reported cases per 100,000 residents in 2024; 3. Reporting procedures unchanged.

breakdown.analysis: How can the count go up while the rate goes down? Rate = cases ÷ population. If cases grew 10% but the rate fell, the population must have grown by more than 10%. It's like a school with more failing students but a lower failure rate: enrollment grew faster. So the population grew proportionally faster than the cases. Most students pick (A) because a falling rate sounds like progress, and progress needs a cause. It fails because the facts give no cause at all; population growth alone explains the numbers.

choices.note: Tempting. A lower rate sounds like safer food, and safer handling is a natural cause. But nothing in the facts mentions restaurants or practices. The falling rate is fully explained by arithmetic: more residents.
Possible, but just one of many stories. The facts don't compare newcomers with long-time residents.
We only have two years. Cases could have dipped and recovered in between.
Too broad. A citywide rate can fall while some age groups get worse. The facts say nothing about age groups.
CORRECT. Rate = cases ÷ population. Cases rose, yet the rate fell, so the denominator must have grown by a bigger percentage than the numerator.

questions.stimulus: A review of 2,000 knee replacement surgeries at Saxby Orthopedic Hospital found that patients who began physical therapy within two days of surgery recovered, on average, three weeks sooner than patients who began it later. At Saxby, surgeons decide when each patient starts therapy, and they routinely postpone it for patients who developed complications during surgery.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?
choices: The difference in average recovery time between the two groups of patients may not be due entirely to when they began therapy.
Starting physical therapy within two days of knee replacement surgery shortens patients' recovery by about three weeks.
Most of the Saxby patients who began physical therapy more than two days after surgery had developed complications during surgery.
Patients who develop complications during knee surgery recover more slowly than other patients regardless of when therapy begins.
Surgeons at Saxby should start physical therapy within two days of surgery for every patient who has a knee replaced.
questions.explanation: Because surgeons push therapy back for patients with complications, the late-therapy group likely contains more complicated cases, and that difference could account for some of the slower recoveries; (A) hedges accordingly. (B) is the dominant trap: it reads the correlation as a cause and even attaches the three-week figure to it. (C) assumes complications explain most delays, (D) is a sweeping claim the review never tested, and (E) is a recommendation built on the causal trap.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Early-therapy patients recovered three weeks sooner on average; 2. Surgeons choose when therapy starts; 3. Surgeons routinely delay therapy for patients with surgical complications.

breakdown.analysis: Who ends up in the late group? Anyone with complications. So the two groups probably aren't alike before therapy even begins. It's like noting that hospital patients who get visitors on day one go home sooner, when the sickest patients aren't allowed visitors. We need an answer that says the timing may not get all the credit. Most students pick (B) because the stimulus opens like a study proving a treatment works. It fails because of fact 3: the groups were sorted by a factor that could slow recovery on its own.

choices.note: CORRECT. The late group is enriched with complicated cases, so part of the gap could come from the complications themselves. "May not be due entirely" is exactly as far as the facts go.
Tempting, because the numbers seem to show it. But this is correlation read as causation, with a precise effect size attached. The facts give a strong reason to doubt that timing alone did it.
Too strong. Surgeons delay therapy for complicated cases, but other patients might start late for other reasons (scheduling, patient choice). We can't say most late starters had complications.
"Regardless of when therapy begins" goes far beyond the review. Nothing here separates complications from timing.
A recommendation that relies on the causal claim in (B). The facts don't support the cause, let alone a policy for every patient.

questions.stimulus: A blood test for a certain thyroid disorder correctly detects the disorder in 95 percent of people who have it, and it wrongly indicates the disorder in 5 percent of people who do not have it. About 1 in every 200 adults in the region of Dresmore has the disorder. Dresmore's health agency plans to give the test to every adult in the region.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?
choices: About 95 percent of the Dresmore adults whose test results indicate the disorder will in fact have the disorder.
The test will fail to detect the disorder in more Dresmore adults who have it than it correctly detects it in.
Only a minority of the Dresmore adults whose test results indicate the disorder will actually turn out to have it.
More Dresmore adults will receive results wrongly showing that they are free of the disorder than results wrongly showing that they have it.
Testing every adult in Dresmore will cost the agency more than treating all of the cases of the disorder that the test detects.
questions.explanation: Out of every 200 adults, about 1 has the disorder and is almost always caught, while about 10 of the 199 who don't have it are wrongly flagged; so roughly 10 of every 11 positive results are false, and (C) follows. (A) is the dominant trap: it confuses the test's 95 percent detection rate with the share of positive results that are correct. (B) and (D) get the error counts backward, and (E) brings in costs the facts never mention.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. The test catches 95% of people who have the disorder; 2. It wrongly flags 5% of people who don't; 3. 1 in 200 adults has it; 4. Every adult will be tested.

breakdown.analysis: Run 200 people. About 1 has the disorder, and the test catches it (0.95 of a person). The other 199 are healthy, and 5% of them, about 10, get flagged anyway. So about 11 positive results, and only about 1 is real. When a condition is rare, false alarms swamp true hits. Most students pick (A) because "95 percent accurate" sounds like "95 percent of positives are right." It fails because the 95% is about people who have the disorder, and almost nobody does.

choices.note: Tempting. It reads "detects 95% of cases" as "95% of positive results are true." Those are different fractions. With a rare disorder, about 10 of every 11 positives are false alarms.
Backward. It catches 95% of real cases and misses 5%. Far more are detected than missed.
CORRECT. Per 200 adults: about 1 true positive versus about 10 false positives. True cases are a small minority of the positive results.
Backward again. Wrongly cleared: 5% of 1 person per 200. Wrongly flagged: 5% of 199. False alarms vastly outnumber missed cases.
Costs never appear in the facts. New information.

questions.stimulus: Sales manager: Two years ago, our Northgate store accounted for 10 percent of the chain's total sales, and last year it accounted for 14 percent. So the Northgate store's sales were higher last year than they were two years ago, and its manager has therefore earned the bonus the chain gives for increased sales.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?
choices: Last year the Corley library's fiction collection grew by 400 volumes, more than any other part of its collection. So fiction now makes up a larger share of the library's collection, and the library should hire another fiction specialist.

Ten years ago, nurses made up 30 percent of the staff at Ellsworth Hospital, and today they make up 36 percent. So Ellsworth employs more nurses today than it did ten years ago, and it has met its goal of expanding its nursing staff.

The share of the region's farmland planted in wheat rose from 20 to 25 percent over five years, during which the region's total farmland also grew. So more land is planted in wheat now, and the growers' association has met its goal of expanding wheat acreage.

Twenty percent of the shoppers surveyed at the Brayfield Mall said they would shop there more often if parking were free. So if the mall made parking free, its total sales would rise by about 20 percent.

Two years ago the Halden bakery's sales rose by 10 percent, and last year they rose by 14 percent. So the bakery's sales grew faster last year than they did two years earlier, and its owner was right to hire an extra baker.
questions.explanation: The manager infers that the store's sales rose from a rise in its share of the chain's sales, ignoring that the chain's total may have shrunk. (B) makes the same move: a larger share of the staff is taken to mean more nurses, though total staff may have fallen. (A) is the strongest trap: it also confuses amounts with shares, but in the opposite direction, from an increase in number to an increase in share. (C) avoids the flaw by stating that the total grew, (E) uses percentages but reasons validly from growth rates, and (D) commits a different error.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Northgate's sales rose, so its manager earned the increased-sales bonus.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Northgate's share of chain sales went from 10% to 14%.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: X's share of a total rose; so X's amount rose (and a reward follows). Overlooks a shrinking total.

breakdown.analysis: A bigger slice of a smaller pie can be less pie. If chain sales dropped from 100 to 60, Northgate went from 10 to 8.4 even with a 14% share. That's the flaw: share up treated as amount up. We need another argument that goes from a rising percentage to a rising count with nothing said about the total. Watch for the mirror-image flaw (count up, so share up) and for versions that fix the problem by mentioning the total.

choices.note: Tempting, since it's also a share-versus-number mistake. But it runs the other way: from a raw increase (400 volumes) to a bigger share. The original goes from share to amount. Same family, opposite direction.

CORRECT. Nurses' share of staff rose (30% to 36%), so the argument concludes there are more nurses. If total staff shrank enough, there could be fewer. Same share-to-amount leap, then the same "goal met" payoff.
This one closes the gap: the total farmland grew, so a bigger share of a bigger total really is more wheat land. Valid, so it doesn't match a flawed original.
A different flaw: it treats what 20% of surveyed shoppers say they'd do as a 20% rise in total sales. Survey intentions to sales figures, not share to amount.
It uses percentages like the original, but these are growth rates, and 14 percent growth really is faster than 10 percent. The reasoning holds, so the flaw is missing.

questions.stimulus: Most of Hadley Media's sales staff work in its Miami office, and every Hadley employee in the Miami office speaks Spanish. Last year, every member of Hadley's sales staff who speaks Spanish received the company's language bonus. Some Hadley employees who are not on the sales staff also received that bonus.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Some members of Hadley's sales staff work in offices other than the one in Miami.
Most of the Hadley employees who received the language bonus last year work in the Miami office.
Every Hadley employee who received the language bonus last year speaks Spanish.
Most of the employees in Hadley's Miami office are members of the company's sales staff.
Fewer than half of Hadley's sales staff went without the language bonus last year.
questions.explanation: Most sales staff are in Miami, everyone in Miami speaks Spanish, and every Spanish-speaking salesperson got the bonus, so most sales staff got the bonus; (E) says the same thing from the other side: fewer than half missed it. (A) is the dominant trap: it reads 'most work in Miami' as 'some work elsewhere', but 'most' is consistent with all. (B) and (D) make proportion claims about groups the facts don't size, and (C) ignores that non-sales recipients needn't speak Spanish.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Most sales staff work in Miami; 2. Miami employee → speaks Spanish; 3. Spanish-speaking salesperson → language bonus; 4. Some non-sales employees also got the bonus.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it: most sales staff → Miami → Spanish → bonus. So most sales staff got the bonus. Flip it around: fewer than half didn't. Most students pick (A) because in everyday talk "most" means "not all." On the LSAT, "most" just means more than half, and that includes every single one. All of Hadley's sales staff could be in Miami.

choices.note: Tempting. "Most work in Miami" sounds like "some don't." But "most" allows "all." Every salesperson could be in Miami, so this isn't guaranteed.
We don't know how many bonus winners there are outside Miami. Spanish-speaking salespeople elsewhere and non-sales recipients could outnumber the Miami group.
Only Spanish-speaking salespeople are guaranteed to have earned it that way. The non-sales recipients in fact 4 might not speak Spanish.
The Miami office could be packed with non-sales employees. We know where most salespeople are, not what most Miami employees do.
CORRECT. Most sales staff got the bonus (Miami → Spanish → bonus). So the ones who didn't are fewer than half. Same fact, viewed from the other side.

questions.stimulus: Last year, the Tamarind Credit Union approved 80 percent of the loan applications it received from its members and 40 percent of those it received from nonmembers. This year it again approved exactly those percentages of each group's applications. Yet the percentage of all its loan applications that the credit union approved was lower this year than last year.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: The credit union received more loan applications from nonmembers this year than it received from them last year.
The credit union approved fewer loan applications in total this year than it approved last year.
Most of the loan applications that the credit union received this year came from nonmembers.
Members' applications made up a smaller share of all applications this year than last year.
The credit union applied stricter lending standards to nonmembers' applications this year than it had last year.
questions.explanation: The overall approval rate is a weighted average of 80 percent and 40 percent, so with both group rates unchanged it can fall only if the mix shifted toward nonmembers, that is, only if members' share of applications shrank, which (D) states. (A) is the dominant trap: it turns a change in share into a change in count, but if total applications fell, nonmember applications could fall too. (B) is about counts as well, (C) needs a specific threshold, and (E) contradicts the identical approval rates.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Approval rates: members 80%, nonmembers 40%, both years; 2. Overall approval rate fell this year.

breakdown.analysis: How can the overall rate fall if neither group's rate changed? The mix changed. The overall rate is a blend of 80% and 40%; more weight on the 40% group pulls it down. So nonmembers are a bigger share and members a smaller share. Most students pick (A) because "more nonmembers" sounds like the same idea. It isn't: suppose applications fell from 1,000 to 500 and nonmembers went from 300 to 250. That's fewer nonmembers but a bigger share (30% to 50%).

choices.note: Tempting. It swaps share for count. If total applications dropped a lot, nonmember applications could drop too while their share rose. Not guaranteed.
Total approvals depend on total applications, which we don't know. The credit union could have approved more loans overall at a lower rate.
The mix moved toward nonmembers, but maybe from 20% to 30%. Nothing forces them past half.
CORRECT. Same rates, lower blend means more weight on the 40% group. That's the same as members making up a smaller share. Stated from the members' side.
Contradicts the facts: it approved exactly 40% of nonmember applications both years. Nothing suggests stricter standards.

questions.stimulus: Wrenfield Books sells new and used books and no other merchandise. Last year, used books made up 60 percent of all the books the store sold, but they brought in only 25 percent of its revenue. The store's revenue last year was higher than in any previous year of its operation.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following CANNOT be true?
choices: Last year Wrenfield took in less money per book sold from its new books than from its used books.
Some of the used books that Wrenfield sold last year sold for higher prices than some of the new books it sold.
Wrenfield earned more profit last year from the used books it sold than it earned from the new books it sold.
Wrenfield's revenue from the sale of used books was lower last year than it had been in the previous year.
Most of the books that Wrenfield sold last year for less than ten dollars apiece were new books rather than used ones.
questions.explanation: Used books were 60 percent of units but 25 percent of revenue, while new books were 40 percent of units and 75 percent of revenue, so a new book brought in about 4.5 times as much as a used book on average; (A), which says new books brought in less per book, cannot be true. (B) is the dominant trap: it looks impossible, but averages allow some used books to cost more than some new ones. (C) concerns profit, which depends on costs, and (D) and (E) are consistent with every fact given.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Only new and used books are sold; 2. Used books: 60% of units, 25% of revenue; 3. Record revenue last year.

breakdown.analysis: We need the one that's impossible. Do the per-book math. Used: 25% of revenue over 60% of units. New: 75% of revenue over 40% of units. New books bring in about 4.5 times as much per book. So any claim that used books brought in more per book is dead. Most students pick (B) because "used books are cheaper" feels absolute. It fails because the facts are averages: a rare first edition can be used and pricey while a new paperback is cheap.

choices.note: CORRECT. Per book, new books earned 75 ÷ 40 ≈ 1.9 units of revenue and used books 25 ÷ 60 ≈ 0.4. Saying new books took in less per book contradicts the facts.
Tempting. It feels like it contradicts "used books are cheaper." But that's only true on average. Some individual used books can easily cost more than some individual new ones. Could be true.
Profit isn't revenue. If used books cost the store almost nothing to acquire, they could earn more profit. Could be true.
Record total revenue doesn't require record used-book revenue. New-book sales could have carried the year. Could be true.
Nothing tells us how cheap books split. Many new paperbacks could sell under ten dollars while most used books sell for more. Could be true.

questions.stimulus: Health inspector: Under the county's rules, a restaurant can earn an A rating only if it passes every one of its kitchen inspections during the year. Cassia Bistro has passed every one of its kitchen inspections this year. So Cassia Bistro will earn an A rating this year.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?
choices: Under the county's rules, a restaurant that fails any of its kitchen inspections during the year cannot earn an A rating. Since the Marsh Street Grill failed one of its inspections this year, it will not earn an A rating.
Under the Delacourt Gallery's policy, a painting may hang in the main hall only if it is fully insured. The portrait of Elena Voss is fully insured, so it will hang in the main hall.
Most restaurants that pass every one of their kitchen inspections during the year go on to earn an A rating. Cassia Bistro has passed every inspection this year, so it will probably earn an A rating.

A student may enroll in the advanced chemistry course only if she has passed introductory chemistry. Nadia has not passed introductory chemistry, so she may not enroll in the advanced chemistry course.
Every restaurant in the county that earned an A rating last year had been inspected by Ms. Ruiz. So Ms. Ruiz must be more lenient in her inspections than the county's other inspectors are.
questions.explanation: The inspector treats a requirement (passing every inspection) as if it guaranteed the result (an A rating). (B) repeats the error: being fully insured is required for hanging in the main hall, but it doesn't ensure that the portrait will be hung. (A) is the trap for readers matching the restaurant topic; it correctly applies the requirement to a restaurant that failed it, which is valid. (C) is a reasonable probabilistic inference, (D) is valid, and (E) commits a different error, inferring leniency from a correlation.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Cassia Bistro will earn an A rating.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A rating → passed every inspection; Cassia passed every inspection.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: A only if B; B; so A. A necessary condition treated as sufficient.

breakdown.analysis: "Only if" introduces a requirement. Passing every inspection is required for an A; it isn't enough for one. Maybe the rating also depends on menus, pests or paperwork. It's like saying you can win the lottery only if you buy a ticket, you bought one, so you'll win. We need another argument that meets a requirement and declares the outcome certain.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's the same rule and another restaurant. But this one uses the rule correctly: failing the requirement rules the A out. Valid reasoning can't match a flawed original.
CORRECT. Insurance is required for the main hall (only if), the portrait is insured, so it "will be hung." Requirement met, outcome assumed. Same mistake.
Reasonable: a "most" premise supports a "probably" conclusion. No necessary-sufficient confusion.
Valid. Passing introductory chemistry is required; Nadia hasn't passed; so she can't enroll. Denying a requirement is the correct move.
A different flaw: it reads a pattern in who inspected the A-rated restaurants as proof of leniency, ignoring other explanations (maybe she inspects the best districts).

questions.stimulus: Every franchise owner in the Juno Coffee network who attended this year's spring training summit has adopted the network's new loyalty app. Most of the franchise owners who adopted the app saw their sales rise last quarter. No Juno franchise owner whose sales rose last quarter has asked the network for a reduction in fees.
questions.stem: Which one of the following can be properly inferred from the statements above?
choices: Some of the franchise owners who attended this year's spring training summit saw their sales rise last quarter.
Most of the franchise owners who attended the spring training summit have not asked the network for a reduction in fees.
Not every Juno franchise owner who has adopted the new loyalty app has asked the network to reduce its fees.
At least one franchise owner who has asked the network for a reduction in fees did not attend the summit.
Most of the Juno franchise owners who have not asked for a reduction in fees adopted the new loyalty app.
questions.explanation: Most app adopters saw sales rise, and no one whose sales rose has asked for a fee cut, so most adopters, and therefore at least some, have not asked; (C) says this as 'not every'. (A) is the dominant trap: summit attendees are a subset of adopters, and that subset could fall entirely in the minority whose sales did not rise. (B) makes the same all-then-most leap, (D) assumes someone has asked for a fee cut, and (E) reverses a 'most' relationship.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Attended summit → adopted app; 2. Most adopters saw sales rise; 3. Sales rose → has not asked for a fee cut.

breakdown.analysis: Chain from the middle: most adopters → sales rose → no fee request. So most adopters haven't asked, which means not every adopter has. The tempting move is to drag the summit attendees along: they're all adopters, so surely some saw sales rise? No. All attendees are adopters, but most adopters having rising sales tells you nothing about which adopters. Picture 10 adopters, 7 with rising sales; the 3 summit attendees could be the other 3. Most students pick (A) for exactly this reason. All → most doesn't chain.

choices.note: Tempting. Attendees are all adopters, and most adopters saw sales rise, so it feels like some attendees must have. But the attendees could all sit in the minority whose sales didn't rise. All + most doesn't give you anything.
Same broken chain, pushed further. The attendees might be exactly the adopters who did ask for a fee cut.
CORRECT. Most adopters saw sales rise, and those owners haven't asked for a fee cut. So at least some adopters haven't asked, which is exactly "not every adopter has asked."
Assumes someone asked for a fee cut at all. Maybe no one did. Even if someone did, they might have attended.
Reverses the direction. We know most adopters haven't asked; we don't know that most non-askers are adopters. Plenty of non-adopters may also not have asked.

questions.stimulus: Of the workers at Corliss Mills' three factories who reported hearing loss last year, 60 percent regularly wore the ear protection that the company supplies. According to company surveys, whose results were confirmed by spot checks on the factory floors, 85 percent of all the workers in those factories regularly wear that ear protection.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?
choices: The ear protection that Corliss supplies does little to prevent hearing loss among the factory workers who wear it regularly.
Regularly wearing the ear protection that Corliss supplies cuts a factory worker's risk of hearing loss by more than half.
Most of the workers in Corliss's factories who do not regularly wear the supplied ear protection reported hearing loss last year.
More of the workers who reported hearing loss last year wore the ear protection irregularly than wore it regularly.
Workers who did not regularly wear the ear protection were more likely than regular wearers to report hearing loss last year.
questions.explanation: Regular wearers are 85 percent of the workforce but only 60 percent of those reporting hearing loss, while non-wearers are 15 percent of the workforce but 40 percent of the reports, so a non-wearer was far more likely to report hearing loss, as (E) says. (A) is the dominant trap: it reads 'most of the people with hearing loss wore protection' without the base rate that most workers wear it. (B) is the second trap: the facts show a correlation, not that the protection itself cut the risk; non-wearers might, for example, work at noisier machines. (C) needs absolute rates the facts don't give, and (D) contradicts the 60 percent figure.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. 60% of workers reporting hearing loss were regular wearers; 2. 85% of all workers are regular wearers (surveys confirmed).

breakdown.analysis: Is 60% a lot? Only compared with 85%. Wearers are 85% of the workforce but only 60% of the hearing-loss reports: under-represented. Non-wearers are 15% of the workforce but 40% of the reports: heavily over-represented. Per 100 reports: 60 from 85 wearer-units (about 0.7 each) and 40 from 15 non-wearer-units (about 2.7 each). That's a higher report rate among non-wearers. Most students pick (A) because "most people with hearing loss wore protection" sounds damning. It ignores the base rate. Others pick (B), which turns the comparison into a cause and adds a number.

choices.note: Tempting. It reads "60% of the injured wore protection" without asking how many workers wear it overall. Since 85% do, wearers are actually under-represented among the injured. Classic base-rate neglect.

Tempting, because the risk gap is big. But the facts show who reports hearing loss, not why. If non-wearers tend to work the loudest machines, the gap could come from the noise, not the gear. A causal claim with a number attached.
We know non-wearers report loss at a higher rate than wearers, not that most of them report it. The absolute rate could be 5%.
Contradicts the facts: 60% of the reports came from regular wearers, so regular wearers outnumber irregular ones among the reports.
CORRECT. Non-wearers are 15% of workers but 40% of reports; wearers are 85% of workers but 60% of reports. So a non-wearer was more likely to report hearing loss. A comparison, not a cause.

questions.stimulus: Economist: In the province of Kelvary, office workers earn more per hour, on average, than restaurant workers do. From 2020 to 2024, the average hourly wage of Kelvary's restaurant workers rose by 18 percent, while that of its office workers rose by only 9 percent. Nonetheless, the difference in dollars between the two groups' average hourly wages was greater in 2024 than in 2020.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: From 2020 to 2024, the average hourly wage of Kelvary's restaurant workers rose by more dollars than that of its office workers did.
In 2024, most of Kelvary's restaurant workers earned less per hour than most of its office workers did.
The average office wage in Kelvary was a larger multiple of the average restaurant wage in 2024 than it was in 2020.
In 2020, Kelvary's restaurant workers earned, on average, less than half as much per hour as its office workers did.
Restaurant wages in Kelvary rose faster than office wages because the province had a shortage of restaurant workers.
questions.explanation: If office pay is O and restaurant pay is R, the dollar gap grows only if 9 percent of O exceeds 18 percent of R, that is, only if R was less than half of O in 2020; (D) states that bound. (A) is the dominant trap: 18 percent sounds bigger than 9 percent, but a bigger percentage of a much smaller base can be fewer dollars, and here it must be. (C) gets the ratio backward (it shrank), (B) reads averages as 'most', and (E) supplies an unsupported cause.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Office average > restaurant average; 2. 2020–2024: restaurant average +18%, office average +9%; 3. The dollar gap widened anyway.

breakdown.analysis: How can the faster-growing group fall further behind in dollars? Only if its base is much smaller. Try restaurant $10, office $30: restaurant gains $1.80, office gains $2.70, gap widens. Try restaurant $20, office $30: restaurant gains $3.60, office $2.70, gap shrinks. The break-even is when 0.09 × office = 0.18 × restaurant, i.e., restaurant = half of office. So restaurant pay must have started below half. Most students pick (A) because 18 beats 9. But a big percentage of a small number can be a small number.

choices.note: Tempting. 18% > 9% feels like more money. But if restaurant workers had gained more dollars, the gap would have shrunk. The facts say it grew, so office workers must have gained more dollars. This is actually false.
Averages don't tell you about "most." A few very highly paid office workers could pull the office average up while many earn less than many restaurant workers.
Backward. Restaurant pay grew faster in percentage terms, so office pay became a smaller multiple of restaurant pay, not a larger one.
CORRECT. The gap widens only if 9% of office pay exceeds 18% of restaurant pay, which means restaurant pay was under half of office pay in 2020.
The facts give no cause for the wage growth. A shortage is one possible story, not something the numbers support.

questions.stimulus: Most of the products that Danforth Outfitters sells under its own label are made overseas, and most of its own-label products are sold at a discount at least once a year. None of the products Danforth sells that are made overseas comes with a lifetime guarantee. Danforth also sells many products made by other companies.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Most of Danforth's own-label products that are sold at a discount at least once a year are made overseas.
Not all of the products that Danforth discounts at least once a year come with a lifetime guarantee.
Some of Danforth's own-label products that are made overseas are never sold at a discount during the year.
Most of the products that Danforth sells at a discount at least once a year carry Danforth's own label.
Some of the products that come with a lifetime guarantee at Danforth are made by other companies.
questions.explanation: Two majorities of the same group (own-label products) must overlap, so at least one own-label product is both made overseas and discounted; being made overseas, it lacks a lifetime guarantee, so some discounted product lacks one, which (B) states as 'not all'. (A) is the dominant trap: the overlap is guaranteed to be at least one product, not a majority of the discounted ones. (C) treats 'most' as 'not all', (D) ignores the other companies' discounted products, and (E) assumes lifetime guarantees exist at all.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Most own-label products are made overseas; 2. Most own-label products are discounted at least once a year; 3. Made overseas → no lifetime guarantee; 4. Danforth also sells other companies' products.

breakdown.analysis: Two "mosts" about the same group must overlap. Picture 10 own-label products: at least 6 made overseas and at least 6 discounted, so at least 2 are both. Each of those lacks a lifetime guarantee (fact 3). So at least one discounted product has no lifetime guarantee. Most students pick (A) because two majorities feel like they line up. They only have to share one member: 6 overseas and 6 discounted out of 10 can overlap in just 2, and 2 of 6 isn't most.

choices.note: Tempting. Most + most feels like it should give most. But 6 overseas and 6 discounted out of 10 might share only 2. Then only 2 of the 6 discounted are overseas, a minority.
CORRECT. The two majorities overlap, so some own-label product is both overseas-made and discounted. Overseas means no lifetime guarantee. So not every discounted product has one.
"Most" can mean "all." Every overseas product could also be discounted at some point. Not required.
Danforth sells many outside products, and those could be discounted constantly. We can't tell what share of discounted goods are own-label.
We don't even know Danforth offers any lifetime guarantees. If it does, they might all be on domestic own-label goods.

questions.stimulus: Hospital administrator: Last year, the average length of stay at Pellard General Hospital fell from 6 days to 5 days for surgical patients and from 4 days to 3.5 days for all other patients. Even so, the average length of stay for all of the hospital's patients taken together was longer last year than it was the year before.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: The total number of days that patients spent at Pellard General Hospital was greater last year than the year before.
Pellard General Hospital treated more surgical patients last year than it had treated the year before.
Most of the patients that Pellard General Hospital treated last year were surgical patients.
In the year before last, fewer than half of the patients treated at Pellard General Hospital were surgical patients.
Some surgical patients at Pellard General Hospital last year stayed longer than any of its other patients did.
questions.explanation: If s is the surgical share of patients, the overall average is 4 + 2s days the year before and 3.5 + 1.5s days last year; even if every patient last year had been surgical, the average would be 5 days, so it can exceed the earlier figure only if 4 + 2s was below 5, that is, only if surgical patients were under half of the earlier year's patients, as (D) states. (B) is the dominant trap: the surgical share must have risen, but a rising share is not a rising count. (A) needs patient totals, (C) does not follow because the earlier share could have been very small, and (E) says nothing averages can establish.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Surgical stays averaged 6 days, then 5; 2. Other stays averaged 4 days, then 3.5; 3. The overall average stay rose.

breakdown.analysis: Both groups got shorter, yet the overall average rose. Only the mix can do that: more weight on the long-stay surgical group. Now push it further. Last year's overall average can't exceed 5 days, since that's what you'd get if every patient were surgical. So the earlier year's overall average must have been under 5. With 6 and 4 as the group averages, that means surgical patients were under half of the earlier year's patients. Most students pick (B) because "the surgical share rose" sounds like "more surgical patients." If the hospital's total patient count fell, the surgical count could fall too while its share rose.

choices.note: Total patient-days depends on how many patients there were, which we don't know. A smaller hospital load could mean fewer total days.

Tempting. The surgical share must have grown. But share isn't count: if total patients dropped from 1,000 to 300, surgical patients could fall from 200 to 190 while their share jumps from 20% to about 63%.
Not required. If surgical patients were 10% of the earlier year's patients, last year's share only needs to top about 47% for the average to rise.

CORRECT. Last year's average is at most 5 days (all surgical). The earlier average, 4 + 2 × (surgical share), must be lower than last year's, so it's under 5, which forces the surgical share under one half.
Averages tell you nothing about the longest individual stays. A nonsurgical patient might have stayed longest.

questions.stimulus: Sales director: Last quarter, the 50 sales representatives at Vantor Medical Supply closed an average of 12 deals each. Exactly 10 of those representatives closed at least 30 deals apiece, and no representative closed more than 45 deals. Every one of the 50 representatives closed at least one deal during the quarter.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?
choices: At least one of Vantor's sales representatives closed fewer than 8 deals last quarter.
Most of Vantor's sales representatives closed fewer than 12 deals each last quarter.
More than half of all the deals that Vantor's representatives closed last quarter were closed by the 10 top performers.
None of Vantor's sales representatives closed between 12 and 29 deals last quarter.
The 10 representatives who closed at least 30 deals each closed an average of more than 35 deals apiece.
questions.explanation: The 50 representatives closed 600 deals, and the top 10 closed at least 300 of them, so the other 40 closed at most 300, an average of no more than 7.5 each, which means at least one of them closed fewer than 8, as (A) says. (B) is the dominant trap: it reads an average as a median, but 20 of the other 40 could have closed 12 or more while the rest closed very few. (C) is the subtler trap: the top 10 must have closed at least half of the deals, but exactly half (30 each) is possible. (D) and (E) are possible but not required.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. 50 reps, average 12 deals → 600 deals total; 2. Exactly 10 reps closed 30+ each; 3. Nobody closed more than 45; 4. Everyone closed at least 1.

breakdown.analysis: Turn the average into a total: 50 × 12 = 600. The top 10 closed at least 10 × 30 = 300. That leaves at most 300 for the other 40, an average of at most 7.5. If 40 people average 7.5 or less, someone is at 7 or below. Most students pick (B) because "average 12" sounds like "typical rep closes about 12." But averages don't tell you how many are above or below. Try it: top 10 at 34 (340), 20 reps at 12 (240), 20 reps at 1 (20). Total 600, and 30 of 50 reps closed 12 or more.

choices.note: CORRECT. 600 total, at least 300 by the top 10, so the other 40 closed at most 300, averaging 7.5 or less. Somebody among them closed fewer than 8.
Tempting. It treats the average as the middle. But see the example in the analysis: 30 of 50 reps can sit at 12 or more. Average isn't "most."
Tempting, because the top 10 closed at least 300 of 600. But "at least half" isn't "more than half." If each top rep closed exactly 30, they closed exactly half.
Nothing rules out a rep with, say, 15 deals among the other 40. The facts allow it.
They might each have closed exactly 30, an average of 30. Their average must be at least 30, not more than 35.

questions.stimulus: Of the 120 people employed by Inverly Textiles, 70 work on the factory floor and 65 have been with the company for more than ten years. Every Inverly employee who has been with the company for more than ten years is enrolled in its pension plan, and some of the company's newer employees are enrolled in the plan as well.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Most of the employees who work on Inverly's factory floor are enrolled in the company's pension plan.
Most of the Inverly employees who are enrolled in the pension plan work on the company's factory floor.
At least 15 of the employees who have been with Inverly for more than ten years work somewhere other than the factory floor.
Fewer than half of the Inverly employees who are not enrolled in the pension plan work on the factory floor.
No more than 55 of Inverly's factory-floor employees are outside the company's pension plan.
questions.explanation: Since 70 + 65 = 135 exceeds the 120 employees, at least 15 floor workers have been with the company more than ten years, and all of them are in the pension plan; so no more than 55 of the 70 floor workers can be outside the plan, which is (E) stated from the unenrolled side. (A) is the dominant trap: two majorities guarantee an overlap of 15, not a majority of the floor workers. (B) and (C) assume particular overlaps, and (D) fails because all of the unenrolled employees could work on the floor.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. 120 employees; 2. 70 work on the floor; 3. 65 have 10+ years; 4. 10+ years → enrolled in pension; 5. Some newer employees are enrolled too.

breakdown.analysis: Two big groups in a fixed total must overlap. 70 + 65 = 135, but there are only 120 people, so at least 15 are in both: floor workers with 10+ years. Those 15 are all enrolled. That leaves at most 55 floor workers who could be unenrolled. Most students pick (A) because both groups are majorities, so it feels like most floor workers are veterans and enrolled. But the guaranteed overlap is only 15 of 70. The other 55 floor workers could all be newer and unenrolled.

choices.note: Tempting. Two majorities feel like they should mostly coincide. But the overlap can be as small as 15 floor workers. If the rest of the floor is newer and unenrolled, only 15 of 70 are enrolled.
Enrollees are at least 65 veterans plus some newer employees. If only 15 of them are on the floor, the floor is a minority of enrollees.
Not required. All 65 veterans could work on the floor (the floor has 70 spots), leaving zero veterans elsewhere.
Every unenrolled employee is a newer one, and the newer employees could all be on the floor. Then all of the unenrolled work on the floor.
CORRECT. At least 15 floor workers are veterans (70 + 65 − 120), and every veteran is enrolled. So at most 70 − 15 = 55 floor workers can be unenrolled.

questions.stimulus: A survey of adults in the city of Wendling found that those who live within a kilometer of a public park are far more likely than other adults to exercise regularly. However, among the surveyed adults who had moved to within a kilometer of a park during the previous five years, the proportion who exercise regularly was the same as it had been before they moved.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Building additional public parks in Wendling would not change the proportion of its adults who exercise regularly.
Most of the adults in Wendling who exercise regularly live within a kilometer of a public park.
Something other than living near a park accounts for at least part of the difference in exercise rates that the survey found.
Adults in Wendling who exercise regularly are more likely than other adults to move to a home near a public park.
Wendling adults who moved within the previous five years exercise less regularly than adults who did not move.
questions.explanation: People who moved near a park did not start exercising more, which suggests that living near a park is not, by itself, what produces the higher exercise rate; (C) draws that modest conclusion. (D) is the dominant trap: self-selection is one way to explain the pattern, but the facts never say that movers were already more active than other adults, only that their rate didn't change. (A) predicts with certainty about new parks, (B) turns a rate into a share, and (E) compares groups the survey never compared.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Adults near parks exercise regularly at a much higher rate; 2. Adults who moved near a park in the last five years exercise at the same rate as before they moved.

breakdown.analysis: If parks made people exercise, the newcomers should have picked it up. They didn't. So proximity probably isn't the whole story behind the gap. That's all the facts support. Most students pick (D) because "active people choose homes near parks" is the obvious alternative explanation. But the survey never says the newcomers were unusually active before moving, only that they didn't change. They might have been couch potatoes before and after. A plausible story is not a supported one.

choices.note: Too strong. The facts suggest proximity isn't the whole cause, not that new parks would change nothing for anyone. Maybe long-term residents do pick up the habit over more than five years.
A rate isn't a share. If few adults live near parks, most regular exercisers could live elsewhere even though the nearby group exercises at a higher rate.

CORRECT. Newcomers' exercise rates didn't budge after the move, so living near a park probably doesn't by itself produce the gap. Something else accounts for at least part of it. Modest, and backed by the facts.
