Tempting: it's the natural alternative explanation. But we don't know the newcomers exercised more than other adults before moving; we only know their rate didn't change. Self-selection is possible, not supported.
The survey never compares movers with non-movers. No basis at all.

questions.stimulus: Economist: Most of the small businesses that received grants from the Strand Valley development fund last year are restaurants, and most restaurants in the province operate at a loss during their first two years. So most of the businesses that received the fund's grants last year are operating at a loss.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?
choices: Most of the businesses that received grants from the development fund last year are restaurants, and every restaurant that received a grant has hired new staff. So most of the businesses that received grants have hired new staff.

Most of the members of the Arden Street choir are retired teachers, and most of the choir's members sing in its alto section. So at least some of the retired teachers in the choir sing in the alto section.
Most of the people who buy season tickets to the Rowan Theater live downtown. So most of the people who live downtown buy season tickets to the Rowan Theater.
A majority of the Quayside apartments' tenants must own a car, since most of them commute to jobs outside the city, and most of the region's out-of-city commuters own a car.
Most of the businesses that received grants from the development fund last year have hired new staff since then. So the grants are what enabled most of those businesses to hire new staff.
questions.explanation: The economist chains two 'most' claims: most grant recipients are restaurants, and most restaurants in the province lose money, so most recipients lose money; but the recipients could be among the profitable minority of restaurants. (D) repeats this most-plus-most chain with its conclusion first: most tenants commute out of the city, most such commuters own cars, so a majority of tenants own cars. (B) is the dominant trap: it also has two 'most' premises, but both are about the same group, so its modest conclusion is valid. (A) is a valid most-plus-every chain, (C) reverses a 'most' claim, and (E) infers a cause.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most grant recipients are operating at a loss.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most recipients are restaurants; most restaurants in the province lose money in their first two years.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Most A are B; most B (in a larger population) are C; so most A are C.

breakdown.analysis: Most + most doesn't chain. The grant-winning restaurants could be the healthy ones; maybe the fund picks winners. It's like saying most of my friends are lawyers, most lawyers are unhappy, so most of my friends are unhappy. We need another argument that links two "most" claims through a middle group and concludes "most." Watch the decoy that has two "mosts" but about one group, which is valid, and the one with "every" in the second slot, also valid.

choices.note: Same fund, same first premise, but the second premise is "every restaurant that received a grant." Most + every → most is valid. A valid argument can't match a flawed one.
Tempting: two "most" premises, just like the original. But both are about the choir's members, so they must overlap, and the conclusion only claims "at least some." That's valid.
A different flaw: it flips "most A are B" into "most B are A." Most season-ticket buyers live downtown doesn't mean most downtown residents buy tickets.

CORRECT. Most tenants commute out (most A are B); most regional out-commuters own cars (most B are C); so most tenants own cars (most A are C). Same broken chain: the tenants might be the out-commuters without cars. The conclusion just comes first.
A causal flaw (hiring after the grant, so the grant caused it), not a quantifier chain. It shares the fund topic only.

questions.stimulus:
Priya: Publishers should hire professional actors, not the authors themselves, to narrate the audiobooks of novels. Most novelists have never been trained to use their voices, and listeners who find a narration flat often stop listening partway through the book.

Colm: An author's reading may lack polish, but only the author knows exactly how each line was meant to sound. For a novel, that knowledge matters more than vocal training, so the author should be the narrator whenever he or she is willing.
questions.stem: Priya and Colm disagree over whether
choices: most authors of novels have never received any training in how to use their voices when reading aloud
listeners who find an audiobook's narration flat often stop listening before they reach the end of the book
the author of a novel knows better than anyone else how each line of the novel was meant to sound
publishers should generally have professional actors, rather than the novels' own authors, narrate the audiobooks of novels
an audiobook narrated by its author is likely to sound less polished than one narrated by a trained actor
questions.explanation: Priya says publishers should hire actors, not authors, to narrate novels; Colm says the author should narrate whenever willing, so they disagree over (D). (C) is the main trap: it is the heart of Colm's case, but Priya never says who knows best how the lines should sound, so she takes no position on it. (A) and (B) are Priya's claims alone, and Colm's concession that an author's reading 'may lack polish' means he doesn't reject (E).

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Priya: Actors, not authors, should narrate novels; most novelists are untrained, and listeners quit flat narrations.; Colm: Authors may lack polish, but only they know how each line should sound, and that matters more; authors should narrate when willing.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other must say no. Find each bottom line. Priya: hire actors instead of authors. Colm: let the author narrate whenever he or she is willing. That's a direct clash over who should narrate. Notice how little else they fight about. Colm never denies that authors are untrained; he even grants that an author's reading "may lack polish." And Priya never says a word about who understands the lines best. Each premise belongs to one speaker only.

choices.note: Priya's claim only. Colm doesn't dispute it. His "may lack polish" comes close to conceding it.
Priya's claim only. Colm never discusses whether listeners quit. He could agree completely and still prefer the author's voice.

Tempting, because it's Colm's main reason and it seems like the obvious thing Priya would reject. But she never addresses it. Her case rests on vocal training and listener patience, not on who understands the text. Silence isn't disagreement.
CORRECT. Priya: hire actors, "not the authors themselves." Colm: "the author should be the narrator whenever he or she is willing." One says yes to actors over authors; the other says no.
No dispute here. Priya implies it, and Colm concedes that an author's reading "may lack polish." At most this is common ground.

questions.stimulus:
Anouk: The Delford Jazz Club should lift its ban on filming during sets. Clips that audience members post online are free advertising, and the club's attendance has been falling for three years.

Ruben: Lifting the ban might well bring in more people. But musicians improvise more freely when they know that a misstep won't end up online, and that freedom is exactly what the club's audiences come to hear. The ban should stay.
questions.stem: Anouk and Ruben disagree over whether
choices: the Delford Jazz Club should allow members of its audiences to film the musicians during sets
lifting the ban on filming would bring more people to the Delford Jazz Club's performances
the freedom to improvise without fear of being recorded is what draws audiences to the club
attendance at the Delford Jazz Club has been declining steadily for the past three years
video clips of live performances that are posted online tend to discourage people from attending in person
questions.explanation: Anouk says the club should lift its filming ban; Ruben says the ban should stay, so they disagree over (A). (B) is the trap: Anouk relies on it, but Ruben grants that lifting the ban 'might well bring in more people,' so he doesn't deny it. (C) is Ruben's claim alone, (D) is Anouk's claim alone, and (E) is a view neither holds.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Anouk: Lift the filming ban; posted clips are free advertising and attendance is falling.; Ruben: Lifting it might bring in more people, but musicians improvise more freely without the risk of being filmed, and that's what audiences come for; keep the ban.

breakdown.analysis: Bottom lines first. Anouk: lift the ban. Ruben: keep it. That's a clean yes versus no. The thing to watch is Ruben's concession. He says lifting the ban "might well bring in more people." So he isn't fighting Anouk on attendance at all. He's saying something else matters more. When a speaker concedes a point, it can't be the point at issue.

choices.note: CORRECT. Anouk: "should lift its ban on filming." Ruben: "The ban should stay." Allowing audiences to film is exactly what one wants and the other rejects.
Tempting, because it's Anouk's main reason. But Ruben concedes it: lifting the ban "might well bring in more people." He doesn't dispute the benefit; he outweighs it.
Ruben's claim only. Anouk says nothing about why audiences come or about how musicians improvise.
Anouk's claim only. Ruben never mentions attendance figures, so he isn't committed either way.
Neither speaker says this. Anouk thinks clips help attendance, and Ruben grants they might. Nobody claims they discourage attendance.

questions.stimulus:
Tamsin: The Westvale school board should not adopt abridged editions of classic novels for its ninth graders. A novel's style is part of what the novel is, and an abridgment that rewrites a novelist's sentences into plainer ones gives students something other than the novel.

Hugo: The abridgments the board is considering do not rewrite a single sentence. They omit whole chapters of subplot and leave every remaining sentence exactly as the novelist wrote it.
questions.stem: Hugo responds to Tamsin by
choices: denying that a novel's style is part of what makes the novel the particular work that it is
arguing that the benefits of abridged editions to ninth graders outweigh any loss to the novels' style
suggesting that Tamsin's objection would apply equally to the unabridged editions that the board now uses
questioning whether ninth graders are able to appreciate the style of a classic novel in the first place
pointing out that the editions at issue lack the feature on which Tamsin's objection depends
questions.explanation: Tamsin's objection targets abridgments that rewrite the novelist's sentences; Hugo replies that the editions under consideration rewrite nothing, so the objection doesn't reach them, as (E) says. (A) is the trap: Hugo never denies that style is part of a novel; in fact his reply assumes it matters, since he stresses that every sentence stays as written. He weighs no benefits (B), mentions no other editions (C), and says nothing about what ninth graders can appreciate (D).

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: (Tamsin) The board shouldn't adopt abridged classics. (Hugo) Implied: Tamsin's objection doesn't apply to these abridgments.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: (Tamsin) Style is part of a novel, and abridgments that rewrite sentences into plainer ones change the novel. (Hugo) These abridgments rewrite no sentences; they only cut subplot chapters.

breakdown.analysis: Ask what Tamsin's objection actually needs. It needs the abridgments to rewrite the novelist's sentences. Hugo says: these don't. He isn't fighting her principle about style. He's saying her principle doesn't touch these books. It's like objecting to a restaurant because it fries everything, and someone answers that this restaurant doesn't fry anything. Prephrase: he shows the editions don't have the feature her objection targets.

choices.note: Tempting, because Hugo is pushing back on Tamsin, so it's natural to think he rejects her premise. But he leaves "A novel's style is part of what the novel is" untouched. If anything, he relies on it: his point is that the style survives because every sentence stays.
choices.example: Example of method: A novel is its plot and characters; the particular sentences are just packaging, so rewriting them changes nothing essential.

choices.note: Hugo never weighs benefits against costs. He doesn't concede any loss to style at all.
choices.example: Example of method: Even if some style is lost, students who finish an abridged classic gain more than students who give up on the full one.

choices.note: Hugo mentions no other editions. He doesn't claim Tamsin's reasoning would condemn the books the board already uses.
choices.example: Example of method: By your reasoning, the annotated editions we use now, with their simplified glosses, aren't the novels either.

choices.note: Hugo says nothing about ninth graders' abilities. This is a different objection to Tamsin.
choices.example: Example of method: Fourteen-year-olds rarely notice prose style, so it hardly matters whether the sentences are rewritten.

choices.note: CORRECT. Tamsin objects to abridgments that rewrite sentences into plainer ones. Hugo points out that these abridgments "do not rewrite a single sentence." So her objection, whatever its merit, doesn't reach these editions.

questions.stimulus:
Lidia: Children beginning the violin should be taught to read music from their first lessons. Students who are taught to play by ear first often resist learning notation later, because reading slows them down compared with the playing they can already do.

Matteo: Some students taught by ear do resist notation later. But children learn language by listening long before they read, and music is no different. Beginners should play only by ear for at least their first year.
questions.stem: Lidia and Matteo disagree over whether
choices: most students who are taught to play the violin by ear go on to resist learning to read music
children who are beginning the violin should be taught to read music from their very first lessons
the process by which a child learns music closely resembles the process by which a child learns language
students who can already play by ear find at first that reading notation slows down their playing
some students who are taught to play the violin by ear later resist learning to read music
questions.explanation: Lidia says beginners should learn to read music from their first lessons; Matteo says beginners should play only by ear for at least a year, so they disagree over (B). (A) is the trap: Lidia says such students 'often' resist notation, which is not 'most,' and Matteo concedes only that some do, so neither is committed to it. (E) is something both accept, and (C) and (D) belong to one speaker each.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Lidia: Teach beginners to read music from the first lesson; ear-first students often resist notation later.; Matteo: Some do resist, but children learn language by listening first, and music is the same; beginners should play only by ear for at least a year.

breakdown.analysis: Lidia: read music from day one. Matteo: only by ear for at least a year. Those can't both happen, so that's the clash. Now watch the quantifiers on the side issue. Lidia says ear-first students "often" resist notation. Matteo grants that "some" do. "Often" and "some" are compatible, so there's no fight there. And neither of them says "most." The LSAT loves to slip a stronger quantifier into a trap.

choices.note: Tempting, because it looks like the factual dispute behind their positions. But Lidia says "often," not "most," and Matteo only concedes "some." Neither speaker is committed to "most," so this can't be what they disagree about.
CORRECT. Lidia: beginners "should be taught to read music from their first lessons." Matteo: beginners "should play only by ear for at least their first year." One says yes, the other says no.
Matteo's claim only ("music is no different"). Lidia never compares music to language.
Lidia's claim only. Matteo never discusses whether reading slows ear-trained players down.
Common ground. Matteo says "Some students taught by ear do resist notation later," and Lidia's "often" implies at least some. Agreement is the opposite of what the stem asks for.

questions.stimulus:
Hadley: The Corran Tribune buries its corrections on page two, where few readers notice them. A correction should run in the same place as the error it corrects; otherwise many readers who saw the error will never learn that it was wrong.

Pruitt: If every correction ran on the front page, trivial slips, like a misspelled name in a sports roundup, would crowd out the news. Corrections of serious errors in front-page stories, though, do belong on the front page.
questions.stem: The dialogue provides the most support for the claim that Hadley and Pruitt agree that
choices: the Tribune should print every one of its corrections on the front page of the paper
few of the Tribune's readers notice the corrections that the paper prints on page two
a correction of a serious error in a front-page story belongs on the Tribune's front page
a correction should be printed in the same size of type as the story that contained the error
misspelling a name in a sports story is too minor an error to require any correction at all
questions.explanation: Hadley holds that every correction should run where the error ran, which puts corrections of front-page errors on the front page; Pruitt says corrections of serious front-page errors belong on the front page, so both accept (C). (A) is the trap: Pruitt rejects it, and Hadley never proposes it, since she wants corrections placed where the errors were, not all on page one. (B) is Hadley's claim alone, and neither speaker says (D) or (E).

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Hadley: Corrections are buried on page two; each correction should run in the same place as the error.; Pruitt: Putting every correction on the front page would let trivial slips crowd out news, but corrections of serious front-page errors belong on the front page.

breakdown.analysis: For an agreement question, you need a claim BOTH speakers are committed to. Hadley's rule: a correction goes where the error was. Apply it to a serious error in a front-page story. Where does the correction go? The front page. Pruitt says exactly that about serious front-page errors. So that narrow case is common ground. Notice that Pruitt is attacking a position Hadley never took. She didn't say every correction goes on page one.

choices.note: Tempting, because Pruitt seems to be answering this, so it feels like Hadley's view. But Hadley wants each correction where its error was, and most errors aren't on the front page. And Pruitt rejects this outright. Not agreement.
Hadley's claim only. Pruitt never says how many readers notice page-two corrections.

CORRECT. Hadley's rule (same place as the error) puts a front-page error's correction on the front page, serious or not. Pruitt explicitly says serious front-page errors' corrections "do belong on the front page." Both are committed.
Neither speaker mentions type size. Hadley talks about placement only.
Pruitt calls such slips "trivial" and says they shouldn't crowd the front page, not that they need no correction. Hadley would correct them. Neither holds this.

questions.stimulus:
Ilse: The unsigned poem 'Low Tide at Carrick' was almost certainly written by Nora Vane. It appeared in the same small magazine as her other early poems, in the same year, and it shares their unusual habit of rhyming only the second and fifth lines of each stanza.

Desmond: Other poets published in that magazine that year, and Vane's rhyme scheme was easy to imitate. Since your evidence doesn't establish that Vane wrote the poem, she did not write it.
questions.stem: Desmond's reasoning is flawed in that it
choices: takes for granted that a claim is false if the evidence offered for it does not establish it
overlooks the possibility that a poet's habits of rhyme can change over the course of his or her career
presumes, without providing justification, that Vane never published a poem without signing it
rejects Ilse's conclusion on the grounds that Ilse has a personal stake in Vane's reputation
draws a conclusion about all of Vane's early poems from evidence about a single unsigned poem
questions.explanation: Desmond's points show at most that Ilse's evidence is inconclusive, yet he concludes that Vane did not write the poem; (A) describes this move from 'not proven' to 'false.' (B) is tempting because it sounds like a real weakness in attributing poems by style, but Desmond never relies on rhyme habits staying fixed. Desmond doesn't presume anything about signing (C), attacks no motive (D), and draws no conclusion about Vane's other poems (E).

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: (Desmond) Vane did not write the poem.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: (Desmond) Other poets published in the magazine that year; Vane's rhyme scheme was easy to imitate; so Ilse's evidence doesn't establish that Vane wrote it.

breakdown.analysis: Desmond's two points are fair. They show Ilse's evidence isn't conclusive. But then he jumps: "your evidence doesn't establish it, so it's false." Does weak evidence for a claim prove the claim is false? No. It's like saying: you haven't proven it will rain, so it won't rain. This is the classic "absence of proof treated as proof of absence" flaw. Worth knowing; it shows up a lot in dialogue replies. Prephrase: he treats a failure to prove something as proof that it's false.

choices.note: CORRECT. Desmond's evidence only undercuts Ilse's case. His conclusion, "she did not write it," needs much more. He moves from "not established" to "false."
Tempting, since changing habits are a real problem for attribution by style. But that problem would hurt Ilse, not Desmond. His reasoning never depends on Vane's rhymes staying the same.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Vane rhymed only the second and fifth lines in 1910, so a poem from 1925 without that pattern can't be hers.

choices.note: Desmond never mentions signing. His argument doesn't need any assumption about whether Vane signed her poems.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Vane signed every poem we know of, so an unsigned poem can't be hers.

choices.note: Desmond says nothing about Ilse's motives or interests. He responds to her evidence.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Ilse is writing Vane's biography, so of course she wants another poem to be Vane's; we can ignore her.

choices.note: Desmond's conclusion is about one poem only. He says nothing about Vane's other early poems.
choices.example: Example of flaw: This one unsigned poem in Vane's style isn't hers, so none of the poems attributed to her early period are hers.

questions.stimulus:
Fenella: History exams at our school should be open-book. Students forget memorized dates within weeks, and what matters is whether they can interpret sources, which an open-book exam tests as well as a closed-book one does.

Osric: An open-book exam can test interpretation, I admit. But students who know they can look facts up during an exam don't bother to learn them, and no one can interpret a source without knowing the events surrounding it. Our exams should stay closed-book.
questions.stem: Fenella and Osric disagree over whether
choices: students at the school tend to forget within a few weeks the dates that they memorize for history exams
an open-book history exam is capable of testing how well students can interpret historical sources
students who expect to be able to look facts up during an exam generally do not bother to learn those facts
the school's history exams should permit students to consult their books while they are taking them
a student cannot interpret a historical source without some knowledge of the events surrounding it
questions.explanation: Fenella wants the school's history exams to be open-book, and Osric wants them to stay closed-book, so they disagree over (D). (C) is the trap: it is central to Osric's case and seems to clash with Fenella's view, but Fenella never says whether students learn facts they can look up. (B) is common ground, since Osric admits it, and (A) and (E) are each one speaker's claim.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Fenella: Make history exams open-book; students forget memorized dates, and open-book exams test interpretation just as well.; Osric: Open-book exams can test interpretation, but students then don't learn the facts, and you can't interpret sources without the facts; keep exams closed-book.

breakdown.analysis: Fenella: open-book. Osric: closed-book. That's the clash. Then check what Osric gives away: "An open-book exam can test interpretation, I admit." So that's not in dispute. The trap will be one of Osric's reasons that Fenella never addresses. Fenella talks about forgetting dates and testing interpretation. She never says whether students study facts they can look up. Silence isn't disagreement.

choices.note: Fenella's claim only. Osric never says whether students forget memorized dates.
Common ground. Osric says "An open-book exam can test interpretation, I admit." A concession can't be the point at issue.

Tempting, because it's Osric's key reason and seems to cut against Fenella. But Fenella never discusses whether students learn facts they know they can look up. She might grant it and think it doesn't matter.
CORRECT. Fenella: exams "should be open-book." Osric: "Our exams should stay closed-book." A clean yes and no on consulting books during exams.
Osric's claim only. Fenella says interpretation is what matters, but she never says it can be done without background knowledge.

questions.stimulus:
Wren: A newspaper may crop a news photograph, but it must never remove anything from within the frame. Once a paper erases even a stray power line, readers cannot know what else it has erased, and its photographs lose their value as evidence.

Kasimir: Cropping removes far more of a scene than erasing a power line does, yet you allow it. Erasing a minor distraction should be permitted, provided that the caption tells readers it was done.
questions.stem: Wren and Kasimir disagree over whether
choices: cropping a news photograph removes more of the scene it depicts than erasing a minor object from it does
readers' trust in news photographs depends on whether newspapers tell them how the photographs were edited
a newspaper can be justified in erasing a minor object from within the frame of a news photograph
a newspaper that secretly erases objects from its photographs undermines the photographs' value as evidence
every way of editing a news photograph diminishes to some degree the photograph's value as evidence
questions.explanation: Wren says a paper must never remove anything from within the frame; Kasimir says erasing a minor distraction should be permitted with a caption, so they disagree over (C). (A) is the trap: Kasimir asserts it, but Wren allows cropping without ever comparing how much it removes, so she isn't committed against it. Kasimir never addresses secret erasures (D), Wren's acceptance of cropping keeps her from holding (E), and (B) is at most implied by Kasimir alone.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Wren: Cropping is fine, but nothing inside the frame may ever be removed; one erasure makes all of a paper's photos worthless as evidence.; Kasimir: Cropping removes more than erasing a power line, yet you allow it; minor erasures should be allowed if the caption says so.

breakdown.analysis: Wren's rule is absolute: never remove anything from within the frame. Kasimir says minor erasures are fine with a caption. That's a yes/no on whether such an erasure can ever be acceptable. Now the trap. Kasimir's lead claim is that cropping removes more than erasing. Does Wren deny that? She never says. She allows cropping, but she doesn't compare amounts. Her rule might rest on something else entirely, like the difference between leaving things out of the frame and altering what's in it. A claim only one speaker addresses can't be the point at issue.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's Kasimir's opening shot and it's aimed at Wren. But Wren never compares how much cropping and erasing remove. She could agree that cropping removes more and still say erasing is different in kind. Only Kasimir is committed.
Kasimir's caption condition hints at something like this, but he never states it, and Wren says nothing about disclosure. Neither is clearly committed.

CORRECT. Wren: a paper "must never remove anything from within the frame." Kasimir: "Erasing a minor distraction should be permitted." One says such an erasure is never acceptable; the other says it can be.
Wren would accept this, since she thinks any erasure undermines a paper's photos. But Kasimir only defends erasures disclosed in captions. He says nothing about secret ones. No disagreement.
Wren doesn't hold this. She allows cropping and never suggests cropping hurts a photo's value as evidence. And Kasimir doesn't address it. Neither speaker is committed.

questions.stimulus:
Rosalind: Merrit Hale asked in her will that her diaries be burned, and her heirs should have honored that request instead of publishing the diaries. A writer's explicit wishes about her private papers should prevail over readers' curiosity.

Bertram: Hale had already drawn two of her novels almost entirely from those diaries. Her request deserved respect, but the diaries shed so much light on the novels that publishing them was justified.
questions.stem: Rosalind and Bertram disagree over whether
choices: Hale's request that her diaries be burned deserved to be taken seriously by her heirs
Hale had made much of the content of her diaries public by drawing on them for two of her novels
a writer's wishes about her private papers should prevail even over the papers' value for understanding her published works
curiosity about a writer's life is never by itself a sufficient reason to publish her private papers
Hale's heirs ought to have burned her diaries, as she had asked, rather than publishing them
questions.explanation: Rosalind says the heirs should have honored Hale's request to burn the diaries rather than publish them; Bertram says publishing them was justified, so they disagree over (E). (C) is the trap: Bertram rejects it, but Rosalind's principle sets a writer's wishes only against 'readers' curiosity,' not against the diaries' value for understanding the novels, so she isn't committed to (C). (A) is common ground, (B) is Bertram's alone, and (D) overstates Rosalind with 'never by itself.'

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Rosalind: The heirs should have burned the diaries as asked; a writer's explicit wishes beat readers' curiosity.; Bertram: The request deserved respect, but the diaries illuminate two novels drawn from them, so publishing was justified.

breakdown.analysis: Start with the case. Rosalind: the heirs should have honored the request (burned the diaries) instead of publishing. Bertram: publishing was justified. That's a direct clash about what the heirs should have done. Now the trap: the general principle. Rosalind's principle pits wishes against "readers' curiosity." Bertram's reason isn't curiosity; it's scholarly light on the novels. Rosalind never weighs wishes against that kind of value. So a principle about scholarly value goes beyond what she said. Watch for a choice that upgrades one speaker's principle into a broader one.

choices.note: Common ground. Rosalind wants the request honored, and Bertram says it "deserved respect."
Bertram's point only. Rosalind never mentions the novels.

Tempting, and the main trap. Bertram clearly rejects it. But Rosalind's principle only says wishes beat "readers' curiosity." She never addresses the diaries' value for understanding the novels, so we can't say she holds this broader principle.

Too strong for Rosalind. She says wishes should prevail over curiosity, which concerns papers a writer wanted kept private, not that curiosity is "never by itself" enough in any case. And Bertram doesn't rest on curiosity at all.

CORRECT. Rosalind: the heirs "should have honored that request instead of publishing." Bertram: "publishing them was justified." If publishing was justified, the heirs weren't obligated to burn the diaries instead.

questions.stimulus:
Editor: Since the Garrow Times redesigned its website last spring, with larger type and fewer ads beside each article, the average time readers spend on an article has risen by 40 percent. The redesign has made our articles easier to read.

Analyst: Last spring the Times also began running long investigative features, and those features account for nearly all of that increase. Readers spend no more time than before on the paper's other articles.
questions.stem: The analyst responds to the editor by
choices: questioning the accuracy of the measurement on which the editor's claim about reading time is based
accepting the editor's figure but showing that how it breaks down tells against the editor's explanation
arguing that the redesign has in fact made the paper's ordinary articles more difficult to read
proposing that the investigative features were introduced in order to take advantage of the redesign
contending that the time readers spend on an article is not a reliable measure of how easy it is to read
questions.explanation: The analyst doesn't dispute the 40 percent rise; he shows that it comes almost entirely from the new long features, while time spent on other articles is unchanged, which undercuts the claim that the redesign made articles easier to read, as (B) says. (E) is the trap: the analyst's point could suggest that reading time is a poor measure, but he never questions the measure itself; he uses it, citing unchanged reading time on other articles. He doesn't challenge the figure (A), claim the redesign hurt readability (C), or speculate about motives (D).

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: (Editor) The redesign made articles easier to read. (Analyst) Implied: the increase doesn't show that.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: (Editor) Average reading time per article rose 40% after the redesign. (Analyst) Nearly all of the rise comes from new long features; time on other articles hasn't changed.

breakdown.analysis: Does the analyst say the 40% figure is wrong? No. He accepts it and splits it up. Nearly all of the increase comes from long features, which take longer because they're long. On everything else, reading time didn't budge, even though everything else got the same larger type and fewer ads. So the aggregate number hid the real story. It's like a restaurant crediting its new menu for a rise in average bill, when the whole rise came from one new wine list. Prephrase: he breaks the editor's number into parts, and the parts point away from the editor's explanation.

choices.note: The analyst never says the figure is inaccurate. He accepts the 40% rise and explains where it comes from.
choices.example: Example of method: Your analytics count a page as read whenever a tab is left open, so the 40 percent figure is inflated.

choices.note: CORRECT. He grants the overall rise but shows it's concentrated in the new features. On the other articles, which also got the redesign, reading time is flat. That breakdown cuts against "the redesign made articles easier to read."
Too strong. The analyst says reading time on other articles is unchanged, not that those articles got harder to read.
choices.example: Example of method: Since the redesign, readers spend less time on ordinary articles and abandon more of them partway, so the new layout is harder to read.

choices.note: The analyst says nothing about why the features were introduced. He only says when, and what they did to the numbers.
choices.example: Example of method: The paper launched long features precisely because the new, cleaner layout finally made long reads practical.

choices.note: Tempting, because his point can feel like an attack on the measure. But he relies on the very same measure: "Readers spend no more time than before" on other articles. He accepts reading time as evidence; he just reads it differently.
choices.example: Example of method: People linger on an article when it's confusing, too, so more time spent reading tells us nothing about ease.

questions.stimulus:
Gerda: The Valmont Opera should not install the sound-enhancement system its board is considering. Opera singers train for years to fill a hall unaided, and an audience that hears amplified voices is no longer hearing opera.

Lorcan: The system would only even out the sound in the balcony, where some words now get lost; no singer would sound louder in the main seats. Still, I would oppose it if it changed the voices' timbre, and the vendor hasn't yet shown that it doesn't.
questions.stem: The dialogue provides the most support for the claim that Gerda and Lorcan agree that
choices: the opera company should not install the system if it would alter the timbre of the singers' voices
the opera company should not install the sound-enhancement system that its board is considering
some of the words sung in performances at the Valmont Opera are now lost on listeners in the balcony
an audience that hears singers' voices amplified is no longer hearing opera in the true sense
the system under consideration would not make any singer sound louder to listeners in the main seats
questions.explanation: Gerda opposes installing the system under any circumstances, so she is committed to opposing it if it would alter the voices' timbre; Lorcan says he would oppose it in that case, so both accept (A). (B) is the trap: Gerda holds it, but Lorcan opposes the system only on a condition the vendor hasn't yet settled, so he isn't committed to rejecting it. (C) and (E) are Lorcan's claims alone, and (D) is Gerda's.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Gerda: Don't install the system; singers train to fill the hall unamplified, and amplified voices aren't opera.; Lorcan: The system only evens out balcony sound and makes no singer louder in the main seats; but he'd oppose it if it changed the voices' timbre, which hasn't been ruled out.

breakdown.analysis: Agreement questions with a conditional are sneaky. Lorcan's position is: oppose the system IF it changes timbre. Gerda's position is: oppose the system, period. If you oppose something in every case, you oppose it in the timbre-changing case too. So both are committed to "don't install it if it alters timbre." Gerda: no in all cases. Lorcan: no in that case. Where do they meet? In that case. What they DON'T share is Gerda's flat "don't install it." Lorcan hasn't decided; he's waiting on the vendor.

choices.note: CORRECT. Gerda opposes the system under all conditions, so she opposes it if it alters timbre. Lorcan says outright, "I would oppose it if it changed the voices' timbre." Both are committed.

Tempting, because Lorcan raises an objection and sounds skeptical. But his objection is conditional, and the condition is unsettled: the vendor "hasn't yet shown" either way. Gerda is committed; Lorcan isn't. Not agreement.
Lorcan's claim only. Gerda never mentions the balcony.
Gerda's claim only. Lorcan never says amplified voices aren't opera. He'd accept the system if it left the timbre alone.
Lorcan's claim only. Gerda never addresses what the system would do in the main seats; her objection is to amplification as such.

questions.stimulus:
Mireille: Graphic novels belong in the high school literature curriculum. Several of them are as complex in structure and theme as any novel students now read, and assigning them draws in students who rarely finish a book.

Anders: A few graphic novels may be that complex. But in practice the titles would be chosen by teachers eager to engage reluctant readers, and their choices would tend toward the simplest titles available. Graphic novels should stay out of the curriculum.
questions.stem: Mireille and Anders disagree over whether
choices: several graphic novels are as complex in structure and theme as the novels that high school students now read
most graphic novels are considerably simpler in structure and theme than most novels are
teachers choosing graphic novels in order to engage reluctant readers would tend to select the simplest titles
graphic novels should be among the works that high school students are assigned in their literature courses
assigning graphic novels in literature courses would draw in students who seldom finish reading a book
questions.explanation: Mireille says graphic novels belong in the literature curriculum; Anders says they should stay out, so they disagree over (D). (A) is the trap: Mireille asserts it, but Anders says only that a few graphic novels 'may be' that complex, so he neither affirms nor denies it. (B) is held by neither speaker, (C) is Anders's claim alone, and (E) is Mireille's, which Anders doesn't contest.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Mireille: Put graphic novels in the curriculum; several are as complex as assigned novels, and they draw in reluctant readers.; Anders: A few may be that complex, but teachers would pick the simplest titles; keep them out.

breakdown.analysis: Bottom lines: Mireille says graphic novels belong in the curriculum; Anders says keep them out. That's the clash. The trap is the complexity claim. Mireille says several ARE as complex. Anders says a few MAY be. "May be" isn't a denial. He sidesteps the question and moves to how teachers would choose. When one speaker hedges with "may," he hasn't taken the other side.

choices.note: Tempting, because it looks like the factual crux. But Anders says a few graphic novels "may be that complex." That's not a denial. He grants the possibility and shifts to how titles would be chosen. Only Mireille is committed.
Neither speaker says anything about most graphic novels compared with most novels. Anders's worry is about which titles teachers would pick, not about graphic novels in general.
Anders's claim only. Mireille doesn't discuss how teachers would choose titles.
CORRECT. Mireille: graphic novels "belong in the high school literature curriculum." Anders: they "should stay out of the curriculum." Yes versus no.
Mireille's claim only. Anders never denies it. If anything, his talk of teachers "eager to engage reluctant readers" goes along with it.

questions.stimulus:
Halvard: Broadcast radio still matters to musicians. In our region, no song has reached the top of the sales charts in the past decade without first being played heavily on at least one regional station.

Signe: That can't be right. Every week, regional stations play dozens of songs heavily, and nearly all of them disappear without a trace. Clearly, heavy airplay does little to make a song a hit.
questions.stem: Signe's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: treats a claim that something guarantees an outcome as if it were a claim that it is required for that outcome
cites evidence that is inconsistent with Halvard's claim about which songs have reached the top of the sales charts
takes for granted that a song's sales are the only reliable indication of whether it has become a hit
infers from the fact that most heavily played songs fail that heavy airplay lowers a song's chances of becoming a hit
treats a claim that something is required for an outcome as if it were a claim that it guarantees that outcome
questions.explanation: Halvard claims that heavy airplay has been necessary for reaching the top of the charts; Signe rebuts him by showing that heavy airplay is not sufficient, since most heavily played songs fail, so (E) describes her error. (A) is the trap: it names the same necessary/sufficient confusion but runs it backward, as though Halvard had claimed that airplay guarantees a hit and Signe had read that as a requirement. (B) fails because her evidence is fully consistent with Halvard's claim, which is exactly why her rebuttal misfires. (C) is not assumed, since both speakers use the same standard of a hit, and (D) overstates her conclusion, which is that airplay does little, not that it hurts.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: (Signe) Halvard is wrong; heavy airplay does little to make a song a hit.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: (Signe) Each week dozens of songs get heavy airplay, and nearly all of them vanish.

breakdown.analysis: Halvard's claim: chart-topper → heavy airplay first. That's airplay as a NECESSARY condition. Signe's evidence: heavy airplay → usually no hit. That shows airplay isn't SUFFICIENT. But Halvard never said it was. Both facts can be true at once: almost every hit needed airplay, and most songs with airplay still flopped. It's like saying a college degree can't matter for becoming a surgeon, because most people with degrees don't become surgeons. Prephrase: she attacks airplay as a guarantee when Halvard claimed it was a requirement. Two choices will describe a necessary/sufficient mix-up. Before you pick, say which claim was which: Halvard's was the requirement; Signe treated it as a guarantee.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap: it uses the right vocabulary and most students pick it on a quick read. But it's backward. Halvard's claim was the requirement (no chart-topper without airplay), and Signe treated it as a guarantee. This choice says Halvard claimed a guarantee and Signe treated it as a requirement. Always pin down which claim is which.
choices.example: Example of flaw: You say a strong cover letter guarantees an interview. But plenty of people get interviews without one, so you're wrong.

choices.note: Backward. Her evidence is perfectly consistent with Halvard's claim: hits can all have had airplay while most songs with airplay flop. That's the problem. Her rebuttal doesn't contradict him, though her "That can't be right" pretends it does. If her evidence really were inconsistent with his claim, her reply would be a good one.
choices.example: A reply that really does cite inconsistent evidence (and so is not flawed): You say every chart-topper had heavy airplay first, but Slow River topped the chart without being played anywhere.

choices.note: Not assumed. Halvard measures success by the sales charts, and Signe's "disappear without a trace" fits the same standard. Her argument would misfire the same way under any measure of a hit.
choices.example: Example of flaw: That song has ten million streams, but it hasn't sold, so it isn't a hit and radio did nothing for it.

choices.note: Overstates her conclusion. Signe says airplay "does little to make a song a hit," not that it hurts a song's chances.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Most heavily advertised products fail, so advertising lowers a product's chances of success.

choices.note: CORRECT. Halvard said airplay is required (no chart-topper without it). Signe answers by showing that airplay doesn't guarantee a hit. That doesn't contradict him at all. She's confused a necessary condition with a sufficient one.

questions.stimulus:
Ottilie: Baroque music should be performed on period instruments. Gut strings and valveless horns produce a quieter, rougher sound than their modern counterparts, and that is the sound the composers were writing for.

Barnaby: The composers did write for the instruments they had, but several of them complained in letters that those instruments were crude. A composer who wished for better instruments would not want his music confined to the ones he was stuck with.
questions.stem: Ottilie and Barnaby disagree over whether
choices: the composers of Baroque music wrote it with the instruments of their own time in mind
performers of Baroque music should limit themselves to instruments of the kinds that its composers had
all of the Baroque composers would have preferred to hear their music played on modern instruments
a composer's own preferences ought to settle how his or her music is performed in later centuries
gut strings and valveless horns produce a rougher sound than the strings and horns that are used today
questions.explanation: Ottilie says Baroque music should be performed on period instruments; Barnaby says the composers would not want their music confined to those instruments, so they disagree over (B). (A) is the trap: it sounds like Ottilie's premise under attack, but Barnaby concedes it ('The composers did write for the instruments they had'). (C) inflates Barnaby's 'several' to 'all,' (D) is a principle neither states, and (E) is Ottilie's claim, which Barnaby doesn't dispute.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Ottilie: Play Baroque music on period instruments; their rougher sound is what composers wrote for.; Barnaby: Composers wrote for what they had, but several called those instruments crude; they wouldn't want their music confined to them.

breakdown.analysis: Ottilie's position: period instruments are how this music should be played. Barnaby's: the music shouldn't be confined to them. That's the clash, stated in Barnaby's own word, "confined." Then check the concession. Barnaby says, "The composers did write for the instruments they had." So he grants Ottilie's premise and fights her conclusion. Also watch "several" in Barnaby: several composers complained, not all.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's Ottilie's key premise and Barnaby seems to be attacking it. But he concedes it: "The composers did write for the instruments they had." He disputes what follows from it, not the fact itself.

CORRECT. Ottilie: the music "should be performed on period instruments." Barnaby: the composers "would not want [their] music confined" to those instruments. That's whether performers should limit themselves to period instruments, yes versus no.
Too strong. Barnaby says "several" composers complained, not all, and Ottilie says nothing about what composers would have preferred.
Neither speaker states this principle. Barnaby appeals to composers' wishes and Ottilie to the sound they wrote for, but neither says a composer's preferences settle the matter.
Ottilie's claim. Barnaby doesn't dispute it; calling the old instruments "crude" fits with it.

questions.stimulus:
Ines: Our district should stop teaching cursive. Hardly any adult writes in cursive anymore, and the hours spent on it could go to keyboarding, a skill every student will need.

Tobias: Most adults rarely write in cursive, true. But students who can't read cursive can't read most of the letters and records in the town archive, which our eighth graders use for their local-history project. So students should at least be taught to read cursive, even if they are not taught to write it.
questions.stem: Ines and Tobias disagree over whether
choices: the district should continue to teach its students how to write in cursive
few adults today write in cursive often enough to make teaching students to write it worthwhile
the district should end all of the instruction in cursive that it now gives its students
keyboarding is a skill that every student in the district will need to have
most of the letters and records held in the town archive were written in cursive
questions.explanation: Ines says the district should stop teaching cursive altogether; Tobias says students should at least be taught to read it, so he rejects ending all cursive instruction, and they disagree over (C). (A) is the trap: Ines rejects it, but Tobias explicitly leaves open whether students should learn to write cursive ('even if they are not taught to write it'), so he isn't committed to it. (B) and (D) are Ines's claims, which Tobias never denies, and (E) is Tobias's alone.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Ines: Stop teaching cursive; hardly anyone writes it, and the time could go to keyboarding.; Tobias: Most adults rarely write it, but students need to read it to use the town archive; teach at least reading cursive, even if not writing.

breakdown.analysis: Ines wants ALL cursive instruction gone. Tobias wants at least reading cursive kept. So they clash over whether every bit of cursive instruction should end. The trap is about writing cursive. It feels like Tobias is defending cursive, so he must want writing taught. But he says "even if they are not taught to write it." He's neutral on writing. That one clause is the whole question: reading versus writing, and "all" versus "some." Read the scope words in each choice.

choices.note: Tempting, and the most-picked trap. Ines rejects it, but Tobias deliberately sets writing aside: students should learn to read cursive "even if they are not taught to write it." He takes no position on writing, so this isn't a disagreement.
Ines's view. Tobias concedes that most adults rarely write cursive and never argues that teaching writing is worthwhile. He isn't committed against this.
CORRECT. Ines: "stop teaching cursive," with no exceptions. Tobias: students "should at least be taught to read cursive." One says end all of it; the other says keep some of it.
Ines's claim only. Tobias never mentions keyboarding. He could agree that every student needs it and still want some time kept for reading cursive.
Tobias's claim only (students who can't read cursive "can't read most of the letters and records"). Ines never mentions the archive.

questions.stimulus: Media analyst: After the Fenwick Daily put its website behind a paywall, the number of people reading it online fell by 60 percent, yet the site's revenue, all of which comes from advertising and subscription fees, rose. Advertisers pay more per reader to reach people who pay for their news, since such readers tend to read more closely. Evidently, then, the Daily now takes in more online advertising revenue than it did before the paywall.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the media analyst's argument depends?
choices: Most of the increase in the Daily's online revenue came from advertisers rather than from subscription fees.
The Daily did not lose any of its online advertisers as a result of putting its website behind a paywall.
Every advertiser that bought space on the Daily's website before the paywall spent more there afterward.
Most of the online readers whom the Daily lost after the paywall had previously visited its website only occasionally.
Subscription fees did not account for the entire increase in the revenue from the Daily's website.
questions.explanation: A paywall brings in subscription fees, which could explain the revenue increase by themselves; the analyst concludes that advertising revenue went up, so she must assume that fees did not account for the whole increase, as (E) says. (A) is the trap: it pushes the same idea too far, since advertising revenue could have risen slightly while fees supplied most of the gain. (C) would guarantee the conclusion, but it isn't required, since some old advertisers could spend less while others spend much more; (B) is likewise too strong, and (D) is irrelevant.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Daily now takes in more online advertising revenue than before the paywall.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Online readers fell 60% but online revenue rose; advertisers pay more per reader to reach paying readers.

breakdown.analysis: Wait, what's the most obvious thing a paywall does to revenue? It brings in subscription fees. So why credit the advertisers at all? If fees covered the whole increase, ad revenue didn't rise at all; with 60% fewer readers, it may even have fallen. Higher rates per reader don't help if there are far fewer readers. The analyst needs only a sliver of the increase to come from somewhere other than fees. Prephrase: not all of the rise came from subscriptions. Then watch for the too-strong version: "most" of it came from ads.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's the right idea. But it's too strong. The conclusion says only that ad revenue went up. If ads produced 30% of the gain, the argument is fine. Negate it and nothing breaks.
choices.negation: Most of the increase did not come from advertisers; at least half came from subscription fees.

choices.note: Too strong. The Daily could lose a few advertisers and still earn more from the rest at higher rates per reader.
choices.negation: The Daily lost at least one online advertiser as a result of the paywall.

choices.note: Tempting, because if it's true, ad revenue certainly went up, so it proves the conclusion. But that makes it sufficient, not required. A few old advertisers could spend less, or leave, while the rest spend far more, and ad revenue would still rise. Negate it and the argument survives.
choices.negation: At least one advertiser that bought space on the Daily's website before the paywall did not spend more there afterward.

choices.note: Irrelevant. How often the lost readers used to visit doesn't decide whether ad revenue went up. At most it explains why losing them hurt less.
choices.negation: Fewer than half of the readers the Daily lost had previously visited its website only occasionally.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: subscription fees accounted for the entire increase. Then advertising revenue didn't go up, and the conclusion is false. Note the modest "not the entire" wording: the argument needs only some of the gain to come from elsewhere.
choices.negation: Subscription fees accounted for the entire increase in the revenue from the Daily's website.

questions.stimulus:
Corinne: The Pellam Prize for fiction should require that entries be judged with the authors' names removed. Judges who know an author's reputation cannot help being swayed by it, and a prize that rewards reputation instead of the book itself fails at its one job.

Aldous: Judges are swayed by reputation. But anonymity wouldn't fix that: established novelists have styles so distinctive that judges would recognize most of their books anyway. Removing names would add cost for little benefit.
questions.stem: Corinne and Aldous disagree over whether
choices: the Pellam Prize ought to have its judges evaluate entries without knowing who wrote them
the judges of the Pellam Prize are influenced by what they know of the reputations of the authors
removing authors' names from entries would do nothing to lessen the effect of reputation on the judges
judges would be able to identify most books by established novelists even if the authors' names were removed
a prize for fiction has no legitimate purpose other than to reward the best book among the entries
questions.explanation: Corinne says the prize should require anonymous judging; Aldous says removing names would add cost for little benefit, so he rejects the requirement, and they disagree over (A). (C) is the trap: Aldous says anonymity wouldn't 'fix' the problem and offers 'little benefit,' but judges would recognize 'most,' not all, established novelists' books, so he isn't committed to anonymity doing nothing. (B) is common ground, (D) is Aldous's claim alone, and (E) goes beyond Corinne's 'one job.'

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Corinne: Require anonymous judging; judges are swayed by reputation, and rewarding reputation defeats the prize's purpose.; Aldous: Judges are swayed, but anonymity wouldn't fix it, since judges would recognize most established novelists anyway; it adds cost for little benefit.

breakdown.analysis: Bottom lines: Corinne wants anonymity required. Aldous says it's not worth the cost. That's the disagreement. Now the quantifier trap. Aldous says anonymity "wouldn't fix" the problem and gives "little benefit," because judges would recognize "most" books. Most isn't all, and little isn't none. So Aldous allows that anonymity would help a bit. A choice saying it would do "nothing" overstates him. Read his hedges as carefully as his claims.

choices.note: CORRECT. Corinne: the prize "should require that entries be judged with the authors' names removed." Aldous: removing names "would add cost for little benefit," so the prize shouldn't do it. Yes versus no.
Common ground. Corinne says judges "cannot help being swayed," and Aldous agrees: "Judges are swayed by reputation."

Tempting, because Aldous is clearly skeptical of anonymity. But he says "little benefit," not none, and judges would recognize "most" books, not all. That leaves some books where anonymity helps. Aldous isn't committed to "nothing," so this isn't the point at issue.
Aldous's claim only. Corinne never says whether judges could identify books without names.

Too strong for Corinne. She says rewarding reputation "fails at its one job," which implies the job is to reward the book. But "no legitimate purpose other than" picking the single best entry goes further, and Aldous never addresses a prize's purpose at all.

questions.stimulus: Educational researcher: First-year students at Marwick College who took the optional study-skills seminar went on to earn higher grades than those who did not take it. Many conclude that the seminar raised their grades. But students who enrolled in the seminar and were turned away only because it was full earned grades just as high as those who took it. So the seminar did not raise its participants' grades.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the educational researcher's argument?
choices: The students turned away from the seminar were chosen at random from among those who had enrolled in it.
Students who enroll in optional seminars are generally more motivated than students who do not enroll in them.
None of the students who were turned away from the seminar consulted any guide to study skills on their own.
The students who were turned away did not, for the most part, acquire the seminar's skills by some other means.
The skills that the seminar teaches are of little use to students in courses that they take after their first year.
questions.explanation: The researcher uses the turned-away students as a comparison group: they wanted the seminar but didn't get it, yet did just as well. That comparison shows nothing if those students mostly learned the same skills elsewhere, so the argument requires (D). (A) is the trap: random selection would make the comparison cleaner, but the comparison can be fair without it, so it's helpful, not required. (C) is too strong, (B) would support the argument without being needed, and (E) is irrelevant.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The seminar did not raise its participants' grades.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Students who enrolled but were turned away because the seminar was full earned grades as high as those who took it.

breakdown.analysis: Clever control group: students who wanted the seminar but didn't get it. They did just as well, so the seminar didn't matter. But ask: did those students really go without the seminar's content? What if they were sent to the library's version of the same workshop, or learned the skills some other way? Then they're not a no-seminar group at all, and their high grades could come from the very skills the seminar teaches. Prephrase: the turned-away students didn't mostly get the same skills elsewhere. Then beware answers that make the control group cleaner but aren't required.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. Random selection would make the comparison airtight, so it feels essential. But it's not required. Students turned away on a first-come basis could still be comparable to those admitted. Helpful isn't necessary.
choices.negation: The students turned away were not chosen at random from those who enrolled.

choices.note: This would support the argument by explaining the original gap (motivated students enroll and also earn better grades). But the argument doesn't depend on it. Negate it and the turned-away comparison still works.
choices.negation: Students who enroll in optional seminars are not generally more motivated than those who do not.

choices.note: Too strong. A few turned-away students reading a study guide wouldn't undermine the comparison. The argument needs only that the group as a whole didn't get the skills elsewhere.
choices.negation: At least one student who was turned away consulted a guide to study skills on his or her own.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: most turned-away students acquired the seminar's skills some other way. Then they aren't a real comparison group, and their high grades are consistent with those skills, and so the seminar's teaching, raising grades. The argument collapses.
choices.negation: For the most part, the students who were turned away did acquire the seminar's skills by some other means.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The argument is about the grades students went on to earn; whether the skills help in later years doesn't affect the comparison.
choices.negation: The skills that the seminar teaches are of considerable use in courses after the first year.

questions.stimulus:
Juror Halloway: The Ferris Biennial should exclude sculptures that were fabricated by hired workshops rather than by the artists themselves. When a workshop does the making, viewers cannot tell how much of what they admire reflects the artist's own skill.

Juror Quist: Yet for years you have argued that the Biennial should keep its printmaking category, and nearly every print in it is pulled by a master printer rather than by the artist. Viewers of those prints cannot tell either.
questions.stem: Quist responds to Halloway by
choices: denying that viewers of a fabricated sculpture are unable to tell how much of it reflects the artist's own skill
pointing out that Halloway's reasoning would also count against something that Halloway has supported
showing that Halloway's conclusion conflicts with a general principle that Halloway has explicitly endorsed
showing that Halloway's reasoning would count against every category of work that the Biennial now accepts
suggesting that the value a work has for viewers does not depend on who physically produced it
questions.explanation: Quist notes that Halloway's reason for excluding fabricated sculpture (viewers can't tell how much reflects the artist's skill) applies equally to prints, a category Halloway has long defended, so Quist exposes an inconsistency, as (B) says. (C) is the trap: it also describes an inconsistency, but Quist cites a position Halloway has argued for (keeping printmaking), not a general principle, and the clash is with Halloway's reasoning, not with the conclusion that fabricated sculpture should go. (D) overstates by a quantifier: Quist extends the reasoning to one other category, not to every category. Quist concedes the point (A) denies, and he never states the principle in (E).

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: (Halloway) Exclude workshop-fabricated sculptures. (Quist) Implied: Halloway's reasoning is inconsistent with a position Halloway holds.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: (Halloway) With fabrication, viewers can't tell how much reflects the artist's skill. (Quist) Halloway defends printmaking, yet master printers pull nearly every print, and viewers can't tell there either.

breakdown.analysis: What does Quist actually conclude? Nothing explicit. He points to a position Halloway already holds (keep printmaking) and shows that Halloway's own reason applies to it just as well. So either Halloway's reason is bad, or Halloway should give up printmaking. It's a consistency challenge. Like telling a friend who refuses takeout because he can't see the kitchen that he eats at his mother-in-law's without seeing her kitchen either. Prephrase: Quist turns Halloway's reasoning against something Halloway supports. Then read the near-misses word by word: a reasoning-versus-position match is right; a conclusion-versus-principle match is not, and "one case" is not "every category."

choices.note: Quist doesn't deny this. He concedes it: viewers of prints "cannot tell either." The word "either" grants Halloway's point about sculpture.
choices.example: Example of method: Experienced viewers can easily tell a workshop's hand from an artist's, so fabrication hides nothing.

choices.note: CORRECT. Halloway's reason (viewers can't tell how much reflects the artist's skill) applies equally to prints pulled by master printers. Halloway has argued for keeping printmaking. Quist shows that the reasoning cuts against Halloway's own position.

Tempting, and the main trap, because Quist really is exposing an inconsistency. But look at its two parts. Halloway's printmaking view is a position about one category, not a general principle. And excluding fabricated sculpture doesn't by itself conflict with keeping prints; what conflicts is Halloway's REASON, which applies to both. Right kind of move, wrong parts.
choices.example: Example of method: You have always said the Biennial should judge every work solely on how it looks, yet now you want to exclude sculptures because of who made them.

choices.note: Close, but too broad. Quist applies Halloway's reasoning to one other category, printmaking. He says nothing about painting, photography, or anything else the Biennial shows. "Every category" is more than he claims.
choices.example: Example of method: By your standard, paintings finished by studio assistants, photographs printed by labs, and films shot by crews would all have to go, so nothing in the Biennial would survive.

choices.note: Quist may believe something like this, but he doesn't state or argue it. His reply works only through the comparison with prints.
choices.example: Example of method: A sculpture moves us by its form, and the form is just as moving whoever cast it.

questions.stimulus: Literary historian: The novelist Ambrose Kell is generally thought to have completed several novels after 1931, but this is a mistake. Kell sent every work he completed to his publisher, Harlow & Finch, and the firm's archive contains his manuscripts from 1904 through 1931 but none from any later year. So Kell completed no work after 1931.
questions.stem: The literary historian's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?
choices: Kell did not begin writing any new novel or story at any time after the year 1931.
Harlow & Finch has never lost or discarded any manuscript sent to it by any author it published.
Had Kell sent Harlow & Finch a manuscript after 1931, the firm's archive would now contain it.
Harlow & Finch accepted for publication every manuscript that Kell ever sent to the firm.
Scholars who believe that Kell completed novels after 1931 have not examined the firm's archive.
questions.explanation: The argument runs: completed → sent to Harlow & Finch; the archive has nothing after 1931; so nothing was completed. That works only if anything Kell sent after 1931 would be in the archive now, which is (C). (B) is the trap: it would guarantee the archive is complete, but it's far stronger than needed, since the firm may have lost other authors' manuscripts, or Kell's from before 1931, without hurting the argument. (D) isn't needed if declined manuscripts were kept, (A) confuses beginning with completing, and (E) is irrelevant.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Kell completed no work after 1931.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Kell sent every completed work to Harlow & Finch; the firm's archive has his manuscripts only through 1931.

breakdown.analysis: Lay out the chain: completed → sent to the firm → in the archive? The first arrow is a premise. The second arrow is missing. Nothing says the archive kept everything it received. If a post-1931 manuscript was lost, thrown out, or returned, the empty archive proves nothing. Prephrase: anything Kell sent after 1931 would still be in the archive. Contrapositive check: not in the archive → not sent → not completed. Here the answer is both necessary and sufficient. The traps are versions that are too strong or that miss the link.

choices.note: Tempting, because it seems to back up the claim that Kell stopped working, but it confuses beginning with completing. The conclusion is only about completed works. Kell could have started novels after 1931 and never finished them.
choices.negation: Kell began writing at least one new novel or story after 1931.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap: it would close the gap. But it's far too strong. It covers every author and every manuscript ever. The firm could have lost another author's manuscript, or one of Kell's from 1910, and the argument wouldn't suffer.
choices.negation: Harlow & Finch has lost or discarded at least one manuscript sent to it by some author it published.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: Kell could have sent the firm a manuscript after 1931 that the archive doesn't now contain. Then the empty archive no longer rules out post-1931 work, and the argument fails.
choices.negation: Even if Kell had sent Harlow & Finch a manuscript after 1931, the firm's archive might not now contain it.

choices.note: Not required. If the firm kept the manuscripts it declined, a rejected post-1931 novel would still show up in the archive. Acceptance doesn't matter; keeping does.
choices.negation: Harlow & Finch declined at least one manuscript that Kell sent it.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Who has or hasn't looked at the archive doesn't affect whether the archive's contents support the conclusion.
choices.negation: Some scholars who believe Kell completed novels after 1931 have examined the archive.

questions.stimulus:
Petra: Last year Hollis Middle School replaced letter grades in its art classes with written comments, and this year the number of students choosing art as an elective jumped by half. Clearly, dropping grades made art less intimidating, and that is what drew the new students.

Ewan: Enrollment did jump. But this year the school also began offering ceramics, and the new ceramics sections account for the entire increase. Enrollment in drawing and painting, which also stopped giving grades, was flat.
questions.stem: Petra and Ewan disagree over whether
choices: replacing letter grades with written comments made the school's art classes less intimidating to students
the number of Hollis students who chose art as an elective rose by about half from last year to this year
enrollment in the school's drawing and painting sections was no higher this year than it was last year
hiring a teacher to offer ceramics did more for the school's art program than eliminating letter grades did
the jump in art enrollment would largely have occurred even if the school had kept its letter grades
questions.explanation: Petra says dropping grades is what drew the new students; Ewan says the new ceramics sections account for the whole increase, so he holds that the jump would have happened anyway, and they disagree over (E). (A) is the trap: it is Petra's stated conclusion, but Ewan attacks only her evidence about enrollment and never denies that comments made art less intimidating. (B) is common ground, (C) is Ewan's alone, and (D) is a comparison neither speaker makes.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Petra: Art elective enrollment jumped by half after grades were dropped; dropping grades made art less intimidating, and that drew the new students.; Ewan: The jump is entirely new ceramics sections; drawing and painting, also ungraded, stayed flat.

breakdown.analysis: Petra makes two claims: (1) dropping grades made art less intimidating, and (2) that's what drew the new students. Ewan attacks (2): the new students all went to ceramics, and the ungraded drawing classes didn't grow. Does he deny (1)? No. Art could be less intimidating now and still not explain the jump. So the dispute is about the cause of the jump. The key says it in counterfactual form: would the jump have happened with grades kept? Petra: no, the grades change drew them. Ewan: yes, ceramics did it. Hard questions often hide the key in a form like this.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's Petra's headline claim and Ewan is clearly disagreeing with her. But Ewan attacks her evidence, not this claim. He never says whether art feels less intimidating now; he only says intimidation isn't what explains the enrollment jump.
Common ground. Ewan begins, "Enrollment did jump."
Ewan's claim only. Petra says nothing about drawing and painting enrollment.
Neither speaker ranks the two changes by their overall benefit to the program. Ewan talks about what explains the enrollment increase, not what did more good.

CORRECT. Petra: dropping grades "is what drew the new students," so without it, the jump wouldn't have happened. Ewan: ceramics "account for the entire increase," so the jump would have happened anyway. Same dispute, stated as a counterfactual.

questions.stimulus: Columnist: Every reporter at the Tollbridge Star who has won the state press association's reporting prize spent at least a year covering the city council before winning it. The council beat, with its budget fights and procedural maneuvering, evidently teaches the skills that prize-winning reporting requires. The Star's editors should therefore keep assigning promising young reporters to that beat.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the columnist's argument?
choices: Not every reporter who has worked at the Star spent a year or more covering the city council.
Most of the Star's reporters who have covered the city council for a year or more have later won the prize.
Promising young reporters will learn more from covering the city council than from any other assignment at the Star.
The prize-winning reporters won the prize for stories that they wrote while they were covering the city council.
The skills that the council beat teaches cannot be learned on any of the other beats at the Star.
questions.explanation: The columnist infers that the council beat builds prize-winning skills because every prize winner covered it. If every Star reporter has covered the council beat, that fact about the winners tells us nothing, so the argument requires (A). (C) is the trap: it seems to bridge to the recommendation, but the editors can be right to use the beat without its being the single best assignment, so (C) is too strong, as are (B) and (E). (D) isn't needed; the skills could pay off later on another beat.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The editors should keep assigning promising young reporters to the council beat (because it teaches prize-winning skills).

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Every Star reporter who won the state prize first spent at least a year on the council beat.

breakdown.analysis: "Every winner covered the council." Sounds impressive. But what if every reporter at the Star covers the council for a year, say as a standard rotation? Then of course every winner did, and so did every loser. The fact would tell us nothing about the beat. It's like noting that every Olympic swimmer once drank water. Prephrase: covering the council isn't something every Star reporter has done. The key is a modest "not every." The traps are the strong versions: most council reporters win, the council beat is the best assignment, nothing else teaches these skills.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: every reporter at the Star has spent a year or more on the council beat. Then the winners' council experience is just something everyone has, and it gives no reason to credit the beat. The argument loses its evidence.
