choices.negation: Every reporter who has worked at the Star has spent a year or more covering the city council.

choices.note: Too strong. The beat could build valuable skills even if only a minority of council reporters go on to win. The prize is rare.
choices.negation: Fewer than half of the Star's reporters who have covered the council for a year or more have later won the prize.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap: it seems to connect the evidence to the recommendation. But "more than from any other assignment" is too strong. The editors can be right to keep using the council beat even if some other beat teaches just as much.
choices.negation: Promising young reporters will learn at least as much from some other assignment at the Star as from covering the council.

choices.note: Not required. The columnist says the beat teaches skills. Those skills could produce prize-winning work later, on a different beat. If anything, winning for later work fits the columnist's story.
choices.negation: At least one prize-winning reporter won for stories written after leaving the council beat.

choices.note: Too strong. Other beats could teach the same skills and the council beat would still be a fine place to learn them.
choices.negation: At least some of the skills the council beat teaches can be learned on another of the Star's beats.

questions.stimulus:
Adaeze: The Corbin school district's required summer reading list should be replaced by a free choice of any book. Students made to read assigned titles over the summer mostly skim them, and a student who reads one book eagerly gains more than one who skims three.

Lucian: Free choice would leave many students reading only the kinds of books they already like. I would keep the list, but let students who read at least two books from a broad shelf of approved titles skip it.
questions.stem: The dialogue provides the most support for the claim that Adaeze and Lucian agree that
choices: students should be free to meet the district's summer reading requirement with any books they choose
most students who are required to read assigned titles over the summer do no more than skim them
a student who reads one book eagerly benefits more than a student who skims several books
students should have some way of meeting the summer reading requirement other than reading titles from the list
given a free choice, many students would read only the kinds of books that they already like
questions.explanation: Adaeze wants students to choose any book in place of the list, and Lucian would let students skip the list by reading two books from an approved shelf, so both are committed to some alternative to the list, as (D) says. (A) is the trap: Adaeze holds it, but Lucian limits the alternative to approved titles, so he rejects free choice of 'any' book. (B) and (C) are Adaeze's claims alone, and (E) is Lucian's.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Adaeze: Replace the required list with free choice of any book; students skim assigned titles, and one book read eagerly beats three skimmed.; Lucian: Free choice lets students stick to what they like; keep the list, but let students who read two books from an approved shelf skip it.

breakdown.analysis: Lucian sounds like he's disagreeing; he opens by attacking free choice. But look at his proposal: students can skip the list by reading from an approved shelf. So he also wants a route around the list. Adaeze's route is wide open (any book). Lucian's is limited (approved titles). What do they share? Some alternative to the list exists. What don't they share? The "any book" part. On agreement questions, the right answer is often the lowest common denominator, stated broadly enough that both positions fit inside it.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's Adaeze's proposal and Lucian also offers an alternative. But Lucian rejects "any books": his alternative is limited to a shelf of approved titles, and he opposes free choice outright. Adaeze yes, Lucian no.
Adaeze's claim only. Lucian never says how students read assigned titles.
Adaeze's claim only. Lucian doesn't weigh eager reading against skimming.

CORRECT. Adaeze: replace the list with free choice, which is one alternative. Lucian: students who read two approved books can "skip" the list, which is another. Both are committed to there being some way around the list.
Lucian's claim only. Adaeze never addresses what students would choose.

questions.stimulus: Organizer: Last year the Tarn Valley Book Fair moved from the town library to the fairgrounds, and attendance fell by a quarter. Some blame the move, but the fairgrounds are no farther from the town center than the library is. Moreover, last year the fair announced its visiting authors two months later than usual, leaving out-of-town visitors too little time to plan trips. So the late announcement, not the move, caused the decline.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the organizer's argument depends?
choices: Most of the people who attended the fair in the years before the move were visitors from out of town.
Distance from the town center is the only feature of a site that affects how many people attend the fair.
Every out-of-town visitor who stayed away last year did so because the authors were announced late.
Other book fairs that have announced their visiting authors late have also seen their attendance decline.
Fewer out-of-town visitors attended the fair last year than in the years before the move.
questions.explanation: The organizer's explanation works only through out-of-town visitors, who lacked time to plan trips. If out-of-town attendance didn't fall, the late announcement explains none of the decline, so the argument requires (E). (B) is the trap: the argument does lean on the fairgrounds being no worse a site, but 'the only feature' is far stronger than needed. (A) and (C) are also too strong, and (D) would support the argument without being required.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The late announcement, not the move, caused the drop in attendance.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The fairgrounds are no farther from the town center than the library; the authors were announced two months late, leaving out-of-town visitors too little time to plan trips.

breakdown.analysis: The organizer's cause works through one group: out-of-town visitors who couldn't plan in time. So ask: did out-of-towners actually stop coming? If the whole drop came from local residents, the late announcement explains nothing, because locals don't need to plan trips. Prephrase: at least some of the decline was among out-of-town visitors. That's minimal. The traps make it bigger: most visitors were from out of town, every absent visitor stayed away for this reason, distance is the only thing that matters.

choices.note: Too strong. Out-of-towners could be a minority of past visitors and still account for a real drop. The argument doesn't need them to be most of the crowd.
choices.negation: At most half of the people who attended in earlier years were visitors from out of town.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. The organizer does dismiss the move on distance alone, so she needs the new site not to be worse in some other way that matters. But "the only feature" goes way beyond that. Parking or signage could matter in general and still not have hurt this year's fair.
choices.negation: Some feature of a site other than its distance from the town center affects how many people attend the fair.

choices.note: Too strong. Some out-of-towners could have stayed away for other reasons; the late announcement only needs to explain the decline as a whole.
choices.negation: At least one out-of-town visitor who stayed away did so for some reason other than the late announcement.

choices.note: This would support the organizer, but it isn't required. Her argument is about this fair; what happened elsewhere doesn't matter if it's negated.
choices.negation: Other book fairs that announced late have not seen their attendance decline.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: out-of-town attendance did not fall. Then the late announcement, which only affected visitors planning trips, accounts for none of the drop, and the conclusion collapses.
choices.negation: At least as many out-of-town visitors attended the fair last year as in the years before.

questions.stimulus:
Orchestra director: Our free open rehearsals bring in people new to orchestral music. Last season, 40 percent of those attending the open rehearsals had never before attended one of our events, compared with 15 percent of those attending our regular concerts.

Trustee: But more newcomers attended our Saturday matinees alone than attended all of last season's open rehearsals combined. So the open rehearsals do little to bring in newcomers.
questions.stem: The trustee's reasoning is flawed because it
choices: confuses the percentage of an audience made up of newcomers with the number of newcomers in that audience
treats the fact that another kind of event draws more newcomers as showing that the open rehearsals draw few
relies on figures about newcomers that are inconsistent with the percentages the orchestra director cites
overlooks the possibility that many newcomers who attended the Saturday matinees will never attend again
presumes, without providing justification, that newcomers who attend open rehearsals will come to concerts later
questions.explanation: The trustee shows only that the matinees drew more newcomers than the open rehearsals did; that comparison doesn't show the rehearsals drew few, since the matinees might simply be a far larger series, so (B) describes the flaw. (A) is the trap: it names the textbook percentage-versus-number error, but the trustee makes no such confusion; he correctly uses numbers and never treats the director's percentages as counts. His figures are consistent with the director's (C), and (D) and (E) concern returning visitors, which neither argument relies on.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: (Trustee) The open rehearsals do little to bring in newcomers.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: (Trustee) More newcomers attended the Saturday matinees alone than all of last season's open rehearsals combined.

breakdown.analysis: The director talks percentages: 40% of rehearsal-goers were newcomers versus 15% at concerts. The trustee switches to counts: the matinees had more newcomers. That switch is legitimate; both facts can be true if the matinees are much bigger. The problem is what he concludes. Being outdrawn by another series doesn't make your contribution small. A school can enroll fewer students than the state university and still enroll thousands. Prephrase: he infers "few" from "fewer than something else." Know the percent-versus-number family, but read carefully: here the trustee isn't mixing them up. He's making a relative-to-absolute jump.

choices.note: Tempting, because percentages and counts are both in play and this is the famous flaw. But the trustee doesn't confuse them. He knowingly answers with a count and never treats the 40% as a number of people. His mistake comes after that: treating "fewer than the matinees" as "few."
choices.example: Example of flaw: Forty percent of rehearsal-goers were newcomers but only 15 percent of concertgoers were, so more newcomers came to rehearsals than to concerts.

choices.note: CORRECT. All the trustee shows is that the matinees drew more newcomers. That's a comparison. It doesn't show the open rehearsals drew few; the matinee series may simply be far larger. He moves from "fewer than another event" to "little".
The figures aren't inconsistent. A big matinee series at 15% newcomers can easily include more newcomers than a small rehearsal series at 40%.
choices.example: Example of flaw: You say 40 percent were newcomers, but I count 300 newcomers out of 500, so your figures can't both be right.

choices.note: Whether matinee newcomers come back has nothing to do with the trustee's argument. He counts how many came, not whether they returned.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The matinees drew many newcomers, so they've built a loyal new audience.

choices.note: Neither speaker relies on rehearsal newcomers coming back later. The director's claim is only that the rehearsals bring newcomers in.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The rehearsals draw newcomers, so they're building the orchestra's future concert audience.

questions.stimulus: Principal: This year Delmont High began requiring every ninth grader taking algebra to attend a weekly algebra lab. This year 84 ninth graders failed algebra, down from 120 last year. Since the lab was the only change in how algebra is taught at Delmont, the lab must have reduced the rate at which our ninth graders fail algebra.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption that the principal's argument requires?
choices: The number of ninth graders taking algebra at Delmont this year was the same as the number last year.
Most of the ninth graders who attended the algebra lab this year went on to pass the algebra course.
The number of ninth graders taking algebra at Delmont did not fall by 30 percent or more this year.
Weekly algebra labs have lowered failure rates at most of the other schools that have adopted them.
Every ninth grader who failed algebra last year would have passed it if the lab had existed then.
questions.explanation: The conclusion is about the failure rate, but the evidence is a count: 84 failures, down from 120, a 30 percent drop. If the number taking algebra fell by 30 percent or more, the rate didn't fall at all, so the argument requires (C). (A) is the trap: the same enrollment both years would make the evidence work, but enrollment could drop somewhat and the rate still fall, so (A) is sufficient, not necessary. (B), (D), and (E) aren't needed.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The lab reduced the rate at which ninth graders fail algebra.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Failures fell from 120 to 84; the lab was the only change in how algebra is taught.

breakdown.analysis: Rate or count? The conclusion is about a RATE. The evidence is a COUNT. 84 is 30% fewer than 120. If 30% fewer ninth graders took algebra this year, the failure rate is unchanged (say 120/400 = 30% and 84/280 = 30%). If enrollment fell by more than 30%, the rate actually rose. So the argument needs enrollment not to have dropped that much. Prephrase: the number taking algebra didn't fall by 30% or more. A small calculation hides the key. The trap is the overkill version: enrollment stayed exactly the same.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap: it would make the counts tell the whole story. But it's sufficient, not necessary. If enrollment fell 5%, the failure rate still fell a lot. Negating it doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: The number taking algebra this year was different from last year's number.

choices.note: Not required. Since every ninth grader taking algebra attended the lab, this just says most passed, which could have been true last year too. It says nothing about a change in the rate.
choices.negation: At least half of the ninth graders who attended the lab failed algebra.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: enrollment fell by 30% or more. Then 84 failures out of the smaller group is the same failure rate as last year, or a higher one, and the rate didn't fall. The conclusion collapses.
choices.negation: The number of ninth graders taking algebra fell by 30 percent or more this year.

choices.note: This would support the principal, but other schools' results aren't required. The argument stands or falls on Delmont's numbers.
choices.negation: Weekly algebra labs have not lowered failure rates at most other schools that adopted them.

choices.note: Far too strong. The lab can reduce the failure rate without rescuing every student who failed last year.
choices.negation: At least one student who failed last year would have failed even with the lab.

questions.stimulus:
Marta: The Kelling Herald's book section should begin reviewing self-published books. Some of the best new fiction in our region is now self-published, and readers rely on the Herald to tell them about the region's best new fiction.

Joaquin: Some fine books are self-published, but they're needles in a haystack: for every one, hundreds of weak ones would arrive. The Herald's two reviewers couldn't screen that many without neglecting the books readers ask about most. The section's policy should stay as it is.
questions.stem: Marta and Joaquin disagree over whether
choices: some of the best new fiction now being written in the region is self-published
the Herald's two reviewers could screen all the self-published books they would receive without neglecting other books
the great majority of the self-published books that the Herald would receive are weak
the Herald's book section ought to depart from its present practice with respect to self-published books
readers depend on the Herald to inform them about the best new fiction from the region
questions.explanation: Marta says the book section should begin reviewing self-published books, which would change its practice; Joaquin says the policy should stay as it is, so they disagree over (D). (B) is the trap: Joaquin denies it, but Marta never addresses whether the reviewers could handle the volume, so she isn't committed to it. (A) is not disputed, since Joaquin grants that some fine books are self-published, and (C) and (E) belong to one speaker each.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Marta: Start reviewing self-published books; some of the region's best new fiction is self-published, and readers rely on the Herald for that.; Joaquin: Some are fine, but they're buried among hundreds of weak ones; two reviewers couldn't screen them without neglecting other books; keep the policy.

breakdown.analysis: Marta: "begin reviewing" self-published books, so change the policy. Joaquin: "The section's policy should stay as it is." That's the clash, but the right answer states it abstractly ("depart from its present practice"), which makes it easy to skip. Meanwhile the trap is Joaquin's strongest point, the reviewers' workload. It feels like the heart of the debate, but Marta never talks about workload. A speaker who ignores an objection isn't committed either way on it.

choices.note: Not disputed. Marta asserts it, and Joaquin grants that "some fine books are self-published." Even if "fine" isn't quite "best," he never denies her claim.
Tempting, and the main trap. Joaquin clearly denies this. But Marta never discusses how many books would arrive or whether two reviewers could cope. She's silent, so it's not the point at issue.
Joaquin's claim only ("for every one, hundreds of weak ones"). Marta doesn't address the ratio.

CORRECT. Marta wants the section to "begin reviewing" self-published books, which is a change in practice. Joaquin: "The section's policy should stay as it is." Yes versus no, just in abstract wording.
Marta's claim only. Joaquin's worry about "the books readers ask about most" neither confirms nor denies it.

questions.stimulus: Music critic: The Vessel Quartet's recordings from the 1940s are, on average, noticeably faster than its recordings from the 1970s. Some attribute this to the players' slowing with age. But the discs the quartet recorded on in the 1940s held at most about four and a half minutes of music per side, and several of the movements it recorded then would run longer than that at a moderate tempo. So the quartet probably played faster in the 1940s to fit its music onto the discs.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the music critic's argument depends?
choices: None of the quartet's players had lost any of their technical skill by the time of the 1970s recordings.
Every movement on the quartet's 1940s recordings was played just fast enough to fit onto one side of a disc.
Other string quartets that recorded in the 1940s also played faster then than they did in later decades.
Listeners in the 1940s generally preferred faster tempos than listeners in the 1970s did.
The quartet did not routinely divide its longer movements between two sides of a disc.
questions.explanation: The critic's explanation assumes the disc limit forced the quartet to speed up, but a long movement could instead be split across two sides. If the quartet routinely did that, the limit gave it no reason to play faster, so the argument requires (E). (A) is the trap: it rules out the rival explanation, but 'none' and 'any' make it far too strong; the players could have lost a little skill and the disc limit could still explain the faster recordings. (B) is too strong, (C) would help without being needed, and (D) points to a different cause.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The quartet probably played faster in the 1940s to fit its music onto the discs.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 1940s discs held about 4.5 minutes per side; several movements the quartet recorded would run longer at a moderate tempo; some blame aging instead.

breakdown.analysis: The critic's story: the disc couldn't hold the movement, so the quartet sped up. But is speeding up the only way to deal with a short disc side? No. You could break the movement in the middle and continue on the other side. If the quartet routinely did that, the time limit put no pressure on its tempos, and the explanation falls apart. Prephrase: the quartet didn't routinely split long movements across sides. That's an alternative to the critic's mechanism, ruled out in the narrowest way. The trap goes after the age explanation instead, and words it far too strongly.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap: it seems to clear away the rival explanation. But "none" and "any" make it too strong. The players could have lost a little skill and the disc limit could still be the main reason the 1940s recordings are faster. The critic says "probably," not "only."
choices.negation: At least one of the quartet's players had lost some technical skill by the time of the 1970s recordings.

choices.note: Too strong. The quartet could have sped up some movements more than needed, or played short movements at normal speed, and the explanation would still hold.
choices.negation: At least one movement on the 1940s recordings was played faster or slower than needed to fit on one side.

choices.note: This would support the critic, since an era-wide pattern points to the technology rather than the players' age. But it isn't required; the argument is about this quartet.
choices.negation: Other quartets recording in the 1940s did not play faster then than later.

choices.note: This is a different explanation for the faster tempos, so it would weaken the argument if anything. Negating it doesn't hurt the critic.
choices.negation: Listeners in the 1940s did not prefer faster tempos than listeners in the 1970s.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the quartet routinely split longer movements across two sides. Then the disc limit gave it no reason to rush, and the critic's explanation of the faster tempos collapses.
choices.negation: The quartet routinely divided its longer movements between two sides of a disc.

sections.title: Skill Builder: Hard Sufficient Assumption & Principle

questions.stimulus: Under the Corwin County notary code, a notary may certify a signature on a document only if the notary has no financial interest in that document. Last week the notary Hollis Brandt was asked to certify his sister’s signature on a deed selling her house to a neighbor. Therefore, Brandt may not certify that signature.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Brandt’s sister will receive a substantial sum of money from the sale of her house to the neighbor next door.
A notary has a financial interest in any document that is signed by a member of the notary’s family.
Any notary who has a financial interest in a document is related to at least one person who has signed that document.
The Corwin County notary code was adopted in order to keep notaries from profiting from the documents they certify.
Notaries in Corwin County seldom certify signatures on deeds that transfer houses from one neighbor to another.
questions.explanation: The rule gives Certify → no financial interest, so the argument needs Brandt to have a financial interest in his sister’s deed. (B) supplies it: family member signs → notary has a financial interest. The tempting trap is (A): the money goes to the sister, and the rule asks about the notary’s interest, not hers. (C) reverses the needed link, and (D) and (E) never connect family to financial interest.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Brandt may not certify his sister’s signature on the deed.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Notary certifies → notary has no financial interest in the document; the document is his sister’s deed.

breakdown.analysis: So what if it’s his sister’s deed? The rule doesn’t mention family at all. It only cares whether the notary has a financial interest. Chain it: Sister signs → ??? → Brandt has a financial interest → Brandt may not certify (contrapositive of Certify → No interest). We need an answer that says a family member’s document gives the notary a financial interest.

choices.note: Tempting. It shows money is at stake, but it’s the sister’s money. The rule is about the notary’s financial interest, and nothing here gives Brandt any.
CORRECT. Family member signs → notary has a financial interest. Chain: sister signs → Brandt has an interest → he may not certify.
This reverses the link we need. It says Interest → related to a signer. We need Related to a signer → interest.
The purpose of the code isn’t the code. Knowing why the rule exists doesn’t tell us that Brandt has a financial interest.
Irrelevant. How often such deeds get certified says nothing about whether Brandt may certify this one.

questions.stimulus: Records officer: Amberleigh’s open records law requires a city agency to release any record a resident requests unless releasing it would endanger someone’s safety. The fire department’s inspection reports on downtown warehouses do not identify any individual by name. And residents have a strong interest in knowing which buildings are unsafe. So the fire department must release those reports to any resident who requests them.
questions.stem: The records officer’s conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Residents’ interest in knowing which buildings are unsafe outweighs any risk that releasing inspection reports could pose to anyone’s safety.
Releasing any record that identifies an individual by name would endanger the safety of that individual.
Fire department inspection reports rarely contain information that could be used to harm the owners of the buildings inspected.
Releasing a record endangers someone’s safety only if the record identifies at least one individual by name.
Most records that identify no individual by name have been released by city agencies without anyone being harmed.
questions.explanation: The law says: release would not endanger anyone → must release. The premise is that the reports name no one, so we need No names → no danger, which is (D) stated in “only if” form (Danger → names). Most students pick (B), which uses the same two ideas in the wrong direction: Names → danger says nothing about records that name no one. (A) leans on the residents’ interest, a decoy the law never weighs, and (C) and (E) are too weak.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The fire department must release the warehouse inspection reports on request.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Must release unless release would endanger someone’s safety; the reports name no individual; residents have a strong interest in the reports.

breakdown.analysis: Why should naming nobody mean nobody is endangered? A report could say which warehouse has its alarm switched off. The argument needs that link. Translate the law: Not endanger → must release. Chain: No names → ??? → not endanger → must release. We need No names → not endanger, or in contrapositive form, Endanger → names. Notice the residents’ interest is a decoy. The law doesn’t weigh interests at all, so the bridge won’t use it.

choices.note: Tempting, because it uses the argument’s most high-minded sentence. But the law has no balancing test. If release would endanger someone, the law simply doesn’t require it, however strong the interest. This never establishes that the reports are safe to release.
This is the reversal, and it’s the main trap. Names → danger. Our reports have no names, so this rule never applies to them. We need Danger → names.
“Rarely” is too weak, and harm to owners is only one kind of danger. It doesn’t guarantee that releasing these reports endangers no one.
CORRECT. Danger → names. Contrapositive: no names → no danger. The reports name no one, so releasing them endangers no one, so the law requires their release.
A track record of “most” records being harmless doesn’t guarantee these reports are. Too weak.

questions.stimulus: Ethicist: Eight months ago, Teodora Vance resigned as director of Marl Province’s forestry agency, and she now works for a timber company. Although the province’s ethics law permits it, she should not lobby the agency on the company’s behalf. Most of the agency’s senior staff owe their positions to her, and officials who owe their positions to someone find it hard to refuse that person’s requests.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the ethicist’s reasoning?
choices: Former officials should not lobby an agency whose staff would find it hard to turn down their requests, even when the law permits it.
A former official may lobby the agency she once directed only if the law of her jurisdiction allows her to do so.
An agency should decline to meet with any lobbyist to whom members of its own senior staff owe their current positions.
No one who has directed a government agency should later take a job with a company whose business that agency oversees.
Former officials should wait at least six months after leaving an agency before lobbying it on behalf of any private employer.
questions.explanation: The ethicist concludes Vance should not lobby the agency, despite the law, because its senior staff would find it hard to refuse her. (A) turns exactly that fact into a “should not lobby” verdict and covers the legal permission. The trap is (C): it uses the right fact but tells the agency what to do, not Vance. (B) states a necessary condition Vance already meets, (D) is about taking the job, and (E) is satisfied at eight months, so it gives no verdict.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Vance should not lobby the forestry agency for the timber company, even though the law permits it.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most senior staff owe their positions to her; people find it hard to refuse someone they owe their positions to.

breakdown.analysis: The law says yes, so where does “should not” come from? From the staff’s difficulty in refusing her. A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says. So we need: if the staff would find it hard to say no to a former official, she shouldn’t lobby them, law or no law. Watch for answers that use the right fact but tell someone else what to do.

choices.note: CORRECT. Staff would find it hard to refuse her → she should not lobby, even if the law allows it. That’s the conclusion, delivered by the premise.
This gives a necessary condition for lobbying: legal permission. Vance has it, so the principle is satisfied and says nothing more. It can’t produce “should not.”
Tempting. Right fact, wrong person. It tells the agency to refuse meetings. The conclusion is about what Vance should do.
Wrong action. The ethicist isn’t criticizing Vance for taking the job, only for lobbying.
Eight months is more than six, so Vance has waited long enough under this rule. It gives no reason she shouldn’t lobby now.

questions.stimulus: Court rules require a judge to withdraw from any case in which her impartiality might reasonably be questioned. Public confidence in the courts depends on judges’ being seen as neutral. Judge Tanaka is presiding over a contract dispute in which the plaintiff’s lawyer, Ruth Dacey, practiced at the same law firm as Tanaka for six years before Tanaka became a judge. So Tanaka must withdraw from the case.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion of the argument to be properly drawn?
choices: A judge’s impartiality might reasonably be questioned in any case in which she has a financial tie to one of the lawyers.
Whenever a judge’s impartiality in a case might reasonably be questioned, one of the lawyers in that case once worked with the judge.
Judges who withdraw from every case in which their neutrality is in doubt do more to sustain public confidence than other judges do.
Most lawyers who once practiced at the same firm as a judge expect that judge to treat them with at least some favor.
A judge’s impartiality is beyond reasonable question only if no lawyer in the case was ever her colleague at a law firm.
questions.explanation: The rule is Impartiality might reasonably be questioned → withdraw, so the argument needs Former firm colleague → impartiality questionable. (E) gives this in disguised form: Beyond question → no former colleague, whose contrapositive is exactly the bridge. Most students pick (A), which bridges through a financial tie, something the stimulus never says Tanaka has. (B) reverses the link, (C) leans on the public-confidence decoy, and (D) is about lawyers’ expectations and is too weak.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Judge Tanaka must withdraw from the contract case.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Impartiality might reasonably be questioned → withdraw; the plaintiff’s lawyer practiced at Tanaka’s old firm for six years.

breakdown.analysis: Is having once shared a firm with a lawyer enough to put a judge’s impartiality in question? The argument just assumes so. Chain: Former colleague → ??? → impartiality questionable → must withdraw. We need Former colleague → questionable. The public-confidence sentence is a decoy; the rule doesn’t mention it. Expect the key in contrapositive form: Not questionable → no former colleague.

choices.note: Tempting, because a financial tie sounds like the classic conflict. But the stimulus never says Tanaka has any financial tie to Dacey. This bridges through a fact we don’t have.
Reversed. Questionable → former colleague. We need Former colleague → questionable.
This praises judges who withdraw, using the decoy about public confidence. It doesn’t say Tanaka’s impartiality might reasonably be questioned, so the rule never kicks in.
What lawyers expect isn’t what a reasonable observer would question, and “most” is too weak anyway.
CORRECT. Beyond question → no former colleague. Contrapositive: former colleague → impartiality questionable. Dacey was Tanaka’s colleague, so Tanaka must withdraw. The “only if” wording hides it.

questions.stimulus: An accountant should decline to audit a company if any member of the accountant’s household owns shares in that company, unless the shares are held through a fund whose investments the household member has no say in choosing.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: Tobias’s wife owns shares in Penn Mills only through a pension fund whose outside managers alone choose all of its investments, so Tobias should accept the assignment to audit Penn Mills.
Dana’s brother, who lives across the country, owns shares in Orrin Textiles, so Dana should decline to audit Orrin Textiles.
Mirela’s husband, who lives with her, owns Calder Freight shares only through a retirement fund whose investments he picks himself, so Mirela should decline to audit Calder Freight.
Luis’s daughter, who lives with him, owns shares in Vey Foods, so Luis should tell Vey Foods’ directors about those shares before he audits the company.
Ana’s roommate owned shares in Strand Paper until he sold them last year, so Ana should decline to audit Strand Paper this year.
questions.explanation: The principle: household member owns shares → decline, unless the shares sit in a fund the member has no say over. Mirela’s husband holds his shares through a fund, but he picks its investments, so the exception fails and she should decline, as (C) says. Most students pick (A) because Tobias satisfies the exception, but the exception only removes the duty to decline; it never says he should accept. (B) involves a non-household member, (D) gives a different verdict, and (E) involves shares no longer owned.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Household member owns shares in the company AND NOT (held through a fund the member has no say over) → accountant should decline the audit.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Find the judgment that meets every condition and concludes the accountant should decline.

breakdown.analysis: The right answer needs: 1. a member of the accountant’s household; 2. who currently owns shares in the company; 3. the exception fails (not a fund the member has no say in); 4. verdict: decline. Be careful with the exception. Shares held through a fund only escape the rule if the member has no say in the fund’s choices. And meeting the exception just switches the rule off; it doesn’t tell you to accept. It’s like “you must wear a helmet unless you’re on a bike path.” Being on the path doesn’t mean you must take the helmet off.

choices.note: Tempting. Tobias’s wife does meet the exception, so the principle doesn’t require him to decline. But it never says he should accept. The verdict goes beyond the rule.
The brother lives across the country, so he isn’t a member of Dana’s household. The principle doesn’t apply.

CORRECT. Husband, same household, owns shares. They’re in a fund, but he picks its investments, so the exception doesn’t apply. Verdict: decline. The fund detail is there to make you think the exception saves her.
The facts trigger the rule, but the verdict is wrong. The principle says decline the audit, not disclose and then audit.
The roommate no longer owns any shares. The rule covers someone who owns shares, so it doesn’t apply this year.

questions.stimulus: Bar examiner: In Tessary, no one may be admitted to the bar unless the admissions board finds that the applicant was fully candid during the application process. Lawyers are entrusted with clients’ money and secrets, so the profession rightly demands honesty. Joel Arrin’s application omitted a lawsuit he once filed against a landlord, although the form asks about every lawsuit an applicant has filed. Hence Arrin will not be admitted.
questions.stem: The bar examiner’s conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: The board finds an applicant fully candid only if the application omits nothing that the form asks about.
The board finds fully candid every applicant whose application omits nothing that the form asks about.
No one who has ever sued a landlord has the good moral character that the practice of law requires.
Anyone who is entrusted with clients’ money and secrets must be scrupulously honest in all dealings.
Most applicants who leave a lawsuit off their bar applications do so deliberately rather than by mistake.
questions.explanation: Admitted → board finds fully candid. Arrin omitted something the form asked about, so we need Omission → board doesn’t find him candid, which is the contrapositive of (A). Most students pick (B), the reversed version: No omission → found candid says nothing about an applicant who did omit something. (C) bridges through moral character, which the rule never mentions, (D) restates the decoy about honesty, and (E) is about motive and is too weak.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Arrin will not be admitted to the bar.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Admitted → board finds applicant fully candid; Arrin’s application omitted a lawsuit the form asked about.

breakdown.analysis: So he left something off. Does that mean the board won’t find him candid? Maybe the board forgives a forgotten lawsuit. The argument needs: Omitted something asked for → not found candid → not admitted. Prephrase: the board finds someone candid only if nothing asked for was left out. The line about lawyers being trusted with secrets is a decoy; the rule turns on the board’s finding, not on honesty in general.

choices.note: CORRECT. Found candid → omitted nothing asked for. Contrapositive: omitted something → not found candid → not admitted.
Tempting, because it uses the same two ideas. But it’s reversed: Omitted nothing → found candid. Arrin did omit something, so this never applies to him.
The rule is about candor, not moral character. Even if Arrin lacked good character, the stated rule wouldn’t bar him on that basis.
This is the decoy premise dressed up as a principle. It doesn’t say what the board will find, and the conclusion depends on the board’s finding.
“Most” is too weak, and it’s about motive. Arrin might have made an honest mistake, and the board might still find him candid.

questions.stimulus: Public defender: Our office should stop accepting new court appointments until our caseloads fall. Each of our attorneys now carries more than 120 open felony cases, a load at which no attorney can investigate every case before advising clients on plea offers. Judges warn that refusing appointments will delay trials, but some delay is better than advice given in ignorance.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the public defender’s reasoning?
choices: Attorneys who are able to investigate each of their cases before advising clients on plea offers should accept every appointment they are offered.
A delay in bringing a case to trial is acceptable only if it results from attorneys’ efforts to investigate their cases with care.
Courts should not appoint a public defender to any felony case unless that public defender currently has fewer than 120 open felony cases.
A defender’s office should refuse new appointments whenever its attorneys have too many cases to investigate each before advising on pleas.
No attorney should ever advise a client about a plea offer without first having looked carefully into the facts of that client’s case.
questions.explanation: The defender concludes the office should refuse appointments because its attorneys can’t investigate every case before advising on pleas; (D) makes exactly that condition sufficient for refusing. Most students pick (E), which condemns uninformed advice but says nothing about appointments; the office could comply simply by delaying advice. (A) is the reversed rule (able to investigate → accept), (B) gives a necessary condition for acceptable delay, and (C) tells courts, not the office, what to do.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The office should stop accepting new appointments until caseloads fall.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: At over 120 cases, attorneys can’t investigate every case before advising on plea offers; delay is better than uninformed advice.

breakdown.analysis: The premise is about investigating before advising. The conclusion is about refusing appointments. A justifying principle must connect them: if caseloads are too high to investigate before advising, the office should refuse new appointments. It’s the condition-to-verdict link that matters. An answer that only says uninformed advice is bad leaves the action (refusing appointments) unjustified.

choices.note: This reverses the idea. Able to investigate → accept. Our attorneys aren’t able to, so this rule says nothing about them.
A necessary condition for acceptable delay. Even if the delay here qualifies, nothing tells the office to refuse appointments.
Tempting because of the 120 figure. But it tells courts what not to do. The conclusion is about what the defender’s office should do.
CORRECT. Too many cases to investigate each before advising → refuse new appointments. That’s the premise feeding straight into the conclusion.

Tempting, since it captures the defender’s worry. But it only forbids advising without investigating. It doesn’t say to stop taking appointments; attorneys could hold off advising instead. It stops short of the conclusion.

questions.stimulus: Under Dalmore’s campaign law, a campaign must return any contribution of $50 or more whose donor the campaign cannot identify. Voters are entitled to know who is financing the candidates they elect. The Hask campaign received a $200 contribution through Donalink, an online service that does not pass donors’ names along to campaigns. So the Hask campaign must return that contribution.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Anyone who contributes through an online service that withholds donors’ names does so because he or she wants to remain unknown to the campaign.
A campaign can identify the donor of a contribution only if the donor’s name was passed along to the campaign with the contribution.
Every campaign that receives a donor’s name along with a contribution is able to identify the donor of that contribution.
Contributions whose donors cannot be identified do more than any other contributions to keep voters from knowing who finances candidates.
Most contributions of $50 or more made through online services come from donors whom campaigns have no other way to identify.
questions.explanation: The law requires return when the campaign cannot identify the donor, and we know only that Donalink didn’t pass the name along. (B) says Identify → name passed along, so no name passed → can’t identify → must return. Most students pick (C), its reversal: Name passed → can identify tells us nothing when no name was passed. (A) bridges through the donor’s wishes, which the law ignores; (D) restates the decoy about voters; (E) is only “most.”

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Hask campaign must return the $200 Donalink contribution.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Contribution of $50+ AND campaign cannot identify donor → must return; Donalink doesn’t pass donors’ names to campaigns.

breakdown.analysis: So the service didn’t send a name. Couldn’t the campaign identify the donor some other way, say from a note or a phone call? The argument assumes not. Chain: Name not passed along → ??? → cannot identify → must return. We need No name passed → can’t identify, or in “only if” form: Identify → name passed along.

choices.note: The law doesn’t care what donors want. A donor who wants secrecy could still be identifiable. This doesn’t establish that the campaign cannot identify the donor.
CORRECT. Identify → name passed along. Contrapositive: no name passed → can’t identify. Donalink passed no name, so the campaign can’t identify the donor and must return the money.
Tempting, because it links names to identification. But it’s reversed: Name passed → can identify. With no name passed, it tells us nothing.
This dresses up the decoy about voters’ right to know. Ranking how harmful anonymous gifts are doesn’t show this donor can’t be identified.
“Most” isn’t “all.” This donor could be one the campaign can identify another way.

questions.stimulus: A veterinarian should not prescribe medication for an animal without first examining it in person unless that veterinarian, or a colleague at the same practice, has examined the animal in person within the past twelve months. Otherwise the prescriber cannot be confident that the animal’s condition is what its owner reports.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: Dr. Halloran examined Pip, a terrier, in person ten months ago, so it was appropriate for her to prescribe Pip a new medication over the phone.
Dr. Ngata examined a cat in person three weeks before prescribing it medication by phone, so he had no need to review the cat’s earlier records.
No one at Dr. Ruiz’s practice had seen the parrot Kiki, though a vet elsewhere examined her last month, so Dr. Ruiz should not have prescribed for Kiki unseen.
Dr. Bauer had last examined a horse in person fourteen months ago and examined it again this morning before prescribing medication, so he acted wrongly.
Because Dr. Osei’s partner examined the rabbit Clover in person eight months ago, Dr. Osei acted wrongly in prescribing Clover medication by phone.
questions.explanation: The principle: no in-person exam now AND no exam within twelve months by the prescriber or a same-practice colleague → don’t prescribe. Kiki was examined last month, but by a vet at another practice, so the exception fails and Ruiz should not have prescribed, as (C) says. The trap is (A): Halloran meets the exception, but the principle never says prescribing is then appropriate. (B) gives a verdict the rule doesn’t address, (D) involves a vet who did examine the horse first, and (E) condemns a case the exception covers.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Prescribe without an in-person exam now AND no in-person exam within 12 months by this vet or a colleague at the same practice → should not prescribe.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Find the case that meets every condition and concludes the vet should not have prescribed.

breakdown.analysis: The right answer needs: 1. the vet prescribed without examining the animal in person; 2. neither that vet nor a colleague at the same practice examined it in the last 12 months; 3. verdict: shouldn’t have prescribed. The rule only ever says “should not.” Read the exception exactly: an exam by a vet at some other practice doesn’t count.

choices.note: Tempting. Halloran meets the exception, so the rule doesn’t forbid her. But it never says prescribing is appropriate. “Not forbidden by this rule” isn’t “appropriate.”
The principle says nothing about reviewing records. Wrong verdict.

CORRECT. Nobody at Ruiz’s practice had examined Kiki, and Ruiz prescribed without seeing her. The recent exam was at another practice, which the exception doesn’t cover. Verdict: shouldn’t have prescribed.
Bauer examined the horse this morning before prescribing. The principle only covers prescribing without an in-person exam, so it doesn’t apply. The 14-month detail is bait.
Osei’s partner examined Clover eight months ago, inside the twelve-month window and at the same practice. The exception applies, so the principle doesn’t condemn Osei.

questions.stimulus: Rent board member: In Carvel, a landlord may raise the rent on a stabilized apartment only if the building passed its most recent safety inspection. Tenants deserve safe housing in return for rising rents. The Orme Street building’s most recent inspection was cut short when the inspector was called away to an emergency, and no inspection has been held there since. So its landlord may not raise rents.
questions.stem: The rent board member’s conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Tenants should not be asked to pay higher rents for apartments in buildings that have not been shown to be safe.
Every building whose most recent safety inspection was completed has passed that inspection.
A building fails a safety inspection whenever the inspector finds an unrepaired violation of the building code there.
Most safety inspections that are cut short would have found violations had the inspector been able to finish them.
No building passes a safety inspection that the inspector was unable to complete.
questions.explanation: Raise rent → passed most recent inspection. The most recent inspection was cut short, so we need Not completed → not passed, which is (E). The trap is (A), the decoy premise turned into a principle: it says what tenants should be asked to pay, not what the law permits, and it never shows the building failed to pass. (B) reverses the link, (C) bridges through violations the stimulus never mentions, and (D) is only “most.”

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Orme Street landlord may not raise rents.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Raise rent → building passed its most recent inspection; the most recent inspection was cut short.

breakdown.analysis: Cut short isn’t the same as failed. Did the building pass or not? The argument assumes an unfinished inspection can’t count as a pass. Chain: Inspection not completed → ??? → not passed → may not raise rent. Prephrase: a building doesn’t pass an inspection that wasn’t finished. The line about tenants deserving safe housing is a decoy.

choices.note: Tempting, since it sounds like the board member’s values. But it’s about what tenants should be asked to pay, not what the law permits, and it doesn’t show the building failed to pass. The legal rule still needs “not passed.”
Reversed. Completed → passed. Our inspection wasn’t completed, so this says nothing about it.
Nobody said any violation was found. This bridges through a fact the stimulus never gives.
“Most” would-have-found-violations doesn’t mean this building didn’t pass. Too weak, and still hypothetical.
CORRECT. Not completed → not passed. The most recent inspection wasn’t completed, so the building didn’t pass it, so the landlord may not raise rents.

questions.stimulus: Ethics officer: Councilor Ruelle should not send her quarterly newsletter to constituents this month, even though the city pays for it and it has gone out every quarter for six years. She is running for reelection next month, and this issue features photographs of her at the openings of projects she championed, which can only help her campaign.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the ethics officer’s argument?
choices: During an election campaign, officials should not use public money to send out material that would promote their candidacy, however routine sending it may be.
An official may use public funds to send a newsletter to constituents only if the official has regularly sent such newsletters to them in the past.
Newsletters paid for by a city should never contain photographs of any official who is running for reelection to the city council.
Any newsletter that an official sends to constituents during an election campaign should state clearly who paid for printing and mailing it.
Officials should stop sending publicly funded newsletters during an election campaign if any of their opponents objects to them.
questions.explanation: The officer concludes Ruelle shouldn’t send this city-paid newsletter, despite the routine, because it would help her campaign; (A) makes those facts sufficient for “should not send.” Most students pick (C), but it only bans the photographs; Ruelle could remove them and send the newsletter, so (C) doesn’t justify the conclusion. (B) states a necessary condition she already meets, (D) asks only for a disclosure of who paid, and (E) depends on an objection the stimulus never mentions.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Ruelle should not send this month’s city-paid newsletter.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The city pays for it; she’s running for reelection next month; this issue would help her campaign; (concession) it’s a long-standing routine.

breakdown.analysis: The conclusion is about not sending this newsletter at all. The reason: public money would promote her campaign, and the routine doesn’t excuse it. We need: during a campaign, publicly funded material that promotes the official’s candidacy shouldn’t go out, routine or not. Beware answers that fix one feature (the photos, who pays) rather than forbidding the mailing.

choices.note: CORRECT. Campaign period + public money + promotes her candidacy → don’t send, even if routine. Every fact lines up, and the verdict matches.
A necessary condition: a history of regular newsletters. Ruelle has one, so the rule is satisfied and gives no verdict. It certainly doesn’t say “don’t send.”

Tempting. It targets the photos, which is what makes this issue promotional. But the conclusion is that she shouldn’t send the newsletter at all. Under this rule she could just pull the photos and mail it.
A disclosure rule. She could comply by adding a line saying the city paid, and then send it. It doesn’t support not sending it.
We don’t know that any opponent objected, so the condition is never met.

questions.stimulus: Under Tavin Province’s licensing rules, an engineer may place her seal only on plans prepared under her direct supervision. Accurate plans are essential to public safety. The plans for the Kessel footbridge were drawn at a firm in another province, and the engineer Mara Ostrow, who never visited that firm’s office, reviewed each draft by video call. So Ostrow may not place her seal on those plans.
questions.stem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Any plan whose preparation an engineer attended in person was prepared under that engineer’s direct supervision.
An engineer may seal plans for a structure only if the firm that drew them is licensed in the province where it will be built.
Plans that are reviewed only by video call are more likely than other plans to contain errors that endanger the public.
No plan is prepared under an engineer’s direct supervision unless the engineer was at some point present where it was prepared.
Most engineers who review drafts only by video call fail to notice at least some errors that would be caught in person.
questions.explanation: Seal → direct supervision. Ostrow was never present where the plans were drawn, so we need Never present → not direct supervision, which is (D) in “unless” form. The main trap is (A), its reversal: Present → direct supervision says nothing about someone who was never present. (B) bridges through the firm’s license, which the stimulus never addresses; (C) and (E) lean on the public-safety decoy and are about errors, not supervision.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Ostrow may not seal the Kessel footbridge plans.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Seal → plans prepared under her direct supervision; she reviewed every draft by video and never visited the firm.

breakdown.analysis: She reviewed every draft. Why isn’t that direct supervision? The argument assumes supervision requires being physically there. Chain: Never present → ??? → not direct supervision → may not seal. Translate “No X unless Y”: X → Y. So the key reads: Direct supervision → present at some point. Contrapositive: never present → no direct supervision.

choices.note: Reversed. Present → direct supervision. Ostrow was never present, so this never applies to her.
We aren’t told whether the firm is licensed in Tavin, so this condition gives no verdict. It bridges through a fact the stimulus never supplies.
This is about error rates, an echo of the public-safety decoy. The rule is about supervision, and this doesn’t say video review isn’t supervision.
CORRECT. Direct supervision → present at some point. Ostrow was never present, so the plans weren’t prepared under her direct supervision, so she may not seal them.
Too weak and off target. Missing errors doesn’t mean she wasn’t supervising.

questions.stimulus: Principle: A legislator should abstain from voting on any bill that would affect his or her own finances, unless the bill would affect them in the same way that it would affect the finances of most residents of the legislator’s district.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?
choices: Representative Lind drives to work each day, as do most residents of his district, so he should abstain from voting on a bill raising the gasoline tax.
Representative Asante owns the only ferry company serving her district, so she should abstain from voting on a bill that would raise the fees ferry operators pay.
A bill cutting the sales tax would benefit Representative Moro exactly as it would benefit most of his constituents, so he should vote in favor of it.
Representative Kahn’s brother owns a vineyard that a proposed water bill would harm, so Kahn should abstain from voting on that bill.
Representative Ilves has campaigned against a proposed highway for years, so she should abstain from voting on the bill that would fund it.
questions.explanation: The principle: bill affects the legislator’s own finances AND not in the same way as most residents’ → abstain. A ferry-fee bill hits Asante, the district’s only ferry owner, differently from most residents, so (B) conforms. The trap is (A): the gas tax does touch Lind’s finances, but exactly as it touches most residents’, so the exception applies and no abstention is called for. (C) gives a verdict the principle never gives, (D) is about a brother’s finances, and (E) is about opinions, not finances.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Bill affects legislator’s own finances AND NOT the same way as most district residents’ → legislator should abstain.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Find the case where the legislator’s own finances are affected in a way most residents’ aren’t, with the verdict “abstain.”

breakdown.analysis: Check each answer for: 1. the legislator’s own finances (not a relative’s, not an opinion); 2. affected differently from most residents’; 3. verdict: abstain. The exception is the subtle part. If everyone’s wallet is hit the same way, the rule is switched off. And switching the rule off doesn’t tell you how to vote.

choices.note: Tempting, since the gas tax does affect Lind’s finances. But it affects them the same way as most residents’, so the exception applies. The principle doesn’t call for abstaining.
CORRECT. Asante’s own business pays ferry fees, and as the only ferry owner she’s affected in a way most residents aren’t. Verdict: abstain.
The exception applies, so the principle is silent. It never tells anyone how to vote.
The vineyard is her brother’s, not hers. The principle is about the legislator’s own finances.
Campaigning against a bill is an opinion, not a financial stake. The principle doesn’t apply.

questions.stimulus: Under Corla’s civil service law, an employee who publicly discloses wrongdoing at her agency is protected from dismissal for that disclosure only if she first reported the wrongdoing to the agency’s inspector general. Agnes Ferrand told only her supervisor about the falsified safety logs before giving them to a newspaper. Admittedly, the public benefited from learning of the logs. Still, Ferrand is not protected from dismissal for the disclosure.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion of the argument to be properly drawn?
choices: A public disclosure of wrongdoing that benefits the public ought to be protected whether or not the employee followed the required steps.
Every employee who first reports wrongdoing to the inspector general is protected from dismissal for later disclosing it publicly.
An employee who discloses wrongdoing to a newspaper before reporting it to the inspector general is not protected from dismissal.
Disclosures of falsified records are protected only if the employee’s own supervisor took part in falsifying them.
The person to whom Ferrand reported the falsified logs was not her agency’s inspector general.
questions.explanation: Protected → first reported to the inspector general. Ferrand reported only to her supervisor, so the argument needs that her supervisor isn’t the inspector general, which is all (E) says. Most students pick (C), but it merely restates the law; whether Ferrand reported to the inspector general is exactly what’s still open. (B) reverses the rule, (A) is the decoy about public benefit and points the other way, and (D) depends on a fact we don’t have.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Ferrand is not protected from dismissal for the disclosure.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Protected → first reported to the inspector general; before going to the newspaper she told only her supervisor.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to see the gap at first, because it looks airtight. But who is her supervisor? If the supervisor happened to be the inspector general, Ferrand did report to the inspector general and might be protected. Chain: Told only her supervisor → ??? → didn’t report to the inspector general → not protected. The missing piece is a plain fact: the supervisor isn’t the inspector general.

choices.note: Opposite direction. This would push toward protecting her, and it’s about what ought to be, not what the law says.
Reversed. Reported to the inspector general → protected. It tells us nothing about someone who didn’t.
Tempting, because it sounds exactly like the conclusion. But it only restates the law. We still don’t know Ferrand failed to report to the inspector general. That’s the gap.
We don’t know whether the supervisor took part. Without that, this condition gives no verdict.

CORRECT. Ferrand told only her supervisor. If the supervisor isn’t the inspector general, she never reported to the inspector general first, so she isn’t protected. A short, plain fact hiding as the key.

questions.stimulus: Statistician: The national statistics office should refuse the police request for the household survey answers it collected in the Tarn district. Granted, the request is lawful, and the answers might help solve a serious crime. But everyone who took part in the survey was promised that their answers would be used for statistical purposes only.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the statistician’s argument?
choices: A government office should share information with the police only if doing so is likely to help them solve a serious crime.
People who are asked to take part in a government survey should be told in advance of any law that would allow the police to see their answers.
An agency that gathered information on a promise to use it only for certain purposes should not release it for other purposes, even if lawfully asked.
A lawful request from the police should be granted unless the information requested was obtained from people who were legally compelled to give it to the government.
Promises that a government office makes to the public should be kept unless breaking them would help prevent serious harm to someone.
questions.explanation: The statistician argues from the promise to the refusal, over a lawful request; (C) supplies exactly that: promised limited use → don’t release for other purposes, even if lawfully asked. The trap is (E): it does say promises should be kept, but its exception (breaking would help prevent serious harm) may well be triggered by a serious crime, so it doesn’t deliver a verdict. (A) gives a necessary condition the request may satisfy, (B) is about advance notice, and (D) would require handing the answers over.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The statistics office should refuse the police request.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Respondents were promised statistical use only; (concessions) the request is lawful and might help solve a serious crime.

breakdown.analysis: The statistician grants the two best reasons to comply and still says no, purely because of the promise. So the principle must say: a promise of limited use beats even a lawful request. Watch for exception clauses that the facts might trigger. A promise-keeping rule with a “prevent serious harm” escape hatch doesn’t clearly win here.

choices.note: A necessary condition for sharing. The answers might help solve a serious crime, so the condition may be met. Either way it never says to refuse.
About telling people in advance. It doesn’t address whether to hand over these answers now.
CORRECT. Promised limited use → don’t release for other purposes, even if the request is lawful. The concession is covered, and the verdict is refusal.
Opposite. Nothing says the respondents were compelled, so this rule says grant the request.

Tempting, since it’s about keeping promises. But helping solve a serious crime may well help prevent serious harm, which triggers the exception. Then the rule gives no verdict. It doesn’t justify refusing.

questions.stimulus: In Quessa, a will is valid only if it was signed in the presence of two witnesses, neither of whom receives anything under it. This rule keeps witnesses from having any motive to misreport how a will was signed. Edda Pryce signed her will in the presence of her nephew and her accountant, and the will leaves her house to the nephew’s nine-year-old son. Thus Pryce’s will is not valid.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: A will that was signed in the presence of two witnesses, neither of whom receives anything under it, is valid.
A witness who is related to the person making a will receives something under it if the will leaves property to that witness.
Anyone whose child stands to gain from a will has a motive to misreport how that will was signed.
A person receives nothing under a will only if the will leaves nothing to any minor child of that person.
Courts in Quessa generally treat property left to a minor as belonging, in practice, to that minor’s parents.
questions.explanation: Valid → neither witness receives anything. The will leaves the house to the nephew’s minor son, so we need that the nephew thereby receives something. (D) says Receives nothing → nothing left to his minor child; the contrapositive is the bridge. Most students pick (C), which captures the rule’s purpose (motive), but the rule turns on receiving, not on motive, so (C) proves nothing about validity. (A) is the reversed rule, (B) needs property left to the witness himself, and (E) says only “generally” and “in practice.”

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Pryce’s will is not valid.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Valid → two witnesses AND neither receives anything under it; the witnesses were her nephew and her accountant; the house goes to the nephew’s nine-year-old son.

breakdown.analysis: The house goes to the boy, not to the nephew. So does the nephew “receive anything”? The argument assumes he does. Chain: House left to nephew’s minor son → ??? → nephew receives something → a witness receives something → not valid. Prephrase: when a will leaves something to your minor child, you count as receiving something. The motive sentence is a decoy. The rule asks who receives, not who has a motive.

choices.note: Reversed. It turns the necessary condition into a sufficient one. That tells you when a will is valid, never when it isn’t.
This covers property left to the witness himself. The will leaves the nephew nothing directly, so this never applies.

Tempting, and most students pick it, because it fits the rule’s purpose. But the rule doesn’t invalidate wills when a witness has a motive. It invalidates them when a witness receives something. Motive doesn’t get you there.

CORRECT. Receives nothing → nothing left to his minor child. Contrapositive: something left to his minor child → he receives something. The nephew is a witness who receives something, so the will is invalid.
“Generally” and “in practice” are too weak, and treating property as the parents’ in practice isn’t the same as their receiving it under the will.

questions.stimulus: Court administrator: Lena Moss should not have accepted the assignment to interpret at the trial of Vasco Pell, even though she had never met Pell and the court could find no other interpreter fluent in his dialect. During the police investigation, Moss had interpreted for the prosecution’s chief witness while that witness described the events at issue.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the court administrator’s judgment?
choices: An interpreter whose earlier work on a case acquainted her with a witness’s account of events should not interpret at the trial, even if no substitute can be found.
An interpreter who has heard a witness’s account of events while working on a case should not interpret at its trial unless no other qualified interpreter is available.
An interpreter should accept a trial assignment only if there is no other qualified interpreter who is fluent in the defendant’s language.
A court should not assign an interpreter to a trial if that interpreter has ever met the defendant or any member of the defendant’s family.
An interpreter who has worked for the prosecution in a case should agree to interpret at its trial only if the defense has consented.
questions.explanation: Moss heard the chief witness’s account during the investigation, and the administrator says she shouldn’t interpret even though no one else could. (A) has the right trigger and expressly overrides the lack of a substitute. Most students pick (B), which has the same trigger but an exception (“unless no other qualified interpreter is available”) that the facts satisfy, so (B) gives no verdict. (C) states a necessary condition Moss meets, (D) depends on her having met Pell, which she hadn’t, and (E) turns on consent we know nothing about.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Moss should not have accepted the trial assignment.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: She interpreted the prosecution’s chief witness’s account during the investigation; (concessions) she’d never met Pell, and no other interpreter was available.

breakdown.analysis: The administrator grants that nobody else could do the job and still says no. So the principle has to forbid it anyway. We need: earlier exposure to a witness’s account → don’t interpret at trial, even with no substitute. Two answers share the trigger. Read their exception clauses word by word. The one that lets the interpreter proceed when no one else is available can’t justify this conclusion.

choices.note: CORRECT. Acquainted with a witness’s account through earlier work → don’t interpret at trial, even with no substitute. That covers Moss and overrides the concession.
Tempting, and most students pick it. Same trigger, but look at the “unless”: no other qualified interpreter was available, so the exception applies and the principle says nothing against Moss.
A necessary condition for accepting. No one else was available, so Moss meets it. This can’t produce “should not have accepted.”
Moss had never met Pell. Nor are we told about his family. The condition isn’t met, and it’s about the court anyway.
We don’t know whether the defense consented, so this gives no verdict. It’s also unclear that interpreting for a witness to the police is “working for the prosecution.”

questions.stimulus: Transit board chair: Our rules require a board member to withdraw from the vote on any contract for which a company that has employed that member within the past three years has submitted a bid. Four of our seven members worked for Halsey Coachworks, a bus manufacturer, within the past three years. So at least four members must withdraw from the vote on the contract for our new bus fleet.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the transit board chair’s argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Every company that has submitted a bid for the contract for the board’s new bus fleet is a manufacturer of buses.
Most bus manufacturers have submitted bids for the contract to supply the board’s new bus fleet.
Each company that manufactures buses has submitted a bid for the contract for the new bus fleet.
Any board member who still owns shares in a company that is bidding on a contract must withdraw from the vote on it.
The three members who did not work for Halsey Coachworks have never worked for any company that makes buses.
questions.explanation: The rule makes the four withdraw if Halsey has bid on the bus fleet contract; all we know is that Halsey makes buses. (C) says every bus maker has bid, which puts Halsey among the bidders. Most students pick (A), its reversal: Bidder → bus maker doesn’t make Halsey a bidder. (B) is “most,” so Halsey could be an exception; (D) bridges through share ownership, never mentioned; (E) is about the other three members and can’t add to the four.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: At least four members must withdraw from the bus fleet vote.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Company that employed member in past 3 years has bid → member withdraws; four members worked for Halsey, a bus manufacturer, in that period.

breakdown.analysis: Did Halsey actually bid? The stimulus never says so. It only says Halsey makes buses. Chain: Halsey makes buses → ??? → Halsey bid → its four former employees withdraw. We need Bus maker → bidder. Watch the reversal: Bidder → bus maker uses the same words and gets you nowhere.

choices.note: Tempting, and most students pick it. But it’s reversed: Bidder → bus maker. Halsey could make buses without having bid at all.
“Most” isn’t “all.” Halsey could be one of the bus makers that didn’t bid.
CORRECT. Bus maker → bidder. Halsey makes buses, so Halsey bid, so all four of its recent employees must withdraw.
Nobody mentioned owning shares. This bridges through a fact we don’t have.
This is about the other three members. It can’t show that the four Halsey alumni must withdraw, because it says nothing about whether Halsey bid.

questions.stimulus: Bar association rule: A law firm may quote a client’s praise of the firm in its advertising only if the client has consented in writing and, in addition, either the client’s matter has concluded or the client is no longer represented by the firm.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the rule stated above?
choices: Orlov consented in writing to having his praise quoted, and his lawsuit has concluded, though the firm still handles his other affairs, so the firm may quote him.
Sato consented in writing to the firm’s quoting her praise, but her case is still pending and the firm still represents her, so the firm should not have quoted her.
Although Petrak never consented to being quoted, his praise of the firm had already appeared on a public review site for anyone to read, so the firm acted properly in quoting it.
Attorney Kell posted a former client’s praise of her work on her personal social media account without asking him, so Kell violated the rule.
Because Wynn’s case is still pending, the firm must wait until the case concludes before asking Wynn for written consent to quote his praise.
questions.explanation: The rule gives only necessary conditions: written consent AND (matter concluded OR client no longer represented). Sato’s case is pending and the firm still represents her, so the “or” fails and quoting her was improper, as (B) says. Most students pick (A): Orlov meets every condition, but the rule never says meeting them makes quoting permissible. (C) contradicts the consent requirement, (D) concerns a personal post rather than the firm’s advertising, and (E) adds a timing rule about asking for consent that the rule doesn’t contain.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Firm quotes client’s praise in advertising → written consent AND (matter concluded OR client no longer represented).

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Find a case where a firm quoted a client in advertising while one of these conditions failed, judged improper.

breakdown.analysis: “May … only if” gives necessary conditions, so the rule can only ever tell you a quote is NOT allowed.
