Requirements: 1. written consent; 2. at least one of: matter concluded, or client no longer represented. Sato has 1 but neither half of 2. Orlov has everything, but that only means this rule doesn’t forbid it.

choices.note: Tempting, and most students pick it. Orlov meets every condition. But they’re necessary conditions. Meeting them doesn’t make quoting him allowed; some other rule might still forbid it.
CORRECT. Written consent, yes, but her case is pending and the firm still represents her, so the “either … or” requirement fails. The firm shouldn’t have quoted her.
Petrak never gave written consent, so the rule forbids the quote. Public posting doesn’t substitute for consent.
The rule covers a law firm’s advertising. A lawyer’s personal social media post is outside its scope as stated.
The rule says nothing about when the firm may ask for consent. It only limits when the firm may quote. Wrong verdict.

questions.stimulus: Under Larkin University’s research code, a study may proceed without obtaining each subject’s consent only if the ethics board determines both that the study poses minimal risk and that obtaining consent would be impracticable. Respect for subjects’ autonomy is the foundation of research ethics. Professor Adair’s study of former patients’ dental records poses minimal risk, and every former patient in it can easily be reached by mail. So Adair’s study may not proceed without each subject’s consent.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion of the argument to be properly drawn?
choices: The ethics board determines that obtaining consent would be impracticable for any study whose subjects cannot easily be reached by mail.
The ethics board never allows a study to proceed without consent if the study poses more than minimal risk to its subjects.
Studies of patients’ medical records must obtain each patient’s consent unless the records have been stripped of identifying details.
Most studies whose subjects can easily be reached by mail are ones for which the ethics board has required consent from every subject.
The ethics board does not find consent impracticable to obtain when each of a study’s subjects can easily be reached by mail.
questions.explanation: Proceed without consent → board determines minimal risk AND impracticable. Minimal risk is conceded, so the argument needs the board not to find consent impracticable for a mail-reachable study; (E) says exactly that. Most students pick (A), the reversal: Not reachable → impracticable says nothing about subjects who are reachable. (B) concerns risk, which is already granted, (C) depends on whether the records were anonymized, which we aren’t told, and (D) is only “most.”

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Adair’s study may not proceed without each subject’s consent.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Proceed without consent → board finds minimal risk AND finds consent impracticable; the study is minimal risk; every subject can easily be reached by mail.

breakdown.analysis: Minimal risk is granted, so that half of the test is no help. The argument has to win on the other half: the board must not find consent impracticable. But the premise is about how easy the subjects are to reach, and the rule is about what the board determines. Chain: Easily reached → ??? → board doesn’t find impracticable → may not proceed without consent. The autonomy line is a decoy.

choices.note: Tempting, and most students pick it. It links reachability to impracticability, but backwards: Not reachable → impracticable. Adair’s subjects are reachable, so this never applies.
The study is minimal risk, so this condition isn’t triggered. It attacks the half of the test the argument concedes.
We don’t know whether the records were stripped of identifying details, so this gives no verdict. It bridges through a fact never stated.
“Most” leaves room for Adair’s study to be an exception.
CORRECT. All subjects easily reached → board doesn’t find consent impracticable. One required finding is missing, so the study can’t proceed without consent.

questions.stimulus: Political theorist: The legislature should not extend the governor’s emergency authority to set fuel prices, even though fuel shortages could recur. That authority was granted to deal with last winter’s shortage, which has now ended, and should a new shortage arise, the legislature could pass price controls itself quickly enough to respond.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the political theorist’s argument?
choices: An emergency power should be allowed to lapse once the emergency that prompted it is over, unless a similar emergency could occur in the future.
An official should keep an emergency power after a crisis ends only if the official used that power responsibly while the crisis lasted.
A legislature should not extend a power that it has granted to an official unless that official has asked for the extension.
Once the crisis that prompted an emergency power has passed, the power should end if the legislature could handle a renewed crisis in time itself.
The power to set prices should be held only by officials who are directly accountable to voters for the prices that they set.
questions.explanation: The theorist’s reasons are that the crisis is over and the legislature could respond in time to a new one, and the conclusion holds even though shortages could recur. (D) uses exactly those two conditions to say the power should end. Most students pick (A), which has the right trigger but an exception (“unless a similar emergency could occur”) that the stimulus concedes is met, so (A) gives no verdict. (B) and (C) depend on facts we lack (responsible use, a request), and (E) doesn’t distinguish the governor from the legislature.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The legislature should not extend the governor’s emergency fuel-price authority.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The shortage that prompted it is over; the legislature could act quickly enough itself if a new shortage came; (concession) shortages could recur.

breakdown.analysis: Notice the concession: shortages could recur. Any principle with a “could recur” exception is switched off by the facts. We need: crisis over + legislature can respond in time → the power should end. Read every “unless” and ask whether the facts trigger it.

choices.note: Tempting, and most students pick it. Right trigger, but the stimulus admits shortages could recur, so the exception applies and the principle gives no verdict.
We aren’t told how the governor used the power. The condition is unknown, so no verdict.
We don’t know whether the governor asked for an extension, so this gives no verdict.
CORRECT. Crisis passed + legislature could handle a renewed crisis in time → the power should end. Both facts are in the stimulus, and the possible recurrence doesn’t matter under this rule.
Governors are elected too, so this doesn’t show the governor shouldn’t hold the power. The theorist’s reasons are about timing and the end of the crisis, not accountability.

questions.stimulus: An antiquity may be exported from Kardia only with a permit, and the culture ministry issues permits only for objects that a state museum has catalogued. The nation’s heritage belongs to all its citizens. The Ostler Gallery wishes to export a bronze mirror, an antiquity found last spring that has so far been examined only by private appraisers. So the mirror cannot legally be exported.
questions.stem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: An object has been catalogued by a state museum only if someone other than a private appraiser has examined it.
Every object that has been examined by the staff of a state museum has been catalogued by a state museum.
The culture ministry issues an export permit for every antiquity that a state museum has catalogued.
No antiquity that belongs to the nation’s heritage should be allowed to leave Kardia for a private gallery abroad.
Most antiquities that have been examined only by private appraisers have not yet been catalogued by any state museum.
questions.explanation: Exported → permit → catalogued by a state museum. The mirror has been examined only by private appraisers, so we need Examined only by private appraisers → not catalogued; (A) is the contrapositive form of that. Most students pick (C) or (B), which reverse links: (C) makes catalogued sufficient for a permit, and (B) makes museum examination sufficient for cataloguing; neither ever yields “not catalogued.” (D) turns the heritage decoy into a “should,” not a legal bar, and (E) is only “most.”

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The mirror cannot legally be exported.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Exported legally → permit → catalogued by a state museum; the mirror has been examined only by private appraisers.

breakdown.analysis: Who said the mirror isn’t catalogued? We only know who has examined it. Could a museum catalogue something its staff never looked at? The argument assumes not. Chain: Examined only by private appraisers → ??? → not catalogued → no permit → no legal export. We need Catalogued → examined by someone other than a private appraiser.

choices.note: CORRECT. Catalogued → examined by someone other than a private appraiser. Contrapositive: only private appraisers → not catalogued → no permit → can’t be legally exported. The “only if” form hides it.
Reversed. Museum examination → catalogued. No museum examined the mirror, so this says nothing.
Tempting, since it’s about the permit rule. But it reverses it: Catalogued → permit. We need to show no permit, and this can’t do that.
This turns the heritage decoy into a “should.” The conclusion is about what’s legal, and this doesn’t show the mirror isn’t catalogued.
“Most” leaves room for this mirror to be catalogued. Too weak.

questions.stimulus: Principle: A therapist should break a client’s confidence only to prevent serious physical harm to an identifiable person, and then only by warning that person or the police. Clients who fear disclosure will not speak frankly, and frank speech is what makes therapy work.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: Dr. Feld’s client said he meant to assault a coworker whom he named, so Dr. Feld acted rightly when he warned that coworker about the client’s threat.
Dr. Aro’s client threatened to injure her former husband, whom she named, but Dr. Aro told no one, so Dr. Aro acted wrongly.
Dr. Ince’s client vowed to break the legs of a neighbor he named, and Dr. Ince alerted the client’s landlord, so Dr. Ince acted wrongly.
Because Dr. Mahr’s client threatened only to slash a named rival’s tires, Dr. Mahr should have warned the rival rather than the police.
Dr. Quist warned a man whom her client had threatened to kill, but she should also have told the police about the client’s threat against him.
questions.explanation: The principle sets two necessary conditions on breaking a confidence: the purpose (preventing serious physical harm to an identifiable person) and the recipient (that person or the police). Ince told the landlord, so the second condition fails and he acted wrongly, as (C) says. Most students pick (A): Feld meets both conditions, but the principle only says when breaking a confidence is NOT allowed, never that it is right. (B) treats the principle as requiring a warning, (D) recommends a breach the principle forbids, and (E) demands a second warning the principle never requires.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Break confidence → (to prevent serious physical harm to an identifiable person) AND (by warning that person or the police).

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Find a breach that fails one of these conditions, judged wrong.

breakdown.analysis: Two “only”s, so two necessary conditions. The principle can tell you a breach was wrong, but never that a breach was right or required. Check: 1. was confidence broken? 2. to prevent serious physical harm to an identifiable person? 3. told that person or the police? A breach failing 2 or 3 is wrong. Everything else goes beyond the rule.

choices.note: Tempting, and most students pick it. Feld meets both conditions, so the principle doesn’t forbid what he did. But it never says such a warning is right. Necessary conditions can’t make something right.
The principle never requires a warning. It only limits when you may give one. Telling no one can’t violate it.
CORRECT. Ince broke the confidence by telling the landlord, who is neither the threatened neighbor nor the police. The second condition fails, so the breach was wrong.
Slashing tires isn’t physical harm to a person, so the principle says not to break the confidence at all. Recommending a warning to the rival contradicts it.
The principle allows warning the person OR the police. It never requires both, so there was no duty to tell the police too.

questions.stimulus: Senate aide: Senate rules require that a judicial nominee be rejected if the state bar association rates the nominee unqualified. Litigants deserve judges who know their way around a courtroom, and most of the nominees the governor has sent us this year have no trial experience. So, under the rules, most of this year’s nominees must be rejected.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the senate aide’s argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Every nominee whom the state bar association rates unqualified is someone who has no trial experience.
Most nominees who have no trial experience are rated unqualified by the state bar association.
The bar association never rates as unqualified a nominee who has already served as a judge in a lower court.
Judges who lack trial experience serve litigants less well than judges who have such experience do.
Only nominees who have trial experience avoid being rated unqualified by the state bar association.
questions.explanation: Rated unqualified → rejected; most nominees lack trial experience. To get “most rejected” we need No trial experience → rated unqualified, which (E) states in “only” form (Avoid unqualified rating → trial experience). Most students pick (B), but most of most doesn’t give most: if 6 of 10 nominees lack experience and only 4 of those 6 are rated unqualified, just 4 of 10 are rejected. (A) reverses the link, (C) is about lower-court judges, which the stimulus never applies, and (D) is the courtroom decoy.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Under the rules, most of this year’s nominees must be rejected.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Rated unqualified → rejected; most of this year’s nominees have no trial experience.

breakdown.analysis: Does lacking trial experience get you rated unqualified? The argument assumes so. Chain: No trial experience → ??? → rated unqualified → rejected. Because the premise is “most,” the bridge has to be all-or-nothing. A “most” bridge leaks. Imagine 10 nominees: 6 lack experience, and only 4 of those 6 are rated unqualified. That’s most of them, but only 4 of 10 nominees get rejected. Not most. “Only A avoid B” translates to: Avoid B → A, so not A → B.

choices.note: Reversed. Rated unqualified → no trial experience. It never gets a nominee without experience rated unqualified.
Tempting, and most students pick it. But most + most doesn’t make most. The rated-unqualified group could be a minority of all nominees.
The stimulus never says any nominee served as a judge. This rule is about who escapes a bad rating and doesn’t help at all.
This is the courtroom decoy. Serving litigants badly isn’t a bar association rating, and the rule turns on the rating.
CORRECT. Avoid an unqualified rating → have trial experience. Contrapositive: no trial experience → rated unqualified → rejected. Most nominees lack experience, so most are rejected.

questions.stimulus: Commentator: Mira Castell was right to tell the city that the parking garage she designed fifteen years ago has drainage flaws that could weaken its supports. True, the city now owns the garage, her contract was with the developer who built it and expired long ago, and the disclosure may expose her to a lawsuit. But none of that changes what she owed.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the commentator’s position?
choices: An architect who learns of a dangerous flaw in a building she designed should promptly inform the client who originally commissioned that design.
Architects who learn that a structure they designed may endanger its users should tell its current owner, whatever their contracts say or the risk to them.
Architects should inform the owners of any flaws in buildings they designed, unless more than ten years have passed since those buildings were first completed.
Architects should disclose flaws in their past designs only if doing so will not expose them to legal liability.
Public bodies that own buildings should have those buildings inspected regularly for flaws that could endanger the public.
questions.explanation: Castell told the current owner (the city) about a danger to users, despite an expired contract and legal risk; (B) requires exactly that and overrides both concessions. Most students pick (A), but the client who commissioned the design was the developer, not the city, so (A) would have her tell the wrong party. (C)’s ten-year exception is triggered at fifteen years, so it gives no verdict; (D) points the other way; and (E) tells the city, not the architect, what to do.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Castell was right to tell the city about the garage’s drainage flaws.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The flaws could weaken the supports; (concessions) the city now owns it, her contract was with the developer and expired, and she may be sued.

breakdown.analysis: Who did she tell? The city, the current owner, not her old client. So the principle has to point to the current owner and survive the concessions: no contract, legal risk, fifteen years. Check every recipient and every exception clause against the facts.

choices.note: Tempting, and most students pick it. But the client who commissioned the design was the developer. This would justify telling the developer, not the city.
CORRECT. Possible danger to users → tell the current owner, regardless of contract or personal risk. The city is the current owner, and both concessions are covered.
Fifteen years have passed, so the exception applies and this principle doesn’t require, or endorse, her telling anyone.
Opposite. She risks a lawsuit, so this principle would tell her not to disclose.
Wrong person. It tells the city what to do, not whether Castell was right to speak up.

questions.stimulus: A lawyer may not act against a former client in a matter substantially related to the earlier work, and if one lawyer at a firm is barred from a case, all the firm’s lawyers are. Nadia Orr, now at Ferris & Lowe, once negotiated water rights for Bellmar Holdings, the parent company of Corvan Mills. A farm wants Ferris & Lowe to sue Corvan Mills in a matter substantially related to that negotiation. So no lawyer at Ferris & Lowe may take the case.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion of the argument to be properly drawn?
choices: Orr is the lawyer at Ferris & Lowe who would most likely be assigned to handle the farm’s case against Corvan Mills.
Any lawyer who has represented a company is to be treated as having represented that company’s parent company as well.
A lawyer may not act against a former client in any matter in which she learned that client’s confidential information.
A lawyer’s former clients include every company whose parent company that lawyer once represented.
Most lawyers who have represented a parent company have also done at least some work for that company’s subsidiaries.
questions.explanation: Orr’s client was Bellmar, but the suit is against its subsidiary Corvan. The argument needs Corvan to count as Orr’s former client; (D) does that, so Orr is barred, and therefore the whole firm. Most students pick (B), which runs the relationship backward (subsidiary’s lawyer → parent’s lawyer). (A) is beside the point because the bar applies to the whole firm anyway, (C) bridges through confidential information, never mentioned, and (E) is only “most” and is about prior work, not client status.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: No lawyer at Ferris & Lowe may take the farm’s case against Corvan Mills.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A lawyer is barred from acting against a former client in a substantially related matter; one lawyer barred → the whole firm barred; Orr represented Bellmar, Corvan’s parent; the matter is substantially related.

breakdown.analysis: Orr’s client was Bellmar. The suit is against Corvan. Is Corvan her former client? The argument assumes so. Chain: Orr represented Corvan’s parent → ??? → Corvan is Orr’s former client → Orr barred → whole firm barred. We need: represented the parent → the subsidiary counts as a former client. Watch the direction of parent and subsidiary in the answers.

choices.note: Irrelevant. If Orr is barred, every lawyer at the firm is barred, whoever gets assigned. And this doesn’t show she’s barred in the first place.
Tempting, and most students pick it. But it runs the wrong way: represented the subsidiary → represented the parent. Orr represented the parent, so this never reaches Corvan.
Nothing says Orr learned Corvan’s confidential information, and Corvan still isn’t shown to be her former client. It bridges through a fact we don’t have.
CORRECT. Represented the parent → the subsidiary is a former client. Corvan becomes Orr’s former client, the matter is substantially related, so Orr is barred, and so is the whole firm.
“Most” isn’t “all,” and doing some work for a subsidiary isn’t shown to be related to this matter.

questions.stimulus: Principle: A public agency should not award a contract without competitive bidding unless a delay would endanger public safety, and it should never award a contract to a firm in which any of its own employees holds a financial interest.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: During last spring’s floods, the roads department hired Tarn Builders without bidding to shore up a failing levee; no employee had a stake in Tarn, so the department acted properly.
After competitive bidding, the parks agency hired Lusk Paving, a firm owned by the cousin of one of the agency’s clerks, so the agency acted wrongly.
The water department hired Pell Contracting without bidding to repave its staff parking lot, so the department should have hired the lowest bidder instead.
After competitive bidding, the housing agency hired Brask Roofing, in which one agency inspector had held shares until selling them a year earlier, so the agency acted wrongly.
When a bridge began to crumble, the highway agency hired Ross Ironworks without bidding to brace it, but an agency engineer owns part of Ross, so it acted wrongly.
questions.explanation: The principle has two parts: no bidding is allowed only when delay would endanger safety, and never with a firm in which an employee holds a financial interest. The crumbling bridge satisfies the safety exception, but an agency engineer owns part of Ross, so the second part is violated, as (E) says. Most students pick (A): Tarn meets both parts, but the principle only forbids; it never says such an award is proper. (B) involves a relative, not an employee, (C) gives a verdict (lowest bidder) the principle never states, and (D) involves an interest already sold.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Rule 1: No bidding → delay would endanger public safety. Rule 2: Employee holds a financial interest in the firm → don’t award to it.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Find an award that breaks either rule, judged wrong.

breakdown.analysis: Two separate rules, both only ever saying “don’t.” The safety exception rescues a no-bid award from Rule 1 but does nothing about Rule 2. So look for a case where an emergency excuses the lack of bidding but a current employee holds a stake. Check each case for: 1. bidding or a safety emergency; 2. no current employee with a financial interest; 3. a verdict of “wrong” when either fails.

choices.note: Tempting, and most students pick it. Tarn passes both rules, but the principle never says anything is proper. It only marks some awards as wrong.
The owner is a clerk’s cousin, not an agency employee. The bidding was competitive. Neither rule is broken.
The no-bid award does break Rule 1, but the verdict is off. The principle calls for competitive bidding, not for hiring the lowest bidder.
The inspector sold the shares a year earlier, so no employee holds an interest now. Neither rule is broken.
CORRECT. The crumbling bridge excuses the lack of bidding, but an agency engineer owns part of Ross, which breaks Rule 2. The agency acted wrongly. The emergency is bait.

questions.stimulus: Licensing official: A home inspector’s license lapses unless the inspector completes forty hours of approved courses during the year. The requirement keeps inspectors current with changes in building codes. Hours count as approved only if the course provider was registered with the board when the course was taken. All forty of Gil Varga’s course hours last year came from the Harrowgate Institute, which registered with the board last June. So Varga’s license has lapsed.
questions.stem: The licensing official’s conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Varga took no courses at all last year from any provider other than the Harrowgate Institute.
Not all of Varga’s Harrowgate course hours last year were completed after the institute registered with the board.
Some home inspectors took courses from the Harrowgate Institute last year before it registered with the board.
Hours from any course offered by a provider that is registered with the board count as approved hours.
None of the courses that the Harrowgate Institute offered last year covered recent changes to the building codes.
questions.explanation: Varga had exactly forty hours, all from Harrowgate, which registered in June. If even one hour came before registration, it doesn’t count, he falls short of forty, and the license lapses. (B) says exactly that, in “not all” form. Most students pick (C), but other inspectors’ early courses tell us nothing about Varga’s. (A) restates what we already know, (D) reverses the approval rule, and (E) bridges through the building-code purpose, which the approval rule never uses.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Varga’s license has lapsed.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: License lapses unless 40 approved hours in the year; hours approved → provider registered when the course was taken; all 40 of Varga’s hours came from Harrowgate, which registered in June.

breakdown.analysis: He had exactly forty hours, and the provider was registered for half the year. So which half did he take them in? If every hour came after registration, he’s fine. The argument needs at least one hour before registration. Chain: some hour taken before registration → that hour isn’t approved → fewer than 40 approved → lapses. The phrase “not all … after” is just “at least one before” in disguise.

choices.note: We already know all forty hours came from Harrowgate. This adds nothing about timing, which is the real gap.
CORRECT. Not all after = at least some before registration. Those hours don’t count, so Varga has fewer than forty approved hours and the license lapses.
Tempting, and most students pick it, because it puts courses before registration. But it’s about some inspectors, not Varga. His hours could all have come later.
Reversed. Registered provider → approved. That helps show hours count, not that they don’t.
The purpose of the requirement is a decoy. Approval depends on registration, not on course content.

questions.stimulus: Planning commissioner: The city should not take the Lindell family’s orchard by eminent domain for the new reservoir, even though the family would be paid full market value and the reservoir meets a genuine public need. The city already owns a disused quarry nearby that could hold the reservoir, though building it there would cost somewhat more.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the planning commissioner’s argument?
choices: A government should take private property for public use only if it pays the owners the full market value of that property.
A government should not take private property for a public project unless the project meets a genuine public need.
A government should not take private land for a project if land that it already owns could serve the project equally well and at no greater cost.
When land a government owns could serve a public project, it should not take private land for the project, even if using its own costs more.
Owners whose land is taken for public use should be paid more than market value if their family has worked that land for generations.
questions.explanation: The commissioner opposes taking the orchard because the city’s own quarry could serve, even at somewhat greater cost. (D) makes that sufficient and expressly covers the higher cost. Most students pick (C), but its condition is “at no greater cost,” and the quarry costs more, so (C) never applies. (A) and (B) give necessary conditions the city already meets, so they can’t yield “should not,” and (E) is about compensation, not whether to take the land.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The city should not take the Lindell orchard for the reservoir.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The city owns a quarry that could hold the reservoir; (concessions) full market value would be paid, the need is genuine, and the quarry would cost somewhat more.

breakdown.analysis: The commissioner gives away three points (fair pay, real need, higher cost) and still says no, because the city has its own land. So the principle must say: if the government’s own land could serve, don’t take private land, even at extra cost. The trap will have the right idea with a cost condition the facts fail.

choices.note: A necessary condition: full market value. The city would pay it, so this is satisfied and gives no verdict.
A necessary condition again. The need is genuine, so it’s satisfied. Nothing here says don’t take the land.
Tempting, and most students pick it. Right idea, but read the condition: “at no greater cost.” The quarry costs more, so this principle never kicks in.
CORRECT. Own land could serve → don’t take private land, even if it costs more. That matches the facts and the concession.
About how much to pay, not whether to take the land at all. And no generations of family work are mentioned.

questions.stimulus: In the Orvel Forest, the oaks produce enormous acorn crops every few years and small crops in the years between. Mice and squirrels eat far more acorns in the bumper-crop years than in other years. Yet it is mainly in the bumper-crop years that large numbers of new oak seedlings take root in the forest.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Acorns from bumper-crop years are, on average, no larger or more nutritious than the acorns that the oaks produce in other years.
In bumper-crop years, the forest's populations of mice and squirrels grow rapidly because their food is then so plentiful.
Even in bumper-crop years the animals eat only a small share of the acorns; in other years they eat nearly all.
Acorns that escape being eaten often fail to sprout when they land on a thick layer of fallen leaves.
Some oak species that grow outside the Orvel Forest produce moderately sized acorn crops every year.
questions.explanation: More acorns eaten (an amount) is compatible with more acorns left over, because what matters for seedlings is how many escape. If the animals eat only a small share of a huge crop but nearly all of a small one, far more acorns survive in bumper years. That is (C). (B) is the trap: it explains why more acorns get eaten, which is one side of the puzzle, and makes the seedling side look even stranger.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Animals eat more acorns in bumper years, but that's when most new seedlings appear.

breakdown.analysis: So what if more acorns get eaten? The question is how many are left. Eating more of a much bigger pile can still leave far more behind. It's like a bakery that gives away more free samples on its biggest baking day and still has more bread to sell. We need an answer that compares the share eaten, not the amount eaten. Most students pick (B) because it ties the animals to the bumper years. It fails because it only explains why more acorns are eaten, which we already knew; it does nothing to explain the seedlings.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Acorn quality being the same across years doesn't explain why more seedlings appear in bumper years.
Tempting. More animals means more acorns eaten, so it fits one side of the puzzle. But that side needed no explaining, and more hungry animals make the seedling boom harder to understand, not easier.
CORRECT. In bumper years the animals eat a bigger amount but a much smaller share. A huge crop with a small share eaten leaves far more acorns to sprout than a small crop that's nearly all eaten.
This happens every year, big crop or small. It doesn't explain a difference between the years.
Other oak species elsewhere tell us nothing about Orvel's seedlings.

questions.stimulus: Over the past fifty years, the average annual rainfall in the Sorrel Plains has not changed. Yet over the same period, the region's farmers have suffered both damaging floods and crop-killing droughts far more often than farmers there did before.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: A growing share of the region's yearly rain now falls in a few intense storms separated by long dry spells.
Many farmers in the Sorrel Plains now grow crops that need considerably more water than the crops grown there fifty years ago.
The rain gauges in the Sorrel Plains were replaced during the period with more accurate electronic instruments.
Average annual rainfall has risen over the same period in several of the regions that border the Sorrel Plains.
Floods in the Sorrel Plains do more damage to crops planted in low-lying fields than to crops planted on higher ground.
questions.explanation: An unchanged average can hide a changed pattern. If the same total now arrives in a few intense storms with long dry gaps between them, the storms cause floods and the gaps cause droughts. That is (A). (B) is the trap: thirstier crops would explain more drought damage, but not more floods.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Average rainfall is the same as fifty years ago, but floods and droughts are both more common.

breakdown.analysis: How can the same amount of rain cause both more floods and more droughts? An average says nothing about how the rain is spread out. A year with ten huge downpours and long dry months has the same average as a year of steady showers. It's like a paycheck: the same yearly salary paid in one lump in December leaves you broke in June. We need an answer about how the rain is distributed. Most students pick (B) because it explains crop-killing droughts. It fails because it explains only the dry half; it says nothing about floods.

choices.note: CORRECT. Same total, different timing. Intense storms cause floods, and the long dry spells between them cause droughts. Both facts fit.
Tempting. Crops that need more water would suffer more in dry spells. But that explains only the droughts. It does nothing for the floods.
If anything this questions the data. It doesn't explain why floods and droughts both increased.
Neighboring regions aren't the Sorrel Plains. Their rainfall doesn't explain local floods or droughts.
This says where floods hurt most. It doesn't explain why floods and droughts became more frequent.

questions.stimulus: Twenty years ago, the grassy hills above the town of Wendmere were replanted with pine forest. Planners expected the trees' roots to help rain soak into the soil and so to raise the flow of Wendmere's streams during the dry season. Instead, the streams' dry-season flow has fallen steadily since the planting.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: The pine forest has greatly reduced the amount of soil that washes from the hills into Wendmere's streams.
Rainfall in the region during the dry season over the past twenty years has been close to its long-term average.
Since the planting, less rain has run off the surface of the hills during storms, so Wendmere's streams flood less often.
Growing pines draw far more water from the soil, and release it into the air, than pasture grasses do.
Several other towns in the region replanted hillside pastures with native hardwood trees rather than with pine.
questions.explanation: The plan assumed the forest would only add water to the ground. If growing pines pull much more water out of the soil and release it into the air than grass did, less water is left to feed the streams in the dry season, even if more rain soaks in. That is (D). (C) is the trap: it confirms that the trees changed how rain enters the ground, which is the side that went as planned, and makes the falling flow more puzzling.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The trees were supposed to help rain soak in and raise dry-season streamflow, but dry-season flow has fallen.

breakdown.analysis: Is helping rain soak in the only thing a forest does to water? Trees also drink. A lot. More water can enter the soil and still less can reach the stream if the trees use it up first. It's like getting a raise and still saving less because you also bought a car. We need an answer showing the forest takes water out. Most students pick (C) because it shows the trees changing the water flow. It fails because less runoff is exactly what the planners expected; it explains the part that worked, not the falling streamflow.

choices.note: Less soil in the streams is a benefit of the forest, but it says nothing about how much water flows.
This rules out a drought as the cause, so it makes the puzzle harder, not easier.
Tempting. It shows the trees changed how water moves. But more rain soaking in instead of running off is what the planners predicted. It deepens the puzzle about why dry-season flow fell.
CORRECT. The pines take far more water out of the soil than grass did. So even if more rain soaks in, less is left over to feed the streams in the dry season.
What other towns planted tells us nothing about Wendmere's streams.

questions.stimulus: Ecologist: Ten years ago, to protect the wildflowers of the Tarrant Prairie from grazing and trampling, we fenced cattle out of one large section of it. Today that fenced section contains fewer wildflower species than the adjacent prairie, where cattle still graze.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: The cattle that graze the Tarrant Prairie avoid eating several of the prairie's most common wildflower species entirely.
Without grazing, tall grasses have grown dense enough in the fenced section to shade out low wildflowers.
Ten years ago, the fenced section contained about as many wildflower species as the rest of the prairie did.
The number of wildflower species in the grazed part of the prairie has stayed about the same over the past ten years.
Cattle on the open prairie trample far more wildflowers during wet springs than they do during dry springs.
questions.explanation: Removing the cattle removed a harm, so something else must have harmed the wildflowers in the fenced section. If, without grazing, a few tall grasses grew dense enough to shade out low plants, the cattle were actually keeping those grasses in check. That is (B). (A) is the trap: it explains why the grazed side keeps its wildflowers, but not why the fenced side lost species.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Cattle were fenced out to protect wildflowers, but the fenced section now has fewer wildflower species than the grazed section.

breakdown.analysis: If cattle hurt wildflowers, why did removing them leave fewer species? Maybe the cattle were also doing something useful, like eating whatever crowds the wildflowers out. It's like firing the only person who ever cleaned the office kitchen. We need an answer showing that the absence of cattle hurt the fenced section. Most students pick (A) because it explains why wildflowers survive grazing. It fails because it explains only the grazed side; surviving grazing doesn't explain dying without it.

choices.note: Tempting. It explains why the grazed side does fine. But the puzzle is why the fenced side did worse, and cattle skipping some flowers doesn't touch that.
CORRECT. The cattle were keeping the tall grasses down. Fence them out and the grasses take over and shade the wildflowers. Both facts now fit.
This rules out a difference that existed from the start, so it sharpens the puzzle instead of solving it.
The grazed side holding steady tells us nothing about why the fenced side lost species.
This is about trampling in the grazed area. It gives no reason the fenced area would lose species.

questions.stimulus: Agronomist: Last spring, half of the bean fields on the Corley research farm were sprayed with an insecticide that kills over 95 percent of the aphids it contacts. A week after spraying, aphids were far scarcer in the sprayed fields. Six weeks after spraying, however, the sprayed fields held considerably more aphids than the fields that had been left unsprayed.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the agronomist's statements?
choices: The aphids that survived the spraying were those that happened to be least exposed, not ones resistant to the insecticide.
Aphids harm bean plants mainly by spreading viral diseases from one plant to another as they feed on sap.
The unsprayed fields were planted with the same bean variety, and on the same dates, as the sprayed fields.
Aphids reproduce so quickly that a population cut by 95 percent can return to its former size within a few weeks.
The insecticide also kills the lacewings and ladybird beetles that eat aphids, and these breed far more slowly.
questions.explanation: The sprayed fields didn't just recover; they ended up with more aphids than unsprayed fields. If the spray also kills the aphids' predators, which breed slowly, the aphids bounce back into fields where nothing is eating them. That is (E). (D) is the trap: fast breeding explains a return to the former level, but not a level higher than the fields that were never sprayed.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The spray killed almost all the aphids, but six weeks later sprayed fields had more aphids than unsprayed ones.

breakdown.analysis: Bouncing back is one thing. Overshooting the untouched fields is another. What keeps aphids down in the unsprayed fields that isn't there in the sprayed ones? Something that eats them. It's like clearing a lawn of weeds with a chemical that also kills the grass: the weeds return to bare ground with no competition and run wild. We need an answer showing the spray removed a check on aphids. Most students pick (D) because it explains the recovery. It fails because recovery only gets you back to where you were; it can't explain ending up worse off than fields that were never sprayed.

choices.note: Whether survivors were lucky or resistant, the puzzle is why the sprayed fields ended up worse than unsprayed ones. This doesn't say.
How aphids harm beans is irrelevant to why their numbers rose.
This rules out a difference between the fields, so it sharpens the puzzle.

Tempting. It explains how aphids could recover. But returning to the former size would leave the sprayed fields about even with the unsprayed fields. It can't explain them ending up with considerably more.
CORRECT. The spray wipes out the aphids' predators too, and the predators come back slowly. Aphids then multiply unchecked in the sprayed fields, while predators keep them down in the unsprayed ones.

questions.stimulus: Water district spokesperson: Last year we began seeding clouds over the Brisk River watershed with silver iodide to increase rainfall. Admittedly, seeding works only on clouds that already contain supercooled water droplets, so many storms cannot be seeded. But last year's rainfall in the watershed was 18 percent above its average for the previous ten years. Clearly, the seeding program is increasing rainfall.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the spokesperson's argument?
choices: The previous ten years were the driest decade on record in the watershed, and last year's rainfall was about normal.
On most days last year when storms passed over the watershed, the clouds held too little supercooled water to be seeded.
Seeding clouds costs the district less per liter of added water than piping water in from neighboring districts does.
Some residents of the watershed object to the program on the grounds that silver iodide may build up in the soil.
Last year the district seeded clouds far more often in the spring than it did in the autumn.
questions.explanation: The spokesperson's evidence is a comparison with the previous ten years. If that decade was unusually dry and last year was merely normal, an 18 percent jump is just a return to normal and shows nothing about seeding. That is (A). (B) is the trap: it sounds like the program rarely worked, but the spokesperson already concedes many storms can't be seeded; seeding could still add rain on the days it was possible.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The seeding program is increasing rainfall.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Rainfall last year was 18 percent above the previous ten-year average (concession: many storms can't be seeded).

breakdown.analysis: Above average compared with what? The baseline is the previous ten years. If those years were a drought, then 18 percent above them could be an ordinary year. It's like a student bragging that his grades jumped after a new study app, when the year before he had mono. We need an answer showing the baseline was unusually low. Most students pick (B) because it seems to show seeding rarely happened. It fails because the spokesperson already admitted that many storms can't be seeded. The claim is only that seeding adds rain, and it could on the days it was used.

choices.note: CORRECT. The comparison year was measured against a record drought. Rainfall merely returning to its long-term average would look like an 18 percent gain without any help from seeding.
Tempting. It sounds like the program barely operated. But the spokesperson already conceded that many storms can't be seeded. Seeding the few suitable clouds could still have added rain.
Cost is a different issue. The argument is about whether seeding increases rainfall, not whether it's a good deal.
Residents' worries about soil don't bear on whether the seeding produced rain.
When seeding happened doesn't tell us whether it worked.

questions.stimulus: Three years ago, wildlife managers began netting invasive banded perch out of Lake Ferrow, removing tens of thousands of them each year. When the program began, banded perch made up 20 percent of the fish in the lake. Surveys now show that banded perch make up 35 percent of the lake's fish.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Most of the banded perch removed from the lake by netting were adults rather than juveniles.
The surveys of Lake Ferrow's fish use the same sampling methods now as they did when the program began.
In the past three years a parasite has killed most of the lake's ciscoes, formerly its most numerous fish.
Netting has reduced the number of banded perch in Lake Ferrow by only about a quarter since the program began.
Banded perch are much easier to catch in nets during their spawning season than at other times of year.
questions.explanation: The perch share is a fraction: perch divided by all fish. It can rise even while the number of perch falls, if the other fish fall faster. A parasite killing most of the lake's most numerous native fish shrinks the denominator, so perch can be fewer and still a larger share. That is (C). (D) is the trap: it sounds like it explains the failure, but a 25 percent cut in perch, with nothing else changing, would lower their share, not raise it.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Managers removed tens of thousands of perch, but perch went from 20 percent to 35 percent of the lake's fish.

breakdown.analysis: Does a bigger share mean more perch? Not necessarily. A share depends on two numbers: perch and everything else. If everything else crashes, perch can be a larger share even after heavy netting. Picture a class where three students drop out but twelve others transfer away: the three remaining troublemakers are a bigger share of a smaller class. We need something that shrank the rest of the fish. Most students pick (D) because 'netting only worked a little' sounds like it explains the rise. It fails: if perch fell by a quarter and other fish held steady, the perch share would drop below 20 percent. It deepens the puzzle.

choices.note: Which perch were removed doesn't change the math: removing perch of any age should lower their share unless something happens to the other fish.
Same methods rules out a measurement quirk. That makes the puzzle stand, not go away.
CORRECT. If the ciscoes, the lake's biggest group of fish, mostly died, the total number of fish fell sharply. Perch can then be fewer than before and still make up a bigger share.
Tempting. It sounds like the program just didn't work well. But fewer perch with everything else unchanged means a smaller perch share, not a bigger one. Percentage versus amount.
When perch are easiest to catch says nothing about why their share rose.

questions.stimulus: Over the past fifteen years, farms in the Wessel River basin have cut the phosphorus washing off their fields into Lake Pember by nearly half. Because phosphorus feeds the algae that cloud the lake each summer, scientists expected the summer algae blooms to shrink. Yet in recent summers the blooms have been as large and frequent as they were fifteen years ago.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: The amount of phosphorus fertilizer that farms in the basin apply to their fields has also fallen during the period.
Algae blooms in several lakes outside the Wessel River basin have become smaller in recent years.
Some of the phosphorus that reaches Lake Pember comes from sources other than farms, such as the sewage of nearby towns.
Phosphorus from past decades of runoff lies in the lake's bottom mud and slowly seeps back into the water.
Large algae blooms make Lake Pember's water unappealing to swimmers and harm many of the fish that live in the lake.
questions.explanation: Cutting what flows in today doesn't remove what's already there. If decades of earlier runoff left phosphorus in the lake-bottom mud that keeps seeping back into the water, the algae can be fed for years after the inflow drops. That is (D): a time lag. (C) is the dominant trap: other sources sound like an answer, but they were there fifteen years ago too, and nothing says they grew enough to make up for halving the farm runoff.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Farm phosphorus runoff into the lake was cut nearly in half, but algae blooms are as big and frequent as ever.

breakdown.analysis: Is the phosphorus coming in each year the only phosphorus the algae can use? What about all the phosphorus that came in before? It's like cutting your credit card spending in half and still being buried, because last year's balance is still on the card. We need a source of phosphorus that the cut didn't touch and that hasn't shrunk. Most students pick (C) because 'other sources' sounds like the missing piece. It fails because those sources existed fifteen years ago too. To explain unchanged blooms after a big cut, they'd have to have grown, and (C) doesn't say that.

choices.note: This just confirms the farms really cut back. It deepens the puzzle.
Other lakes improving makes Lake Pember's lack of improvement more puzzling, not less.

Tempting. Other sources sound like the answer. But they were already there fifteen years ago. Halving the farm runoff should still have cut the total unless those other sources grew, and (C) doesn't say they did.
CORRECT. Phosphorus from earlier decades is stored in the mud and keeps leaking back into the water. The algae are still being fed even though less phosphorus now comes in from the farms.
This describes harm from the blooms. It doesn't explain why they haven't shrunk.

questions.stimulus: Every winter, volunteers in the Ardley Hills count the gray-crowned sparrows they see along a fixed set of routes. These winter counts have roughly doubled over the past twenty years. Yet surveys of the species' breeding grounds, hundreds of kilometers to the north, show that its total population has declined over the same period.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Gray-crowned sparrows that winter in the Ardley Hills return each spring to the same breeding grounds as those that winter elsewhere.
As winters grew milder, many of these sparrows stopped flying past the Ardley Hills and now winter there.
Gray-crowned sparrows eat mostly seeds in the winter and mostly insects during the breeding season.
Much of the gray-crowned sparrow's breeding habitat in the north has been cleared for farming over the past few decades.
Breeding-ground surveys count singing males, and nearly every adult male gray-crowned sparrow sings in the spring.
questions.explanation: The winter count covers only the birds that winter in the Ardley Hills, not the whole species. If milder winters have led many birds that used to winter farther south to stop in the Ardley Hills instead, more of a shrinking population ends up there. That is (B). (D) is the trap: habitat loss explains the falling total, but that side of the puzzle wasn't the mystery, and it makes the doubled winter count stranger.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Winter counts in the Ardley Hills have doubled, but the species' total population has fallen.

breakdown.analysis: Does the winter count measure the whole species? No. It measures how many birds are in one place in winter. A smaller population can still put more birds in one spot if more of them choose that spot. It's like a shrinking chain of restaurants whose downtown branch gets busier because the suburban branches closed. We need an answer that shifts where the birds spend the winter. Most students pick (D) because it explains a decline. It fails because it explains only the decline; it gives no reason more birds would show up in the Ardley Hills.

choices.note: Where the birds breed doesn't explain why more of them are counted in the Ardley Hills in winter.
CORRECT. The population shrank, but a bigger share of it now winters in the Ardley Hills. More birds there, fewer birds overall: both fit.
Diet changes between seasons don't explain why the winter count rose.
Tempting. It gives a cause for the population decline. But the decline was never the mystery. It does nothing to explain the doubled winter count.
This supports the breeding surveys' accuracy, which makes the puzzle firmer.

questions.stimulus: Geologist: On the floor of Lake Tamsin, a lava flow lies buried beneath 60 centimeters of fine lake sediment. Measurements over the past several decades show that sediment now settles on the lake floor at about 1 centimeter per century. Therefore, the lava flow must be roughly 6,000 years old.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the geologist's argument?
choices: Lava flows of similar chemical composition found elsewhere in the region have been dated to between 5,000 and 7,000 years ago.
The lava flow is chemically similar to rock produced by a volcano near the lake that is now extinct.
The sediment in Lake Tamsin contains pollen from plant species that grow in the surrounding hills today.
The rate at which sediment settles in Lake Tamsin has been measured only over the past few decades, not over centuries.
For millennia after the last ice age, meltwater streams carried far more silt into the lake than streams do today.
questions.explanation: The estimate works only if sediment has always piled up at today's rate. If meltwater after the ice age carried far more silt into the lake, much of the 60 centimeters could have been laid down quickly, and the flow could be much younger than 6,000 years. That is (E). (D) is the trap: it points at the short measuring period, which is a premise the geologist states openly, but it gives no reason to think the rate was ever different.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The lava flow is roughly 6,000 years old.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 60 cm of sediment covers it; sediment settles today at about 1 cm per century.

breakdown.analysis: Who says sediment has always settled at today's rate? The math is 60 divided by 1 per century, which only works if the rate never changed. It's like measuring a candle's height and how fast it burns now, then figuring how long it's been lit, without knowing someone had it near a fan for the first hour. We need an answer showing the rate was different in the past. Most students pick (D) because it sounds like it undermines the measurement. It fails because it only repeats what the stimulus already said and gives no evidence the rate changed. A doubt isn't a weakener.

choices.note: This fits the geologist's estimate, so it strengthens.
Which volcano produced the lava doesn't tell us when.
Pollen from today's plants says nothing about how fast the sediment built up.

Tempting. It seems to attack the rate. But the geologist already says the rate comes from recent decades. Without a reason to think it was different before, this is just a possibility, not a weakener.
CORRECT. Sediment poured in much faster for thousands of years after the ice age. So the 60 centimeters didn't need 6,000 years to build up, and the flow could be much younger.

questions.stimulus: Over the past thirty years, the land area of the Ossa River delta has shrunk steadily as the sea has claimed land along its coastal edge. Yet measurements show that the Ossa delivers as much sediment to its mouth each year as it did thirty years ago, and in earlier centuries that much sediment was enough to keep the delta growing.
questions.stem: Each of the following, if true, helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above EXCEPT:
choices: Heavy pumping of groundwater from beneath the delta over the past thirty years has caused the delta's land surface to sink.
Levees built along the river's lower channel now carry most of its sediment past the delta and out into deep water offshore.
Silt from expanding farms upstream has made up for the sediment that a dam built thirty years ago now traps.
Sea level along the coast near the Ossa delta has risen faster over the past thirty years than in earlier centuries.
Mangrove forests that once shielded the delta's coastal edge from storm waves were mostly cleared about thirty years ago.
questions.explanation: Four answers give a reason the delta can shrink even with the same sediment arriving: the land sinks (A), the sediment is carried past the delta (B), the sea rises (D), or waves erode the edge faster (E). (C) explains only why the sediment supply stayed the same, which is one side of the puzzle; it gives no reason the delta shrinks. The trap is (B): it can look as if it contradicts 'delivers as much sediment to its mouth,' but the sediment can reach the mouth and still be carried past the delta into deep water.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The river brings as much sediment as ever, an amount that used to build the delta, but the delta is shrinking.

breakdown.analysis: EXCEPT question: four answers resolve the puzzle and one doesn't. A resolver must give a reason the delta loses ground even though the sediment supply is unchanged: the land sinks, the sea rises, waves hit harder, or the sediment doesn't stay. The odd one out will explain something else, or only one side. Most students pick (B) as the exception, thinking it contradicts the stimulus. It doesn't: the stimulus says sediment reaches the river's mouth, not that it settles on the delta. Levees can shoot it right past.

choices.note: Resolves it. If the land is sinking, the delta can lose area even while the same sediment arrives.

Tempting to pick as the exception, because it seems to clash with 'delivers as much sediment to its mouth.' It doesn't: the sediment still reaches the mouth but is carried past the delta into deep water, so it no longer builds land. This resolves the puzzle.
CORRECT. This only explains why the sediment supply stayed the same despite the dam. That half of the puzzle was a given. It offers no reason the delta is shrinking.
Resolves it. A faster-rising sea can drown land faster than the same old sediment supply can build it.
Resolves it. Without the mangroves, storm waves erode the delta's edge faster than the sediment can replace it.

questions.stimulus: During last summer's severe drought in the Quillan Lowlands, the number of mosquitoes there fell to less than half its usual level. Nonetheless, cases of Varo fever, a disease that mosquitoes transmit from infected birds to people, were more numerous in the Quillan Lowlands last summer than in any previous year on record.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Birds and mosquitoes crowded around the few pools left by the drought, so a larger share of mosquitoes became infected.
Varo fever tends to cause more severe illness in elderly people than it does in younger adults who catch it.
Several bird species that carry Varo fever left the Quillan Lowlands early last summer to search for water in other, wetter regions.
The mosquitoes that carry Varo fever breed in standing water, much of which the drought eliminated.
Health officials in the Quillan Lowlands sprayed to control mosquitoes last summer just as they do every summer.
questions.explanation: Disease cases depend on how many mosquitoes are infected, not just how many mosquitoes there are. If the drought crowded birds and mosquitoes at the same few pools, a far larger share of mosquitoes would pick up the virus, so fewer mosquitoes could still infect more people. That is (A). (D) is the trap: it explains why mosquitoes declined, which is the side that needed no explaining.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Mosquitoes fell by more than half, but the mosquito-borne disease hit a record high.

breakdown.analysis: Fewer mosquitoes, more disease? What matters is not how many mosquitoes there are but how many carry the virus. Half as many mosquitoes, each three times as likely to be infected, means more infected mosquitoes. It's like a smaller crowd at a party where everyone is crammed into one room: fewer people, but a cold spreads faster. We need an answer that raises the infection rate among mosquitoes. Most students pick (D) because it ties the drought to mosquitoes. It fails because it explains only the drop in mosquitoes, not the rise in cases.

choices.note: CORRECT. Crowding at the few remaining pools brought mosquitoes and infected birds together. A much larger share of the remaining mosquitoes carried the virus, so cases rose even as mosquito numbers fell.
Who gets sickest doesn't explain why there were more cases.
Fewer infected birds should mean fewer cases. This deepens the puzzle.
Tempting. It explains why mosquito numbers dropped. But that was never the mystery. It gives no reason cases rose.
Same spraying as always. This changes nothing about last summer.

questions.stimulus: Climatologist: Winters around Lake Morrow have warmed over the past forty years. Since warmer winters bring a larger share of precipitation as rain rather than snow, one would expect snowfall in the towns just downwind of the lake to have declined. Instead, those towns now receive more snow each winter, on average, than they did forty years ago.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the climatologist's statements?
choices: Rain falls in the downwind towns more often in early and late winter than it does in midwinter.
Snowfall in the downwind towns is measured by trained volunteers who use the same standard methods each year.
Most of the snow in the downwind towns comes from storms that form over the lake itself.
The lake now freezes much later in winter, so cold winds crossing it pick up moisture for more weeks than before.
Winters in many regions far from any large lake have also grown warmer over the past forty years.
questions.explanation: Warming should mean less snow, unless it also adds moisture. If the lake now stays open far longer each winter, cold winds keep picking up water over it and dumping it as snow downwind for many more weeks. That is (D). (C) is the trap: it says the snow comes from lake storms, which is half the mechanism, but it doesn't say why those storms would now produce more snow.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Winters warmed, which should cut snowfall, but downwind towns get more snow than before.

breakdown.analysis: What could warming do that adds snow? Snow needs cold and moisture. The towns still get cold winds; what if the lake supplies more moisture than before? A frozen lake gives wind nothing to pick up. An open lake does. It's like a fan blowing across a bowl of water: cover the bowl and the air stays dry. We need something that changed and increased the moisture. Most students pick (C) because it links the snow to the lake. It fails because it describes where the snow comes from without saying anything changed. A source that was always there can't explain an increase.

choices.note: When rain falls doesn't explain why snow increased.
This confirms the measurements are reliable, which keeps the puzzle in place.
Tempting. It's the right neighborhood: lake storms. But it describes a constant, not a change. It doesn't explain why there is more snow now than forty years ago.
CORRECT. Warming keeps the lake open longer. Open water feeds moisture to cold winds for more weeks of winter, so the downwind towns get more snow even though winters are warmer.
Warming elsewhere is irrelevant to why these particular towns get more snow.

questions.stimulus: In the cliffs of the Brackwater Basin, each sediment layer laid down before about 100 million years ago contains, on average, fossils of more clam species than does each layer laid down since then. Yet paleontologists studying the basin are confident that more clam species lived there at any one time after 100 million years ago than before.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Paleontologists have found fossils of other kinds of shellfish in both the older and the younger layers of the basin.
Each of the older layers built up over a far longer span of time than does each of the basin's younger layers.
Many clam species that lived in the basin before 100 million years ago became extinct at about that time.
The basin's climate was considerably warmer before 100 million years ago than it has been since then.
Clams that lived in the basin after 100 million years ago were, on average, larger than earlier clams.
questions.explanation: A layer's fossil count reflects every species that lived there during the whole time the layer formed. If each older layer took far longer to build up, it collects many successive communities, so it can hold more species than a younger layer even though fewer species lived at any one moment. That is (B): a count per layer is not a count per moment. (C) is the trap: mass extinction sounds like it explains why the older layers are richer, but it means fewer species after 100 million years ago, which deepens the conflict with the paleontologists' view.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Older layers hold more clam species per layer, but more species lived at any one time in the later period.

breakdown.analysis: What does one layer measure? Not a snapshot. It's everything that settled during the time the layer formed. A layer that took a million years to build holds a million years of clams. A layer that formed in ten thousand years holds far fewer. It's like comparing two photo albums by how many different people appear: the one covering forty years beats the one from a single wedding, even if the wedding had a bigger crowd. Hard to prephrase; watch for a difference in what each layer represents. Most students pick (C) because extinction sounds like a reason for fewer later species. It fails because it supports the layers' story, not the paleontologists'. It makes the conflict worse.

choices.note: Other shellfish are irrelevant to why clam counts per layer and clam diversity disagree.
CORRECT. Each older layer covers much more time, so it piles up fossils from many successive communities. More species per layer doesn't mean more species at once.

Tempting. It sounds like a reason the later layers have fewer species. But if many species died out, there really were fewer species afterward. That contradicts the paleontologists instead of reconciling them with the fossils.
Climate could affect diversity in either direction. It doesn't explain the gap between the layer counts and the paleontologists' view.
Clam size doesn't explain how many species each layer holds.

questions.stimulus: Meteorologist: The number of tornadoes recorded each year in the Dellin Plains has tripled since the 1960s. Some take this as evidence that tornadoes there have become more frequent. But in the 1990s the region installed Doppler radars that can detect brief, weak tornadoes that once touched down unnoticed in empty farmland. So the rise reflects improved detection, not a real increase in tornadoes.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the meteorologist's argument?
choices: Tornadoes in the Dellin Plains occur most often in late spring and early summer.
Weather services in several other regions installed similar radar networks at about the same time.
Doppler radar can detect the rotation in a storm that precedes a tornado but cannot confirm that a tornado has touched down.
Tornado damage in the Dellin Plains has risen sharply, largely because many more buildings now stand in the region.
Over the same period, the yearly number of tornadoes strong enough to destroy farm buildings has also roughly tripled.
questions.explanation: Radar explains more weak tornadoes being recorded, because weak ones used to go unnoticed. Tornadoes strong enough to destroy farm buildings were never going to go unnoticed. If those tripled too, better detection can't explain it, which points to a real increase. That is (E). (C) is the trap: it seems to attack the radar, but if radar can't confirm touchdowns, some recorded 'tornadoes' may not be real, which would support the meteorologist's conclusion that the rise isn't real.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The rise in recorded tornadoes reflects improved detection, not a real increase.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Since the 1990s, radar detects weak, brief tornadoes that used to go unnoticed.

breakdown.analysis: Better detection explains more of what used to be missed. So which tornadoes were never missed? The big, destructive ones: they leave wreckage behind. If those rose just as fast, detection can't be the whole story. It's like a doctor saying more cancer diagnoses just reflect better scans, when even the late-stage cases that were always caught have tripled. We need evidence of an increase among tornadoes that were always detectable. Most students pick (C) because it sounds like a knock on the radar. It fails because it cuts the other way: if radar inflates the count with storms that never touched down, the recorded rise is even less likely to be real.

choices.note: Timing within the year has nothing to do with whether tornadoes increased.
Other regions' radars don't tell us whether Dellin tornadoes became more frequent.
Tempting. It sounds like it attacks the radar premise. But if radar counts storms that never touch down, the recorded rise is inflated, which helps the meteorologist.
Damage rising because of more buildings explains damage, not tornado frequency. It even suggests a non-weather reason for alarm.
CORRECT. Tornadoes that flatten farm buildings never went unnoticed, so radar can't explain their rise. A tripling there points to a real increase.

questions.stimulus: Over the past forty years, the average summer temperature in the Ruska Valley, a farming region, has risen by about one degree Celsius. Over the same period, however, the number of summer days on which the temperature in the valley climbs above 32 degrees Celsius has fallen by nearly a third.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: The valley's weather stations record the temperature every hour of the day and night throughout the summer.
The valley's hottest days usually come during droughts, which have become less frequent there in recent decades.
Expanded irrigation in the valley has cooled its summer afternoons slightly but made its summer nights much warmer.
Average summer temperatures have risen by a similar amount in the other farming valleys throughout the region.
Crops in the valley suffer heat damage mainly on days above 32 degrees Celsius.
questions.explanation: An average summer temperature includes nights; a count of days above 32 degrees depends only on afternoon highs. If irrigation has made afternoons a little cooler while making nights much warmer, the average can rise while hot afternoons become rarer. That is (C). (B) is the trap: fewer droughts explains fewer hot days, but it gives no reason the average went up; if anything it should pull the average down.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The average summer temperature rose, but days above 32 degrees became much rarer.

breakdown.analysis: What goes into an average summer temperature? Every hour, day and night. What goes into 'days above 32'? Only the afternoon peak. So the average can climb from warmer nights while the peaks drop. It's like a team whose average score rises because its worst players improved, even though its star scores less. We need an answer that separates nights from afternoons. Most students pick (B) because it explains the drop in hot days. It fails because it explains only that half: fewer scorching droughts should lower the average, not raise it.

choices.note: Interesting, and it hints that nights count in the average. But it doesn't say anything changed. By itself it explains neither the rise nor the drop.
Tempting. It explains why hot days are rarer. But fewer hot droughts would pull the average down. It handles one side and deepens the other.
CORRECT. Warmer nights push the average up; slightly cooler afternoons mean fewer days pass 32 degrees. Both facts fit.
A similar rise elsewhere doesn't explain why hot days fell here.
This is about crop damage, not why hot days became rarer as the average rose.

questions.stimulus: Ecologist: In forest plots from which we removed the invasive gray buckthorn, native tree seedlings became three times as numerous as in plots where buckthorn remained. Admittedly, buckthorn roots release compounds that slow the germination of some native seeds in laboratory dishes. But buckthorn leafs out weeks before native plants each spring, deeply shading the forest floor. So buckthorn suppresses native seedlings mainly by shading them.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the ecologist's argument?
choices: Where buckthorn was removed and replaced by shade cloth casting equally deep shade, native seedlings still tripled.
The compounds released by buckthorn roots remain in the soil for several years after the shrubs themselves have been removed.
Native seedlings in the plots cleared of buckthorn grew taller in their first year than seedlings in the uncleared plots.
Some native shrubs also leaf out early in spring, though none of them shades the forest floor as deeply as buckthorn does.
Gray buckthorn produces large quantities of berries that birds carry to forest plots where the shrub does not yet grow.
questions.explanation: The study shows removing buckthorn helps seedlings, but not that shade is why. Shade cloth tests exactly that: same shade, no buckthorn. If seedlings boomed under the cloth anyway, the shade wasn't what held them back. That is (A). (B) is the trap: it sounds like a point for the chemical explanation, but if the compounds linger after removal, seedlings tripled despite them, which makes chemicals a worse explanation and shade a better one.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Buckthorn suppresses native seedlings mainly by shading them.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Removing buckthorn tripled native seedlings; buckthorn leafs out early and shades the forest floor (concession: its roots release compounds that slow some germination in the lab).

breakdown.analysis: The removal experiment shows buckthorn hurts seedlings. Does it show how? Removing the shrub removed the shade, the roots, the leaf litter, everything at once. To pin it on shade, you need to put the shade back without the shrub. It's like proving your headaches come from screen glare because they stopped when you quit your job: maybe it was the boss. We need an answer that separates shade from the other effects of buckthorn. Most students pick (B) because it seems to favor the chemical explanation. Read it again: if the chemicals stay in the soil after removal, seedlings tripled even with them present. That makes chemicals look less important and helps the ecologist.

choices.note: CORRECT. Same deep shade, no buckthorn, and the seedlings still boomed. So shade wasn't what was holding them back; something else about the shrub was.

Tempting. It mentions the root compounds, so it feels like support for the rival explanation. But if the compounds stay after removal, the seedlings tripled while the compounds were still there. That points away from chemicals and toward shade.
Faster growth after removal fits any explanation. It doesn't separate shade from anything else.
This says buckthorn's shade is unusually deep, which if anything helps the ecologist.
How buckthorn spreads has nothing to do with how it suppresses seedlings.
