questions.stimulus: At the Lisk fish hatchery, netting was stretched over half of the ponds stocked with young carp, to keep herons from feeding in them; the other ponds were left open. Two years later, the netted ponds held more carp in total than the open ponds did, but they held fewer carp large enough to be sold.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Herons that feed at the hatchery also take frogs and large insects from the open ponds.
Herons catch small carp far more often than large ones, since large carp are too big for them to swallow.
The netted ponds and the open ponds were stocked with equal numbers of young carp of similar size.
Carp in crowded ponds compete for limited food, and carp that get too little food stay small.
The hatchery sells carp only after they have reached a certain minimum length.
questions.explanation: The netted ponds kept more fish, and more fish in the same pond means more competition for food. If underfed carp stay small, a crowded pond can produce fewer large carp than a thinned-out one. That is (D). (B) is the dominant trap: herons eating small carp would give the open ponds a larger share of large carp, but it can't give them a larger number of large carp; herons remove fish, they don't add large ones.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Netted ponds, protected from herons, have more carp overall but fewer large carp than open ponds.

breakdown.analysis: How can protecting fish leave you with fewer big fish? Not fewer as a share: fewer, period. Herons can only take fish away. So something about having more fish must keep them from growing. It's like a garden where you skip thinning the seedlings: you get more carrots, all of them stunted. We need an answer where crowding limits growth. Most students pick (B) because it explains why open ponds would be heavy on large fish. It fails on the numbers: eating small fish raises the large fish's share, but the netted ponds have fewer large carp in absolute terms, and (B) can't produce that by itself.

choices.note: Other heron prey doesn't explain why the netted ponds have fewer large carp.

Tempting. It explains why open ponds would have a higher proportion of large carp. But the netted ponds have fewer large carp outright. Herons skipping large fish can't make the open ponds have more of them. Share versus number.
Equal stocking rules out a head start. It sharpens the puzzle.
CORRECT. Protected from herons, the netted ponds stayed crowded, food ran short, and the carp stayed small. The herons thinned the open ponds, so the survivors had enough food to grow.
This just defines 'large enough to be sold.' It explains nothing.

questions.stimulus: Agronomist: Some claim that no-till farming, in which crops are planted without plowing, improves soil and so raises crop yields. Admittedly, any such benefit would take years to appear. But in the Calla district, even fields farmed without tillage for over a decade yield about 10 percent less corn per hectare, on average, than plowed fields do. So no-till farming does not raise corn yields.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the agronomist's argument?
choices: Plowing a field requires considerably more fuel and labor than planting the same field without tillage.
Corn yields in the Calla district vary a great deal from year to year, depending on the amount of rainfall.
Improvements in soil structure from no-till farming often take five years or more to produce higher yields.
Some farmers in the Calla district who once used no-till methods have since gone back to plowing their fields.
Calla farmers have mostly used no-till methods on their steepest, most eroded fields, where plowing had washed away topsoil.
questions.explanation: The agronomist compares no-till fields with plowed fields, but that works only if the two groups of fields are otherwise alike. If farmers chose no-till for their worst land, those fields would yield less no matter what; no-till could still be raising their yields above what plowing would give. That is (E). (C) is the trap: it sounds like a reason the benefit hasn't shown up, but the agronomist already concedes the delay and uses fields farmed this way for over a decade.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: No-till farming does not raise corn yields.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: In Calla, fields farmed without tillage for 10+ years yield about 10 percent less than plowed fields (concession: benefits take years).

breakdown.analysis: Are the no-till fields and the plowed fields the same kind of land? If the no-till fields started out worse, comparing them with good plowed land proves nothing about no-till. It's like saying a tutor doesn't help because her students score lower than other students, when she only takes students who are failing. We need an answer showing the no-till fields differ in a way that lowers yields. Most students pick (C) because a delayed payoff sounds like a reason the data mislead. It fails because the agronomist already concedes the delay and answers it by looking at fields with over a decade of no-till.

choices.note: Cost is a different question. The argument is about yields.
Year-to-year swings affect both kinds of fields. They don't explain a steady 10 percent gap.
Tempting. It sounds like the benefit just hasn't arrived. But the agronomist already concedes that and looks at fields with over ten years of no-till. Five years has long passed.
A few farmers switching back tells us nothing about whether no-till raises yields.
CORRECT. The no-till fields are the district's worst land. They'd yield less under any method, so their lower yields don't show that no-till fails. It may be helping them.

questions.stimulus: In the Ardel orchards, warm weather in early spring reliably brings the cherry trees into bloom early. Last year, both the winter and the early spring in the region were the warmest on record. Yet the Ardel cherry trees bloomed later last year than they had in any of the previous ten years.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Warm winter weather can cause cherry buds to swell early, leaving them open to damage from any later frost.
Cherry buds cannot respond to spring warmth until they have been exposed to a certain total amount of cold weather.
The trees in the Ardel orchards belong to several cherry varieties whose usual blooming dates differ by a few days.
Several of the previous ten winters in the region were colder than the region's long-term average.
The bees that pollinate the cherry blossoms become active earlier in warm springs than in cool ones.
questions.explanation: The stimulus says early-spring warmth brings early bloom, but last year's winter was also warm. If buds must first get a set amount of cold before warmth can trigger them, a record-warm winter delays that requirement, and the buds can't use the spring warmth until it's met. That is (B). (A) is the trap: warm winters harming buds sounds like an explanation, but frost damage would kill buds, not delay blooming, and nothing says a frost came.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Early-spring warmth brings early bloom, and last spring was record-warm, but the trees bloomed later than in any of the last ten years.

breakdown.analysis: What's different about last year besides the warm spring? The winter was warm too. Could a warm winter matter? Only if the trees need something from winter. It's like an oven that won't start baking until it's preheated: turn the dial up all you want, nothing cooks until the preheat finishes. We need an answer where the warm winter blocks the spring trigger. Most students pick (A) because it ties the warm winter to the buds. It fails because it describes possible frost damage, which would mean fewer blossoms, not later ones, and the stimulus never mentions a frost.

choices.note: Tempting. It links the warm winter to the buds. But it's about frost damage, which kills blossoms rather than delaying them, and there's no frost in the story.
CORRECT. The buds need a dose of cold before warmth can wake them. A record-warm winter delayed that dose, so the warm spring couldn't trigger bloom on time.
Varieties differing by a few days happens every year. It can't explain last year's record-late bloom.
Earlier cold winters don't explain why last year's bloom came late.
Bees have no effect on when the trees bloom.

questions.stimulus: Botanist: Thrushes eat the berries of the hollin shrub and later excrete its seeds. In our trials, hollin seeds collected from thrush droppings germinated at twice the rate of seeds sown inside whole berries picked from the same shrubs. We conclude that passing through a thrush's digestive tract alters hollin seeds in some way that promotes their germination.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the botanist's argument?
choices: Thrushes often excrete hollin seeds far from the parent shrub, where the young seedlings face less competition.
Many hollin seeds swallowed by thrushes are crushed and destroyed in the birds' digestive tracts.
Hollin seeds removed from their berries by hand and washed clean germinated about as often as seeds from droppings.
Seeds of several other shrubs germinate at higher rates after passing through the digestive tracts of birds.
Hollin seeds germinate best in soil that is kept moist but drains well after rain.
questions.explanation: The comparison seeds were sown inside whole berries, so they differ from the dropping seeds in two ways: they never passed through a bird, and they were still wrapped in fruit. If hand-cleaned seeds germinate just as well, removing the fruit is what matters, not anything the digestive tract does. That is (C). (B) is the trap: crushed seeds sound bad for the theory, but the conclusion is about the seeds that come through intact.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Passing through a thrush's gut alters hollin seeds in a way that promotes germination.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Seeds from droppings germinated at twice the rate of seeds sown inside whole berries.

breakdown.analysis: What else is different between the two groups of seeds? The control seeds were still inside the fruit. Maybe the fruit is what holds them back, and the bird just happens to strip it off. It's like concluding a car wash makes cars faster because washed cars beat cars still covered by a tarp. We need an answer that separates 'passed through a bird' from 'no longer inside a berry.' Most students pick (B) because it sounds like the gut hurts seeds. It fails because the claim is only about seeds that survive the trip. Losing some seeds says nothing about whether the gut helps the rest germinate.

choices.note: This is about where seedlings grow up, not whether passage through the gut makes seeds germinate. The trials measured germination.
Tempting. It sounds damaging to the gut theory. But the botanist's claim is about seeds that come out whole. Some seeds being destroyed doesn't show the survivors weren't helped.
CORRECT. Clean seeds germinate just as well without ever passing through a bird. So the boost comes from getting the seed out of the berry, not from anything the thrush's gut does to it.
Other shrubs behaving this way makes the botanist's claim more plausible, if anything.
Ideal soil conditions are irrelevant to the comparison.

questions.stimulus: Each autumn, biologists net a sample of the walleye in Gorran Reservoir and weigh them. Over the past ten years, the average weight of the walleye sampled has fallen by almost a fifth. Yet within every age group, from one-year-olds to the oldest fish, the walleye sampled now weigh more, on average, than walleye of the same age did ten years ago.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: The nets used in the autumn sampling catch walleye of all sizes about equally well.
Walleye in Gorran Reservoir keep growing in length and weight throughout their lives.
Abundant food has allowed walleye in Gorran Reservoir to grow faster than walleye in nearby lakes.
Eight years ago the state began releasing large numbers of hatchery-raised young walleye into the reservoir every spring.
The water level in Gorran Reservoir has varied little from year to year over the past decade.
questions.explanation: An overall average depends on the mix of ages as well as the weight within each age. If the state has been adding large numbers of young fish every year, the population is now weighted toward light young fish, so the overall average can fall even as every age group gets heavier. That is (D). (C) is the trap: abundant food explains why each age group is heavier, which is only one side, and makes the falling average more puzzling.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The average walleye is lighter than ten years ago, but walleye of every age are heavier.

breakdown.analysis: How can every group gain weight while the average loses it? Change the mix. If the sample is now mostly young fish, it averages light even if each age is heavier than before. Imagine a school where every grade's average height rose, but the school just opened two new kindergarten classes: the school-wide average drops. We need an answer that shifts the population toward young fish. Most students pick (C) because good feeding sounds relevant. It fails because it explains only why each age group is heavier; it gives no reason the overall average fell.

choices.note: This rules out a sampling quirk, which leaves the puzzle in place.
Fish growing all their lives is a background fact. By itself it doesn't change the age mix, so it explains nothing new.
Tempting. It explains why each age group is heavier. But that's the side we already understood. It makes the drop in the overall average harder to explain.
CORRECT. Yearly stocking floods the reservoir with young fish. With far more light young fish in the mix, the overall average falls even though each age group is heavier than before.
Stable water levels change nothing about the weights.

questions.stimulus: Ornithologist: Over the past thirty years, springs in the Kessel Marshes have warmed considerably, and many birds that breed there now arrive weeks earlier than they once did. But the tawny reed warbler, which winters in central Africa, still arrives in the marshes on almost the same dates as thirty years ago. So this warbler must time its spring migration by day length, which has not changed, rather than by temperature.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the ornithologist's argument?
choices: Spring temperatures in the tawny reed warbler's central African wintering grounds have changed very little in thirty years.
The tawny reed warbler's arrival dates in the Kessel Marshes have been recorded each year by the same team of observers.
Tawny reed warblers in the marshes now raise fewer chicks than before, because the insects their chicks eat peak earlier.
Many bird species that are known to time their migrations by day length spend the winter in central Africa.
Some of the birds that breed in the Kessel Marshes spend the winter only a short distance to the south.
questions.explanation: The ornithologist rules out temperature by pointing to warming in the Kessel Marshes. But a bird in central Africa can't feel spring in the marshes. If temperatures where the warbler actually starts its journey haven't changed, a temperature cue there would predict unchanged arrival dates too. That is (A). (C) is the trap: it sounds like bad news for the warbler, but it's about the cost of arriving on time, not what triggers departure.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The tawny reed warbler times its migration by day length, not temperature.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Marsh springs warmed and many birds arrive earlier, but the warbler, which winters in central Africa, arrives on the same dates.

breakdown.analysis: Temperature where? The warming happened in the marshes. The warbler decides when to leave from central Africa. If Africa hasn't warmed, a temperature-driven bird would leave on the usual dates and arrive on the usual dates. It's like concluding a coworker ignores the weather because she wore a coat on a warm day here, when she flew in from somewhere cold. We need an answer showing temperature at the starting point didn't change. Most students pick (C) because it suggests the warbler's timing is a problem. It fails because whether arriving late hurts the warbler says nothing about what cue sets its departure.

choices.note: CORRECT. The warbler starts out in central Africa, where spring temperatures haven't changed. A temperature cue there would produce the same arrival dates, so the unchanged dates don't single out day length.
Consistent observers make the arrival data more reliable. That helps the argument.
Tempting. It sounds like evidence about the warbler's timing. But it's about a consequence of the timing, fewer chicks, not about what triggers migration.
This makes day length a familiar cue for birds wintering there, which helps the ornithologist.
Short-distance migrants feel local warming; that explains why they shifted, and it fits the argument.

questions.stimulus: In field trials, the drought-tolerant millet variety Sura consistently outyields the standard variety in dry years and matches it in wet years. Yet a survey of farms in the Kenna district found that fields planted with Sura produced less millet per hectare, on average, than fields planted with the standard variety, even in last year's severe drought.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Seed for Sura costs Kenna farmers somewhat more per hectare than the seed for the standard variety does each year.
Sura was developed by crossing the standard variety with a wild millet native to a desert region.
Last year's drought reduced millet yields throughout the Kenna district by roughly the same percentage on nearly every farm.
Sura produces somewhat less grain than the standard variety does in years of unusually heavy rain or flooding.
Kenna farmers who grow both varieties usually save their best fields for the standard variety and plant Sura elsewhere.
questions.explanation: The trials compare the varieties on the same land; the survey compares them on whatever land farmers chose. If farmers put Sura on their worst fields, Sura's fields can yield less even in a drought while Sura is the better variety on any given field. That is (E). (D) is the trap: lower yields in very wet years could drag down a multiyear average, but the survey found the gap even in the drought year, where (D) says nothing.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: In trials Sura beats or matches the standard variety, but on Kenna farms Sura fields yield less, even in a drought year.

breakdown.analysis: Are the Sura fields and the standard fields the same kind of land? In trials, yes; on farms, not necessarily. If Sura gets the worst ground, it can lose the comparison while still being the better seed. It's like a hospital's best surgeon having the worst survival rate because she gets the hardest cases. We need a hidden difference between the fields. Most students pick (D) because it gives Sura a weakness. It fails because the gap showed up in the drought year, when Sura's wet-year weakness doesn't apply. It also contradicts the trial finding that Sura matches the standard variety in wet years.

choices.note: Seed cost doesn't affect how much grain a field produces.
Where Sura came from doesn't explain how it performs on Kenna farms.
A drought that hit everyone equally doesn't explain why Sura fields did worse.
Tempting. It gives Sura a weak spot. But the survey found Sura behind even in last year's drought, and heavy rain has nothing to do with that.
CORRECT. Sura goes on the worst land. On any given field it may be better, but the fields it's planted on are much poorer, so its average yield can still trail the standard variety's.

questions.stimulus: Conservationist: Every June for twenty-five years, volunteers have stopped at the same fifty points along rural roads in Ferrin County and recorded every golden meadowlark they could hear singing within three minutes. The counts have fallen by 40 percent. Since the counts are made the same way at the same places every year, they show that the county's meadowlark population has declined sharply.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conservationist's argument?
choices: Volunteers at the count points also record every other bird species they hear or see during the three minutes.
Traffic on the county's rural roads has grown much heavier, and passing vehicles drown out birdsong.
Meadowlarks nest on the ground in grassy fields, much of which in Ferrin County has been converted to cropland.
Golden meadowlarks live for only a few years, so the county's meadowlark population turns over frequently.
The count points are spaced far enough apart that a bird singing at one point cannot be heard at another.
questions.explanation: The counts measure birds heard, not birds present. Using the same method only helps if the birds are just as easy to hear now as before. If traffic noise now drowns out songs at roadside points, counts would fall even with no change in the population. That is (B). (C) is the trap: lost nesting habitat gives a reason the population might have declined, which supports the conclusion rather than weakening it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The county's meadowlark population has declined sharply.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Counts of singing meadowlarks heard at the same roadside points, made the same way each year, fell 40 percent.

breakdown.analysis: Same method, same places, sure. But are the birds just as easy to hear? The volunteers count by ear, at the side of the road. If the road got louder, the same number of birds would produce a smaller count. It's like judging how many people are at a party by how many voices you can pick out from the hallway, when someone just turned up the music. We need a change that lowers the count without lowering the population. Most students pick (C) because it sounds like an alternative cause. But the conclusion isn't about why meadowlarks declined. It's that they declined, and (C) gives a reason to expect exactly that.

choices.note: What else volunteers record doesn't affect the meadowlark count.
CORRECT. The counts depend on hearing the birds. Louder roads mean fewer songs heard at roadside points, so the counts could fall even if the population didn't.
Tempting. It sounds like an alternative explanation. But the conclusion is only that the population declined, and habitat loss is a reason to expect a decline. It supports the argument.
Fast turnover doesn't tell us whether the population is up or down.
This rules out double counting, which makes the counts more trustworthy.

questions.stimulus: Geologist: A lava flow that runs into Lake Ostrin cooled about 3,000 years ago, according to the radiocarbon ages of charcoal from plants it buried. Yet shells of freshwater snails that lived on the flow's submerged surface, and that remain cemented where they grew, give radiocarbon ages of about 5,000 years.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the geologist's statements?
choices: Freshwater snails of the kind found on the lava flow live for only two or three years.
Lava flows of about the same age are found at several other places around Lake Ostrin.
Charcoal can give radiocarbon ages that are too old if the burned wood came from trees that were already centuries old.
Snails in the lake build their shells partly from carbon dissolved out of limestone too old to contain any radiocarbon.
Some of the snail shells on the flow are broken, apparently by the birds that feed on the snails there.
questions.explanation: Radiocarbon dating assumes a shell started with the normal amount of radiocarbon. If the snails built their shells partly from carbon dissolved out of ancient limestone, which has no radiocarbon left, the shells looked old the day they formed. That is (D). (C) is the trap: it seems to say the dates are unreliable, but an old-wood error makes the charcoal date too old, which means the lava is even younger and the gap even wider.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The lava is about 3,000 years old, but snails that lived on top of it date to about 5,000 years.

breakdown.analysis: Something living on a surface can't be older than the surface. So one of the dates must be off, and in a particular direction: the shells must look older than they are, or the lava younger. It's like a birth certificate dated before the parents' wedding: either a typo or someone backdated it. We need a reason the shells read too old. Most students pick (C) because 'charcoal dates can be wrong' feels like a way out. Check the direction: if the charcoal reads too old, the lava is younger than 3,000 years, and the snails are even more out of place.

choices.note: Snail lifespan is a few years. It can't account for a 2,000-year gap.
Other flows around the lake don't explain why these shells date older than this flow.
Tempting. It shows radiocarbon dates can be off. But it pushes the wrong way: if the charcoal date is too old, the lava is younger still, and the gap gets bigger.
CORRECT. Carbon from ancient limestone has no radiocarbon. Shells built partly from it look old from the start, so snails living on a 3,000-year-old flow can date to 5,000 years.
Broken shells have nothing to do with their radiocarbon ages.

questions.stimulus: Engineer: Five years ago a highway was cut into the slopes of the Morrow Valley. Since then, the slopes along the highway have had twelve landslides, while slopes elsewhere in the valley have had only three. Admittedly, the past five years have been unusually rainy. But both sets of slopes received the same heavy rain, so cutting the highway must be what made its slopes prone to sliding.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the engineer's argument?
choices: Landslides along the highway have closed it for a total of several weeks over the past five years.
The highway's builders used explosives to cut through rock at several points along the route.
The slopes elsewhere in the valley are covered by the same type of forest as the slopes along the highway.
Rainfall in the Morrow Valley over the past five years has been the heaviest in a century of record keeping.
The highway runs along the valley's north side, which rests on crumbly shale; most other slopes rest on granite.
questions.explanation: The engineer compares highway slopes with other slopes and controls for rain. But if the two sets of slopes differ in their rock, crumbly shale on the highway side and granite elsewhere, the highway slopes could slide more with or without the highway. That is (E). (D) is the trap: record rainfall sounds like an alternative cause, but the engineer already concedes the heavy rain and points out it fell on both sets of slopes.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Cutting the highway made its slopes prone to sliding.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Highway slopes had 12 landslides vs. 3 elsewhere in the valley; both got the same heavy rain (concession: it's been unusually rainy).

breakdown.analysis: The engineer controlled for rain. Did he control for everything else? Two groups of slopes can differ in steepness, soil, or rock. If the highway runs along the weak side of the valley, it would see more slides anyway. It's like blaming a new coach for losses when the team also switched to a league full of stronger opponents. We need a pre-existing difference between the two sets of slopes. Most students pick (D) because heavy rain is the obvious rival cause. It fails because the engineer already admits the rain and shows that it fell on both sets of slopes. Rain alone can't explain a difference between them.

choices.note: Closures show the slides were costly, not what caused them.
Blasting gives a way cutting the highway could weaken slopes. That supports the engineer.
This rules out a forest difference, which makes the comparison look fairer and helps the engineer.
Tempting. Record rain sounds like a rival cause. But the engineer already concedes the heavy rain and notes both sets of slopes got it. It can't explain why one set slid four times as often.
CORRECT. The highway slopes sit on weak shale; the others sit on granite. That difference could produce more slides on the highway side whether or not the highway was ever built.

questions.stimulus: Psychologist: In a recent study, forty adults kept a gratitude journal, writing down each evening three things for which they were thankful. After eight weeks, the group’s average score on a standard life-satisfaction questionnaire was markedly higher than it had been when the study began. Clearly, keeping a gratitude journal increases a person’s satisfaction with life.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Do people who already report high life satisfaction tend to describe themselves as grateful more often than other people do?
Would the participants’ scores have risen even further if the study had continued for more than eight weeks?
Did the life-satisfaction scores of comparable adults who kept no journal change over the same eight weeks?
Is writing down three things each evening the most effective way for a person to keep a gratitude journal?
Did any of the participants find it hard to think of three new things to write down each evening?
questions.explanation: The study has no comparison group: scores rose over eight weeks, but they might have risen anyway, say because the study began in a gloomy season. (C) supplies the missing group: if similar adults without journals rose just as much, the journal did nothing; if their scores stayed flat, the journal looks responsible. (A) is the trap because it raises a reverse-causation worry, but the study tracked the same people before and after, so a link between being grateful and being satisfied can’t explain why their scores went up.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Keeping a gratitude journal increases a person’s satisfaction with life.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Forty adults kept gratitude journals; after eight weeks their average life-satisfaction score was markedly higher than at the start.

breakdown.analysis: Higher than what? Higher than their own starting point. But people’s moods drift. The study might have started in February and ended in April, when almost everyone feels better. Without a group that kept no journal, we can’t tell whether the journal did anything. It’s like taking a vitamin while you have a cold, getting better in a week, and crediting the vitamin. We want a question about that missing comparison: did people who kept no journal also improve? Most students who miss this pick (A), because “satisfied people are grateful anyway” sounds like a causation problem. But the study measured change in the same people, and a fixed trait can’t produce a rise.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like reversed causation. But the evidence is a rise within the same forty people. Whether satisfied people tend to be grateful doesn’t explain why these people’s scores went up, so either answer leaves the argument where it was.
So? Whether the gains would keep growing tells us nothing about whether the journal caused the gains we already have. A yes or a no leaves the argument unchanged.

CORRECT. This is the missing comparison group. If similar adults who kept no journal improved just as much, something else (the season, the attention of being studied) explains the rise, and the argument collapses. If their scores stayed flat, the journal looks like the cause.
Irrelevant. The argument says journaling helps, not that this is the best way to do it. A better method elsewhere wouldn’t undercut the result.
Interesting fact, but not relevant. Some participants struggling with the task doesn’t tell us whether the journaling caused the rise in scores.

questions.stimulus: Eight months ago, Fenwray Airport installed self-service bag-drop machines in the terminal used by Skyvale Airlines. Since then, the average time Skyvale passengers wait to check their bags has fallen from fourteen minutes to nine. So the machines have substantially shortened the wait to check bags.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Did bag-check waits also fall over the same period for Fenwray airlines whose terminals got no machines?
Do most Skyvale passengers who use the machines find them easy to operate without any help from airline staff?
Did the bag-drop machines cost Fenwray Airport more than hiring additional check-in staff would have cost?
Do passengers who check no bags at all make up a large share of the passengers who fly with Skyvale?
Are self-service bag-drop machines already in use at most other airports that are about the size of Fenwray?
questions.explanation: The argument credits the machines for a drop in waiting time but gives no comparison with check-in lines that didn’t get machines. (A) asks for exactly that: if waits fell just as much at the other airlines’ counters, something airport-wide (fewer travelers, a slow season) explains the drop; if they didn’t, the machines look responsible. (B) is the tempting choice, but the waits have already fallen, so whether passengers find the machines easy can’t undo that, and a yes adds nothing new.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The bag-drop machines have substantially shortened the wait to check bags.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Since the machines were installed, Skyvale passengers’ average wait to check bags fell from fourteen minutes to nine.

breakdown.analysis: Fell compared with what? Only with Skyvale’s own past. Eight months is long enough for the travel season to change. If the whole airport got quieter, every line got shorter, machines or not. It’s like buying a new umbrella in May and crediting it for keeping you drier than in March. We want the comparison group: what happened to waits at counters that got no machines?

choices.note: CORRECT. This is the comparison group the manager skipped. If other airlines’ waits fell by a similar amount, the drop probably comes from something airport-wide, like fewer passengers. If their waits stayed the same, the machines get the credit.

Tempting, because ease of use sounds like it should matter. But we already know the waits fell. If passengers find the machines easy, that’s no news; if they don’t, the waits still fell. Neither answer tells us what caused the drop.
Wrong dimension. The argument is about waiting time, not about cost. A cheaper alternative doesn’t change whether the machines shortened the wait.
Irrelevant. The figures are about passengers who check bags. How many passengers check none doesn’t affect that average.
So? What other airports do says nothing about whether the machines caused the drop at Fenwray.

questions.stimulus: To learn how residents of Wenlow feel about extending the city’s commuter rail line, the transit authority surveyed 1,500 people waiting on the line’s station platforms during the morning rush hour. Of those surveyed, 72 percent favored the extension. The authority concluded that most Wenlow residents favor extending the line.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Was the survey conducted at every station on the line rather than only at the line’s busiest stations?
Would the extension shorten the daily commutes of most people who now ride the commuter rail line?
Do residents of other cities with commuter rail lines generally favor proposals to extend those lines when surveyed?
Have Wenlow residents supported most of the other transit projects proposed during the past decade?
Do Wenlow residents who ride the line view the extension differently from residents who do not?
questions.explanation: The sample is people waiting for the train, but the conclusion is about all residents. (E) tests whether that matters: if riders view the extension differently from nonriders, the 72 percent tells us little about residents in general; if the two groups think alike, the sample is a fair stand-in. (A) is the trap: covering every station would make the sample more representative of riders, but it would still contain only riders, so either answer leaves the real gap open.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most Wenlow residents favor extending the commuter rail line.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 72 percent of 1,500 people surveyed on the line’s platforms during the morning rush favored the extension.

breakdown.analysis: Who did they ask? People standing on a train platform. Of course train riders might like more train. The conclusion jumps to all residents, most of whom may never ride it. It’s like polling people in a gym about whether the city should build another gym. We need to know whether riders and nonriders see the extension the same way.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like a check on how representative the sample is. But even a survey at every station reaches only riders. Whatever the answer, the problem of leaving out nonriders remains.
Wrong dimension. Whether the extension would help riders is a question about its merits, not about how residents feel about it.
Irrelevant. Other cities’ residents tell us nothing about what Wenlow’s residents think.
So? Past support for other projects doesn’t tell us whether this sample reflects residents’ views on this one.

CORRECT. If riders favor the extension more than nonriders do, a platform survey overstates support and the conclusion is in trouble. If riders and nonriders think alike, the sample works fine. Either answer changes the argument’s strength.

questions.stimulus: Highway engineer: Two years ago we built a sound barrier of recycled-rubber panels along the east side of Route 9 and a conventional concrete barrier along the west side. Since then, residents living behind the rubber barrier have filed far fewer noise complaints than residents living behind the concrete one. So rubber panels block highway noise better than concrete does.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Do recycled-rubber panels last as long as concrete barriers do before they need to be repaired or replaced?
Did east-side residents already file fewer noise complaints than west-side residents before either barrier was built?
Have residents on either side of Route 9 complained about the appearance of the new barriers since they were built?
Is traffic on Route 9 heavier now than it was before the two barriers were built?
Were the rubber panels made from used tires that had been collected within the region?
questions.explanation: The engineer compares complaints on the two sides only after the barriers went up. (B) asks about the baseline: if east-side residents already complained less before the barriers, the gap says nothing about the materials; if both sides complained equally before, the rubber looks better. (D) is the trap, since heavier traffic sounds like a noise factor, but it would affect both sides of the same road, so it can’t explain the difference between them.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Rubber panels block highway noise better than concrete does.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Since the barriers were built, residents behind the east-side rubber barrier have filed far fewer noise complaints than residents behind the west-side concrete barrier.

breakdown.analysis: Were the two sides ever equal? Maybe the east side always complained less: fewer homes, homes set farther back, a hill in the way. Then the barriers changed nothing and the gap was there all along. It’s like crediting your new running shoes for beating your friend, when you were always faster. We need the before picture.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. Durability is a different question from how well each barrier blocks noise.

CORRECT. This is the baseline. If the east side already complained less before the barriers, the difference isn’t evidence about rubber versus concrete. If both sides complained about equally before, the drop on the east side points to the rubber.
Irrelevant. Complaints about looks aren’t complaints about noise.
Tempting, because more traffic means more noise. But Route 9’s traffic passes both barriers. Heavier traffic would raise noise on both sides alike, so it can’t explain why one side complains less.
Interesting fact, but not relevant. Where the tires came from has nothing to do with how well the panels block sound.

questions.stimulus: Last quarter, the accounting firm Garroway & Venn installed software that blocks access to personal e-mail and social media sites on its office computers during working hours. This quarter, the firm’s employees completed 15 percent more client projects than they did last quarter. Evidently, blocking those sites made the firm’s employees more productive.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Did the blocking software cost the firm more to purchase and install than the firm had expected?
Do the firm’s employees now spend more time on social media sites in the evenings than they used to?
Did a few of the firm’s employees find ways to reach the blocked sites despite the software?
Before the software was installed, did employees spend much working time on the now-blocked sites?
Would most of the firm’s employees prefer to have the blocked sites available during their lunch breaks?
questions.explanation: Blocking the sites can free up working time only if employees were spending real time on them. (D) tests that precondition: if they spent a lot of time there, the 15 percent gain is plausibly the software’s doing; if they spent very little, blocking recovered almost nothing and something else explains the gain. (C) is the trap: a few people getting around the block would only slightly dilute the effect, and if no one did, that wouldn’t show the block caused the gain.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Blocking personal e-mail and social media sites made the firm’s employees more productive.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: After the software was installed, employees completed 15 percent more client projects than in the previous quarter.

breakdown.analysis: Blocking what, exactly? If nobody was on those sites much anyway, cutting them off saved no time. Then a 15 percent jump has to come from somewhere else. It’s like locking the cookie jar and crediting the lock for your weight loss when you never ate the cookies. We need to know whether there was wasted time for the software to recover.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. Cost has nothing to do with whether the software raised productivity.
Irrelevant. What employees do in the evenings doesn’t bear on their productivity during working hours.
Tempting, because it questions whether the block worked. But it only matters one way: a few people slipping through wouldn’t erase a firm-wide gain, and a no wouldn’t prove the software caused it.

CORRECT. This is the precondition the argument needs. If employees had been losing lots of time to those sites, the software plausibly explains the gain. If they barely used them, blocking recovered almost nothing, and the gain must have another cause.
So? Employees’ preferences say nothing about whether the block made them more productive.

questions.stimulus: Researchers gave the same set of logic puzzles to sixty volunteers. Thirty of the volunteers worked at standing desks and thirty worked seated, and on average those who stood solved more of the puzzles in the time allowed. The researchers concluded that standing while working improves a person’s ability to solve problems.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Were the volunteers who stood given puzzles of the same difficulty as the volunteers who sat?
Did the volunteers decide for themselves whether they would stand or sit while working on the puzzles?
Did the volunteers who stood report feeling more tired at the end of the session than those who sat?
Do people who work at standing desks every day tend to prefer them to ordinary desks?
Would the volunteers who stood have solved even more puzzles if they had been given additional time?
questions.explanation: The groups were compared, but nothing says how volunteers ended up in each one. (B) asks: if volunteers picked for themselves, the more energetic or confident ones may have chosen to stand, and that difference could explain the result; if they were assigned at random, standing looks responsible. (A) is the trap: puzzle difficulty would matter, but the stimulus already says both groups got the same set.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Standing while working improves a person’s ability to solve problems.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Of sixty volunteers given the same puzzles, the thirty who stood solved more on average than the thirty who sat.

breakdown.analysis: Who chose to stand? If the volunteers picked, the people who chose a standing desk might be more alert or more eager to do well. Then the desk didn’t make them better; better solvers chose the desk. It’s like noticing that people who order salads are thinner and concluding salad made them thin. We need to know how the groups were formed.

choices.note: Tempting, because unequal puzzles would ruin the comparison. But the stimulus says both groups got the same set of puzzles. This is already answered, so knowing it adds nothing.

CORRECT. If volunteers chose, the standers may have differed from the sitters in energy or confidence, and that could explain their scores. If they were assigned at random, the difference points to standing itself.
Irrelevant. How tired they felt doesn’t change how many puzzles they solved or why.
So? Liking standing desks isn’t the same as solving problems better at them.
Irrelevant. The question is whether standing caused the difference in the time given, not what more time would do.

questions.stimulus: Safety analyst: Of the drivers involved in crashes on the Marlinch Expressway last year, 65 percent were using a navigation app on their phones at the time of the crash. Clearly, using such an app while driving substantially increases a driver’s risk of crashing on the expressway.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Were drivers who crashed on other expressways in the region also frequently using navigation apps at the time?
Did the total number of crashes on the Marlinch Expressway rise last year compared with the year before?
Were the app users who were involved in crashes more likely to be injured than the other drivers who crashed?
Were most drivers on the Marlinch Expressway last year using a navigation app while they drove?
Were some of the drivers who crashed while using an app also distracted by other things, such as passengers?
questions.explanation: Sixty-five percent of crashing drivers used an app, but that means something only if app users are a smaller share of all drivers on the expressway. (D) asks for that base rate: if most drivers there use an app anyway, app users crash no more than their share; if few do, they are heavily overrepresented among crashes. (A) is the trap: finding the same pattern on other expressways looks like confirmation, but it repeats the same missing base rate, so a yes or a no leaves the gap open.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Using a navigation app while driving substantially increases a driver’s risk of crashing on the expressway.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 65 percent of the drivers in crashes on the expressway last year were using a navigation app.

breakdown.analysis: 65 percent compared with what? If 65 percent of all drivers on the expressway use an app, then app users crash exactly as often as everyone else. If only 10 percent use one, the figure is alarming. It’s like noting that most drivers in crashes were wearing shoes. We need the base rate: how common is app use among all drivers there? Most students who miss this pick (A), because the same pattern on other roads feels like extra proof. But it’s the same number with the same hole: it still doesn’t tell us how common app use is among drivers who don’t crash.

choices.note: Tempting, because a pattern that repeats elsewhere feels stronger. But it has the same missing base rate. If 65 percent of crashing drivers everywhere use apps because 65 percent of all drivers do, the repetition proves nothing. Either answer leaves the gap.
So? More or fewer total crashes doesn’t tell us whether app users crash more than other drivers.
Wrong measure. The argument is about the risk of crashing, not about how badly people are hurt once they crash.

CORRECT. This is the base rate. If most drivers on the expressway use an app, app users are no more common among crashes than on the road, and the argument collapses. If few do, app users are far overrepresented, and the argument gets much stronger.
Only matters one way, and barely. Some app users also being distracted by passengers wouldn’t undo the pattern, and a no wouldn’t show app use raises risk.

questions.stimulus: Researchers found that teenagers who play action video games for at least five hours a week score markedly higher on tests of visual attention than teenagers who rarely play such games. The researchers concluded that playing action video games improves a person’s visual attention.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Did the teenagers who play frequently already score higher on such tests before they began playing action games regularly?
Do teenagers who play action video games frequently spend less time on homework than those who rarely play them?
Is the advantage shown by the frequent players large enough to make a difference in everyday tasks such as driving?
Did the study include any teenagers who play action video games for fewer than five hours a week?
Are action video games more popular among teenagers than among adults over the age of thirty?
questions.explanation: A correlation between gaming and attention fits two stories: games sharpen attention, or teenagers with sharp attention are drawn to fast games. (A) asks about time order: if the frequent players already scored higher before they started playing, the games can’t be the cause; if they scored no higher then, the games look responsible. (C) is the trap, because it questions how much the advantage matters, but the conclusion only says the games improve attention, not that the improvement is large.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Playing action video games improves a person’s visual attention.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Teenagers who play action games at least five hours a week score markedly higher on visual attention tests than those who rarely play.

breakdown.analysis: Which came first? Maybe teens with quick eyes enjoy action games, because they’re good at them, and keep playing. Then the attention came first and the gaming followed. It’s like noticing that tall kids play basketball and concluding basketball makes you tall. We need to know whether the gamers were already ahead before they started. Most students who miss this pick (C), because it seems to question whether the effect is real. But the conclusion claims only that games improve attention; a small improvement is still an improvement.

choices.note: CORRECT. This checks the time order. If the frequent players were already ahead before they started playing, their attention explains their gaming, not the other way around, and the argument fails. If they started out even with everyone else, the games look like the cause.
Irrelevant. Homework time isn’t part of the argument. Less homework wouldn’t explain better visual attention.
Tempting, because it questions whether the effect matters. But the conclusion is only that games improve attention. Whether the gain is big enough to help with driving doesn’t touch that claim.
Already answered. The comparison group is teenagers who rarely play, so the study did include people under five hours a week.
So? Popularity among adults says nothing about whether games improve attention.

questions.stimulus: Of the forty pumps at the Ressel water treatment plant, the twelve fitted with a new seal design have needed seal repairs only twice in the past five years, while the twenty-eight with the older design have needed thirty seal repairs. So the new design makes pump seals far more reliable.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Do pumps fitted with the new seal design cost more to buy than pumps fitted with the older design?
Does the plant have more pumps with the older seal design than pumps with the new seal design?
Were the pumps with the new seal design put into service only within the past year or so?
Were some of the seal repairs on pumps with the older design needed because of mistakes made during installation?
Would replacing the older seals with the new design require shutting down the plant for several days?
questions.explanation: The comparison counts repairs over five years, which is fair only if both groups of pumps were running for all five years. (C) checks this: if the new-design pumps have been in service for only a year or so, they’ve had far less time to fail and the comparison means little; if they’ve run the whole period, the new design looks much better. (B) is the trap: it raises the count-versus-rate worry, but the stimulus already gives both counts (12 and 28), and per pump the new design still wins easily.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new seal design makes pump seals far more reliable.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Over the past five years, the twelve new-design pumps needed two seal repairs; the twenty-eight older-design pumps needed thirty.

breakdown.analysis: Were the new pumps even running for five years? If they were installed last year, two repairs in one year is no better than the old pumps’ record, and new parts usually fail least. It’s like comparing the dents on a car you bought last month with the dents on a car you’ve driven for five years. We need to know how long the new-design pumps have been in service. Most students who miss this pick (B), the count-versus-rate trap. But the stimulus already gives both counts: 2 repairs for 12 pumps versus 30 for 28. Per pump, the new design still looks far better, so that question is answered.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. Price has nothing to do with reliability.

Tempting, and the main trap. More older pumps would mean more repairs even at the same rate. But the stimulus gives the counts, 12 and 28, so we already know the answer. Per pump, the new design is still far ahead.

CORRECT. This is about time in service. If the new-design pumps started running only a year or so ago, they’ve had a fraction of the time to fail, and new parts rarely fail early anyway. If they’ve been running all five years, the comparison is fair and the new design looks much better.
Only matters one way. A few installation mistakes would barely dent a 30-to-2 gap, and a no wouldn’t make the comparison any fairer.
Irrelevant. The cost of switching over is a practical issue, not evidence about which seal is more reliable.

questions.stimulus: A six-month study tested a phone app meant to help people drink fewer sugary beverages. Of the 200 people who enrolled, 80 were still using the app at the end of the study, and those 80 were drinking, on average, 60 percent fewer sugary beverages than when they enrolled. The app’s developers concluded that the app is highly effective at helping people cut back on such beverages.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Would the app be equally effective at helping people cut back on salty or fried snack foods?
Did some of the 80 people who kept using the app cut back by much more than 60 percent?
Is drinking fewer sugary beverages one of the most effective ways for a person to improve his or her health?
Did most of the 80 people who kept using the app say they would recommend it to a friend?
Did people who stopped using the app tend to stop because they were not managing to cut back?
questions.explanation: The results come only from the 80 people who stayed, and those who stayed may be the ones who were succeeding. (E) tests that selection effect: if people quit because they weren’t cutting back, the 60 percent figure reflects only the success stories and overstates the app’s effectiveness; if they quit for unrelated reasons, the 80 are a fair sample. (B) is the trap: it sounds like a probe of the 60 percent figure, but that figure is already an average, so some people cutting back by more is expected and changes nothing.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The app is highly effective at helping people cut back on sugary beverages.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Of 200 enrollees, the 80 still using the app after six months were drinking 60 percent fewer sugary beverages than at enrollment.

breakdown.analysis: What about the other 120? Only the people who stuck with the app were counted. If people quit because it wasn’t working for them, the 80 who stayed are the success stories, and of course they did well. It’s like a diet company bragging about the weight lost by customers who renewed their memberships. We need to know why the dropouts dropped out. Most students who miss this pick (B), because it seems to test the 60 percent figure. But 60 percent is an average; some people beating it is just what an average implies.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Snack foods are outside the argument, which is only about sugary beverages.
Tempting, because it seems to test the key number. But 60 percent is an average, so some people cutting back by more is built in. A yes or a no leaves the argument unchanged.
Irrelevant. The argument is about whether the app works, not about how much cutting back helps health.
So? Being willing to recommend the app is opinion, not evidence that it caused the drop. And it still comes only from the people who stayed.

CORRECT. This targets who was left in the sample. If the dropouts quit because they were failing, the 80 who remained are a filtered group of successes and the app looks better than it is. If they quit for unrelated reasons, like changing phones, the result is far more trustworthy.

questions.stimulus: City official: Since rentable electric scooters arrived in Kelderby two years ago, the rate of emergency-room visits for head injuries among residents aged 18 to 35, the group that rides the scooters most, has risen by 25 percent. So the scooters are responsible for much of the recent rise in head injuries among Kelderby’s young adults.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Has the number of Kelderby residents aged 18 to 35 grown over the past two years?
Over the same two years, did the rate of such visits among Kelderby residents over 35 rise by a similar percentage?
Were some of the head injuries treated in Kelderby’s emergency rooms caused by falls from bicycles?
Do the companies that rent scooters in Kelderby require all riders to be at least 18 years old?
Would requiring scooter riders in Kelderby to wear helmets substantially reduce the number of head injuries they suffer in crashes each year?
questions.explanation: The official blames the scooters because the rise hit the age group that rides them most, but never checks the groups that rarely ride them. (B) supplies that comparison: if older residents’ rate rose just as much, something citywide (such as a change in how emergency rooms record visits) is the likelier cause; if it didn’t, the scooters look responsible. (A) is the trap: a larger population would explain more visits, but the figure is a rate, so population growth is already accounted for.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The scooters are responsible for much of the recent rise in head injuries among Kelderby’s young adults.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Since scooters arrived, the rate of ER visits for head injuries among residents aged 18 to 35, the heaviest riders, rose 25 percent.

breakdown.analysis: Did everyone else’s rate rise too? If head-injury visits went up 25 percent among people over 35, who rarely ride scooters, then something that hit the whole city is at work, and the scooters are off the hook. It’s like blaming your new pillow for a stiff neck when everyone in your office has one this week. We need a comparison with a group the scooters don’t reach. Most students who miss this pick (A), because population growth is a classic count problem. But the official cites a rate, so more young residents wouldn’t raise it.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. More young residents would mean more visits. But the official gives a rate, not a count. Population growth is already built in, so the answer doesn’t matter.

CORRECT. This is the comparison group. Older residents rarely ride scooters. If their rate rose by about as much, the cause is probably citywide, not the scooters. If their rate held steady, the scooters look like the cause.
Only matters one way. Some injuries coming from bicycles is expected and doesn’t show the scooters didn’t cause much of the rise. A no wouldn’t prove they did.
Irrelevant. An age rule for renters doesn’t tell us what caused the rise among 18- to 35-year-olds.
So? Helmets reducing scooter injuries says nothing about how much of the rise the scooters caused in the first place.

questions.stimulus: Columnist: Among users of the Mailvane e-mail service, those who have turned on two-step verification are more likely than other users to report that their accounts have been broken into at some point. Two-step verification, then, does nothing to protect accounts from intruders and may even make them easier to break into.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions most helps in evaluating the argument?
choices: Does two-step verification make it more inconvenient for users to sign in to their Mailvane accounts?
Do intruders who break into accounts protected by two-step verification usually do so by stealing the user’s phone?
Were some of the break-ins reported by Mailvane users carried out by people whom the users knew personally?
Is the number of Mailvane users who report break-ins larger this year than it was last year?
Did most users who reported a break-in turn on two-step verification only after that break-in occurred?
questions.explanation: The columnist treats two-step verification as coming before the break-ins, but the users report break-ins that happened “at some point.” (E) asks about time order: if most of them turned the feature on after being broken into, the break-ins caused the verification, not the reverse, and the argument fails; if they had it on beforehand, the columnist’s worry gains force. (B) is the trap: it describes how protected accounts get broken into, but a method of beating the feature doesn’t show it does nothing, and a no wouldn’t help the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Two-step verification does nothing to protect accounts and may make them easier to break into.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Mailvane users with two-step verification turned on are more likely than other users to report having been broken into at some point.

breakdown.analysis: Which came first, the lock or the burglary? People often add security right after something goes wrong. If most of these users turned on two-step verification after an intruder got in, the break-ins explain the feature, not the other way around. It’s like noticing that houses with alarm systems are more likely to have been burgled and concluding alarms attract burglars. We need to know when the feature was switched on. Most students who miss this pick (B), because it’s about how two-step accounts get broken into. But knowing one way to beat the feature can’t show it never helps.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. Inconvenience isn’t protection. The argument is about whether the feature keeps intruders out.

Tempting, because it seems to explain how two-step accounts get broken into. But a way around a protection doesn’t show the protection does nothing, and a no doesn’t make the argument any weaker or stronger. One-sided at best.
So? Some intruders being acquaintances doesn’t bear on whether two-step verification protects accounts.
Irrelevant. A year-to-year change in total break-ins says nothing about whether users with the feature are more vulnerable.

CORRECT. This is the time order. If most of these users turned the feature on after an intruder got in, the break-in caused the feature, and the correlation says nothing against it. If they had it on before, the columnist’s concern looks more serious.

questions.stimulus: Automaker: Most car buyers who decide against an electric car say that worry about running out of charge on the road is their main reason. Yet in a survey of people who own our electric cars, 90 percent said they rarely or never worry about running out of charge. So most buyers who now reject electric cars for this reason would stop worrying about it once they owned one.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Did most of the owners surveyed worry little about running out of charge even before they bought their cars?
Do most car buyers who decide against an electric car give worry about running out of charge as their main reason?
Are the automaker’s electric cars more expensive than the gasoline-powered models that it also sells?
Did some of the owners surveyed actually run out of charge on the road at least once during the past year?
Would the automaker sell more electric cars if more charging stations were built along major highways?
questions.explanation: The owners surveyed are people who chose electric cars, so they may never have shared the worry that keeps other buyers away. (A) tests that selection effect: if the owners worried little even before buying, their calm says nothing about what owning one would do for anxious buyers; if many of them worried beforehand, ownership looks like it cured the worry. (B) is the trap, since it targets the argument’s first premise, but the stimulus already states it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most buyers who reject electric cars because of range worry would stop worrying once they owned one.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most buyers who reject electric cars cite range worry; 90 percent of the automaker’s electric-car owners rarely or never worry about it.

breakdown.analysis: Who buys an electric car? Probably the people who weren’t worried about running out of charge in the first place. If so, the owners’ calm is a filter, not a transformation. It’s like surveying people at a roller coaster’s exit and concluding that riding cures fear of heights. We need to know whether the owners worried before they bought. Most students who miss this pick (B), because it goes straight at a premise. But the stimulus already tells us the answer, so asking it adds nothing.

choices.note: CORRECT. This targets who ended up in the sample. If the owners were unworried even before buying, their answers tell us nothing about what ownership would do for worried buyers, and the argument collapses. If many of them worried before, owning the car seems to have removed the worry.
Tempting, because it targets a premise. But the stimulus states this as fact. It’s already answered, so it can’t help us evaluate anything.
Irrelevant. Price is a different reason to reject a car. The argument is about the worry over charge.
Only matters one way, if at all. Some owners running out of charge and still not worrying doesn’t touch whether worried buyers would calm down.
So? Building stations is a separate plan. Whether it would boost sales doesn’t test whether ownership ends the worry.

questions.stimulus: Last spring, new control software was installed in eight of the twenty elevators in the Tolvane Tower. Each of those eight has broken down less often since then than it did in the year before, while the other twelve have broken down about as often as they did before. So the new software reduces elevator breakdowns.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Have the twelve elevators without the software broken down about as often since last spring as the year before?
Do elevators in other buildings that use the new software break down less often than those in the Tolvane Tower?
Were any of the breakdowns in the eight elevators before last spring caused by mechanical faults rather than by software faults?
Were the eight elevators chosen to receive the software because they had broken down more often than the others the year before?
Did installing the new software in the eight elevators cost more than repairing their old control systems would have cost?
questions.explanation: The argument even has a comparison group, which makes the argument look airtight. But if the eight elevators were picked because they’d just had an unusually bad year, they would likely break down less the next year anyway, the way an unusually bad stretch tends to be followed by a more ordinary one. (D) tests this: a yes means the improvement may be a return to normal; a no (say, the eight were picked at random) makes the software the best explanation. (A) is the trap: it checks the comparison group, but the stimulus already says the other twelve broke down about as often as before.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new software reduces elevator breakdowns.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The eight elevators that got the software each broke down less often than in the year before; the twelve without it broke down about as often as before.

breakdown.analysis: Why those eight? If someone picked the elevators that had the worst year, some of that bad year was probably bad luck, and bad luck rarely repeats. Next year they’d look better with or without new software. It’s like a coach benching his worst shooters for a week of special drills, then crediting the drills when their shooting returns to normal. This is called regression to the mean; it’s worth knowing. We need to know how the eight were chosen. Most students who miss this pick (A), because checking the comparison group feels rigorous. But the stimulus already answers it.

choices.note: Tempting, because it checks the control group. But the stimulus already says the other twelve broke down about as often as before. Asking it again adds nothing.
So? Other buildings differ in age, use and maintenance. Their numbers don’t tell us whether the software caused the change in the Tolvane Tower.

Only matters one way. Some breakdowns being mechanical just means the software can’t fix everything. It doesn’t show the software didn’t cut the rest, and a no wouldn’t answer how the eight were picked.

CORRECT. If the eight were chosen for their bad year, part of their improvement is just a return to their usual rate, and the comparison with the other twelve isn’t fair. If they were chosen at random, the twelve make a fair control and the software looks responsible.
Wrong dimension. Cost doesn’t tell us whether the software reduced breakdowns.

questions.stimulus: Transit researcher: In a survey of riders on Corlin’s subway, 70 percent of those who said they had had a phone or wallet stolen while riding reported that the theft happened on a crowded train. So riding on a crowded train makes a passenger more likely to have something stolen.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Do riders on crowded trains find it harder to notice when someone is reaching into their pockets or bags?
Were thefts on crowded trains reported to the police less often than thefts on trains that were not crowded?
Are most of the rides on Corlin’s subway taken on trains that are crowded with passengers?
Did riders who had something stolen ride the subway less often after the theft than they did before it?
Are thefts more common on Corlin’s subway than on the subways of other cities of similar size?
questions.explanation: Seventy percent of thefts happened on crowded trains, but if 70 percent or more of all trips are taken on crowded trains, crowded trains get no more than their share. (C) asks for that base rate: if most trips are on crowded trains, the figure shows nothing; if crowded trips are uncommon, they are badly overrepresented and the argument holds up. (A) is the trap: it offers a plausible way crowding could help thieves, but that only supports the claim if the numbers already show a link, and a no wouldn’t weaken the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Riding on a crowded train makes a passenger more likely to have something stolen.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 70 percent of surveyed riders who had something stolen said it happened on a crowded train.

breakdown.analysis: Seventy percent compared with what? If most subway rides happen at rush hour, most thefts would happen on crowded trains even if crowding made no difference at all. It’s like finding that most car crashes happen within five miles of home: that’s where most driving happens. We need the share of all trips taken on crowded trains. Most students who miss this pick (A), because it gives a mechanism, and a mechanism feels like support. But a mechanism only helps if the numbers show a link, and a no wouldn’t weaken anything. One-sided.

choices.note: Tempting, because it explains how crowding could help thieves. But it only pushes one way: a yes makes the claim plausible without showing the figure means anything, and a no doesn’t weaken it (thieves could still favor crowds for other reasons). It doesn’t touch the base rate.
Irrelevant. The figure comes from a survey of riders, not police reports, so how often thefts reach the police doesn’t matter.

CORRECT. This is the base rate. If most trips are taken on crowded trains, 70 percent of thefts happening there is just what you’d expect, and the argument collapses. If crowded trips are a small share, crowded trains are badly overrepresented and the argument is strong.
So? What riders did after the theft doesn’t tell us whether crowding made the theft more likely.
Irrelevant. A comparison with other cities says nothing about crowded versus uncrowded trains in Corlin.

questions.stimulus: Two years ago, the Pressick transit agency installed screens showing real-time bus arrival times at the stops along six of its bus routes. Since then, ridership on those six routes has risen by 15 percent, while ridership on the agency’s other routes has stayed flat. So the screens have drawn new riders to the agency’s buses.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Has ridership on the routes without the screens stayed about the same over the past two years?
In the years before the screens were installed, had ridership on the six routes already been rising faster than ridership on the other routes?
Do riders who board at stops with the screens rate the agency’s service more highly than riders at other stops do?
Would installing screens along the remaining routes cost more per stop than installing them along the first six did?
Did the transit agency raise fares on all of its routes at some point during the past two years?
questions.explanation: The argument compares the six routes with the rest, but a difference that appears after the screens may have been there before them. (B) asks whether the six routes were already growing faster: if so, the 15 percent rise may just continue that trend, perhaps the very reason those routes were picked; if not, the screens look responsible. (A) is the trap: it checks the comparison, but the stimulus already says ridership on the other routes stayed flat.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The screens have drawn new riders to the agency’s buses.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Since screens were installed on six routes, their ridership rose 15 percent; ridership on the other routes stayed flat.

breakdown.analysis: Were those six routes already growing? A transit agency might well put its new screens on its up-and-coming routes, the ones with new apartments and offices along them. If ridership there was already climbing faster, the 15 percent rise is just the trend continuing. It’s like moving your fastest-growing plants to a new pot and crediting the pot. We need the trend before the screens. Most students who miss this pick (A), because it checks the comparison routes. But the stimulus has already told us those routes stayed flat.

choices.note: Tempting, because it checks the comparison group. But the stimulus says ridership on the other routes stayed flat. That’s already answered, so it can’t help us evaluate.

CORRECT. This targets what was happening before. If the six routes were already outgrowing the others, the post-screen rise may be the same trend, and the screens get no credit. If the routes were growing no faster before, the jump after the screens points to them.

So? Ratings come from people who already ride. Whether they rate the service higher or lower doesn’t tell us whether the screens drew new riders, and riders on different routes may rate service differently for reasons that have nothing to do with screens.
Irrelevant. The cost of future screens says nothing about whether these screens drew riders.
So? A fare increase on all routes hits the six routes and the others alike. It can’t explain why only the six grew.

questions.stimulus: Dean: In a trial, a new software tool correctly flagged 95 percent of a set of essays known to have been produced by text-generating programs. So if we use the tool to screen the essays our students submit, nearly every essay it flags will be one that was produced by such a program.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Did the tool flag 95 percent of the program-produced essays no matter which text-generating program had produced them?
Can the tool also identify which particular text-generating program produced each essay that it flags?
Is the tool able to screen a full term’s worth of the school’s student essays in less than a day?
Are essays produced by text-generating programs generally of lower quality than essays written by students?
Does the tool often flag essays that were written entirely by students without the help of such programs?
