questions.explanation: The trial shows the tool catches most program-produced essays, but the conclusion is about the essays it flags, and that depends on how often it flags honest work too. (E) asks exactly that: if the tool often flags student-written essays, then among the school’s many honest essays it will flag plenty, and many flagged essays will be innocent; if it rarely does, flagged essays will mostly be program-produced. (A) is the trap: it sounds like a rigorous check of the 95 percent figure, but that figure only concerns essays the tool should catch, so either answer says nothing about false alarms.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Nearly every essay the tool flags will be one produced by a text-generating program.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: In a trial, the tool flagged 95 percent of essays known to be produced by such programs.

breakdown.analysis: Catching most of the guilty isn’t the same as accusing only the guilty. Suppose 1,000 essays come in and 50 are program-made. Even if the tool catches 95 percent of those (about 48), it could also flag 10 percent of the 950 honest essays, about 95. Then most flagged essays are honest. It’s like a smoke alarm that never misses a fire but also goes off whenever someone makes toast: most of its alarms are toast. We need to know how often the tool flags honest work. Most students who miss this pick (A), because it digs into the 95 percent figure. But that figure is about catching program essays; it can’t tell us how many honest essays get flagged.

choices.note: Tempting, because it probes the trial result. But that result is about how many program essays the tool catches. Whether it catches all kinds equally says nothing about how often it flags honest work, which is what the conclusion depends on.
Irrelevant. Naming the program is an extra feature. It doesn’t tell us how many flagged essays are actually program-made.
Wrong dimension. Speed isn’t accuracy.
So? Quality differences don’t tell us how often the tool flags honest essays.

CORRECT. This is the false-alarm rate, and with many more honest essays than program-made ones, it decides everything. If the tool often flags honest essays, most flags could be false alarms and the conclusion fails. If it rarely does, flagged essays will mostly be program-made.

questions.stimulus: Sociologist: Employers in Dresk have been required since 2010 to record every complaint of workplace bullying. In 2019 a new law gave bullying its first precise legal definition, and since then the number of complaints recorded per thousand employees has risen by 60 percent. Clearly, bullying has become far more common in Dresk’s workplaces since 2019.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions most helps in evaluating the argument?
choices: Does the 2019 definition count as bullying some kinds of conduct that employees would not previously have reported as bullying?
Were employers in Dresk required to keep a record of bullying complaints before the new law took effect?
Has the total number of people employed in Dresk grown since the new law took effect in 2019?
Do most of the complaints recorded since 2019 come from employees of large companies rather than small ones?
Will the rise in recorded complaints lead Dresk’s employers to adopt stricter workplace policies?
questions.explanation: The sociologist reads a rise in complaints as a rise in bullying, but the rise began when the definition changed. (A) tests whether the measure itself shifted: if the new definition covers conduct people didn’t report before, complaints could rise with no more bullying than before; if it covers the same conduct, the rise more likely reflects real change. Two traps are already answered by the stimulus: (B), since records have been required since 2010, and (C), since the figure is per thousand employees.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Bullying has become far more common in Dresk’s workplaces since 2019.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Employers have recorded bullying complaints since 2010; since a 2019 law precisely defined bullying, recorded complaints per thousand employees rose 60 percent.

breakdown.analysis: More complaints, or more things counted as complaints? When a law draws a new line around a term, conduct that used to be shrugged off can suddenly count. Then the records rise even if workplaces behave exactly as before. It’s like a school redefining “late” as one minute instead of ten and announcing that lateness has soared. We want to know whether the definition widened what gets reported. Two answers look strong but are already settled by the stimulus: the record-keeping rule dates to 2010, and the figure is already per thousand employees.

choices.note: CORRECT. If the 2019 definition sweeps in conduct people didn’t report before, the rise could come from the new definition rather than from more bullying, and the argument collapses. If it covers the same conduct people already reported, the rise is more likely real.
Tempting, because a new recording rule would explain a jump in records. But the stimulus says employers have had to record complaints since 2010. Already answered.
Tempting, because more workers would mean more complaints. But the figure is per thousand employees, so workforce growth is already accounted for. Already answered.
So? Where complaints come from doesn’t tell us whether bullying itself became more common.
Irrelevant. Future policy changes are a consequence, not evidence about whether bullying increased.

questions.stimulus: Researcher: When interviewers asked a random sample of Brindmoor residents in person whether they had driven after drinking alcohol in the past year, 18 percent said yes. In an anonymous online survey of a different random sample of residents, 31 percent said yes. Since people are reluctant to admit such behavior to an interviewer, the online survey gives the more accurate estimate.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Were the residents in both surveys chosen at random from Brindmoor’s adult population?
Is driving after drinking more common in Brindmoor than in the towns that surround it?
Do residents of other towns also report driving after drinking more often online than in person?
Are people answering anonymous surveys inclined to claim risky behavior in which they have not actually engaged?
Would the online survey’s estimate have been higher still if it had asked about the past two years?
questions.explanation: The researcher assumes the gap between the surveys is due only to underreporting in person. (D) raises the other possibility: if anonymous respondents sometimes claim risky behavior they never engaged in, the 31 percent may be inflated and the truth could lie anywhere between the two figures; if they don’t, the higher online figure is the more believable one. (C) is the trap: the same gap in other towns makes the pattern look real, but a gap can come from underreporting or from overreporting, so a repeat of it can’t tell us which figure is accurate. (A) is already answered.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The anonymous online survey gives the more accurate estimate of how many Brindmoor residents drove after drinking.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 18 percent said yes in person; 31 percent said yes in an anonymous online survey of a different random sample; people are reluctant to admit such behavior to an interviewer.

breakdown.analysis: Is the gap all one-sided? The researcher explains it by people hiding things from interviewers. But anonymity cuts both ways: with no one watching, some people may also exaggerate or joke. If so, the online figure is too high and the truth could be anywhere in between. It’s like assuming the louder of two scales is the right one. We need to know whether anonymous respondents overreport. Most students who miss this pick (C), because finding the same gap in other towns feels like confirmation. But a gap produced by overreporting online would show up in every town too, so it can’t tell us which figure is right.

choices.note: Tempting, because random sampling is what makes surveys comparable. But the stimulus already says both samples were random. Already answered.
Irrelevant. How Brindmoor compares with nearby towns doesn’t tell us which survey measured Brindmoor correctly.

Tempting, and the main trap. A gap that shows up in other towns too looks like a real effect of the survey method. But it would show up either way: from people hiding things in person or from people exaggerating online. Either answer leaves open which figure is accurate.

CORRECT. This is the overlooked alternative behind the gap. If anonymous respondents tend to claim risky things they didn't do, the 31 percent is inflated and the online survey may be no more accurate than the interviews. If they don't, underreporting to interviewers is the best explanation, and the online figure is the better estimate.
So? Asking about a longer period would measure something different. It doesn’t tell us which survey measured the past year accurately.

questions.stimulus: Last year, brighter LED streetlights were installed along twenty streets in Orsk’s eastern district. Over the following twelve months, nighttime burglaries of homes on those streets fell by 30 percent compared with the twelve months before. Evidently, the brighter lighting deterred many would-be burglars.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Did the brighter streetlights use less electricity than the streetlights they replaced on the twenty streets?
Do residents of the twenty streets report feeling safer walking outside at night since the brighter lights were installed?
Over the same period, did daytime burglaries of homes on the twenty streets fall by a similar percentage?
Were the homes burglarized at night on those streets more often entered through windows than through doors?
Did the brighter streetlights make it easier for police on patrol to see what was happening on those streets at night?
questions.explanation: Streetlights can affect burglaries only after dark, so daytime burglaries on the same streets are a natural comparison. (C) asks for it: if daytime burglaries fell by a similar amount, something else that changed on those streets (a police crackdown, an arrest) is the likelier cause; if they didn’t fall, the drop looks specific to the hours the lights are on. (B) is the trap: residents feeling safer sounds like a sign the lights work, but feelings aren’t burglaries, and a no wouldn’t weaken the argument either. (E) only offers a route by which lighting could work.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The brighter lighting deterred many would-be burglars.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: After brighter streetlights went in on twenty streets, nighttime burglaries of homes there fell 30 percent from the year before.

breakdown.analysis: What else changed on those streets? Maybe police stepped up patrols there, or a prolific burglar was caught. Those would cut burglaries at all hours. The lights, though, only work at night. So look at the daytime: if daytime burglaries also fell 30 percent, the lights probably aren’t the reason. It’s like crediting your new night-light for fewer bad dreams when you also stopped watching horror movies; check whether your daytime moods improved too. Most students who miss this pick (B), because feeling safer sounds like evidence. But how residents feel isn’t a burglary count, and a no wouldn’t hurt the argument.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. Energy use has nothing to do with whether the lights deterred burglars.

Tempting, because feeling safer sounds like the lights working. But perceptions aren’t burglaries, and residents could feel safer whether or not burglars were deterred. A no wouldn’t weaken the argument either.

CORRECT. Daytime burglaries are a comparison the lights can’t touch. If they fell just as much, something else that changed on those streets explains the drop. If they didn’t, the drop is specific to the hours when the lights are on, which points to the lighting.
Irrelevant. How burglars got in doesn’t tell us whether the lighting made them try less often.

Only matters one way. It describes one way lighting might deter burglars, so a yes fits the argument without showing the lights caused the drop, and a no doesn’t rule out the lights deterring burglars directly.

questions.stimulus: In the Orsley housing estate, buildings in which each entrance and stairwell serves only four apartments suffer far less vandalism than buildings in which each entrance serves twenty or more apartments. Evidently, residents who share an entrance with only a few households come to recognize one another, and so they readily notice and challenge strangers who enter their building.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Repair records confirm that the housing authority spends much less money fixing vandalism damage in the small-entrance buildings than in the others.
Vandalism in Orsley's large-entrance buildings is concentrated in the stairwells, which in those buildings are long, windowless, and poorly lit.
Orsley's small-entrance buildings are scattered among its large-entrance buildings rather than grouped together in one part of the estate.
Several housing estates in other cities have recently been redesigned so that each entrance serves fewer apartments than before.
Residents of Orsley's large-entrance buildings are more likely than other residents to say that they would move elsewhere if they could.
questions.explanation: The argument credits entrance size, through neighbors recognizing each other, for the vandalism gap. One rival is location: if the small-entrance buildings sat together in a quieter or better-patrolled corner, place rather than design could explain the gap. (C) rules that out, since the two building types are mixed together across the estate. (A) is the main trap: lower repair costs just restate that the small-entrance buildings suffer less vandalism, which is the premise, not the explanation. (B) offers a rival cause (dark stairwells) and so weakens.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Small-entrance buildings have less vandalism because residents recognize one another and challenge strangers.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: In Orsley, buildings with four apartments per entrance have far less vandalism than buildings with twenty or more per entrance.

breakdown.analysis: The correlation is given. The question is why. Could something other than entrance size be doing the work? Lighting, tenants, or plain location: maybe the small buildings all sit in a quiet corner by the police station. We need an answer that knocks out a rival or backs the recognize-the-neighbors story. Think of two cafés with different seating where one gets fewer thefts; before you credit the seating, check they aren't on different streets. Most students pick (A) because it mentions vandalism in the small-entrance buildings. It fails because cheaper repairs just repeat the premise in money terms. It says nothing about why.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. Lower repair bills are what you'd expect if there's less vandalism, which we already know. Confirming a premise doesn't touch the gap between the correlation and the explanation.
This points to a rival cause: dark, windowless stairwells invite vandalism. If anything it weakens the recognition story.

CORRECT. If the small-entrance buildings are mixed in among the large ones, they share the same streets, patrols and surroundings. That rules out location as the explanation and leaves design, and the recognition mechanism, standing.
So? Other estates copying the design doesn't show the design works, let alone why it works.
Interesting fact, but not relevant. Wanting to move out could reflect noise, size or anything else. It doesn't link entrance size to vandalism.

questions.stimulus: Architect: The proposal to replace the Halsey Building's original steel-framed windows with sealed modern units should be rejected. Because occupants could no longer open their windows on mild days, sealed units would make the building more dependent on mechanical ventilation. And that added dependence would cancel most of the energy savings the units' better insulation is supposed to provide, which is the proposal's chief justification.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the architect's argument by the claim that sealed units would make the building more dependent on mechanical ventilation?
choices: It is the argument's main conclusion, which is supported by the claim that occupants could no longer open their windows on mild days.
It is a premise offered in direct support of the main conclusion, and no other claim in the argument is offered in support of it.
It is a claim that the proposal's supporters use to justify replacing the windows, and the architect seeks to refute it.
It is an objection to the proposal that the architect concedes is outweighed by the energy savings that better insulation would bring.
It is a conclusion drawn from one claim and offered in support of another claim that bears on the argument's main conclusion.
questions.explanation: The claim is supported by the 'because' clause (occupants could no longer open the windows) and in turn supports the next claim, that the added dependence would cancel most of the savings, which undercuts the proposal's chief justification and so supports rejecting it. That makes it an intermediate conclusion, as (E) says. (B) is the trap: it treats the claim as a bare premise, but the 'because' clause supports it. (A) mistakes it for the main conclusion, which is the first sentence.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The proposal to replace the Halsey Building's windows with sealed units should be rejected.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Occupants couldn't open sealed windows on mild days; so the building would depend more on mechanical ventilation; that would cancel most of the insulation savings, the proposal's main justification.

breakdown.analysis: Map the chain: 1. occupants can't open windows → 2. more dependence on mechanical ventilation → 3. most savings cancelled → conclusion: reject the proposal. Our claim is step 2. It gets support ("Because ...") and gives support ("that added dependence would cancel..."). Something that's both supported and supporting is a subsidiary, or intermediate, conclusion. Most students pick (B) because the claim sits early and reads like a reason. It fails because B says nothing supports the claim, and the "Because" clause does.

choices.note: Wrong role. The main conclusion is the first sentence: reject the proposal. This claim is one step on the way there.

Tempting, and the main trap. It's right that the claim helps support the conclusion. But B adds that nothing supports it, and the "Because occupants could no longer open their windows" clause is offered precisely to support it.
The proposal's supporters rely on insulation savings, not on ventilation. And the architect asserts this claim; she doesn't refute it.
Backward. The architect doesn't concede that the savings outweigh anything. She argues the ventilation problem cancels most of the savings.
CORRECT. It's drawn from the claim about opening windows and supports the claim that the savings would be cancelled, which in turn bears on rejecting the proposal.

questions.stimulus: Before last season, the Coastal Hockey League reduced the maximum width of goaltenders' leg pads, and goals per game then rose by nearly 15 percent. Some attribute the rise to the league's simultaneous crackdown on obstruction penalties. But the narrower pads are the more likely cause, since they simply leave more of the net uncovered.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Almost all of the extra goals last season were shots that went in low near the posts, where the old pads had extended.
Goaltenders' save percentages fell last season to their lowest level in a decade, and few goaltenders had strong records.
Goals scored while one team had a player serving a penalty rose more last season than goals scored with both teams at full strength.
Several goaltenders predicted before the season began that the narrower pads would make it much harder for them to stop shots.
The league has changed its rules on goaltenders' equipment several times in the past without any noticeable effect on scoring.
questions.explanation: Two changes happened together, and the argument picks the pads because they leave more net uncovered. (A) confirms that mechanism: the new goals came precisely where the old, wider pads used to block shots, which the obstruction crackdown would not predict. (B) is the main trap: falling save percentages are just another way of saying more goals went in, and both explanations predict that. (C) supports the rival explanation, since penalty crackdowns produce more power plays.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The narrower pads, not the crackdown on obstruction penalties, most likely caused the rise in scoring.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Pads were narrowed and goals rose about 15 percent; a penalty crackdown happened at the same time; narrower pads leave more net uncovered.

breakdown.analysis: Two suspects, one crime. What would point to the pads specifically? If the pads are the cause, the extra goals should go in where the pads used to be. If the crackdown is the cause, you'd expect more power-play goals instead. We want an answer that fits only the pads. It's like a store that changed its locks and its alarm the same week, and break-ins dropped: if the thieves stopped coming in through the doors specifically, credit the locks. Most students pick (B) because it sounds like goalies got worse. It fails because both explanations predict lower save percentages.

choices.note: CORRECT. The added goals came through exactly the area the old pads covered. That's the fingerprint of narrower pads, and the obstruction crackdown gives no reason to expect it.
Tempting, and the main trap. Lower save percentages are just more goals described from the goalie's side. Both suspects predict that, so it doesn't favor the pads.
This helps the other side. Bigger growth in power-play goals points to the penalty crackdown, so it weakens the argument.
Predictions aren't evidence. Goalies expecting trouble doesn't show the pads caused the rise.
If anything this weakens: past equipment changes made no difference, so why credit this one?

questions.stimulus: Anthropologist: Researchers studying the Kaleru, a forest people, conclude that the Kaleru have no concept of private property, since Kaleru hunters share every kill with the whole village. Admittedly, the sharing of game is nearly universal among the Kaleru. But each hunter's arrows bear his personal mark, and no one else may use them without his consent. So the researchers' conclusion is mistaken.
questions.stem: The claim that the sharing of game is nearly universal among the Kaleru plays which one of the following roles in the anthropologist's argument?
choices: It is a premise that, together with the claim about the hunters' arrows, supports the argument's main conclusion.
It is the conclusion that the researchers draw from their observations of how Kaleru hunters behave.
It is a claim that the anthropologist attempts to refute by describing how the Kaleru treat hunters' arrows.
It acknowledges that the researchers' evidence is accurate while denying that it establishes their conclusion.
It is evidence the anthropologist uses to show that the Kaleru distinguish game from other kinds of possessions.
questions.explanation: 'Admittedly' marks a concession: the anthropologist grants the researchers' evidence (game is shared) but then argues, from the arrows, that their conclusion (no private property) is wrong. (D) says exactly that. (A) is the trap: the sharing claim doesn't support the conclusion that the researchers are mistaken; it is the very fact the researchers relied on. (E) invents a conclusion about the Kaleru distinguishing kinds of possessions that the anthropologist never draws.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The researchers' conclusion that the Kaleru have no concept of private property is mistaken.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Each hunter's arrows bear his mark and can't be used without his consent. (Conceded: sharing game is nearly universal.)

breakdown.analysis: "Admittedly" is the flag: a point for the other side is coming. The researchers' evidence is that hunters share every kill. The anthropologist grants it. Then "But": arrows are private. So does the sharing claim help show the researchers are wrong? No. It helps the researchers. That's a concession: true, granted, and not enough to save their conclusion. Most students pick (A) because the claim sits in the middle of the anthropologist's own speech. It fails because a fact that favors the researchers can't support the claim that they're mistaken.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. The content is right (the anthropologist asserts it), but the function is wrong. Universal sharing pushes toward the researchers' view, so it can't support the conclusion that they're mistaken. Only the arrows do that work.
The researchers' conclusion is that the Kaleru have no concept of private property. Sharing game is their evidence, not their conclusion.
The anthropologist doesn't refute it. "Admittedly" means she accepts it. The arrows are used against the researchers' conclusion, not against this claim.
CORRECT. She grants that the evidence is accurate (game really is shared) and then denies it proves there's no private property, using the arrows as a counterexample.
The anthropologist never concludes that the Kaleru sort possessions into kinds. That might be a fair thought, but the argument doesn't use the claim to show it.

questions.stimulus: Dozens of intact clay jars have been recovered from the bottoms of wells in the ancient town of Hesk. Some researchers think the jars were simply dropped by people drawing water. But a jar dropped down a deep shaft would almost always shatter against the stones lining it or at the bottom, so the jars must have been lowered deliberately, most likely as offerings.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Families in Hesk sometimes kept perishable food cool by lowering it in jars to just above the water in their wells.
None of the jars from Hesk's wells has the lugs or narrow neck that Hesk's potters gave to the vessels they made for drawing water.
Jars of the same types as those found in the wells have also been recovered in large numbers from the ruins of houses throughout Hesk.
Inscriptions indicate that offerings at Hesk's temples consisted mostly of small metal figurines rather than of pottery.
Several of the wells in Hesk were abandoned and filled with debris within a few decades of being dug.
questions.explanation: The argument rejects the view that the jars were dropped while drawing water. (B) strengthens it by showing the jars lack the features of Hesk's water-drawing vessels, so they likely weren't water vessels at all. (A) is the trap: it shows jars were sometimes lowered into wells deliberately, but for keeping food cool, an everyday purpose that competes with the offering explanation.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The jars were lowered into the wells deliberately, most likely as offerings.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The jars are intact; a jar dropped down a deep shaft would almost always shatter.

breakdown.analysis: Notice the two steps. Step 1, not dropped, so lowered on purpose: the premise handles that. Step 2, lowered on purpose, so offerings: nothing handles that, and the researchers' rival story is that these were ordinary water jars lost in the well. We want an answer that shows the jars weren't water jars. (B) does: they lack the features Hesk's potters gave to water-drawing vessels. Most students pick (A) because it shows people really did lower jars into wells on purpose. It fails because it gives a non-offering reason for doing so, which competes with the conclusion instead of supporting it.

choices.note: Tempting, because it shows people did deliberately lower jars into wells, which fits 'lowered deliberately.' But it supplies an everyday reason for doing so, which competes with the offering explanation instead of supporting it.

CORRECT. The rival view is that the jars were water vessels dropped while drawing water. These jars lack the features Hesk's potters gave to vessels made for drawing water, so they probably weren't water vessels at all. That removes the leading rival and leaves deliberate placement, most likely as offerings, as the best explanation.
If anything this suggests the jars were ordinary household ware, which fits the water-drawing story better than the offering story.
This cuts against the argument: if offerings were usually metal figurines, pottery offerings look less likely.
Irrelevant. When the wells were abandoned says nothing about how the jars got to the bottom.

questions.stimulus: Sportswriter: Many fans credit the Brockhurst Comets' new manager for the team's rise from last place to second this season, noting that the team won far more games after he arrived. But the team's two best hitters missed most of last season with injuries and have played nearly every game this season. Almost any manager would look brilliant with a healthy lineup. So the fans' evidence gives little reason to think the new manager deserves much of the credit.
questions.stem: The claim that the team won far more games after the new manager arrived figures in the sportswriter's argument in which one of the following ways?
choices: It is a premise that the sportswriter uses to support the conclusion that the new manager deserves little credit for the team's rise.
It is a claim that the sportswriter attempts to show is false by pointing to the return of the team's two best hitters.
It is evidence offered for a view that the sportswriter argues this evidence does little to support.
It is the sportswriter's main conclusion, which is supported by the claim that any manager would look good with a healthy lineup.
It is offered as an explanation of why the team's two best hitters were able to play in nearly every game this season.
questions.explanation: The fans cite the jump in wins ('noting that') as evidence for crediting the manager. The sportswriter accepts the jump but argues it is explained by the healthy hitters, so it does little to support the fans' view. (C) captures that. (A) is the trap: the sportswriter doesn't use the jump in wins to show the manager deserves little credit; the hitters' return does that work. (B) is wrong because the sportswriter never disputes that the team won more games.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The fans' evidence gives little reason to think the new manager deserves much of the credit.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The two best hitters were hurt last season and healthy this season; almost any manager would look brilliant with a healthy lineup.

breakdown.analysis: "Noting that" tells you whose evidence this is: the fans'. The fans say: more wins since he arrived, so credit the manager. The sportswriter doesn't deny the wins. He offers another explanation (healthy hitters) and concludes the evidence is weak. So the claim is the other side's evidence, accepted as fact but drained of force. It's like a student crediting a new pen for his better grades when he also started studying: the grades did go up; the pen just isn't why. Most students pick (A) because the claim is true and appears in the sportswriter's own speech. But it supports the fans, not him.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. The sportswriter accepts the claim, but he doesn't use it to show the manager deserves little credit. More wins is the fans' reason for crediting him. The hitters' return is what supports the sportswriter.
He never says the team didn't win more. He grants the improvement and explains it differently.
CORRECT. It's the fans' evidence for crediting the manager, and the sportswriter's whole point is that it gives that view little support.
Wrong role. The main conclusion is the last sentence, about the fans' evidence giving little reason for credit.
Backward and unsupported. The wins don't explain the hitters' health. If anything, the hitters' health helps explain the wins.

questions.stimulus: On the island of Mera, households that own large fishing canoes host far more public feasts than other households do. Since a large canoe cannot be paddled without a crew drawn from several households, canoe owners probably hold these feasts to secure the labor of the men who will crew their boats.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Canoe owners on Mera hold most of their feasts in the weeks just before the main fishing season, when crews are assembled.
Accounts left by visitors show that canoe-owning households on Mera have hosted more feasts than other households for at least a century.
Large canoes are costly to build, and on Mera only the wealthiest households have ever been able to afford one.
Feasts on Mera are also held to mark marriages and funerals, whether or not the host household owns a canoe of any size.
Some of the men who attend canoe owners' feasts on Mera never serve on the crew of any canoe at all.
questions.explanation: The argument reads a correlation (canoe owners feast more) as having a purpose (recruiting crews). (A) supports that purpose by timing: the feasts cluster right when crews are being assembled, which is what crew recruitment predicts and a general display of wealth does not. (B) is the main trap: a century of records only shows the correlation is long-standing, which is still just the premise. (C) suggests a rival, wealth, that would explain the extra feasts without any recruitment motive.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Canoe owners on Mera probably hold feasts to secure the labor of their crews.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Households with large canoes host far more feasts; a large canoe needs a crew drawn from several households.

breakdown.analysis: Why might canoe owners feast more? Recruitment is one story. Another is simply that canoe owners are rich and rich people throw parties. We need something that fits recruitment better than wealth. Timing is the classic tool: if feasts are for hiring crews, they should come when crews are hired. It's like a company that throws parties every spring; if spring is hiring season, the parties probably have a purpose. Most students pick (B) because it sounds like more evidence. It fails because it only shows the correlation goes back further, not why it exists.

choices.note: CORRECT. Feasts bunch up right before fishing season, when crews come together. That's exactly what recruitment predicts, and wealth display gives no reason for that timing.
Tempting, and the main trap. A longer record of the same correlation is still the same correlation. It doesn't tell us the feasts are for recruiting.
This points to a rival explanation: canoe owners are the wealthiest households and might feast simply because they can. That weakens the argument.
Irrelevant. Other occasions for feasts don't explain why canoe owners host more of them.
This slightly weakens: if feast guests include men who never crew, the feasts may not be about recruiting crews.

questions.stimulus: Councillor Ostrowe argues that the old grain elevator on Quensel's waterfront must be preserved because it is the last structure of its kind in the city. But by that standard the city would be obliged to preserve the last of anything, from its last 1950s gas station to its last tannery, however derelict or dangerous the building. Clearly, being the last of its kind cannot by itself make a building worth preserving.
questions.stem: The argument proceeds by
choices: disputing the accuracy of the claim that the grain elevator is the last structure of its kind remaining in the city
concluding that the grain elevator should not be preserved because preserving it would set an undesirable precedent for other buildings
citing buildings that were preserved for being the last of their kind and that later proved to be dangerous
questioning Councillor Ostrowe's motives for wanting the grain elevator preserved rather than some other old building
showing that a criterion on which an opposing argument relies would have unacceptable implications if it were applied generally
questions.explanation: The argument takes Ostrowe's standard (the last of its kind must be preserved), applies it to a derelict gas station and a tannery, and rejects the standard because those results are unacceptable. (E) describes that. (B) is the trap: the argument concludes only that being last isn't enough by itself to justify preservation; it never says the elevator shouldn't be preserved, and it never mentions precedent. (A) is wrong because the argument doesn't dispute that the elevator is the last of its kind.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Being the last of its kind cannot by itself make a building worth preserving.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: If 'last of its kind' were enough, the city would have to preserve its last 1950s gas station, its last tannery, and so on, however derelict or dangerous.

breakdown.analysis: This is the classic "by that logic..." move. Take the opponent's standard, apply it everywhere, and show it gives silly results. Then reject the standard. Notice how modest the conclusion is: being last isn't enough BY ITSELF. The author never says tear the elevator down. It's like answering "we must keep this sweater because it's the last one I have from 2009" with "by that logic you'd keep your last 2009 sock with holes in it." Most students pick (B) because the argument clearly opposes Ostrowe. It fails because the argument rejects his reason, not his verdict.

choices.note: The argument never questions that the elevator is the last of its kind. It grants that and attacks what follows from it.

Tempting, and the main trap. The argument opposes Ostrowe's reason, but it never concludes that the elevator shouldn't be preserved. Maybe it should, for other reasons. And it says nothing about precedent; the gas station and tannery are hypothetical results of a rule, not buildings that would follow this case.

The argument cites no buildings that were actually preserved. The gas station and tannery are hypothetical applications of the standard. Example of this method: "The Rowe mill was saved as the last of its kind and collapsed on a tour group."
No motives are discussed. Example of this method: "Ostrowe wants the elevator saved only because his brother owns the café beside it."
CORRECT. The criterion is "last of its kind"; applied generally, it would force the city to save derelict and dangerous buildings. That's unacceptable, so the criterion fails.

questions.stimulus: In 1790 the toll on the bridge across the river Arle at Doveny was abolished, and over the next twenty years the number of stalls at Doveny's weekly market nearly doubled. Doveny lies on the river's eastern bank, so ending the toll must have drawn traders from the villages to the west, who could now bring their goods across the river at no cost.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Traders had complained about the toll for decades, and several petitions asking for it to be abolished survive from the 1770s and 1780s.
The market's surviving accounts show that the fees collected from stallholders at Doveny rose sharply in the two decades after 1790.
During the 1790s, several roads leading into Doveny from towns to its east were widened and given new surfaces.
Most stalls added to Doveny's market after 1790 sold cheese and wool, goods produced mainly in villages west of the Arle.
A few traders from the western villages had been selling their goods at Doveny's market for many years before the toll ended.
questions.explanation: The argument infers from timing that ending the toll brought in western traders. (D) confirms that unstated link: the new stalls sold goods that came chiefly from west of the river, so the growth came from the side the toll had burdened. (B) is the main trap: rising fees only restate that the market grew, which the premise already says. (A) shows traders disliked the toll, a different claim from the toll's removal causing the growth, and (C) offers a rival cause on the eastern side.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Ending the bridge toll drew traders from west of the river to Doveny's market.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The toll was abolished in 1790; over the next twenty years the market's stalls nearly doubled; Doveny is on the eastern bank.

breakdown.analysis: Timing alone is weak. Lots of things change over twenty years. If the toll is the cause, who should the new traders be? People from the west, who had to cross the bridge. We want something showing the new stalls came from across the river. The answer may not say "west" in plain words; it might name goods that come from there. Most students pick (B) because it shows the market really boomed. It fails because we already knew the market boomed. The question is who caused the boom.

choices.note: Tempting. Complaints show the toll was unpopular, but disliking a toll isn't the same as being kept away by it. This supports a different claim (traders minded the toll), not that its removal grew the market.
Tempting, and the main trap. More fees collected just means more stalls, which the premise already tells us. It doesn't say where the new traders came from.
This points to a rival cause: better roads from the east could explain the growth with no help from the bridge. It weakens.
CORRECT. The new stalls sold goods made mostly west of the Arle. That ties the growth to the side of the river the toll had burdened, which is exactly what the argument's explanation predicts.
So? A few western traders before 1790 tells us nothing about who filled the new stalls afterward.

questions.stimulus: Historian: Some scholars hold that the city of Pellacre declined in the fourteenth century because its harbor silted up, pointing out that the volume of goods taxed at the harbor fell sharply after 1340. Yet the tax records also show that the harbor's duties nearly tripled in 1338. Merchants facing such duties would have shipped their goods through other ports whatever the harbor's depth. So the silting explanation is doubtful.
questions.stem: The claim that the harbor's duties nearly tripled in 1338 plays which one of the following roles in the historian's argument?
choices: It is offered as evidence that Pellacre's harbor did not in fact silt up at any time during the fourteenth century.
It is part of an alternative account of a fact that has been cited in support of the position the historian disputes.
It is cited by some scholars as support for their view that Pellacre declined because its harbor silted up.
It is the argument's main conclusion, which is supported by the claim that merchants would have shipped their goods through other ports.
It is a concession that the historian makes to the scholars before arguing that the silting explanation is doubtful.
questions.explanation: The scholars cite falling trade volume as evidence of silting. The historian points to the tripled duties, which, together with the claim about merchants rerouting, explain that same fall without silting. So the duties claim is part of an alternative account of the scholars' evidence, as (B) says. (A) is the trap: the historian concludes only that the silting explanation is doubtful, not that the harbor never silted. (C) assigns the claim to the scholars, who cite the fall in volume, not the duties.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The explanation that Pellacre declined because its harbor silted up is doubtful.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Duties at the harbor nearly tripled in 1338; merchants facing such duties would ship through other ports whatever the harbor's depth.

breakdown.analysis: The scholars' evidence: taxed goods fell after 1340. Their explanation: silting. The historian's move: here's another reason the goods would fall, the duties tripled. That's an alternative explanation of the same evidence, and it drains the evidence of force. Notice the conclusion is mild: "doubtful." The historian never says the harbor stayed deep. Most students pick (A) because the claim clearly argues against silting. It fails because the historian attacks the explanation, not the fact. The harbor may have silted; the evidence just doesn't show it caused the decline.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. Too strong. The historian argues that the evidence for silting can be explained another way, so the silting explanation is doubtful. Nothing here shows the harbor never silted.
CORRECT. The fact cited by the scholars is the fall in taxed goods. The tripled duties, plus merchants rerouting, give a different account of that fall, which undercuts the silting view.
Wrong side. The scholars cite the fall in volume. The duties are the historian's evidence.
Wrong role. The main conclusion is the last sentence. This claim supports the merchants claim, not the other way around.
The historian doesn't grant this to the scholars; it's her own point against them. A concession would favor their side.

questions.stimulus: Last winter the outdoor rink at Lorne Park began lending skates free of charge, and attendance rose 40 percent over the previous winter. Since last winter was no colder than usual, the increase must have come mainly from people who had stayed away in earlier years because renting skates cost more than they could easily afford.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Weather records confirm that the number of days cold enough for the rink to open last winter was close to the long-term average.
The free skates were in such demand last winter that the rink's lending counter often ran out of the most popular sizes.
The number of visitors who brought their own skates to the rink last winter was about the same as in the previous winter.
Before last winter, the rink had charged less to rent skates than most other rinks in the region charged.
Several other outdoor rinks in the region, none of which lend skates, also reported higher attendance last winter.
questions.explanation: If the rink simply became more popular, people with their own skates should have come more often too. (C) says they didn't, so the whole 40 percent rise came from skaters without their own skates, the group the free loans served. (B) is the main trap: heavy use of the free skates fits the argument, but those users could be the same people who used to pay for rentals, which would add no attendance at all. (A) only restates the premise about the weather, and (E) points to a regional trend, which weakens.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The attendance rise came mainly from people who had stayed away because renting skates cost too much.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Free skate loans began last winter; attendance rose 40 percent; last winter was no colder than usual.

breakdown.analysis: The argument has ruled out weather. What else could explain a 40 percent jump? Maybe the rink just got trendier, and everyone came more, skate owners included. Split the crowd in two: people who bring skates and people who don't. If free loans are the cause, the rise should be all on the no-skates side. Most students pick (B) because a run on free skates sounds like proof. It fails because the borrowers might be last year's paying renters. Switching from renting to borrowing adds no one to the crowd.

choices.note: Restates a premise. The argument already said the winter was no colder than usual. Confirming it adds nothing about who the new visitors were.
Tempting, and the main trap. Popular free skates are consistent with the argument, but the borrowers could be the same people who paid to rent last year. That changes who pays, not how many come.

CORRECT. Own-skate visitors stayed flat, so the whole increase came from people relying on the rink's skates. That rules out general popularity and points to the cost of rentals as what had kept people away.
This weakens: if rentals were already cheap compared with other rinks, cost is a less likely barrier.
This weakens: rinks without free skates also grew, which suggests a regional trend rather than the loan program.

questions.stimulus: The carved stone at Brynmor is not a boundary marker, as the museum's label claims. Boundary markers in this region were always set upright at the edge of a field, but the Brynmor stone was found lying flat in the floor of a house. Moreover, its carvings are worn smooth only on the side that faced up, so it must have been walked on for many years, which no boundary marker would have been.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the argument by the claim that the stone must have been walked on for many years?
choices: It is the main conclusion of the argument, and the claim about the stone's worn carvings is offered in support of it.
It is a premise offered in support of the claim that boundary markers in this region were always set upright.
It is a hypothesis that the argument raises in order to reject it in favor of the view on the museum's label.
It is the claim made on the museum's label, which the argument is intended to refute.
It is a subsidiary conclusion that is offered in support of the claim that the stone is not a boundary marker.
questions.explanation: The worn carvings support the claim that the stone was walked on for years ('so it must have been'), and that claim, with the added premise that no boundary marker would have been walked on, supports the first sentence: the stone is not a boundary marker. That makes it a subsidiary conclusion, as (E) says. (A) is the trap: 'so ... must' makes the claim look like the main conclusion, but it serves the opening claim, which everything in the argument supports.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Brynmor stone is not a boundary marker.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Boundary markers were set upright at field edges, but this stone lay flat in a house floor; its carvings are worn only on the upper side, so it was walked on for years, which no boundary marker would have been.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. Here it's the first sentence. Two lines of support follow. The second has its own little argument: worn carvings → walked on for years → (no boundary marker is walked on) → not a boundary marker. The walked-on claim gets support and gives support. That's a subsidiary conclusion. Most students pick (A) because "so ... must" sounds like the finish line. It isn't: the argument cares about being walked on only because it shows the stone isn't a marker.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. "So it must have been" looks like a conclusion indicator, and it is one, but for a sub-argument. The main conclusion is the first sentence, which the walked-on claim helps support.
Nothing supports the claim about upright markers; it's a separate premise. The walked-on claim doesn't bear on it.
The argument accepts that the stone was walked on and uses that against the museum's label. It doesn't reject it.
The label says the stone is a boundary marker. That's the claim being refuted, not this one.
CORRECT. It's drawn from the worn carvings and then used, with the point that no marker would be walked on, to support the main conclusion that the stone isn't a boundary marker.

questions.stimulus: Anthropologist: Children among the Ouli, herders who cross the northern desert, memorize long songs that name dozens of landmarks. Ouli adults describe the songs as mere entertainment. Yet Ouli herders, few of whom can read a map, find widely scattered waterholes without difficulty. So the songs very likely serve, whatever the adults say, to pass on the routes between waterholes.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the anthropologist's argument?
choices: In each song the landmarks are named in the order in which they would be passed by someone traveling between two particular waterholes.
Ouli herders who cannot read maps find waterholes as reliably as herders from neighboring peoples who navigate with the help of maps.
Ouli adults sing the songs mostly at evening gatherings, where they are performed for audiences that include people of all ages.
Some of the songs name landmarks that lie far outside the territory through which Ouli herders now move their animals.
The songs are sung in an older form of the Ouli language, which many Ouli children do not fully understand.
questions.explanation: The argument infers a function for the songs (passing on routes) from two facts: the songs name landmarks, and herders navigate well without maps. Nothing connects the songs to routes. (A) does: the landmarks are sung in travel order between waterholes, which is how a route would be encoded and which entertainment alone would not explain. (B) is the dominant trap: it shows Ouli navigation is excellent, but that only strengthens the premise; it doesn't show the skill comes from the songs. (C) supports the adults' entertainment account.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Ouli songs very likely serve to pass on the routes between waterholes.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Children memorize songs naming dozens of landmarks; herders, few of whom read maps, find scattered waterholes easily.

breakdown.analysis: Two facts sit side by side: songs with landmarks, and herders who navigate well. The anthropologist glues them together. But the herders might learn routes by traveling with their parents, and the songs might be just songs. What would make a song work as a map? The landmarks would have to come in the order you'd meet them on the trail. A list of ten pretty places isn't a route; ten places in walking order is. Most students pick (B) because it's about navigating without maps, which sounds like the heart of the argument. It fails because it beefs up the premise (they navigate well) without tying that skill to the songs.

choices.note: CORRECT. Landmarks in travel order between two waterholes is exactly how a route would be stored in a song. That's the missing link between the songs and navigation, and the entertainment story gives no reason for it.
Tempting, and the main trap. It makes the herders' navigation look even more impressive, but that's the premise again. It doesn't show where the skill comes from, and the songs aren't mentioned.
This fits the adults' account: songs performed at gatherings for all ages sound like entertainment. It doesn't help the route theory.
This weakens. Landmarks far outside the herders' range are useless for finding their waterholes.
This weakens a little: songs the children don't understand are a poor way to teach them anything, routes included.

questions.stimulus: Commentator: The Torvale tennis federation's new rule requiring junior players to use lower-compression balls will do little to reduce wrist injuries among juniors. It is true that these balls strike the racket with less force, so each stroke strains the wrist less. But because the balls bounce lower and travel more slowly, rallies will last longer, and juniors will therefore hit far more strokes in each match.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the commentator's argument?
choices: Junior players using lower-compression balls will hit far more strokes in each match than they did before the rule.
Because lower-compression balls strike the racket with less force, each stroke a junior hits will strain the wrist less.
Rallies in junior matches will last longer because lower-compression balls bounce lower and travel more slowly.
Requiring juniors to play with lower-compression balls is unlikely to bring about a substantial reduction in their wrist injuries.
The Torvale tennis federation should not have required junior players to use lower-compression balls in their matches.
questions.explanation: The first sentence is the conclusion: the rule will do little to reduce wrist injuries. The rest supports it: less strain per stroke is conceded, but longer rallies mean far more strokes. (D) paraphrases that first sentence. (A) is the dominant trap: it carries 'therefore,' but it is an intermediate conclusion that supports the claim about injuries. (B) is the concession and (E) adds a verdict about the federation's decision that the commentator never draws.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new ball rule will do little to reduce wrist injuries among juniors.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Granted, each stroke strains the wrist less; but the balls bounce lower and slower, so rallies last longer, so juniors will hit far more strokes.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. The last sentence ends with "therefore," but what is "far more strokes" for? It's there to cancel the per-stroke benefit, which is there to explain why injuries won't drop. So the first sentence is the point. This is the rate-versus-total idea: less strain per stroke times many more strokes may equal the same total strain. Most students pick (A) because "therefore" screams conclusion. It fails because more strokes only matters as a reason injuries won't fall.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. It's flagged by "therefore," but it's an intermediate conclusion. It exists to support the claim that injuries won't drop much.
This is the concession ("It is true that..."). The commentator grants it and then explains why it doesn't help much.
A premise step. Longer rallies support "more strokes," which supports the main point.
CORRECT. A fair paraphrase of the first sentence, "will do little to reduce wrist injuries." Everything else is offered to support it.
Too far. Saying a rule won't do much about injuries isn't saying it shouldn't have been adopted. The commentator never gives that verdict.

questions.stimulus: After the lanes on Fenn Avenue were repainted to be a meter narrower, average speeds there fell by eight kilometers per hour. Some officials credit the speed cameras installed on the avenue that same month. But the cameras photograph only cars exceeding the limit by a wide margin, and most drivers on the avenue never came close to that margin, so the narrower lanes must account for most of the drop.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Since they were installed, the cameras on Fenn Avenue have photographed very few of the cars that travel the avenue on any given day.
On Mabry Street, where identical cameras were installed that month but the lanes were left unchanged, average speeds hardly changed.
Signs warning drivers about the new speed cameras were posted at both ends of Fenn Avenue when the cameras were installed.
Accidents on Fenn Avenue have become less frequent in the months since the lanes were repainted and the cameras were installed.
Before the lanes were repainted, average speeds on Fenn Avenue had been rising slowly for several years.
questions.explanation: The argument dismisses the cameras because they photograph only extreme speeders. But cameras can slow ordinary drivers who don't know where the threshold lies. (B) tests the cameras alone: on a street with identical cameras and unchanged lanes, speeds barely moved, so the cameras by themselves don't slow traffic much. (A) is the dominant trap: few photographs seems to confirm that few drivers speed badly, but it is equally what you'd see if the cameras had frightened drivers into slowing down. (C) makes a deterrent effect more likely and so weakens.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The narrower lanes, not the new cameras, account for most of the drop in speeds on Fenn Avenue.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Lanes narrowed and cameras went in the same month; speeds fell 8 km/h; the cameras photograph only cars far over the limit, and most drivers never came close.

breakdown.analysis: The argument's case against the cameras is about what they photograph. But do drivers know that? A camera on a pole slows lots of people who were never at risk of a ticket. So the gap is: maybe the cameras slowed ordinary drivers just by being there. The clean test is a street with the cameras and none of the lane change. It's like two kids who both got a tutor and new glasses, and only one improved. Most students pick (A) because few photographs seems to prove the argument's premise. It fails because it fits both stories: few photos could mean the cameras scared everyone into slowing down.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. Few photographs looks like support for "most drivers never came close." But it's just as consistent with deterrence: drivers slowed down because of the cameras, so few got photographed. It can't tell the two causes apart.
CORRECT. Same cameras, same month, no lane change, and speeds barely moved. So the cameras alone don't do much, which leaves the narrower lanes as the main cause on Fenn Avenue.
This weakens. Warning signs make it likely drivers slowed because of the cameras.
Irrelevant to which change did the work. Both causes would predict fewer accidents.
Background trend only. It doesn't help decide between lanes and cameras.

questions.stimulus: Historian: Some historians hold that the Treaty of Marlenz was drafted in haste, on the grounds that it contains no provision for the return of prisoners. Yet in that era prisoner exchanges were customarily settled by separate agreement, and the surviving drafts of the treaty show that its wording was revised many times over several months. The treaty's silence on prisoners thus reflects custom, not haste.
questions.stem: The claim that the treaty contains no provision for the return of prisoners plays which one of the following roles in the historian's argument?
choices: It is a premise that the historian uses, together with the evidence of the surviving drafts, to show that the treaty was not drafted in haste.
It is a claim that the historian seeks to discredit by showing that the surviving drafts once contained such a provision.
It is the conclusion that some historians draw from their study of the surviving drafts of the treaty.
It is offered as an illustration of the custom of settling prisoner exchanges by means of separate agreements.
It is accepted by the historian, who offers an account of it that removes the support it was taken to give a rejected view.
questions.explanation: 'On the grounds that' marks the missing prisoner provision as the other historians' evidence for haste. The historian accepts the fact and explains it by custom, concluding that the silence reflects custom rather than haste; that strips the fact of its support for the haste view, as (E) says. (A) is the dominant trap: the omission is not the historian's evidence against haste; the custom and the many revisions are. (D) reverses the relation: the custom explains the omission, not the other way around.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The treaty's silence on prisoners reflects custom, not haste.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Prisoner exchanges were customarily settled by separate agreement; surviving drafts show the wording was revised many times over months.

breakdown.analysis: "On the grounds that" tells you this is someone else's evidence. Other historians: no prisoner clause, so it was rushed. Our historian doesn't deny the clause is missing. She explains the gap differently: custom put prisoners in a separate deal. Then the conclusion is about the silence itself. So the claim is a fact everyone accepts, reinterpreted so it no longer supports the rejected view. Most students pick (A) because the claim is true and the historian talks about it. It fails because the missing clause doesn't support "not hasty"; it's what the haste camp relies on. The drafts and the custom do the historian's work.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. The historian accepts the claim, but she doesn't use the missing clause to show the treaty wasn't rushed. If anything, a missing clause looks like haste. The custom and the drafts carry that load.
The historian never says the drafts had a prisoner clause. She accepts that the treaty lacks one.
Wrong role. The other historians' conclusion is that the treaty was drafted in haste. The missing clause is their evidence.
Reverses the relation. The custom is offered to explain the omission; the omission isn't offered as an example of the custom.
CORRECT. She accepts the fact (no clause), explains it by custom, and so removes its support for the haste view she rejects.

questions.stimulus: At the Bronze Age site of Kettu, a row of stone storerooms stands beside the settlement's largest house. Some scholars think each storeroom belonged to a separate household. But the storerooms are identical in size and construction, which indicates that they were built as a single project, so they were most likely controlled by whoever lived in the large house.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Analysis of the stone shows that all of the storerooms were built of blocks cut from a single quarry at about the same time.
Storerooms of similar size have been found standing beside ordinary houses at several other Bronze Age sites in the region.
Sealings from every storeroom door bear the impression of one seal, which also appears on sealings found in the large house.
The large house at Kettu was built several generations after the row of storerooms had been completed.
Some of the storerooms at Kettu held pottery that had been made in regions far from the settlement.
questions.explanation: The argument has two steps: identical design shows a single building project, and a single project shows control by the large house. The second step is the gap, since a community could build storerooms together and still give one to each household. (C) bridges it: the storerooms were all closed under one seal, also used in the large house, which points to one controller and to that house. (A) is the dominant trap: it supports the first step (one project), which the argument already reached; it leaves the household-ownership view standing. (D) weakens.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Kettu storerooms were most likely controlled by whoever lived in the large house.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The storerooms are identical in size and construction, so they were built as one project; they stand beside the largest house.

breakdown.analysis: Spot the chain: identical → one project → controlled by the big house. The first arrow is fine. The second is shaky. A village can pool labor to build ten identical sheds and still hand one to each family, the way a housing developer builds identical homes for different owners. So we need evidence of a single controller, ideally the big house. Most students pick (A) because one quarry at one time sounds like strong archaeological proof. It fails because it proves the step we already had: one project. One project doesn't mean one owner.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. Same quarry, same time: more proof of a single building project. But that's the intermediate conclusion the argument already reached. It doesn't show who controlled the rooms once built.
If anything this weakens: similar storerooms beside ordinary houses elsewhere suggest households could have their own.
CORRECT. One seal on every door means one authority controlled access, and the same seal turns up in the large house. That links the storerooms to that household and undercuts separate ownership.
This weakens. If the large house came generations later, its occupants didn't plan or originally control the storerooms.
Irrelevant. Imported pottery tells us about trade, not about who controlled the rooms.

questions.stimulus: Planner: Opponents of the proposed tram line on Drayton Road argue that it would hurt local shops, since construction would block the street for two years. That cost is real: shops on the city's other tram routes lost business while those lines were being built. But once the lines opened, those same shops saw sales rise well above their earlier levels. So the opponents' concern, though not baseless, does not justify rejecting the tram line.
questions.stem: The claim that shops on the city's other tram routes lost business while those lines were being built plays which one of the following roles in the planner's argument?
choices: It supports a point that the planner concedes, even though that point is used by others in arguing for a position the planner rejects.
It is evidence that the planner offers in direct support of the conclusion that the tram line should not be rejected.
It is a claim that the planner attempts to discredit by noting that the shops' sales later rose above their earlier levels.
It is the opponents' main conclusion, which the planner argues is undermined by the later rise in the shops' sales.
It is offered to show that construction of the Drayton Road tram line ought to be completed in less than two years.
questions.explanation: The planner concedes 'That cost is real' and backs the concession with the other routes' construction losses. The opponents use that cost to argue against the tram line, a position the planner rejects. (A) captures this. (B) is the dominant trap: the claim is the planner's own statement, but it pushes toward rejecting the tram line, not away from it; the later sales rise is what supports her conclusion. (C) is wrong because the planner accepts the losses; the later rise outweighs them without discrediting them.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The opponents' concern about shops does not justify rejecting the tram line.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Shops on other tram routes saw sales rise well above earlier levels once the lines opened. (Conceded: construction is a real cost, as shown by losses on other routes.)

breakdown.analysis: Track the layers. Opponents: construction hurts shops, so reject the tram. Planner: "That cost is real" (concession), and here's proof, shops on other routes lost business. "But" after opening, sales rose above earlier levels. So the claim is evidence for a concession, and the conceded point is the opponents' reason. Does it help the planner's conclusion? No, it pulls the other way. Most students pick (B) because the planner says it herself and it's specific evidence. It fails because evidence that construction hurts shops can't support "don't reject the tram."

choices.note: CORRECT. It backs up "That cost is real," which the planner concedes, and that cost is the opponents' reason for rejecting the tram line, a position she rejects.
Tempting, and the main trap. The planner does assert it, but losses during construction support the opponents' worry, not her conclusion. Her support is the later rise in sales.
She doesn't discredit the losses. She grants them and argues they're temporary and outweighed.
The opponents' conclusion is that the tram line should be rejected because it would hurt shops. This claim is evidence about other routes, not their conclusion.
The planner never proposes a shorter construction schedule. This adds a recommendation the argument doesn't make.

questions.stimulus: Recorded shipwrecks near the port of Calvadi fell sharply after 1840, the year a lighthouse was built at the harbor mouth. Some attribute the decline to the replacement of sailing ships by steamships, which became common in the region in the same decade. But steamships were wrecked on open coasts about as often as sailing ships were, so the lighthouse was most likely responsible for the decline.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Insurance records from the period show that, throughout the region, steamships and sailing ships were lost on open coasts at similar rates.
Calvadi's lighthouse was paid for by a tax on the cargoes of ships entering the harbor during its first decade.
After 1840, many ships entering Calvadi's harbor took on local pilots who knew the channels and hazards near the harbor mouth.
After 1840, sailing ships still using Calvadi's harbor were wrecked near its mouth at about the same rate as steamships were.
Shipwrecks also fell sharply after 1840 near several other ports in the region that had no lighthouse at the time.
questions.explanation: The argument dismisses the steamship explanation using open-coast wreck rates, but Calvadi's wrecks happen near a harbor, where steamships, which don't depend on the wind, might be far safer than sailing ships. (D) closes that gap: near Calvadi's harbor mouth, sailing ships after 1840 wrecked no more often, relative to their numbers, than steamships did, so the shift to steam can't explain the decline there. (A) is the dominant trap: it confirms the open-coast premise, which was never the weak point. (C) and (E) weaken.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The lighthouse, not the switch to steamships, most likely caused the drop in shipwrecks near Calvadi.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Wrecks fell after 1840, when the lighthouse was built; steamships became common the same decade; steamships wrecked on open coasts about as often as sailing ships.

breakdown.analysis: Notice where the premise is about and where the wrecks are. The premise compares ship types on OPEN COASTS. The wrecks we care about are near a HARBOR. Maybe steamships, which don't depend on the wind, handle tricky harbor entrances much better. Then the switch to steam could explain everything. We want an answer that compares the ship types at Calvadi's harbor itself, as a rate. Most students pick (A) because insurance records sound authoritative. It fails because it just confirms the open-coast premise; it says nothing about harbors.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. Insurance records back up the open-coast premise, but that premise was stated as fact already, and open coasts aren't the issue. The question is whether steamships were safer entering harbors.
Irrelevant. How the lighthouse was paid for doesn't tell us whether it prevented wrecks.
This weakens: local pilots are a rival cause of fewer wrecks near the harbor mouth.

CORRECT. Right where it matters, at Calvadi's harbor mouth, sailing ships were no more wreck-prone than steamships, measured as a rate. So swapping sail for steam can't account for the drop there, which leaves the lighthouse.
This weakens: ports with no lighthouse saw the same decline, which suggests a regional cause such as steamships.

questions.stimulus: Archaeologist: Dr. Szabo dates the burial of the Lisk coin hoard to the reign of Aldric, because the latest coins in it were minted under Aldric. But a hoard's latest coin shows only the earliest date at which the hoard could have been buried. And since Aldric's successor minted far fewer coins, a hoard buried during the successor's reign could easily contain none of them. So Szabo's dating, though possible, is not established.
questions.stem: The archaeologist's argument proceeds by
choices: rejecting Szabo's conclusion as false on the grounds that the evidence offered in support of it is insufficient
arguing that the evidence Szabo relies on is compatible with an alternative to the conclusion he draws from it
questioning the reliability of the methods by which Szabo determined when the coins in the hoard were minted
offering a date for the burial of the hoard that the available evidence supports better than Szabo's date
showing that Szabo's conclusion conflicts with other evidence about when coins from Aldric's reign were buried
questions.explanation: The archaeologist shows that Szabo's evidence (the latest coins are Aldric's) fits equally well with burial under the successor, whose scarce coins could easily be missing, and so concludes the dating is possible but not established. (B) describes that. (A) is the dominant trap: it names a familiar flaw, rejecting a conclusion as false because its support is weak, but the archaeologist explicitly says Szabo's dating is 'possible.' (D) is wrong because no better date is offered; the successor's reign is raised only as a possibility.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Szabo's dating of the hoard, though possible, is not established.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A hoard's latest coin gives only the earliest possible burial date; the next ruler minted few coins, so a hoard buried under him could easily lack them.

breakdown.analysis: The archaeologist never says Szabo is wrong. Read the last line: "though possible, is not established." The move is: your evidence fits your conclusion, but it fits this other scenario just as well. It's like a detective saying the suspect's footprints prove he was at the scene, and his partner replying that the prints only show he was there at some point after the mud formed. Most students pick (A) because it sounds like what critics usually do. It fails because the archaeologist is careful not to call the dating false.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. This describes a real flaw, but the archaeologist doesn't commit it. "Though possible" means she isn't calling Szabo's date false, only unproven. Example of this method: "There's little evidence the hoard dates from Aldric's reign, so it must date from some other time."
CORRECT. Latest coins from Aldric fit both burial under Aldric and burial under his successor. Showing the evidence fits an alternative is exactly how she gets to "not established."

She accepts that the coins were minted under Aldric. Her point is about what that implies, not about how it was determined. Example of this method: "Szabo dated the coins by their style alone, which often misleads."

She proposes no better date. The successor's reign is raised as a possibility, not defended as the answer. Example of this method: "The hoard was most likely buried under Aldric's successor, since its pot is of a later type."
No other evidence about burials is introduced. Example of this method: "Every other Aldric hoard lies above the flood layer, but this one lies below it."

questions.stimulus: Cycling club secretary: Last year, members of the Renfield Cycling Club who did most of their riding in groups reported fewer crashes, on average, than members who rode mostly alone. So riding in a group makes cycling safer, presumably because drivers more readily notice, and give room to, a group of cyclists than a lone rider.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the secretary's argument?
choices: Members of the club who rode mostly in groups were also less likely than members who rode mostly alone to report being injured in a crash.
Members who rode mostly alone were more likely than those who rode mostly in groups to do much of their riding after dark.
