Most of the club's members say that they feel safer when riding with others than when riding by themselves.
Crashes in which several riders fall at once can happen only when cyclists are riding together in a group.
On average, members who rode mostly in groups covered more kilometers last year than members who rode mostly alone.
questions.explanation: The evidence is a count, fewer crashes per member, but safety is a rate: crashes per kilometer ridden. If group riders simply rode less, their lower count would show nothing. (E) rules that out: group riders rode more and still crashed less, so their crash rate per kilometer is lower still. (A) is the dominant trap: fewer injuries follow from fewer crashes, so it repeats the premise in a new form and has the same exposure problem. (B) offers a rival cause, night riding.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Riding in a group makes cycling safer.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Last year, club members who rode mostly in groups reported fewer crashes on average than members who rode mostly alone.

breakdown.analysis: Fewer crashes per member isn't the same as safer. What if the group riders just rode less? Someone who rides 100 km a year will have fewer crashes than someone who rides 5,000, even on the same roads. Safety is a rate: crashes per kilometer. We need the group riders' exposure to be at least as high. Watch for count-versus-rate traps; this is the classic one. Most students pick (A) because fewer injuries sounds like more proof of safety. It fails because it has the very same problem: group riders who ride less will also get hurt less.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. Fewer injuries is what you'd expect from fewer crashes, so it adds nothing new. And it has the same hole: if group riders ride less, they'd get hurt less no matter how safe groups are.
This weakens. Night riding is a rival explanation for the solo riders' extra crashes.
Feeling safe isn't being safe. This supports what members believe, not the claim that groups reduce crashes.
If anything this weakens: it names a kind of crash that only group riders can have.
CORRECT. Group riders logged more kilometers and still had fewer crashes, so their crash rate per kilometer is clearly lower. That rules out "they just rode less" as the explanation.

questions.stimulus: Anthropologist: It is often said that the Vashari began terracing their hillsides only after their population outgrew the valley floor. But this view reverses the actual sequence: it was terracing that made the population growth possible. The oldest terraces date from a time when much of the valley floor was still uncultivated, and the region's villages began to grow only two centuries later, by which time terrace harvests had become the Vashari's main food supply.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the anthropologist's argument?
choices: By the time the region's villages began to grow, the harvests from terraces had become the Vashari's main source of food.
The oldest Vashari terraces were built at a time when much of the valley floor had not yet been brought under cultivation.
The Vashari began terracing their hillsides only after their population had grown too large to be fed from the valley floor.
Terracing was not the Vashari's response to population growth but was instead what made that growth possible.
Farming peoples who live in valleys generally begin to terrace hillsides only once all the flat land has been cultivated.
questions.explanation: The conclusion sits in the middle: the common view reverses the sequence, and terracing made the population growth possible. The last sentence supports it with dates and with the terraces' role as the main food supply. (D) states it. (A) is the dominant trap: it paraphrases the final clause, which sounds like a payoff but is evidence for the conclusion. (C) is the view the anthropologist rejects, and (E) is a generalization nobody in the argument makes.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Terracing made the Vashari population growth possible, rather than following from it.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The oldest terraces date from when much of the valley floor was uncultivated; villages grew only two centuries later, when terrace harvests were the main food supply.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. Sentence 1 is the popular view. Sentence 2, after the colon, is the anthropologist's own position. Sentence 3 is all evidence: dates, then food supply. Here the conclusion is in the middle, and the last sentence ends on a strong-sounding fact. Most students pick (A) because the final clause feels like where the argument lands. It fails because it's a reason: the terraces fed people before villages grew, which shows terracing enabled growth.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. It's the last clause and it sounds like a result. But it's evidence: it shows terraces were feeding people when growth began, which supports the claim that terracing made growth possible.
A premise. The early date of the terraces supports the conclusion; it isn't the conclusion.
This is the view the anthropologist rejects. Picking it means missing the "But this view reverses..."
CORRECT. It combines both halves of the middle sentence: the popular sequence is backward, and terracing made the growth possible.
A general claim about all valley farmers that no one in the argument makes, and it's close to the rejected view anyway.

questions.stimulus: Critic: Defenders of the glass-walled Varnholt Tower point out that its energy bills during its first year were well below those of comparable office towers. But the tower was barely half occupied that year, and an office building's energy use rises steeply with the number of people working in it. So the first year's bills reveal little about the tower's efficiency, and the defenders' case for its design is weaker than they suppose.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the critic's argument by the claim that the tower was barely half occupied during its first year?
choices: It is offered as evidence that the Varnholt Tower is in fact less energy efficient than comparable office towers of similar size are.
It is a premise that the tower's defenders use to support their own claim that the tower's design is highly energy efficient.
It supports a claim that is in turn used to cast doubt on the evidence cited by the design's defenders.
It is the main conclusion of the argument, and it is supported by the claim about how occupancy affects energy use.
It is a concession the critic makes before arguing that the tower's design is less successful than its defenders claim.
questions.explanation: The half-occupancy claim, with the point that energy use rises with occupancy, supports the intermediate conclusion that the first-year bills reveal little about efficiency. That in turn undercuts the defenders' evidence and supports the main conclusion that their case is weaker than they suppose. (C) traces this chain. (A) is the dominant trap: the critic never says the tower is inefficient, only that the bills don't show it is efficient. (E) misreads the claim as a concession, though it works against the defenders.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The defenders' case for the Varnholt Tower's design is weaker than they suppose.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The tower was barely half occupied in its first year; energy use rises steeply with occupancy; so the first year's low bills reveal little about efficiency.

breakdown.analysis: Map it: 1. half empty + energy use tracks occupancy → 2. first-year bills reveal little about efficiency → 3. defenders' case is weaker than they think. Our claim feeds step 2, and step 2 knocks out the defenders' evidence. Note what the critic doesn't say: that the tower is inefficient. Low bills in a half-empty building are like a restaurant bragging about low food costs during a month it was half closed. That doesn't prove the kitchen is wasteful, just that the number tells you nothing. Most students pick (A) because it sounds like the critic's attitude. It fails because undermining evidence isn't proving the opposite.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. Too strong. The critic says the bills reveal little about efficiency, not that the tower is inefficient. Showing evidence is weak isn't showing its conclusion is false.
Wrong side. The defenders cite low bills. The occupancy point is the critic's, and it works against them.
CORRECT. It supports "the first year's bills reveal little," and that claim is used to undercut the defenders' evidence, the low bills.
Wrong role. The main conclusion is that the defenders' case is weaker than they suppose. The occupancy claim is a premise at the bottom of the chain.
Not a concession: it doesn't grant anything to the defenders. And the critic's conclusion is about their case being weaker, not about the design being less successful.

sections.title: Skill Builder: Hard Dialogue, Assumption & Structure

questions.stimulus:
Priya: The Tessick Inn should stop cleaning every occupied room daily and clean rooms only when guests ask. Most guests staying two or three nights would rather not have staff entering their rooms daily, and the change would cut our labor costs.

Owen: Guests rarely ask for daily cleaning, but they notice when a room looks tired and complain in online reviews. Our bookings depend on those reviews, so whatever we saved on labor we would lose in bookings. We should keep cleaning every day.
questions.stem: Priya and Owen disagree over whether
choices: guests are more bothered by staff entering their rooms each day than by rooms that look tired
the condition of the inn's rooms has some effect on what guests write about the inn in online reviews
cleaning rooms only when guests ask would reduce the amount the inn spends on labor
the Tessick Inn should continue its practice of cleaning every occupied room each day of a guest's stay
guests who stay several nights are more likely than other guests to ask to have their rooms cleaned
questions.explanation: Priya says the inn should stop cleaning every occupied room daily; Owen says it should keep cleaning every day, so they disagree over (D). (A) is the trap: it sounds like the trade-off at stake, but neither speaker compares how much guests mind staff visits against tired rooms. (C) is common ground, since Owen grants the labor savings ('whatever we saved on labor'), and (B) is Owen's point alone.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Priya: Stop daily cleaning and clean only on request; short-stay guests don't want staff in their rooms daily, and it would cut labor costs.; Owen: Guests notice tired rooms and say so in reviews; bookings depend on reviews, so lost bookings would eat the labor savings; keep cleaning daily.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Bottom lines first: Priya says stop daily cleaning; Owen says "keep cleaning every day." That's a clean yes versus no. Now look at what Owen gives away. He doesn't deny the savings ("whatever we saved on labor"), and he doesn't deny that guests don't ask for daily cleaning. He fights on different ground: reviews and bookings. So the only spot where both speakers take opposite sides is the policy itself.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like the trade-off the two are weighing. But neither speaker ranks the two annoyances. Priya says short-stay guests would rather not have staff in daily; Owen says guests notice tired rooms. Both could be true, and neither says which bothers guests more.
Owen's claim only. Priya never mentions reviews, so we can't say she rejects this.
Common ground. Priya says the change would cut labor costs, and Owen speaks of "whatever we saved on labor." He accepts the savings and argues they'd be outweighed.
CORRECT. Priya: the inn "should stop cleaning every occupied room each day." Owen: "We should keep cleaning every day." One says yes, the other says no.
Neither speaker compares how often different kinds of guests ask for cleaning. Priya talks about what short-stay guests would rather have, not who asks more often.

questions.stimulus: Supermarket manager: Cashiers at our stores who have taken the company's optional customer-service workshop receive higher scores from mystery shoppers than cashiers who have not taken it. So if we required every cashier to take the workshop, the cashiers who now skip it would begin to receive higher scores from mystery shoppers.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the manager's argument?
choices: The higher scores of cashiers who took the workshop are not due entirely to traits that led them to sign up for it.
Cashiers who took the workshop receive higher scores from mystery shoppers solely because of what the workshop taught them.
Most cashiers who have not taken the workshop would be willing to take it if the company required them to do so.
Mystery shoppers' scores are the measure of a cashier's performance that the company values more highly than any other.
No cashier who has taken the workshop has ever received a lower score from a mystery shopper than some cashier who has not taken it.
questions.explanation: The workshop is optional, so the cashiers who took it chose themselves; the argument needs the workshop, not just the kind of cashier who signs up, to account for at least some of the score gap, which is (A). (B) is the trap: it would make the conclusion follow, but it is far stronger than needed, since the workshop could explain only part of the gap and required attendance would still help. (E) is also too strong; a gap in average scores doesn't require that every attendee outscore every non-attendee.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: If the workshop were required, cashiers who now skip it would start getting higher mystery-shopper scores.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Cashiers who chose to take the optional workshop score higher than those who didn't.

breakdown.analysis: Who takes an optional customer-service workshop? Probably the cashiers who already care most about customer service. So maybe the workshop does nothing and the eager cashiers would score higher anyway. It's like noticing that people who buy gym memberships are fitter and concluding a membership would make anyone fit. We need an answer that says the workshop itself accounts for at least some of the difference. Negate each choice and see whether the argument falls apart.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the higher scores are due entirely to traits that led those cashiers to sign up. Then the workshop adds nothing, and making the others take it won't raise their scores. The argument collapses.
choices.negation: The higher scores of cashiers who took the workshop are due entirely to traits that led them to sign up for it.

choices.note: Tempting, because if it's true the conclusion looks airtight. But it's too strong. Negate it: the workshop is not the only reason attendees score higher. Fine; it could still be part of the reason, and requiring it would still help. The argument survives, so this isn't required.
choices.negation: Cashiers who took the workshop do not receive higher scores solely because of what the workshop taught them.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The conclusion is about what happens if attendance is required. Whether cashiers would be willing doesn't matter; required is required.
choices.negation: Most cashiers who have not taken the workshop would not be willing to take it if the company required them to.

choices.note: So? The argument is about whether the scores would rise, not about how much the company values them.
choices.negation: Mystery shoppers' scores are not the measure the company values more highly than any other.

choices.note: Too strong. The premise is about which group scores higher, presumably on average. One attendee scoring below one non-attendee doesn't touch that.
choices.negation: At least one cashier who has taken the workshop has received a lower score from a mystery shopper than a cashier who has not.

questions.stimulus: Restaurant consultant: On weekend evenings, diners at Fennimore's often wait forty minutes for a table even while several tables sit empty, because the kitchen cannot keep up with more than about sixty diners at a time. The owners' plan to add tables would therefore do nothing to shorten the wait. Instead, Fennimore's should hire a second cook for weekend evenings.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the consultant's argument by the claim that the owners' plan to add tables would do nothing to shorten the wait?
choices: It is the argument's main conclusion, and the claim about the kitchen's capacity is offered in support of it.
It is a proposal that the consultant attributes to the owners of Fennimore's in order to argue against adopting it.
It is a premise offered in order to support the claim that the kitchen cannot keep up with more than about sixty diners at once.
It is a claim that the consultant concedes before going on to recommend an alternative remedy for the wait.
It is a conclusion drawn from a claim about the kitchen, and it is offered as support for the main conclusion.
questions.explanation: The kitchen's limited capacity supports the claim that adding tables won't help ('therefore'), and that claim in turn supports the recommendation to hire a second cook ('Instead'), so it is an intermediate conclusion, as (E) says. (A) is the trap: the claim carries a conclusion indicator, but the argument's final point is what Fennimore's should do. (B) gets the content half right; the plan is the owners', but the claim in question is the consultant's own verdict on that plan.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Fennimore's should hire a second cook for weekend evenings.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The kitchen can't handle more than about sixty diners, which is why diners wait while tables sit empty; therefore adding tables would do nothing to shorten the wait.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The kitchen bottleneck supports "adding tables would do nothing" (that's what "therefore" signals). And "adding tables would do nothing" helps support the recommendation: since tables aren't the fix, "instead" hire a cook. The conclusion is the one everything else supports, and that's the recommendation. So the claim in the stem is a middle step: supported by one thing, supporting another. That's an intermediate (subsidiary) conclusion.

choices.note: Tempting, because "therefore" sits right in that sentence. But the argument doesn't stop there. "Instead, Fennimore's should hire a second cook" is what the whole argument is building to. A "therefore" claim that feeds a later claim is an intermediate conclusion, not the main one.

Right content, wrong function. The owners' plan is to add tables. The claim in the stem is the consultant's verdict on that plan, that it wouldn't work. The consultant doesn't attribute that verdict to the owners.
Backwards. The kitchen's capacity supports the claim about tables, not the other way around.
The consultant doesn't concede this; she argues for it. A concession is something granted that cuts against the author's view. This claim is part of her case.
CORRECT. It's supported by the kitchen-capacity claim ("therefore") and it supports the recommendation to hire a cook ("Instead"). Supported and supporting: an intermediate conclusion.

questions.stimulus:
Sunita: The breakfast buffet at the Alder Ridge ski lodge wastes a great deal of food, since the trays have to stay full until closing whether or not anyone eats from them. We should cook breakfasts to order instead.

Marco: Whatever is left on the trays at closing goes to the shelter in town, which serves it at lunch. Besides, skiers hurrying to catch the first lift won't wait for eggs cooked to order. The buffet should stay.
questions.stem: The dialogue provides the most support for the claim that Sunita and Marco disagree over whether
choices: cooking breakfasts to order would reduce the total amount of food that the lodge prepares each morning
the lodge's breakfast buffet causes a substantial amount of food to go to waste each morning
some of the lodge's guests are unwilling to wait for breakfasts that are cooked to order
food served from a buffet tray is less appealing to guests than food that is cooked to order
the shelter in town would be able to serve its lunches without the food left over from the lodge
questions.explanation: Sunita says the buffet wastes a great deal of food; Marco replies that the leftovers go to a shelter that serves them, so the food isn't wasted, which puts (B) at issue. (C) is the trap: it's Marco's second reason, but Sunita never addresses whether guests would wait. (A) is implied by Sunita's plan, but Marco never denies it; he argues the leftovers aren't wasted.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Sunita: The buffet wastes a lot of food because trays stay full until closing; cook to order instead.; Marco: Leftovers go to the town shelter, which serves them at lunch; skiers won't wait for cooked-to-order food; keep the buffet.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Marco gives two reasons, and only one of them answers something Sunita said. His shelter point is a direct reply to her waste claim: if the leftovers feed people at lunch, they aren't wasted. His point about hurried skiers is new territory; Sunita never said anything about waiting. So the dispute Marco actually engages is whether the buffet wastes food. (The policy itself is also at issue, but it isn't offered.)

choices.note: Tempting, because it's the idea behind Sunita's plan. But Marco never says cooking to order wouldn't cut how much food is prepared. His point is that the buffet's leftovers aren't wasted, not that the buffet uses no extra food. Only Sunita is committed here.
CORRECT. Sunita: the buffet "wastes a great deal of food." Marco: the leftovers go to the shelter, which serves them, so they aren't wasted. Yes versus no.

Tempting, because it's one of Marco's two reasons and it argues against Sunita's plan. But Sunita never says whether guests would wait. Maybe she agrees some won't and still prefers cooking to order. Only one speaker takes a side.
Neither speaker compares how appealing the two kinds of food are. Sunita's complaint is waste, not taste.
Neither speaker says anything about whether the shelter could manage without the lodge's food.

questions.stimulus: Chef: Our restaurant buys its chicken already cut into breasts and thighs. Whole chickens cost 35 percent less per pound, and our cooks could butcher them during the slow afternoon hours, when they are on duty but have little to do. So if we bought whole chickens and cut them up ourselves, we would spend less on chicken.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the chef's argument depends?
choices: Chicken that the restaurant's own cooks cut up would taste at least as good to diners as the precut chicken does.
The restaurant could find a use in its dishes for every part of a whole chicken, including the back and the bones.
Unusable parts do not make up enough of a whole chicken's weight to offset its lower price per pound.
The price of whole chickens will remain lower than the price of precut chicken for at least the next several years.
The restaurant's cooks are more skilled at butchering chickens than the workers who now cut up its chicken are.
questions.explanation: A whole chicken is cheaper per pound, but the restaurant pays for every pound, including the parts it can't use; the argument needs the unusable share to be small enough that the usable meat still costs less, which is (C). (B) is the trap: if every part could be used the conclusion would follow, but that is far more than required, since the restaurant can waste some of each bird and still come out ahead. Labor isn't the gap, because the chef says the cooks are on duty with little to do.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Buying whole chickens and butchering them in-house would reduce what the restaurant spends on chicken.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Whole chickens cost 35 percent less per pound; the cooks have idle time in the afternoons to butcher them.

breakdown.analysis: Cheaper per pound of what? A whole chicken's pounds include the back, the neck and the bones. If the restaurant only uses breasts and thighs, it has to buy a lot more pounds of whole bird to get the same amount of usable meat. It's like buying a whole watermelon because it's cheaper per pound than precut chunks, then throwing out the rind. The chef already dealt with labor (the cooks are idle anyway). We need an answer that says the unusable part isn't big enough to wipe out the 35 percent discount.

choices.note: The argument is about spending, not taste. Negate it and the restaurant might serve worse chicken, but it would still spend less.
choices.negation: Chicken the restaurant's cooks cut up would taste worse to diners than the precut chicken does.

choices.note: Tempting, because if every part is used, the savings are obvious. But it's too strong. Negate it: the restaurant can't use some part, say the bones. It can still come out ahead as long as the waste is small. The argument survives.
choices.negation: There is at least one part of a whole chicken that the restaurant could not use in its dishes.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the unusable parts are heavy enough to offset the lower price. Then the usable meat costs as much or more, and the restaurant won't spend less. The argument falls apart.
choices.negation: Unusable parts make up enough of a whole chicken's weight to offset its lower price per pound.

choices.note: The conclusion is about what would happen if they bought whole chickens now. A price gap that closes in a few years doesn't stop them from saving in the meantime.
choices.negation: The price of whole chickens will not remain lower than the price of precut chicken for the next several years.

choices.note: Too strong and beside the point. The cooks don't need to be better than the current butchers; they just need to do the job.
choices.negation: The restaurant's cooks are not more skilled at butchering chickens than the workers who now cut up its chicken.

questions.stimulus: Consumer columnist: For most home cooks, the 'professional' version of a kitchen blender is not worth its extra cost. The professional models' chief advantage is a motor that can run for an hour without overheating, which matters in a restaurant kitchen. But home cooks rarely run a blender for more than a few minutes at a time, so for them that advantage would almost never come into play.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the columnist's argument?
choices: Most home cooks would not gain enough from a professional blender to justify paying its extra cost.
Home cooks would gain no benefit at all from buying a professional blender instead of a standard model.
A blender motor that can run for an hour without overheating is of real value mainly in restaurant kitchens.
For most home cooks, the chief advantage of a professional blender's motor would almost never come into play.
Restaurant kitchens should buy professional blenders rather than standard ones, because only professional models run for an hour.
questions.explanation: Everything in the argument supports the opening claim that a professional blender isn't worth its extra cost for most home cooks, which (A) restates. (D) is the trap: it is flagged with 'so,' but it is a step toward the opening claim, explaining why the extra cost isn't worth paying. (B) overstates the conclusion ('not worth the extra cost' is not 'no benefit at all'), and (E) adds a recommendation for restaurants that the columnist never makes.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: For most home cooks, a professional blender isn't worth its extra cost.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The pro models' chief advantage is a motor that runs an hour without overheating; home cooks rarely blend more than a few minutes; so that advantage would almost never matter to them.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. Here the last sentence has a "so," which pulls your eye. But what does "the advantage would almost never come into play" support? It supports the first sentence: if the thing you're paying extra for never matters to you, it isn't worth the extra money. So the first sentence is the main conclusion, and the "so" claim is a middle step. Main conclusions often come first with no indicator word at all.

choices.note: CORRECT. A paraphrase of the first sentence: for most home cooks, the pro version isn't worth the extra cost. The rest of the argument exists to back this up.

Too strong. The columnist says the pro model isn't worth its extra cost and that its advantage would "almost never" come into play. That leaves room for some small benefit; it just isn't worth the price. "No benefit at all" overshoots.
Close to a premise, stretched. The columnist says the long-running motor "matters in a restaurant kitchen," not that its value is mainly there. Either way, it's support, not the conclusion.

Tempting, because it carries the "so." But it's an intermediate conclusion. It answers "why isn't the pro model worth it?" and so supports the first sentence rather than being the point of the argument.
The columnist never tells restaurants what to buy, and never says only pro models can run for an hour. This adds a recommendation the argument doesn't make.

questions.stimulus:
Tomas: Rennick must be confident that its suitcases are built to last. After all, it offers a lifetime warranty on every one of them.

Lena: Not necessarily. Rennick repairs a suitcase under the warranty only if the owner pays to ship it both ways, and few owners bother. A warranty that is seldom used costs a company very little, however flimsy its products are.
questions.stem: Lena responds to Tomas by
choices: denying that Rennick actually offers a lifetime warranty on each and every one of the suitcases it sells
arguing that Rennick's suitcases are not in fact built to last as long as Tomas believes they are
questioning whether owners of Rennick suitcases are satisfied with the terms of the warranty
showing that the fact Tomas cites is consistent with Rennick's lacking the confidence he ascribes to it
claiming that Rennick's warranty costs the company more than the warranties offered by its competitors cost them to provide
questions.explanation: Tomas infers Rennick's confidence from its lifetime warranty; Lena explains that the warranty costs Rennick little no matter how flimsy its suitcases are, so offering it doesn't show confidence, which is (D). (B) is the trap: her phrase 'however flimsy its products are' sounds like an accusation, but she never says Rennick's suitcases are flimsy; she only says the warranty would be cheap even if they were. (A) is wrong because she accepts that the warranty exists.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: (Tomas) Rennick must be confident its suitcases are built to last.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: (Tomas) Rennick offers a lifetime warranty on every suitcase. (Lena) Owners must pay shipping both ways, few bother, and a seldom-used warranty costs little even for flimsy products.

breakdown.analysis: Tomas's logic: you'd only offer a lifetime warranty if you expected few claims, so Rennick must trust its suitcases. Lena cuts the link. Few claims could come from the shipping hassle, not from sturdy suitcases. So the warranty is cheap for Rennick either way, and it tells us nothing about confidence. Notice what she doesn't do: she doesn't say the suitcases are bad. She says Tomas's evidence doesn't prove they're good. Showing the evidence doesn't support a conclusion is not the same as showing the conclusion is false.

choices.note: She accepts the warranty exists. She talks about how Rennick handles claims under it.
choices.example: Example of method: Rennick doesn't offer a lifetime warranty at all; that's only on its premium line.

choices.note: Tempting, because "however flimsy its products are" sounds like a dig at Rennick. But read it closely: the warranty would cost little even if the suitcases were flimsy. She never says they are. Maybe they're excellent; her point is only that the warranty can't show it.
choices.example: Example of method: Rennick's suitcases fall apart within two years, so they clearly aren't built to last.

choices.note: She doesn't ask whether owners are satisfied. She says few owners use the warranty because of the shipping cost, which is about cost to Rennick, not satisfaction.
choices.example: Example of method: But do Rennick's customers actually like the warranty terms?

choices.note: CORRECT. The fact Tomas cites is the lifetime warranty. Lena shows that a company with no confidence in its suitcases could offer the same warranty cheaply, so the warranty doesn't establish the confidence Tomas infers.
She never compares Rennick's costs with its competitors'. In fact she says the warranty costs Rennick very little.
choices.example: Example of method: Rennick's warranty is far more expensive for it than its rivals' warranties are for them.

questions.stimulus: Campground manager: Nearly all of the noise complaints we receive come from campers at the sites along the river, and our evening campfire circle, where guests gather to sing and talk until midnight, is also along the river. If we move the campfire circle to the clearing on the hill, we will receive fewer noise complaints.
questions.stem: The manager's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?
choices: Campers at the sites along the river spend more of their evenings at the campfire circle than other campers do.
At least some of the noise that disturbs campers at the sites along the river comes from the campfire circle.
Most of the noise that campers at the sites along the river hear at night comes from the campfire circle.
Guests would be as willing to gather at a campfire circle on the hill as at one beside the river.
The river itself is not loud enough at night to disturb the campers whose sites are closest to it.
questions.explanation: The manager blames the complaints on the campfire circle merely because both are along the river; the plan works only if the circle is at least part of what disturbs the river campers, which is (B). (C) is the trap: 'most' is more than the argument needs, since moving the circle reduces complaints even if it is only one noise source among several. (E) isn't required either; the river could be noisy and the circle could still add to the complaints.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Moving the campfire circle to the hill will reduce noise complaints.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Nearly all complaints come from river sites; the campfire circle is along the river.

breakdown.analysis: Being near each other isn't the same as one causing the other. Maybe the river campers are bothered by something else entirely, like a road or the river itself. Then moving the campfire circle changes nothing. We need an answer that says the circle is at least one source of the noise those campers complain about. Watch for answers that say "most" or "only": the plan can work even if the circle is a small part of the problem.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Negate it: river campers spend no more evenings at the circle than others. The circle could still be keeping them awake from their tents.
choices.negation: Campers at the sites along the river do not spend more of their evenings at the campfire circle than other campers do.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: none of the noise bothering the river campers comes from the circle. Then moving it does nothing for them, and the complaints don't fall. The argument collapses.
choices.negation: None of the noise that disturbs campers at the sites along the river comes from the campfire circle.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like the reason the plan should work. But it's too strong. Negate it: the circle makes less than half the noise. Removing even a third of the noise could still cut complaints. The argument survives.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most of the noise that campers at the river sites hear at night comes from the campfire circle.

choices.note: Negate it: guests would be less willing to gather on the hill. That means fewer late-night singers, which if anything helps the plan. Not required.
choices.negation: Guests would be less willing to gather at a campfire circle on the hill than at one beside the river.

choices.note: Tempting as a defender, but too strong. Negate it: the river is loud enough to disturb some campers. The campfire circle could still be part of the problem, so moving it could still reduce complaints.
choices.negation: The river itself is loud enough at night to disturb the campers whose sites are closest to it.

questions.stimulus:
Yusuf: Tour companies in Castelmar should be required to limit their walking tours to twelve people. Large groups clog the old town's narrow lanes, and residents are growing hostile to tourists in general.

Hana: Large groups do clog the lanes, but a cap would only mean more groups, led through the same lanes at the same hours. If the city wants to help residents, it should route tours away from the residential lanes altogether.
questions.stem: The dialogue provides the most support for the claim that Yusuf and Hana disagree over whether
choices: large tour groups are partly responsible for the crowding in the narrow lanes of Castelmar's old town
large tour groups are the main source of the crowding in the narrow lanes of Castelmar's old town
the residents of Castelmar have been growing increasingly hostile toward tourists in general
Castelmar should route its walking tours away from the residential lanes of the old town
limiting walking tours to twelve people would relieve the crowding in the old town's lanes
questions.explanation: Yusuf proposes the twelve-person cap because large groups clog the lanes, so he takes the cap to relieve the crowding; Hana says a cap would just produce more groups in the same lanes at the same hours, so it wouldn't, which is (E). (A) is the trap: it uses the dialogue's words, but Hana concedes the point ('Large groups do clog the lanes'). (B) raises 'partly' to 'main source,' which neither speaker claims, and (D) is Hana's view alone.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Yusuf: Cap walking tours at twelve; large groups clog the lanes and residents are growing hostile.; Hana: Large groups do clog the lanes, but a cap would just mean more groups in the same lanes at the same hours; route tours away from residential lanes instead.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Start with Hana's "do": "Large groups do clog the lanes." That's a concession, so it's off the table. Her real objection is about the cap's effect: split one group of thirty into three groups of ten and the same thirty people walk the same lanes at the same hour. Yusuf proposes the cap precisely as a fix for clogged lanes, so he's committed to it helping. The fight is over whether the cap would work.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's Yusuf's premise in nearly his words. But Hana grants it: "Large groups do clog the lanes." When the second speaker concedes a point, it can't be the point at issue.
Too strong for either speaker. Both say large groups clog the lanes; neither says they're the main source of the crowding.
Yusuf's claim only. Hana mentions helping residents but never says whether they're growing hostile.
Hana's proposal only. Yusuf never discusses routing, so we can't say he rejects it.

CORRECT. Yusuf offers the cap as the remedy for clogged lanes, so he thinks it would help. Hana says it would only produce more groups in the same lanes at the same hours, so it wouldn't. Yes versus no.

questions.stimulus: Appliance maker: Our new Aquila dishwasher uses 30 percent less water per cycle than the Corvel, the model it replaces, because its redesigned spray arm reaches every rack with less water. So households that trade in their Corvels for Aquilas will, on average, use less water running their dishwashers than they did before.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the appliance maker's argument?
choices: The Aquila cleans dishes at least as thoroughly on its standard cycle as the Corvel did on its standard cycle.
Households that switch to the Aquila will, on average, run it no more often than they ran the Corvel.
Households that switch to the Aquila will, on average, run it less than half again as often as they ran the Corvel.
Most households that now own a Corvel will replace it with an Aquila rather than with a competitor's dishwasher.
The Aquila uses less electricity per cycle than the Corvel does, as well as using less water per cycle.
questions.explanation: Water use is water per cycle times number of cycles; an Aquila run 1.5 times as often as a Corvel uses 0.7 x 1.5 = 1.05 times as much water, so the argument needs households not to run it that much more often, which is (C). (B) is the trap: it would guarantee the conclusion, but households could run the Aquila somewhat more often, say 20 percent more, and still save water (0.7 x 1.2 = 0.84). (A) isn't required, because a less thorough clean doesn't by itself mean more cycles.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Households that switch from the Corvel to the Aquila will, on average, use less water running their dishwashers.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The Aquila uses 30 percent less water per cycle.

breakdown.analysis: Less water per cycle isn't less water in total. Total water = water per cycle x number of cycles. What if people run the efficient machine more often? It's like a car that gets better mileage: you only save gas if you don't start driving a lot more. Do the math: 30 percent less per cycle means the household saves water unless it runs the Aquila about 43 percent more often (1 / 0.7). So the argument needs only that households won't run it at least 50 percent more often. It doesn't need them to run it the same amount. This is rate versus total: know it.

choices.note: Negate it: the Aquila cleans less thoroughly. Maybe some households rerun loads, maybe not. A weaker clean doesn't by itself mean more water used, so the argument survives.
choices.negation: The Aquila does not clean dishes as thoroughly on its standard cycle as the Corvel did.

choices.note: Tempting, because it makes the conclusion airtight. But it's too strong. Negate it: households run the Aquila somewhat more often, say 20 percent more. Water use: 0.7 x 1.2 = 0.84 of before. Still less. The argument survives, so this isn't required.
choices.negation: Households that switch to the Aquila will, on average, run it more often than they ran the Corvel.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: on average they run it at least half again as often. Then water use is at least 0.7 x 1.5 = 1.05 of before, which is more, not less. The conclusion fails.
choices.negation: Households that switch to the Aquila will, on average, run it at least half again as often as they ran the Corvel.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The conclusion is about households that do switch. How many Corvel owners switch doesn't matter.
choices.negation: Most households that now own a Corvel will not replace it with an Aquila.

choices.note: The argument is about water, not electricity.
choices.negation: The Aquila does not use less electricity per cycle than the Corvel does.

questions.stimulus: Travel writer: Visitors to the island of Ardsay in November will find many of its restaurants closed and its ferry running only twice a day. Even so, November is the best month for most visitors to come. The cliff walks that draw most visitors to Ardsay are dangerously crowded in summer, while in November they are nearly empty and the weather on them is still mild.
questions.stem: The claim that visitors to Ardsay in November will find many of its restaurants closed and its ferry running only twice a day plays which one of the following roles in the travel writer's argument?
choices: It describes drawbacks that the argument implicitly treats as outweighed by the advantages that it then cites.
It describes drawbacks that the argument goes on to show are less serious than they might at first appear.
It is offered as evidence that few visitors come in November, which supports the claim that the walks are nearly empty.
It is a premise that, together with the claim about the weather, directly supports the argument's main conclusion.
It is the main conclusion of the argument, which the claims about the cliff walks are offered to support.
questions.explanation: The writer opens with drawbacks of a November visit, says 'Even so, November is the best month,' and then cites the empty, mild cliff walks; the drawbacks are conceded and treated as outweighed, which (A) says without using the word 'concession.' (B) is the trap: it also sees the claim as a set of drawbacks the argument has to deal with, but the writer never minimizes them; she grants them in full and argues that the cliff walks matter more. (C) reads the concession as support, but the writer states directly that the walks are nearly empty and 'Even so' marks the closures as points on the other side.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: November is the best month for most visitors to come to Ardsay.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The cliff walks most visitors come for are dangerously crowded in summer but nearly empty and still mild in November. (Conceded: many restaurants are closed and the ferry runs only twice a day.)

breakdown.analysis: "Even so" is the key. It means: despite what I just said. So the closed restaurants and the twice-a-day ferry are points against November that the writer admits. She doesn't argue them away; she says the cliff walks outweigh them. That's a concession, and the right answer describes it without the label: drawbacks treated as outweighed. There are two ways to get this wrong. One is to read the closures as support (few tourists, so empty walks), but the writer never makes that move. The subtler one is to say the argument shrinks the drawbacks. Granting a cost and outweighing it is not the same as showing the cost is small. It's like saying "Yes, the commute is long, but the job is worth it": you haven't made the commute shorter.

choices.note: CORRECT. The closures and the limited ferry are drawbacks of a November visit. "Even so" grants them, and the cliff-walk advantages that follow are what the writer weighs against them. That's a concession described by what it does.

Tempting, because it also sees the claim as drawbacks the argument has to answer, and that half is right. But the writer never says the closures or the ferry are less of a problem than they seem. She grants them fully and argues that the cliff walks matter more. Outweighing a cost isn't shrinking it.

Tempting if you think closed restaurants hint at few tourists. But the writer doesn't use the claim that way. She states that the walks are "nearly empty" on her own, and "Even so" marks the closures as points against November, not evidence for it.
Backwards. The claim doesn't support the conclusion that November is best; it cuts against it. That's why the writer has to say "Even so."
The main conclusion is that November is the best month to come. The claim about closures is something the writer grants, not the point she argues for.

questions.stimulus:
Ingrid: If we based our furniture showroom's sales bonuses on the team's total sales rather than on each person's own sales, the squabbling over customers on the showroom floor would stop. That squabbling drives customers away, so team bonuses would raise our total sales.

Felix: Team bonuses would end the squabbling, but our best salespeople could then earn more elsewhere, and they would leave. Losing them would cost us more sales than the squabbling does.
questions.stem: Ingrid and Felix disagree over whether
choices: the squabbling among the showroom's sales staff causes the showroom to lose some sales
basing bonuses on the team's total sales would put an end to the squabbling over customers
the showroom's best salespeople would leave if bonuses were based on the team's total sales
switching to bonuses based on the team's total sales would increase the showroom's total sales
the showroom's best salespeople are responsible for most of the squabbling over customers
questions.explanation: Ingrid concludes that team bonuses would raise total sales; Felix says the sales lost when the best salespeople leave would exceed the sales lost to squabbling, so total sales would fall, which puts (D) at issue. (C) is the trap: it is Felix's key claim, but Ingrid never says whether the best salespeople would stay. (A) and (B) are common ground: Felix grants that team bonuses would end the squabbling and, by comparing losses, that the squabbling costs sales.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Ingrid: Team bonuses would end the squabbling; squabbling drives customers away; so team bonuses would raise total sales.; Felix: Team bonuses would end the squabbling, but the best salespeople would leave, and losing them costs more sales than the squabbling does.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Felix agrees with a lot. He says team bonuses "would end the squabbling," and by saying losing the stars would cost more sales "than the squabbling does," he admits the squabbling costs sales too. So what's left? The bottom line. Ingrid: net effect is more sales. Felix: the loss from departures beats the gain from ending squabbles, so net effect is fewer sales. Watch for answers that are one speaker's reason; the other speaker has to take the opposite side.

choices.note: Common ground. Ingrid says squabbling drives customers away, and Felix's comparison ("more sales than the squabbling does") assumes the squabbling costs sales.
Common ground. Felix says it outright: "Team bonuses would end the squabbling."

Tempting, because it's the heart of Felix's objection and it seems Ingrid must reject it. But Ingrid never mentions the best salespeople. She might even agree some would leave and still be wrong about the totals, or right. Only Felix takes a side.
CORRECT. Ingrid: "team bonuses would raise our total sales." Felix: the departures would cost more sales than ending the squabbling recovers, so total sales would fall. Yes versus no.
Neither speaker says who does the squabbling.

questions.stimulus: Human resources director: Many managers treat exit interviews as their most reliable guide to why employees quit. They are wrong to do so. Departing employees usually still want good references, so they tend to cite inoffensive reasons for leaving, such as a better offer elsewhere, rather than complaints about their managers. Exit interviews thus systematically understate the role that poor management plays in employees' departures.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the director's argument?
choices: Exit interviews systematically understate how often poor management leads employees to quit their jobs.
Managers should not regard exit interviews as their most reliable source of information about why employees quit.
Poor management is a more common reason for employees to quit than are better offers from other employers.
Managers who want to learn why their employees quit should rely on sources of information other than exit interviews.
Managers who rely on exit interviews are more likely than other managers to overlook their own shortcomings.
questions.explanation: The director rejects a view ('They are wrong to do so') and then supports that rejection: departing employees want references, so they give inoffensive reasons, so exit interviews understate poor management, so they aren't a reliable guide. (B) restates the rejection. (A) is the trap: it is the last sentence and carries 'thus,' but it is an intermediate conclusion offered as the reason managers are wrong to rely on exit interviews. (D) overshoots: denying that exit interviews are the most reliable guide doesn't mean managers should stop relying on them, and (C) compares two reasons the argument never ranks.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Managers are wrong to treat exit interviews as their most reliable guide to why employees quit.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Departing employees want good references; so they cite inoffensive reasons instead of complaints about managers; thus exit interviews understate the role of poor management.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. "They are wrong to do so" is a flat rejection of what many managers do. Everything after it is the case for that rejection. Why are they wrong? Because exit interviews understate poor management. Why do they understate it? Because people want references. So the "thus" sentence at the end is a middle step: it's supported by the references point and it supports the rejection. Classic setup: the main conclusion comes early, right after the opposing view, and the last sentence is an intermediate conclusion with an indicator word.

choices.note: Tempting, because it comes last and carries "thus." But it answers the question "why are the managers wrong?" That makes it support for the main conclusion, not the main conclusion itself.
CORRECT. This is "They are wrong to do so" spelled out: managers shouldn't treat exit interviews as their most reliable guide to why people quit. Every other claim backs this up.
Too strong. The director says exit interviews understate poor management's role. That doesn't mean poor management is a more common reason than better offers.

Tempting, because it sounds like the practical upshot of "They are wrong to do so." But it's stronger than what the director says. Exit interviews aren't the most reliable guide; that doesn't mean managers should stop using them. They could still be one useful source among several.
The director never compares managers who rely on exit interviews with other managers. This adds a claim the argument doesn't make.

questions.stimulus: Restaurant manager: Our servers spend about a fifth of each shift walking to the order terminal by the kitchen and waiting their turn to use it. Handheld devices would let them enter orders right at the table. With handhelds, then, each server could cover more tables, and we could schedule fewer servers per shift without slowing service.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the manager's argument depends?
choices: Time is the only factor that limits how many tables a single server is able to cover during a shift.
Servers equipped with handhelds would spend all of the time they saved waiting on additional tables.
Handheld devices would cost the restaurant less each year than it would save by scheduling fewer servers.
Most diners would rather have their orders entered at the table than at a terminal by the kitchen.
How many tables a server can cover is limited at least partly by the time spent getting orders to the kitchen.
questions.explanation: Freeing a fifth of a server's shift lets each server cover more tables only if that time is part of what limits how many tables a server can handle, which is (E). (B) is the trap: if servers spent all the saved time on more tables, the plan would work, but they could spend some of it elsewhere and still cover more tables. (A) is too strong in the same way, and (C) addresses cost, which the conclusion never mentions.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: With handhelds, each server could cover more tables, so the restaurant could schedule fewer servers without slowing service.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Servers spend about a fifth of each shift walking to the kitchen terminal and waiting to use it; handhelds let them enter orders at the table.

breakdown.analysis: So what if servers get time back? That only helps if time is what stops a server from taking more tables. What if the limit is something else, like how many tables fit in a section, or how fast the kitchen can cook? Then the freed time just turns into idle time. It's like giving a cashier a faster scanner when the line is held up by the card reader. We need an answer that says the time spent on the terminal trip is at least part of what limits a server's table count. Watch for answers that say "only" or "all".

choices.note: Too strong. Negate it: something other than time also limits how many tables a server can cover. Fine; time could still be one of the limits, so freeing time could still help.
choices.negation: Some factor other than time also limits how many tables a single server is able to cover during a shift.

choices.note: Tempting, because if it's true the plan clearly works. But it's more than the argument needs. Negate it: servers spend some of the saved time on other things. They could still use the rest on more tables. The argument survives.
choices.negation: Servers equipped with handhelds would not spend all of the time they saved waiting on additional tables.

choices.note: The conclusion is that the restaurant could schedule fewer servers without slowing service, not that it would save money overall. Cost isn't part of the claim.
choices.negation: Handheld devices would cost the restaurant at least as much each year as it would save by scheduling fewer servers.

choices.note: Diners' preference doesn't affect how many tables a server can cover.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most diners would rather have their orders entered at the table.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the terminal trips don't limit how many tables a server can cover at all. Then saving that time lets no server take on more tables, and the restaurant can't cut servers without slowing service. The argument collapses.
choices.negation: How many tables a server can cover is not limited at all by the time spent getting orders to the kitchen.

questions.stimulus: Food writer: Some critics define street food as any dish sold to be eaten standing up or on the move. But by that definition, the hot dogs sold at a baseball stadium's concession stands would count as street food, and no one regards a stadium hot dog that way. So street food must be defined at least partly by where it is sold, not solely by how it is eaten.
questions.stem: The food writer's argument proceeds by
choices: using a case that a proposed criterion misclassifies to argue that the criterion should be replaced by one based only on location
showing that a proposed definition fails to apply to some dishes that everyone regards as street food
using a case that a proposed criterion misclassifies to argue that some further factor must figure in the definition
arguing that the critics' definition must be mistaken because the critics disagree among themselves
appealing to the way food is sold at baseball stadiums in order to establish how street food ought to be eaten
questions.explanation: The critics' criterion counts stadium hot dogs as street food, which no one accepts, and the writer concludes that where food is sold must be part of the definition, at least partly, which is (C). (A) is the trap: it describes the same move but gives the writer a stronger conclusion; she says 'at least partly by where it is sold, not solely by how it is eaten,' so how a dish is eaten can stay in the definition. (B) has the right kind of move in the wrong direction; stadium hot dogs are wrongly included, not a real street food left out.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Street food must be defined at least partly by where it's sold, not only by how it's eaten.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The critics' definition (any dish eaten standing up or on the move) would count stadium hot dogs as street food, and no one regards them that way.

breakdown.analysis: Testing a definition against a case is a classic method. Here the definition lets in stadium hot dogs, which no one calls street food, so it's too broad. Now read the conclusion word by word: "at least partly by where it is sold, not solely by how it is eaten." The writer adds a factor; she doesn't throw out the old one. So the right description has to match both the move (a case the criterion gets wrong) and the size of the conclusion (add something, don't replace everything). Two traps each miss one of those: one gets the move right and the conclusion too strong; one gets the direction of the misfit backwards.

choices.note: Tempting, because the first half is exactly right: a case the critics' criterion misclassifies. But the conclusion is too strong. The writer says "at least partly" by location and "not solely" by how it's eaten, so how a dish is eaten can still count. She never says location alone should decide.
choices.example: Example of method: Stadium hot dogs prove the eat-on-the-move test is useless; street food should be defined purely by being sold on a public street.

choices.note: Right kind of move, wrong direction. Stadium hot dogs are something the definition wrongly includes, not a real street food it leaves out.
choices.example: Example of method: Defining street food as food sold from a cart leaves out the noodle stalls of Bangkok, which everyone calls street food.

choices.note: CORRECT. The misclassified case is the stadium hot dog. The writer's lesson is modest: location has to be part of the definition, at least partly. That's "some further factor must figure in the definition."
The writer never says the critics disagree among themselves.
choices.example: Example of method: Even the critics can't agree on what street food is, so their definition can't be right.

choices.note: The stadium case is used to test a definition, not to say how street food ought to be eaten. The conclusion is about where it's sold.
choices.example: Example of method: Fans eat stadium hot dogs standing up, so street food should be eaten standing up too.

questions.stimulus:
Desmond: Diners plainly like our new house salad dressing better than the old one. Since we switched recipes in March, the number of diners who ask for extra dressing has nearly doubled.

Paloma: In March we also started putting a third less dressing on each salad, to cut costs.
questions.stem: Paloma responds to Desmond by
choices: citing a fact that suggests another explanation for a change that Desmond attributes to diners' preferences
showing that the change Desmond cites could not have resulted from diners' liking the new recipe better
offering evidence that the new recipe was adopted mainly as a way to reduce the restaurant's costs
pointing out that the change Desmond cites began before the restaurant adopted the new recipe
suggesting that the requests for extra dressing show that diners like the new dressing less than the old
questions.explanation: Desmond attributes the rise in requests for extra dressing to diners' liking the new recipe; Paloma points out that the salads now come with a third less dressing, which could explain the requests just as well, so (A) is right. (B) is the trap: it describes the right target but makes Paloma's move too strong; smaller portions offer a rival explanation, but they don't rule out that diners also like the new recipe. (E) turns her reply into a counter-conclusion, (C) attaches the cost cutting to the recipe rather than the portions, and (D) misreads 'also' in March as an earlier start.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: (Desmond) Diners like the new dressing better than the old one.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: (Desmond) Requests for extra dressing nearly doubled after the recipe switch. (Paloma) At the same time, the restaurant cut the dressing on each salad by a third.

breakdown.analysis: Desmond sees a change and picks one cause: the new recipe tastes better. Paloma names something else that changed in the same month. If each salad has a third less dressing, of course more people ask for extra. That's an alternative explanation, and it leaves Desmond's evidence proving nothing. But notice how little Paloma claims. She doesn't say the recipe had nothing to do with it, and she doesn't say diners dislike the new dressing. Maybe they love it. She just shows the doubled requests don't tell us. Every wrong answer here describes a nearby move: too strong, aimed at the wrong change, or turned into the opposite conclusion.

choices.note: CORRECT. The change is the doubling of requests for extra dressing. Desmond credits the new recipe; Paloma cites the smaller portions, which would explain the requests whether or not diners like the new recipe.

Tempting, because it aims at the right target: Desmond's explanation of the change. But "could not have resulted" is too strong. Smaller portions give a rival explanation; they don't rule out that diners also like the new recipe and ask for more because of it.
choices.example: Example of method: The requests rose only among diners who never tasted the new recipe, so liking it can't be the reason.

choices.note: Wrong target. The cost cutting Paloma mentions is the smaller portion, not the recipe change. She says nothing about why the recipe was changed.
choices.example: Example of method: We only switched to the new recipe because its ingredients are cheaper.

choices.note: Misreads the timing. "In March we also started" means the portion cut came at the same time as the recipe switch, not before it.
choices.example: Example of method: Requests for extra dressing started climbing in January, two months before we changed the recipe.

choices.note: Tempting, because Paloma's reply sinks Desmond's argument, and it's easy to hear it as "diners don't like it." But she draws no conclusion about which dressing diners prefer. Knocking out someone's evidence doesn't prove the opposite of their conclusion.
choices.example: Example of method: All those requests for extra dressing mean diners find the new dressing too thin, so they like it less.

questions.stimulus:
Alvaro: A restaurant guide should rate restaurants on their food alone. Service and décor matter to diners, of course, but a single rating that blends them with the food tells a diner who wants the best cooking almost nothing.

Beatriz: Few people open a guide to find the best cooking; most want to know where they will have the best evening out. A guide that rated only the food would send them to places where superb dishes arrive cold after an hour's wait.
questions.stem: Alvaro and Beatriz disagree over whether
choices: a single rating that combines food, service, and décor tells diners who want the best cooking very little
a guide should rate a restaurant lower because of poor service even if the restaurant's food is superb
most people who consult a restaurant guide want to know where they will have the best evening out
the service and décor of a restaurant affect how much diners enjoy an evening spent there
a restaurant guide should give separate ratings for a restaurant's food, its service, and its décor
questions.explanation: Alvaro holds that ratings should reflect food alone, so poor service should never lower a rating; Beatriz objects that a food-only rating would steer diners to places with cold dishes after an hour's wait, so she thinks service should count, which puts (B) at issue. (C) is the trap: it is Beatriz's claim, and it seems to clash with Alvaro, but Alvaro never says what most guide readers want; he speaks only of 'a diner who wants the best cooking.' (A) is Alvaro's claim, which Beatriz never contests, and (D) is common ground.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Alvaro: Rate restaurants on food alone; a blended rating tells a diner who wants the best cooking almost nothing.; Beatriz: Most people want the best evening out, not the best cooking; a food-only rating would send them to places with cold food and long waits.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no, and with hard dialogue items the answer is often a specific case of the general dispute. Alvaro: food alone. So a restaurant with superb food and terrible service gets a top rating. Beatriz: that's exactly the restaurant a food-only guide would wrongly send people to. So she thinks the bad service should pull the rating down. Now be careful with the claims about what diners want. Beatriz says most diners want a good evening. Alvaro never says what most diners want; he talks about "a diner who wants the best cooking." Those claims can both be true.

choices.note: Alvaro's claim, and Beatriz never denies it. She can grant that blended ratings don't help cooking-seekers and still say most diners aren't cooking-seekers.

CORRECT. Alvaro's "food alone" means poor service can't lower the rating. Beatriz's objection, that a food-only guide would send people to places with cold food and an hour's wait, means she thinks service should count against a restaurant. Yes versus no.

Tempting, because it's Beatriz's opening claim and it sounds like a direct reply to Alvaro. But Alvaro never says what most guide readers want. His point is conditional: for a diner who wants the best cooking, a blended rating says little. He takes no side on how many diners that is.
Common ground. Alvaro says service and décor "matter to diners, of course," and Beatriz's whole point depends on that.
Neither speaker proposes separate ratings. Alvaro wants one rating based on food; Beatriz wants ratings that reflect the whole evening.

questions.stimulus: Last year Talon kettles made up 30 percent of the electric kettles sold by Brightwell Stores but 60 percent of the kettles that customers returned to Brightwell. So a Talon kettle bought at Brightwell last year was more likely to be defective than a kettle of another brand bought there.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: At least half of the Talon kettles that customers returned to Brightwell last year were in fact defective.
Brightwell sold more Talon kettles last year than it sold kettles of any other single brand.
A defective kettle of another brand was at least as likely to be returned to Brightwell as a defective Talon kettle was.
Talon buyers were not so much more prone to return working kettles that this alone explains the gap in return rates.
Most customers who returned a Talon kettle to Brightwell last year did not buy another Talon kettle to replace it.
questions.explanation: Talons were returned at a much higher rate (60 percent of returns from 30 percent of sales), and the argument reads that gap as a gap in defects; it needs the gap not to be explained entirely by Talon buyers' returning working kettles more readily, which is (D). (A) is the trap: it sounds necessary, but the return-rate gap is so large that even if fewer than half of returned Talons were defective, Talons could still be the more defect-prone brand. (C) is too strong; defective kettles of other brands could be returned slightly less often without erasing the gap.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: A Talon kettle bought at Brightwell last year was more likely to be defective than another brand's kettle.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Talons were 30 percent of kettles sold but 60 percent of kettles returned.

breakdown.analysis: First, the numbers. Say Brightwell sold 1,000 kettles and got 100 back. Talons: 300 sold, 60 returned, a 20 percent return rate. Others: 700 sold, 40 returned, under 6 percent. So Talons come back at more than three times the rate. The argument turns that into "more likely to be defective." But people return kettles for lots of reasons: they were a gift, they're the wrong color, they're too loud. What if Talon buyers just return things more readily? We need an answer that says that difference in return habits isn't the whole story. And watch the trap that asks for too much: with a gap this big, the argument doesn't need most returned Talons to be defective. If only 25 of the 60 returned Talons were defective, that's still about 8 percent of Talons against at most about 6 percent of the others.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like it must be true for returns to mean defects. But run the numbers from the analysis. Even if only about 40 percent of returned Talons were defective, Talons' defect rate (about 8 percent) still beats the others' maximum (about 6 percent). Negate it and the argument survives.
choices.negation: Fewer than half of the Talon kettles that customers returned to Brightwell last year were defective.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The argument compares rates, not which brand sold the most. Negate it and nothing changes.
choices.negation: Brightwell sold at least as many kettles of some other single brand as it sold Talon kettles.

choices.note: Too strong. Negate it: a defective non-Talon was somewhat less likely to be returned than a defective Talon. A small difference like that can't explain a return rate more than three times as high. The argument survives.
choices.negation: A defective kettle of another brand was less likely to be returned to Brightwell than a defective Talon kettle was.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: Talon buyers were so much more prone to return working kettles that this alone explains the gap. Then the higher return rate says nothing about defects, and the conclusion has no support.
choices.negation: Talon buyers were so much more prone to return working kettles that this alone explains the gap in return rates.

choices.note: What customers bought next has nothing to do with whether the returned kettles were defective.
choices.negation: Most customers who returned a Talon kettle to Brightwell last year bought another Talon kettle to replace it.

questions.stimulus: Restaurant consultant: Some owners favor open kitchens, in which diners can watch the cooks at work, on the grounds that cooks who know they are being watched are more careful about hygiene. But diners can see only the cooking line, not the prep rooms and walk-in coolers where most contamination of food begins. So open kitchens do little to make restaurant food safer, however much they may reassure diners.
questions.stem: The claim that cooks who know they are being watched are more careful about hygiene figures in the consultant's argument in which one of the following ways?
choices: It is a claim that the consultant argues is false, on the grounds that diners cannot see the prep rooms.
It is offered as support for the consultant's further view that open kitchens may well reassure diners.
It is cited in support of a position that the main conclusion of the argument opposes.
It is a premise that, together with the claim about prep rooms and coolers, supports the main conclusion.
It is the main conclusion of the owners' argument, a conclusion that the consultant accepts only in part.
questions.explanation: The owners cite the claim to support their view that open kitchens make food safer; the consultant concludes that open kitchens do little for safety, so the claim supports a position the conclusion opposes, as (C) says. (A) is the trap: the consultant argues against the owners' view, but not against this claim; she grants that watched cooks may be more careful and argues that it matters little, because most contamination begins where diners can't see. (E) misplaces the claim, which is the owners' reason, not their conclusion.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Open kitchens do little to make restaurant food safer.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Diners see only the cooking line, not the prep rooms and coolers where most contamination begins. (Opposing view: open kitchens improve safety, because watched cooks are more careful about hygiene.)

breakdown.analysis: Whose claim is this? "On the grounds that" tells you: it's the owners' reason for favoring open kitchens. So it supports their view, that open kitchens make food safer, and the consultant's conclusion opposes that view. Now the hard part: does the consultant say the claim is false? No. She never denies that watched cooks are more careful. Her move is that it doesn't matter much: the cooks being watched aren't where most contamination starts. Rejecting an argument doesn't mean rejecting each of its premises. It's like saying "Sure, the bouncer checks IDs at the front door, but people come in through the back."

choices.note: Tempting, because the consultant clearly argues against the owners, and this is the owners' premise. But she never says watched cooks aren't more careful. Her point about the prep rooms shows the extra care on the line wouldn't make much difference, not that it doesn't exist.
The reassurance point comes at the end and isn't supported by this claim. Cooks being more careful is about safety, not about how diners feel.

CORRECT. The owners offer the claim as their reason for thinking open kitchens improve safety. The consultant's main conclusion, that open kitchens do little to make food safer, opposes that position.
The prep-room claim supports the consultant's conclusion; this claim supports the other side. They don't work together.
It's the owners' reason, not their conclusion. Their conclusion is that open kitchens make food safer; "on the grounds that" introduces their support.

questions.stimulus:
Kofi: Our catering company should never discipline an employee for reporting a safety hazard, even if the report turns out to be false. Employees who fear punishment will keep quiet about real hazards.

Dana: I agree that honest mistakes should go unpunished. But last month one of our drivers reported a gas leak he knew was imaginary, just to get out of a delivery, and he was rightly suspended for it.
questions.stem: Kofi and Dana disagree over whether
choices: an employee whose report of a hazard proves mistaken should go unpunished if the report was made in good faith
fear of punishment would lead some employees to keep quiet about hazards that are real
the driver who reported a gas leak did so in order to get out of making a delivery
the catering company should adopt a written policy stating when employees may be disciplined
the driver who reported an imaginary gas leak deserved to be disciplined for making that report
questions.explanation: Kofi's rule is that an employee should never be disciplined for reporting a hazard, even if the report is false; the driver's report was a false hazard report, so Kofi is committed to saying the driver should not have been disciplined, while Dana says he was rightly suspended, which is (E). (A) is the trap: it is the issue the dialogue seems to be about, but both speakers agree on it, Kofi by his 'even if the report turns out to be false' and Dana by 'honest mistakes should go unpunished.' (B) is Kofi's claim alone, and (C) is Dana's.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Kofi: Never discipline an employee for reporting a hazard, even if the report is false; fear of punishment silences real reports.; Dana: Honest mistakes should go unpunished, but a driver who knowingly invented a gas leak to skip a delivery was rightly suspended.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Dana opens with "I agree," so the honest-mistake case is settled.
