The trick is that Kofi's rule is broader than honest mistakes. "Never ... even if the report turns out to be false" covers every false report, including one the employee made up. Rule: hazard report → no discipline. The driver made a hazard report. So by Kofi's rule, no discipline. Dana says he was rightly suspended. Kofi never mentions the driver, but his "never" commits him anyway. Absolute words like "never" lock a speaker into cases he didn't think about.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's the issue Kofi seems to be raising. But both agree on it. Kofi's rule protects false reports, honest ones included, and Dana says "honest mistakes should go unpunished." Agreement can't be the point at issue.
Kofi's claim only. Dana never says whether fear of punishment would silence employees; she just carves out deliberate lies.
Dana's claim only. Kofi says nothing about the driver or his motives.
Neither speaker mentions a written policy.

CORRECT. Kofi's "never discipline ... even if the report turns out to be false" covers the driver's false report, so Kofi is committed to no. Dana says the driver "was rightly suspended," so she says yes.

questions.stimulus: Hospitality researcher: Over the past two years, hotels in the Rossmere chain that replaced their printed room-service menus with menus shown on each room's television saw room-service orders fall by about a quarter. The likely reason is that guests find a menu on a television screen harder to browse than a printed one.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the researcher's argument?
choices: Guests at the hotels that switched find on-screen menus harder to browse than any other kind of menu they encounter.
Room-service orders at Rossmere hotels that kept their printed menus did not fall at all over the same two years.
Every guest who stopped ordering room service after the switch did so because the on-screen menu was hard to browse.
Room-service orders did not fall by a similar proportion over those two years at Rossmere hotels that kept printed menus.
Guests at Rossmere hotels order room service more often when they travel on business than when they travel for pleasure.
questions.explanation: If orders fell by about a quarter at Rossmere hotels that kept printed menus too, the decline reflects something affecting all the hotels and the on-screen menus explain nothing, so the argument needs (D). (B) is the trap: it is the same comparison pushed to an extreme; orders at the printed-menu hotels could have dipped a little, and a much larger fall at the switching hotels would still point to the screens. (C) is too strong in the same way, since the screens need explain only much of the decline.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The likely reason room-service orders fell is that guests find on-screen menus harder to browse.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: At Rossmere hotels that switched to on-screen menus, room-service orders fell by about a quarter over two years.

breakdown.analysis: Fell compared with what? The researcher only tells us about hotels that switched. Two years is plenty of time for something else to change: delivery apps, fewer business travelers, higher prices across the chain. If the hotels that kept paper menus lost a quarter of their orders too, the screens have nothing to do with it. We need the comparison group to have done better. But how much better? Not perfectly. The argument needs only that the hotels that kept paper didn't fall by about as much. Watch for the answer that demands "not at all."

choices.note: Too strong. The argument needs on-screen menus to be harder to browse than printed ones, not harder than every menu guests ever see.
choices.negation: Guests at the hotels that switched find some other kind of menu at least as hard to browse as on-screen menus.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's the right comparison group. But "not at all" is too strong. Negate it: orders at the printed-menu hotels fell a little, say 3 percent. A 25 percent drop at the switching hotels still stands out and still points to the screens. The argument survives.
choices.negation: Room-service orders at Rossmere hotels that kept their printed menus fell at least somewhat over the same two years.

choices.note: Too strong. "The likely reason" doesn't mean every lost order is due to the screens. Negate it: one guest stopped ordering for some other reason. The argument barely notices.
choices.negation: At least one guest who stopped ordering room service after the switch did so for some reason other than the on-screen menu.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the printed-menu hotels saw a similar drop. Then the decline happened with or without the screens, and the screens can't be the likely reason. The argument collapses.
choices.negation: Room-service orders fell by a similar proportion over those two years at Rossmere hotels that kept printed menus.

choices.note: Interesting fact, but not relevant. Why guests travel doesn't tell us whether the menus caused the drop.
choices.negation: Guests at Rossmere hotels do not order room service more often when they travel on business than when they travel for pleasure.

questions.stimulus: Management consultant: The Quarle Company's plan to save money by letting its experienced office assistants go and hiring temporary workers in their place will probably end up costing the company more than it saves. Temporary workers would need weeks to learn the company's filing and scheduling systems. After all, those systems were designed in-house and are used nowhere else, so no temporary worker could already know them.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the consultant's argument by the claim that temporary workers would need weeks to learn the company's filing and scheduling systems?
choices: It is the argument's main conclusion, and the claim that the systems are used nowhere else is offered in support of it.
It is a claim for which the argument offers support and which in turn helps explain why the plan would probably prove costly.
It is a premise that supports the argument's main conclusion and is not itself supported by any other claim in the argument.
It is a consideration that the consultant concedes to the company before arguing that the plan will cost more than it saves.
It is offered as support for the claim that the company's filing and scheduling systems are used nowhere else.
questions.explanation: The claim is backed by the 'After all' sentence (the systems are unique to Quarle, so no temporary worker could know them), and it is the reason the plan would probably cost more than it saves; (B) describes that intermediate role without naming it. (A) is the trap: support follows the claim directly and the opening sentence has no indicator, so the claim looks like the conclusion, but it is itself a reason for the opening prediction. (C) gets the support for the main conclusion right but misses that 'After all' introduces support for the claim.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The plan to replace experienced assistants with temporary workers will probably cost Quarle more than it saves.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The systems were designed in-house and are used nowhere else; so no temporary worker could already know them; so temporary workers would need weeks to learn them.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The first sentence is a prediction with no indicator, and everything else serves it: why would the plan cost money? Because temps would need weeks to learn the systems. Why would they need weeks? "After all" tells you: the systems are unique to Quarle, so nobody arrives knowing them. So the claim in the stem sits in the middle, propped up from below and propping up the prediction above it. The right answer never says "intermediate conclusion"; it says the claim gets support and helps explain why the plan would backfire. Most students pick (A), because the "After all" sentence attaches directly to this claim and the opening sentence looks like background. It isn't background; it's what the whole argument is for.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. The "After all" sentence does support this claim directly, and the opening sentence has no indicator word. But the claim is itself a reason for the opening prediction: the plan costs money because temps need weeks to get up to speed. A claim that supports another claim isn't the main conclusion.

CORRECT. The argument supports the claim (unique systems, so no temp already knows them), and the claim is why the plan would probably cost more than it saves. Supported and supporting: an intermediate conclusion, described without the label.
Half right. It does support the main conclusion. But "After all" introduces support for it, so it isn't unsupported, and half right is wrong on role questions.
Nothing is conceded to the company. The claim is the consultant's own reason against the plan, not a point granted to the other side.
Backwards. The fact that the systems are used nowhere else supports this claim, not the other way around.

questions.stimulus:
Marisol: The Torvald Hotel's fee for early check-in is unfair as the hotel applies it. Guests are charged the fee even when their rooms happen to be ready hours before the official check-in time.

Gavin: It's only fair for a hotel to charge for a service that costs it extra money, and early check-in does: housekeepers must rush to prepare the room ahead of schedule, and that means paying for extra staff. So the fee is fair.
questions.stem: Gavin's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: takes for granted that any fee that a hotel's guests are willing to pay must be a fair one
misrepresents Marisol as objecting to each and every fee that the Torvald Hotel charges to its guests
fails to consider the possibility that rushing to prepare a room does not require a hotel to pay for extra staff
presumes, without providing justification, that the Torvald Hotel's official check-in time is a reasonable one
relies on a consideration that does not apply to the cases on which Marisol bases her criticism
questions.explanation: Marisol objects only to charging guests whose rooms are already ready; Gavin defends the fee by citing the cost of rushing to prepare rooms early, which doesn't arise when a room is already ready, so his reason misses her cases, as (E) says. (C) is the trap: it attacks Gavin's premise that rushing requires extra staff, but the trouble is not that this premise may be false; even if it is true, it doesn't apply to the guests Marisol is talking about. (B) is wrong because Gavin never attributes any broader objection to Marisol.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: (Gavin) The early check-in fee is fair.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: (Gavin) Charging for services that cost the hotel extra is fair; early check-in costs extra because housekeepers must rush, which requires extra staff. (Marisol's objection: guests are charged even when rooms are ready hours early.)

breakdown.analysis: What exactly did Marisol object to? Not the fee in general. The fee "as the hotel applies it": charging guests whose rooms are already ready. Now look at Gavin's reason: early check-in costs money because housekeepers must rush. When the room is already ready, nobody rushes. So Gavin's justification covers the cases Marisol never complained about and skips the ones she did. It's like defending a delivery charge by citing fuel costs when the complaint was about being charged for in-store pickup. Watch for answers that attack Gavin's premise; the flaw isn't that his facts are wrong, it's that they don't apply.

choices.note: Gavin never mentions what guests are willing to pay. His reason is the hotel's extra cost.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Guests keep paying the early check-in fee without complaint, so it must be fair.

choices.note: Tempting, because Gavin does answer a broader question than the one Marisol raised. But misrepresenting someone means attributing a position to them. Gavin never says what Marisol believes; he just defends the fee in general, which is what (E) describes.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Marisol thinks hotels shouldn't charge for anything beyond the room itself, and that's absurd.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's a real-sounding hole in Gavin's story. But it attacks his premise. On the LSAT, you take premises as given. Even if rushing really does require extra staff, Gavin's reason still misses Marisol's point, because in her cases there's no rushing at all.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Rushing doesn't cost anything, since the housekeepers are on salary; Gavin overlooks this.

choices.note: The official check-in time plays no part in Gavin's reasoning, and nothing turns on whether it is reasonable.
choices.example: Example of flaw: A 4 p.m. check-in is standard, so charging guests who arrive earlier is fair.

choices.note: CORRECT. Gavin's consideration is the cost of rushing to prepare a room early. Marisol's cases are guests whose rooms are already ready, where no rushing happens. His reason doesn't touch her complaint.

questions.stimulus: Company spokesperson: Before Dunlow Hardware began pairing each new hire with an experienced mentor, 40 percent of its new hires were still with the company two years after being hired. Now 55 percent are. So the mentoring program has made new hires less likely to leave the company during their first year.
questions.stem: The spokesperson's argument requires the assumption that
choices: the rise in the share of new hires still employed after two years is not due entirely to fewer second-year departures
most new hires who would have left in their first year without a mentor stayed at least two years because of their mentors
no change at Dunlow Hardware other than the mentoring program has had any effect on how long new hires stay with the company
the percentage of Dunlow Hardware's new hires who leave the company during their second year has not risen since the program began
new hires who were paired with mentors rate their satisfaction with their jobs more highly than earlier new hires did
questions.explanation: The evidence is about who is still employed after two years, but the conclusion is about leaving in the first year; if the entire rise came from fewer second-year departures, first-year departures didn't fall at all, so the argument needs (A). (D) is the trap: it sounds like a needed defender, but if second-year departures rose while two-year retention still climbed, first-year departures must have fallen even more, which helps the argument. (B) and (C) are far stronger than the argument needs.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The mentoring program has made new hires less likely to leave in their first year.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Before mentoring, 40 percent of new hires were still there after two years; now 55 percent are.

breakdown.analysis: The evidence covers two years; the conclusion covers one. Two-year retention can rise in two ways: fewer people leave in year one, or fewer leave in year two. What if all of the improvement is in year two? Say 30 percent used to leave in year one and 30 percent in year two (40 left). Now 30 percent still leave in year one and only 15 percent in year two (55 left). Year one didn't change at all, and the conclusion is false. So the argument needs at least some of the rise to come from year one. A total can hide what's happening in its parts.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the whole rise came from fewer second-year departures. Then first-year departures didn't drop, and the conclusion is wrong. The argument collapses.
choices.negation: The rise in the share of new hires still employed after two years is due entirely to fewer second-year departures.

choices.note: Too strong. Negate it: mentoring kept fewer than half of the would-be first-year leavers. It could still have made new hires somewhat less likely to leave in year one. The argument survives.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most new hires who would have left in their first year without a mentor stayed at least two years because of their mentors.

choices.note: Too strong. Negate it: some other change also affected how long new hires stay. Mentoring could still have reduced first-year departures. The argument survives.
choices.negation: Some change at Dunlow Hardware other than the mentoring program has affected how long new hires stay with the company.

choices.note: Tempting, because it looks like it rules out a complication. But negate it: second-year departures rose. Two-year retention went up anyway, so first-year departures must have fallen by even more. That helps the argument. Not required.
choices.negation: The percentage of Dunlow Hardware's new hires who leave during their second year has risen since the program began.

choices.note: Satisfaction isn't the issue. The conclusion is about whether new hires leave, not how they feel.
choices.negation: New hires who were paired with mentors do not rate their job satisfaction more highly than earlier new hires did.

questions.stimulus: Union representative: The Mirefield Department Store's handbook says that a salesclerk should be rated 'exemplary' only if no customer has ever complained about that clerk. But some customers will complain about anyone. Under that standard, then, even Miriam Ostrow, whom the handbook itself holds up as a model for new clerks, could not be rated exemplary. The standard is plainly unreasonable and should be revised.
questions.stem: The claim that even Miriam Ostrow could not be rated exemplary under the handbook's standard plays which one of the following roles in the union representative's argument?
choices: It is a judgment about Miriam Ostrow that the representative endorses in order to show that the handbook's praise of her is undeserved.
It is the main conclusion of the argument, and the claim that some customers will complain about anyone is offered to support it.
It is offered as evidence that some customers will complain about any salesclerk, however good that clerk is.
It is a consequence the representative draws from the handbook's standard, offered to show that the standard is unreasonable.
It is a premise that the handbook itself relies on to support the standard that the representative goes on to criticize.
questions.explanation: The representative derives the claim from the handbook's standard ('then') and uses its absurdity, that the store's own model clerk would fail, to support the conclusion that the standard is unreasonable, as (D) says. (A) is the trap: it takes the claim as the representative's own verdict on Ostrow, but the representative doesn't think Ostrow falls short; the claim is a result of the standard that the representative rejects. (B) misses that the claim supports the final sentence, which is the main conclusion.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The handbook's standard for an 'exemplary' rating is unreasonable and should be revised.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Exemplary → no customer has ever complained; some customers complain about anyone; so even Miriam Ostrow, the handbook's own model clerk, couldn't be rated exemplary.

breakdown.analysis: Spell out the rule: exemplary → no complaints, ever. Contrapositive: any complaint → not exemplary. Add "some customers will complain about anyone," and nobody qualifies, not even the clerk the handbook itself holds up as a model. The representative doesn't believe Ostrow is less than exemplary. That's the absurd result used to sink the rule. If a rule says your star employee fails, the rule is the problem. So the claim is a consequence drawn from the standard, offered to show the standard is unreasonable.

choices.note: Tempting, because the sentence is a statement about Ostrow, and it's in the representative's mouth. But the representative doesn't endorse it as a verdict on her. It's what the handbook's standard would imply, and the representative treats that as proof the standard is broken, not that Ostrow is overrated.

It carries "then," so it is drawn from earlier claims, but it isn't where the argument ends. The final sentence, that the standard is unreasonable and should be revised, is what this claim is used to support.
Backwards. "Some customers will complain about anyone" is a premise used to derive the claim about Ostrow, not the other way around.

CORRECT. The claim follows from the standard plus the premise about complainers ("then"), and the representative uses it to show the standard is unreasonable. It's a consequence the author rejects, used to sink the rule.
The handbook doesn't use this claim at all. The handbook praises Ostrow; the representative is the one pointing out that its standard would exclude her.

sections.title: Skill Builder: Hard Sufficient Assumption, Principle & Parallel

questions.stimulus: Under the bylaws of the Corliss Court housing cooperative, a member may sublet an apartment only if the cooperative's board has approved the subtenant, and the board approves no subtenant who has not been interviewed by at least two board members. Most subtenants the board approved last year were relatives of members. Joaquin's proposed subtenant cannot attend any of the board's interview sessions. Hence, Joaquin may not sublet his apartment to that person.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Any proposed subtenant who has been interviewed by at least two board members will be approved by the board.
The board is less likely to approve a proposed subtenant who is not a relative of the member who wishes to sublet.
Board members interview proposed subtenants only during the interview sessions that the cooperative's board holds for that purpose.
At least two board members will be unavailable to meet with Joaquin's proposed subtenant before the sublet would begin.
A member who sublets without the board's approval may be required by the cooperative to give up his or her membership.
questions.explanation: The chain runs: sublet → board approval → interviewed by at least two board members. The premises say only that the subtenant can't attend the board's sessions, so the argument needs interviews to happen nowhere else, which is (C). (A) reverses the interview rule, telling us what happens when someone is interviewed rather than when they aren't. (D) is tempting but too weak: two members being unavailable leaves the others free to interview. (B) leans on the decoy about relatives, and (E) describes a penalty the conclusion never needs.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Joaquin may not sublet to his proposed subtenant.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Sublet → board approved the subtenant → subtenant interviewed by at least two board members; the subtenant can't attend any of the board's interview sessions; (most approved subtenants were relatives).

breakdown.analysis: So the subtenant can't come to the board's sessions. So what? Who says the board only interviews at its sessions? Maybe two members meet him for coffee. The chain is: Sublet → approved → interviewed by 2+. We need to get from "can't attend the sessions" to "not interviewed." We need an answer that says interviews happen only at those sessions. It's like saying "I can't make any of the open-house dates, so I won't see the apartment," which works only if the landlord never shows it any other time. The line about relatives is a decoy; the conclusion never needs it.

choices.note: This reverses the interview rule. The stimulus says interviewed is necessary for approval; (A) makes it sufficient. And it tells us about people who were interviewed, while our subtenant is someone who (we hope) wasn't.
Built on the decoy premise about relatives. We don't even know whether this subtenant is a relative, and "less likely" can never prove "may not."
CORRECT. If interviews happen only at the board's sessions and the subtenant can't attend any, he can't be interviewed. Not interviewed → not approved → no sublet. The chain is complete.

Tempting, because it sounds like proof he can't get his two interviews. But it's too weak. If the board has seven members, two being unavailable leaves five who could still interview him. Even "at least two unavailable" doesn't mean fewer than two available.
So? This describes what happens after an unapproved sublet. The conclusion is about whether he may sublet in the first place, and this choice doesn't connect the subtenant to the approval rule.

questions.stimulus: Most of the people who donate to the Corwin Literacy Fund give through automatic monthly payments, and everyone who gives through automatic monthly payments is sent the fund's quarterly report. It follows that most of the Corwin Literacy Fund's donors are sent its quarterly report.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Most of the apartments in the Belvane complex are leased on two-year terms, and every apartment there that is leased on a two-year term comes with a reserved parking space. So most of the Belvane complex's apartments come with one.

Most of the members of the Fairhill hiking club own waterproof boots, and most of the people who own waterproof boots also own trekking poles. So most of the members of the Fairhill hiking club own trekking poles.

Every agent at the Ellery Realty office has passed the state licensing exam, and most people who have passed that exam have also taken an appraisal course. So most of the agents at the Ellery Realty office have taken an appraisal course.

Most of the vendors at the Saturday market in Hale accept credit cards, and every vendor at the market that sells produce accepts credit cards. So most of the vendors at the Saturday market in Hale sell produce.

Most of the novels on the Ravel Library's new-arrivals shelf were written by local authors, and every novel written by a local author is listed in the regional catalog. So most of the library's novels are listed in the regional catalog.
questions.explanation: The argument is valid: most A are B, every B is C, so most A are C. (A) matches exactly with apartments, two-year leases and parking spaces. (C) reuses the quantifiers in the wrong order, all-then-most, which is invalid. (B) chains two "most" statements, (D) reverses the "every" link, and (E) shifts its conclusion from the new-arrivals shelf to all of the library's novels.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most of the fund's donors are sent the quarterly report.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most donors give by automatic monthly payment; everyone who gives that way is sent the report.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Most A are B; all B are C; so most A are C.

breakdown.analysis: Is this valid? Yes. If most donors are monthly givers and every monthly giver gets the report, those same donors (more than half) all get it. Most A are B; all B are C; so most A are C. Picture 10 donors: 6 give monthly, all 6 get the report, so at least 6 of 10 get it. We need a choice with "most" first, "every" second, linking in the same direction, and a "most" conclusion about the original group. Ignore topic and match the quantifiers and their order. A choice that uses the same words in different slots is the decoy.

choices.note: CORRECT. Most apartments are two-year leases (most A are B); every two-year lease has parking (all B are C); so most apartments have parking (most A are C). Same quantifiers, same direction, same group in the conclusion.
Most + most doesn't chain. The boot owners who own poles could be people outside the club. Most A are B, most B are C, so most A are C is invalid; the original is valid.

Same words, wrong slots. Every agent passed the exam (all A are B), and most exam-passers took the course (most B are C), so most agents took it? Invalid: the agents could all be among the minority of exam-passers who skipped the course. The original runs most-then-every; this runs every-then-most.
This reverses the "every" link. It says every produce seller accepts cards (all C are B), not that every card-taker sells produce. From that you can't conclude most vendors sell produce.

Close, but the conclusion jumps to a different group. The premises are about novels on the new-arrivals shelf, and the conclusion is about all of the library's novels. The original concludes about the same group it started with.

questions.stimulus: Principle: A financial adviser should recommend to a client an investment that pays the adviser a commission only if the adviser has told the client about the commission and no comparable investment that pays no commission would serve the client better.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: Dana told her client about the commission on the bond fund she recommended, and no commission-free fund would have served the client better, so she was right to recommend it.
Malik never mentioned to his client that a stock he recommended had nearly doubled in price the year before, so Malik should not have recommended that stock.
Inez recommended a commission-free index fund without mentioning that a fund paying her a commission would have served her client slightly better, so she should not have recommended it.
Because Tomas's client learned about the commission only after buying the annuity Tomas had recommended, Tomas should give the client a refund of that commission.
Ruth told her client about the commission on the annuity she recommended, but a commission-free annuity would have served the client better, so Ruth should not have recommended it.
questions.explanation: The principle sets two necessary conditions for recommending a commission-paying investment: disclosure, and no better commission-free option. Ruth disclosed but failed the second condition, so she should not have recommended the annuity, as (E) says. (A) is the trap: Dana meets both conditions, but meeting necessary conditions doesn't make a recommendation right. (C) applies the rule to a commission-free fund, which it doesn't cover; (B) concerns a stock whose commission status is unknown; and (D) reaches a verdict (a refund) the principle never mentions.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Should recommend a commission-paying investment → told client about the commission AND no comparable commission-free investment would serve the client better.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Find a case where a commission-paying investment was recommended and one of the two conditions failed, concluding the adviser should not have recommended it.

breakdown.analysis: "Only if" introduces necessary conditions. So the principle can only tell you when an adviser should NOT recommend something: if either condition fails, the recommendation was improper. It can never tell you a recommendation was right. Contrapositive: not told OR a better commission-free option existed → should not recommend. We need an answer where: 1. the investment pays a commission; 2. disclosure was missing or a better commission-free option existed; 3. verdict: should not have recommended it. It's like "you may drive only if you have a license and insurance." Having both doesn't mean you should drive; missing either means you shouldn't.

choices.note: Tempting, because Dana checks every box. But checking every necessary box doesn't make the recommendation right. The principle never says when a recommendation is proper, so "right to recommend it" goes beyond the rule.
Wrong topic. The principle is about disclosing a commission, not past price gains. We don't even know whether this stock paid Malik a commission.
Wrong half of the rule. The principle governs recommending an investment that pays a commission. Inez recommended a commission-free fund, so the principle doesn't apply at all.
Wrong verdict. The principle tells you whether to recommend, not what to do afterward. Refunds appear nowhere in it.

CORRECT. The annuity paid Ruth a commission, and a commission-free annuity would have served the client better. That second condition fails, so the principle says she should not have recommended it. Her disclosure doesn't save her; both conditions are required.

questions.stimulus: Banker: At Eastholm Savings, a checking account is charged a monthly maintenance fee unless its holder either keeps a balance above $1,500 or also holds a savings account with us. Accounts opened through our student program rarely keep balances that high. Leila's checking account was opened through the student program, and its balance has never exceeded $400. So Leila's account is charged the monthly fee.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the banker's argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Every Eastholm checking account that is charged the monthly maintenance fee has a balance at or below $1,500.
No one who opened a checking account through Eastholm's student program holds any other account at the bank.
Most customers who opened checking accounts through the student program have never held a savings account at any bank.
Leila's checking account balance is unlikely to rise above $1,500 at any time while the account remains open.
Customers who hold a savings account at Eastholm Savings are never charged the monthly maintenance fee on their checking accounts.
questions.explanation: "Unless" gives: no balance above $1,500 AND no savings account → fee. Leila's balance is covered, so the argument needs her to have no Eastholm savings account. (B) supplies that for every student-program customer, Leila included. (A) reverses the rule, (C) is only "most" and about any bank, (D) re-proves the balance half that is already settled, and (E) restates the exemption without saying whether Leila has a savings account.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Leila's account is charged the monthly fee.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Fee unless balance above $1,500 or a savings account at the bank; Leila's balance has never exceeded $400; her account came through the student program (whose accounts rarely have high balances).

breakdown.analysis: Translate the "unless": NOT balance over $1,500 AND NOT savings account → fee. Leila's balance never tops $400, so the first escape hatch is closed. What about the second? Nobody says she lacks a savings account. That's the gap. We need an answer that rules out a savings account for Leila. It's like a gym that waives the fee for members who attend twice a week or have a family plan: knowing you never show up doesn't settle your bill until we know you have no family plan. The "rarely keep balances that high" line is a decoy, since Leila's own balance is already known.

choices.note: This reverses the rule. The stimulus says low balance (plus no savings) → fee; (A) says fee → low balance. It tells us nothing about whether Leila is charged.

CORRECT. If student-program customers hold no other Eastholm account, Leila has no savings account there. Both escape hatches are closed: balance ≤ $400 and no savings → fee. It's phrased as a general rule about the program, which hides it a bit, but it covers Leila.
Too weak. "Most" leaves room for Leila to be in the minority with an Eastholm savings account. And "at any bank" adds nothing useful.
This re-proves the half we already have. Her balance has never exceeded $400. The open question is the savings account, and this choice ignores it.
This just repeats the exemption in the rule. It doesn't tell us whether Leila holds a savings account, so the gap stays open.

questions.stimulus: Every homeowner in the Sorrel Hill subdivision who bought flood insurance this year attended the county's information session on flood risk. But some homeowners in the subdivision did not attend that session. Therefore, some homeowners in the Sorrel Hill subdivision did not buy flood insurance this year.
questions.stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Every member of the Arden choir who sings solos has taken private voice lessons, and some members of the Arden choir have taken private voice lessons. Therefore, some members of the Arden choir sing solos.

Every tenant in the Larch Street building who joined the renters' association later signed the group's petition. But some tenants in the building never joined the association. Therefore, some of them did not sign the petition.

Most of the tenants at Morrow Tower who signed two-year leases received a rent discount. But some tenants at Morrow Tower received no rent discount. Therefore, some tenants at Morrow Tower did not sign two-year leases.

Some nurses at the Pine Hill clinic are not certified in pediatric care, since every nurse there who is certified in pediatric care has completed the Larsen program, and some of the clinic's nurses have not.

Every bakery in Fenton that sells sourdough bread bakes it on the premises. But some bakeries in Fenton bake nothing on the premises. Therefore, those bakeries should begin baking on the premises so that they can sell sourdough.
questions.explanation: The argument is valid: every insured homeowner attended, some homeowners didn't attend, so those homeowners aren't insured (all A are B; some C not B; so some C not A). (D) has the same skeleton with its conclusion stated first: every certified nurse completed the program, some nurses didn't, so some nurses aren't certified. (B) mirrors the wording but reverses the conditional, (A) affirms the necessary condition, (C) weakens "every" to "most," and (E) ends in a recommendation.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Some Sorrel Hill homeowners did not buy flood insurance this year.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Bought flood insurance → attended the session; some homeowners did not attend.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Every A is B; some members of the group are not B; so some members of the group are not A.

breakdown.analysis: Bought insurance → attended. Contrapositive: didn't attend → didn't buy. Some homeowners didn't attend, so those homeowners didn't buy. Valid. The match needs an "every" rule, a "some are not" fact that denies the rule's necessary condition, and a "some are not" conclusion. Watch out: a correct answer can put its conclusion first ("X, since..."). Don't let the order fool you; rebuild the skeleton.

choices.note: This affirms the necessary condition. Solos → lessons; some have lessons; so some sing solos. Having lessons doesn't mean you sing solos. Invalid, unlike the original.

Tempting, because it mirrors the stimulus sentence for sentence. But the rule is flipped: joined → signed. Not joining tells you nothing about signing; nonmembers could have signed too. That's denying the antecedent, a reversed conditional dressed in the original's wording.
"Most" isn't "every." If only most two-year signers got the discount, the people without a discount could all be the signers who missed out. The conclusion doesn't follow, while the original's does.

CORRECT. Conclusion first, then the premises. Certified → completed Larsen; some nurses didn't complete it; so some nurses aren't certified. Every A is B; some not B; so some not A. Exactly the original's pattern.
The premises line up, but the conclusion is a recommendation ("should begin baking"). The original concludes a fact. Different conclusion type, different pattern.

questions.stimulus: Board member: The Pellham Hospice should not hold its benefit gala again this year. Last year the gala cost more to stage than it raised, though it did attract several new volunteers. By contrast, each of the hospice's other fundraising events brought in more money than it cost to hold.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the board member's argument?
choices: A charity should hold a fundraising event again whenever that event raised more money than it cost the last time the charity held it.
A charity should not repeat a fundraising event that cost more than it raised the last time it was held, even if the event had other benefits.
A charity should value an event that attracts new volunteers more highly than one that merely raises money from people who already give.
A charity's board should review the costs of each of its fundraising events at least once a year before deciding which ones to hold again.
A charity should drop whichever of its fundraising events raises the smallest total amount in donations over the course of each year.
questions.explanation: The conclusion is that the gala should not be held again; the support is that it lost money last time, despite bringing in volunteers. (B) says exactly that: don't repeat an event that cost more than it raised, even if it had other benefits. (A) is the trap: it tells a charity when to repeat an event, and the gala doesn't meet its condition, so it says nothing about dropping it. (E) needs the gala to raise the smallest total, which we don't know; (C) points the other way; and (D) concerns procedure.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The hospice should not hold its gala again this year.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Last year the gala cost more than it raised (though it attracted volunteers); every other event raised more than it cost.

breakdown.analysis: The board member wants to drop the gala because it lost money, and brushes off the volunteers it attracted. A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says: not hold the gala. So we need: lost money last time → don't repeat, and the volunteer benefit shouldn't change that. Lost money → should not repeat. Watch for an answer that only tells you when to hold an event. That's the other half of the rule and can't justify cancelling anything.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's about the money test. But it gives a sufficient condition for holding an event again: raised more than it cost → hold it. The gala fails that condition, and failing a sufficient condition tells you nothing. It can't justify cancelling.
CORRECT. Cost more than it raised last time → don't repeat, even with other benefits. The gala lost money and its benefit (volunteers) is set aside. That gives exactly the conclusion.
Opposite direction. If anything this favors the gala, since it brought in new volunteers.
Procedure, not verdict. Reviewing costs every year doesn't tell you what to decide about the gala.
We don't know the gala raises the smallest total. The stimulus compares profit and loss, not total donations. A money-losing event might still raise a lot in gross terms.

questions.stimulus: Real estate agent: Harlow Mortgage will finance a house only if it has passed an inspection by an inspector on Harlow's approved list, and every inspector on that list examines both the foundation and the roof of each house inspected. The house on Quill Street has a cracked foundation that any such examination would reveal. So Harlow will not finance the house on Quill Street.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the real estate agent's conclusion to be properly drawn?
choices: No house passes an inspection by an inspector on Harlow's approved list if the inspection reveals a cracked foundation.
Every house that fails an inspection by an inspector on Harlow's approved list has either a cracked foundation or a damaged roof.
No house with a damaged roof passes an inspection by any of the inspectors on Harlow's approved list.
Most of the inspectors on Harlow's approved list would refuse to pass a house whose foundation is cracked.
Harlow finances every house that has passed an inspection by an inspector on its approved list, unless the house is overpriced.
questions.explanation: Finance → passed an approved inspection, and any approved inspection would reveal the crack. The missing link is that a revealed crack means failing, which is (A). (B) reverses that link (fail → crack), (C) bridges through the roof, which the argument never applies to this house, (D) is only "most," and (E) reverses the financing rule.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Harlow will not finance the Quill Street house.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Finance → passed an inspection by an approved inspector; approved inspectors check foundation and roof; any such check would reveal the crack.

breakdown.analysis: So the inspector will see the crack. So what? Seeing a crack isn't the same as failing the house. Maybe it's a minor crack the inspector notes and passes. The chain is: Finance → passed approved inspection. We know: approved inspection → crack revealed. We need: crack revealed → not passed. It's like saying "the referee will see the foul, so the goal won't count." Only if seeing the foul means disallowing the goal. The roof is a decoy; nothing says this roof is damaged.

choices.note: CORRECT. Crack revealed → not passed. Any approved inspection reveals the crack, so the house can't pass one. No pass → no financing. Chain complete.
This reverses the needed link: it says fail → crack or roof problem. We need crack → fail. Knowing what failing houses have in common doesn't tell us this house fails.
It bridges through the roof, but the stimulus never says this roof is damaged. Only the foundation is cracked, so this choice never touches our house.
"Most" isn't enough. The house might be inspected by one of the inspectors who would pass it anyway.
This reverses the financing rule (passed → finance) and adds an exception. We need to show Harlow won't finance, so a rule about when it will finance doesn't help.

questions.stimulus: Unless the Dunleigh Literacy Council wins the Tolland grant, it will end its evening classes. If the council ends its evening classes, it will move its tutors to its weekend program. The council will not win the Tolland grant this year. So the council will move its tutors to its weekend program.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Unless the Wickham Street food co-op hires a second buyer, it will close its bulk aisle. If it hires a second buyer, it will extend its weekend hours. The co-op will hire a second buyer. So it will extend its weekend hours and keep its bulk aisle open.

If the Dorseys refinance their mortgage, they will lower their monthly payment. If they lower their monthly payment, they will add to their savings. The Dorseys added to their savings this year. So they must have refinanced their mortgage.

Unless Halima gets a raise, she will cancel her gym membership. If she cancels her gym membership, she will buy a used rowing machine. Halima will not get a raise this year. So she will buy a used rowing machine.

Unless the Kerr Street clinic hires another nurse, it will shorten its hours. If it shortens its hours, it will lose some of its patients. The clinic will lose some of its patients. So it will not hire another nurse.

Mill Road will be repaved unless the city's budget is cut, and if Mill Road is repaved, traffic will be diverted onto Elm Street. The budget probably will not be cut. So traffic will probably be diverted onto Elm Street.
questions.explanation: The argument chains two conditionals and triggers the first: not grant → end classes → move tutors; no grant; so move tutors. (C) matches term for term. (E) has the same chain but hedges its premise and conclusion with "probably," so its certainty doesn't match. (B) and (D) reason backward from the last result, and (A) opens the same way but reaches a conclusion its premises don't support.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The council will move its tutors to the weekend program.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: No grant → end evening classes; end evening classes → move tutors; no grant this year.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Unless A, B; if B then C; not A; so C.

breakdown.analysis: "Unless A, B" means not A → B. So: no grant → end classes → move tutors. The council won't get the grant, so it ends classes and moves tutors. Valid, stated with certainty. The match needs the same two-link chain, a fact that triggers the first link, a certain conclusion that reaches the end of the chain, and no hedging. Check certainty words: "probably" changes the pattern.

choices.note: Same "unless" opening, different logic. "Unless it hires a buyer, it closes the aisle" only tells you what happens without the buyer. With one, nothing says the aisle stays open, so "keep its bulk aisle open" doesn't follow. The wording matches; the structure doesn't.
This runs backward. It starts from the end of the chain (added to savings) and concludes the beginning (refinanced). That's affirming the consequent; the original moves forward.
CORRECT. No raise → cancel gym → buy rowing machine; no raise; so rowing machine. Unless A, B; if B then C; not A; so C. Same chain, same certainty.
Backward again: it affirms the end (lose patients) and concludes about the start. Losing patients could have other causes. Invalid, unlike the original.

Tempting, because the chain is the same shape: not cut → repave → divert. But the trigger and conclusion are only "probably." The original is certain throughout. Parallel answers must match the certainty level.

questions.stimulus: Treasurer: Our museum spends from its endowment's principal only when the trustees have declared a financial emergency, and the trustees declare one only when the museum's operating reserves are exhausted. Admittedly, attendance fell sharply last year. But the new roof will be paid for entirely by the capital campaign, not from operating reserves. So the museum will not spend from its endowment's principal this year.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: A sharp drop in attendance has never by itself exhausted the operating reserves of a museum that has a capital campaign under way.
If the museum's operating reserves are exhausted this year, the trustees will declare a financial emergency.
The capital campaign will raise enough money to pay for the new roof before any payment for the roof comes due.
The trustees have never before declared a financial emergency in a year in which the museum's attendance fell.
The museum's operating reserves will be exhausted this year only if they are used to pay for the new roof.
questions.explanation: Principal → emergency → reserves exhausted, so the argument needs the reserves not to be exhausted. All it offers is that the roof won't come out of reserves. (E) makes the roof the only way the reserves could run out, which closes the gap. Most students pick (A) because it answers the conceded attendance drop; but ruling out attendance leaves every other expense that could drain the reserves. (B) reverses the trustees' rule, (C) corroborates a premise already given, and (D) is a past pattern.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The museum will not spend from its endowment's principal this year.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Spend principal → emergency declared → operating reserves exhausted; the roof won't be paid from reserves; (attendance fell sharply).

breakdown.analysis: The chain: Spend principal → emergency → reserves exhausted. Contrapositive: reserves NOT exhausted → no emergency → no principal spending. So the treasurer must show the reserves won't run out. Does keeping the roof off the reserves prove that? Only if the roof was the one thing that could drain them. Salaries, utilities, an attendance slump could do it too. We need: reserves exhausted → paid for the roof. It's like saying "my brother is paying for the car repair, so I won't overdraw my account." True only if the repair was the only big bill coming. The attendance concession is bait for the trap.

choices.note: Tempting, and most students pick it, because the treasurer conceded the attendance drop and this seems to neutralize it. But it rules out only one threat. Payroll, utilities or an emergency repair could still exhaust the reserves. It's also oddly limited to attendance acting "by itself." Not enough.
This reverses the trustees' rule. The stimulus says emergency → reserves exhausted; (B) says reserves exhausted → emergency. We need to show the reserves aren't exhausted, and this doesn't help.
Irrelevant corroboration. The stimulus already tells us the campaign will pay for the roof entirely. Shoring up that premise doesn't touch the real gap: other expenses.
A past pattern isn't a guarantee. "Never before" doesn't mean "not this year," and attendance isn't the issue anyway.

CORRECT. Reserves exhausted → used for the roof. Contrapositive: not used for the roof → not exhausted. The roof is off the reserves, so they won't be exhausted, so there's no emergency and no principal spending. The "only if" form hides it, but it's the bridge.

questions.stimulus: Columnist: Ilona should not use her savings to pay off her car loan early. Doing so would leave her with less than three months' living expenses in savings, and her job is not secure. It is true that the loan's interest rate is higher than the rate her savings earn, but that advantage does not outweigh the risk.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the columnist's argument?
choices: A person should pay off a loan early only if the loan's interest rate is higher than the rate that the person's savings earn.
A person whose job is secure may let his or her savings fall below three months' living expenses in order to pay off a costly loan.
Paying off a loan early is advisable whenever doing so would leave the borrower with at least three months' living expenses in savings.
No one whose job is not secure should take any step that would leave him or her with less than three months' living expenses in savings.
A person should keep at least three months' living expenses in savings unless the interest rate on his or her debt is higher than the rate savings earn.
questions.explanation: Ilona's job is insecure and paying the loan would drop her savings below three months' expenses; the columnist concludes she shouldn't. (D) says anyone with an insecure job should avoid any step that leaves savings that low, and paying off the loan is such a step. Most students pick (A) because it's about the interest-rate comparison; but it states a necessary condition that Ilona meets, so it can never tell her not to pay. (E) has an exception that Ilona satisfies, (B) covers people with secure jobs, and (C) covers cases with at least three months saved.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Ilona should not use her savings to pay off her car loan early.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Paying would leave less than three months' expenses saved; her job isn't secure; (concession: the loan rate beats the savings rate, but that doesn't outweigh the risk).

breakdown.analysis: The columnist's verdict is a NO. The facts that trigger it: insecure job + savings would fall below three months. The rate advantage is conceded and set aside. A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says. So we need: insecure job AND would leave < 3 months → should not do it. Careful with "only if" answers: a necessary condition Ilona already meets gives no verdict at all. It's like "you may borrow the car only if you have a license." Having a license doesn't mean you should take the car, and it doesn't mean you shouldn't.

choices.note: Tempting, and the most common wrong pick, because the interest rates are right there in the stimulus. But it's a necessary condition for paying early, and Ilona meets it (her loan rate is higher). Meeting a necessary condition gives no verdict either way. Nothing here says she should not pay.
Wrong group. This is about people with secure jobs. Ilona's job isn't secure, and the principle says nothing about her.
Wrong case. This covers paying off a loan when you'd keep at least three months saved. Ilona wouldn't, so it doesn't apply, and it points toward paying anyway.

CORRECT. Insecure job → don't take any step that leaves savings under three months. Paying off the loan is such a step, so Ilona shouldn't do it, and the principle makes the rate advantage irrelevant, just as the columnist does.

This one backfires. Its exception kicks in when the debt's rate beats the savings rate, which is Ilona's situation. So it no longer requires her to keep three months saved. It removes the support rather than adding it.

questions.stimulus: Under Ostwick Bank's rules, the funds from a deposited check become available on the next business day unless the check is flagged for review, and any check that is for more than $5,000 or is drawn on a foreign bank is flagged. Most of the checks that Ostwick flags turn out to be legitimate. Pilar deposited a check for $3,200 on Monday, so its funds will be available on Tuesday.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Ostwick Bank flags no check for review unless the amount of the check is more than $5,000.
The check that Pilar deposited on Monday was not drawn on a foreign bank.
Every check that Ostwick Bank does not flag for review is for an amount of $5,000 or less.
Most checks for $5,000 or less that are drawn on domestic banks are not flagged for review by Ostwick Bank.
If a check that Ostwick Bank flags for review turns out to be legitimate, its funds become available within two business days.
questions.explanation: Not flagged → available next business day, so the argument needs Pilar's check to escape flagging. The stimulus gives only sufficient conditions for flagging (over $5,000, or foreign), so other reasons for flagging remain possible. (A) makes being over $5,000 a necessary condition for flagging, and Pilar's $3,200 check therefore isn't flagged. Most students pick (B), which rules out the foreign-bank trigger; but the stimulus never says those two triggers are the only ones. (C) reverses the amount link, (D) is only "most," and (E) relies on the decoy about legitimate checks.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The funds from Pilar's check will be available Tuesday.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Not flagged → available next business day; over $5,000 OR foreign bank → flagged; Pilar's check is for $3,200; (most flagged checks are legitimate).

breakdown.analysis: Over $5,000 or foreign → flagged. That's a sufficient condition. It tells you some ways a check gets flagged, not the only ways. So knowing the check is small doesn't show it's unflagged. Even knowing it's domestic wouldn't. We need something that guarantees no flag: a rule that makes flagging require a feature Pilar's check lacks. Flagged → over $5,000. It's like "anyone with a fever or a rash is sent home." No fever and no rash doesn't mean you stay; maybe a cough gets you sent home too.

choices.note: CORRECT. "No check is flagged unless it's over $5,000" = flagged → over $5,000. Contrapositive: $5,000 or less → not flagged. Pilar's $3,200 check isn't flagged, so its funds are available the next business day. The "unless" phrasing makes it look like a restatement, but it's the reverse of the given rule, and that's what we need.

Tempting, and most students pick it: it knocks out the one trigger we didn't address. But the stimulus lists sufficient conditions for flagging, not the only ones. A check could be flagged for an unusual signature, a new account, anything. Ruling out both listed triggers still leaves the door open.
This reverses the needed link. It says not flagged → $5,000 or less. We need $5,000 or less → not flagged. Knowing what unflagged checks look like doesn't tell you this small check is unflagged.
Too weak. "Most" small domestic checks aren't flagged, so Pilar's could be one of the ones that is. It also assumes her check is domestic, which we don't know.
Built on the decoy about legitimate checks. It tells you what happens if the check is flagged, but the conclusion needs the check not to be flagged at all. Two business days isn't Tuesday anyway.

questions.stimulus: Principle: A homeowners' association should fine a resident for making an unapproved change to the outside of his or her home only if the resident had received written notice of the relevant rule beforehand or the change creates a safety hazard.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?
choices: Because Wen had received written notice of the rule against unapproved satellite dishes before installing one, the association should fine her for installing it.
Rafael had never received written notice of the rule, so the association should not fine him for his unapproved deck, even though the deck's railing is unsafe.
The association should not fine Gus for his unapproved fence, since he had received no written notice of the rule and the fence creates no safety hazard.
The association should not fine Oona for repainting her shutters an unapproved color, because the new color creates no safety hazard of any kind.
Because Lionel removed his unapproved awning soon after receiving written notice of the rule, the association should not fine him for having put it up.
questions.explanation: Fine → (notice beforehand OR safety hazard); contrapositive: no notice AND no hazard → don't fine. Gus had neither, so (C) conforms. Most students pick (A), since Wen meets the notice condition; but meeting a necessary condition never makes a fine required. (B) ignores the hazard half of the "or," (D) knows only one of the two conditions, and (E) involves notice that came after the change while saying nothing about a hazard.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Should fine for an unapproved exterior change → resident had written notice beforehand OR the change creates a safety hazard.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: The principle only yields "should not fine," and only when BOTH: no prior written notice AND no safety hazard.

breakdown.analysis: "Only if" sets a necessary condition, and here it's an "or": notice OR hazard. Contrapositive: NO notice AND NO hazard → should not fine. That's the only verdict this principle can deliver. It never says when you SHOULD fine. So the right answer must: 1. be about an unapproved exterior change; 2. have no notice beforehand; 3. have no hazard; 4. conclude no fine. Each trap leaves one of these unknown or flips the verdict. It's like "you get a ticket only if you were speeding or ran a light." Speeding doesn't mean you must get a ticket.

choices.note: Tempting, and the most common wrong pick: Wen clearly had notice, so the fine seems earned. But notice is only necessary for a fine. Satisfying a necessary condition never makes the fine required. The principle never says "should fine."

This ignores the "or." The railing is unsafe, so the hazard half is satisfied, and the principle no longer rules out a fine. Concluding "should not fine" contradicts nothing but isn't supported either.
CORRECT. No written notice and no safety hazard, so both halves of the "or" fail. The necessary condition for fining is missing, so the association should not fine Gus. Every condition is checked.
Half the picture. No hazard, fine, but we're never told whether Oona had prior notice. If she did, the principle doesn't forbid the fine.
Notice came after the awning went up, so there was no notice beforehand. But we don't know whether the awning was a hazard. Removing it quickly isn't a condition in the principle at all.

questions.stimulus: A Tamberly pet insurance policy covers a condition only if the condition was not present before the policy began, and a condition counts as present before the policy began if a veterinarian recorded any symptom of it before that date. Mira's dog was diagnosed with hip dysplasia two months after her policy began, and a veterinarian's notes from last year record that the dog limped after long walks. So Tamberly will not cover the dog's hip dysplasia.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion of the argument to be properly drawn?
choices: Limping after long walks is among the most common early symptoms of hip dysplasia in dogs of every breed.
Whenever a dog that is later found to have hip dysplasia limps, that limping is a symptom of the dysplasia.
Every condition that was present before a Tamberly policy began had a symptom that a veterinarian recorded before that date.
Most conditions that are diagnosed within a few months after a pet insurance policy begins were already present when it began.
Tamberly does not cover any condition that a veterinarian diagnosed before the date on which the pet's policy began.
questions.explanation: The chain is covered → not present before; symptom recorded before → present before. So the argument needs last year's limping to have been a symptom of this dog's dysplasia. (B) guarantees that: any limping by a dog later found to have dysplasia counts as a symptom of it. Most students pick (A); but saying that limping is a common symptom doesn't make this dog's limping a symptom, since dogs limp for many reasons. (C) reverses the definition, (D) is a "most" claim about timing, and (E) is about diagnosis, which came after the policy began.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Tamberly won't cover the dog's hip dysplasia.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Covered → not present before the policy; symptom recorded before the policy → present before; a vet recorded limping last year; dysplasia diagnosed after the policy began.

breakdown.analysis: Chain: symptom recorded before → present before → not covered. The vet recorded limping. Was the limping a symptom of dysplasia? Dogs limp from sore paws, sprains and thorns. The argument just takes for granted that this limp was the dysplasia. We need an answer that makes this dog's limp a symptom of its dysplasia. It's like an insurer saying "you mentioned a headache last year, so your migraine was pre-existing." Only if that headache was the migraine.

choices.note: Tempting, and most students pick it, because it links limping to dysplasia. But "among the most common symptoms" is a general fact. It doesn't make THIS dog's limp a symptom. Plenty of limps come from other causes, so the gap stays open.

CORRECT. Any limping by a dog later found to have dysplasia is a symptom of it. Mira's dog was later found to have dysplasia, so last year's recorded limp was a symptom. Recorded symptom → present before → not covered. Strongly worded, but that's fine for a sufficient assumption.
This reverses the definition. The stimulus says recorded symptom → present before; (C) says present before → recorded symptom. We need to establish "present before," and this choice starts from it.
"Most" can't prove a conclusion about one dog, and timing of diagnosis isn't the test Tamberly uses. The test is a recorded symptom.
Diagnosis is a different trigger, and the dog was diagnosed two months after the policy began. This rule never touches the case.

questions.stimulus: Director: Our scholarship fund should accept the Garland family's gift, even though the family has asked that the scholarship be named after them. Naming the scholarship gives the family public credit, but it gives them no say over which students receive awards; those decisions will remain with our independent selection committee.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the director's reasoning?
choices: A nonprofit should accept a gift that comes with conditions only if none of the conditions gives the donor any say over whom the nonprofit serves.
A nonprofit should refuse any gift whose donor seeks public credit for giving it, unless the gift is too large for the nonprofit to do without.
Donors who give in order to receive public credit deserve less gratitude than anonymous donors, even when their gifts are equally useful.
A nonprofit's selection committee should remain independent both of the nonprofit's fundraising staff and of all of the nonprofit's donors.
If the conditions a donor attaches to a gift give the donor no say over whom a nonprofit serves, the nonprofit should accept the gift.
questions.explanation: The director concludes the fund should accept because the naming condition gives the donor no say over who gets awards. (E) supplies that rule: no say over whom the nonprofit serves → accept. Most students pick (A), which uses the same words; but its "only if" makes "no say" merely necessary for accepting, so it can't conclude that the fund should accept. (B) points toward refusal, (C) is about gratitude, and (D) supports a premise rather than the conclusion.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The scholarship fund should accept the Garland gift.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The only condition is naming, which gives public credit but no say over who receives awards; the committee stays independent.

breakdown.analysis: The director's argument: condition gives no say over recipients → accept. A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says, which is accept. So the principle must make "no say" SUFFICIENT for accepting: no say → accept. Two answers will look almost identical; the difference is whether "no say" is in the if-clause or the only-if clause. Necessary vs. sufficient is the whole question. It's the difference between "you may enter only if you have a ticket" and "if you have a ticket, you may enter."

choices.note: Tempting, and the most common pick, because it uses the stimulus's exact idea. But "accept only if no say" makes "no say" necessary, not sufficient. Accept → no say. The Garland gift meets the condition, and meeting a necessary condition gives no verdict. It can't tell you to accept.
This points the other way: the Garlands want public credit, so it tells you to refuse unless the gift is indispensable, which we aren't told.
About gratitude, not acceptance. Even if the Garlands deserve less thanks, that says nothing about whether to take the gift.
This supports a premise (the committee stays independent), not the conclusion. It never says to accept anything.

CORRECT. No say over whom the nonprofit serves → accept. The naming condition gives the Garlands no say over which students get awards, so the fund should accept. Sufficient condition matches the facts; result matches the conclusion.

questions.stimulus: In Fallow County, a lender may issue a mortgage on a property in the floodplain only if the buyer carries flood insurance on it, and flood insurance cannot be bought for a property that lacks an elevation certificate. Only licensed surveyors issue elevation certificates, and most of the county's surveyors are booked for months. The Penrose cottage has no elevation certificate. So no lender may issue a mortgage on the Penrose cottage now.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Any property in Fallow County that has an elevation certificate is located outside the county's floodplain.
Most properties in Fallow County that have no elevation certificate are located within the county's floodplain.
No surveyor in Fallow County could issue an elevation certificate for the Penrose cottage in the near future.
Every property in Fallow County that lies outside the floodplain already has an elevation certificate.
Every property in Fallow County that lies outside the floodplain and was built after 1980 already has an elevation certificate.
questions.explanation: The mortgage rule applies only to floodplain properties, and nothing says the cottage is in the floodplain. (D) handles this indirectly: its contrapositive is no certificate → in the floodplain, so the cottage is in the floodplain, needs flood insurance, and can't get it. Most students pick (E), which has the right shape but is too narrow: it covers only properties built after 1980, and the cottage's age is never given. (A) is the reversed version of (D), (B) is only "most," and (C) bridges through the surveyor decoy.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: No lender may issue a mortgage on the Penrose cottage now.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Mortgage on a floodplain property → flood insurance → elevation certificate; the cottage has no certificate; (surveyors are scarce).

breakdown.analysis: Run the chain: mortgage on a floodplain property → flood insurance → certificate. No certificate → no flood insurance → no mortgage... IF the cottage is in the floodplain. Is it? Nobody says. Outside the floodplain the insurance rule never kicks in. So we need: the Penrose cottage is in the floodplain. The right answer probably won't say it directly. Look for something that forces it. Contrapositive trick: "outside → has a certificate" means "no certificate → inside." It's like a rule that says "everyone over 21 has a wristband." If you see someone without a wristband, they're under 21. The surveyor line is a decoy: the cottage has no certificate now, and that's all the argument uses.

choices.note: This is the reversed version of the right idea. Certificate → outside. The cottage has no certificate, so this tells us nothing about where it is. Its contrapositive (inside → no certificate) also leaves the cottage's location open.
"Most" is too weak for a sufficient assumption. The cottage could be one of the certificate-less properties outside the floodplain, where no flood insurance is needed.
Built on the surveyor decoy. Whether a certificate could be issued soon doesn't matter; the cottage lacks one now. And this still never puts the cottage in the floodplain.

CORRECT. Outside floodplain → has a certificate. Contrapositive: no certificate → inside the floodplain. The cottage has none, so it's in the floodplain. Floodplain mortgage → flood insurance → certificate; no certificate, so no mortgage. The stand-in wording hides the bridge.

Tempting, and the most common wrong pick, because it's nearly the right bridge. But it's too narrow: it covers only properties built after 1980, and we're never told when the cottage was built. An older cottage could sit outside the floodplain with no certificate, and then the insurance rule never applies.

questions.stimulus: Principle: A landlord who keeps part of a tenant's security deposit to pay for damage is justified in doing so only if the damage goes beyond ordinary wear and the landlord sent the tenant an itemized list of it within 30 days after the tenant moved out. The list is not required, however, if the tenant left no forwarding address.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: Keller kept $200 of a deposit to repair walls the tenant had gouged, but sent the itemized list to the tenant's forwarding address 45 days after move-out, so Keller was not justified.
Ortiz sent a former tenant an itemized list showing a broken window two weeks after the tenant moved out, so Ortiz was justified in keeping part of the deposit to replace it.
Dunn kept part of a deposit to repair a door the tenant had broken, and the tenant left no forwarding address; because Dunn sent no list at all, Dunn was not justified.
Sato kept part of a tenant's deposit to cover a month of unpaid rent without ever sending an itemized list, so Sato was not justified in keeping that money.
Lund returned a tenant's full deposit even though the tenant had badly damaged the kitchen floor, so Lund acted wrongly in giving back the entire amount.
questions.explanation: Keeping deposit money for damage is justified only if the damage is beyond ordinary wear and an itemized list went out within 30 days, with the list waived when there's no forwarding address. Keller had a forwarding address and sent the list late, so a necessary condition fails and Keller was not justified (A). Most students pick (C), but the tenant there left no forwarding address, so the list wasn't required and the principle can't condemn Dunn. (B) treats necessary conditions as sufficient, (D) is about rent rather than damage, and (E) gives a verdict on returning money, which the principle never addresses.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Justified in keeping deposit money for damage → damage beyond ordinary wear AND (itemized list within 30 days OR tenant left no forwarding address).

setup.label: Application
setup.text: The principle can only conclude "not justified," for money kept to pay for damage, when one condition fails: ordinary wear only, or a forwarding address existed and no timely list was sent.

breakdown.analysis: Two layers. 1. "Only if" means the principle gives necessary conditions; it can condemn a landlord but never approve one. 2. The "however" sentence is an exception that removes the list requirement when there's no forwarding address. So the right answer needs: money kept for damage; and either the damage was ordinary wear, or the tenant left a forwarding address and the list came late or never; verdict: not justified. Note the scope: damage only. Rent isn't covered. It's like "you may park here only if you have a permit, unless it's Sunday." Parking without a permit on Sunday isn't a violation, and having a permit doesn't mean you're fine in every other way.

choices.note: CORRECT. Money kept for damage. The tenant left a forwarding address, so the exception doesn't apply and the list was required within 30 days. Keller sent it at 45 days. A necessary condition fails, so Keller was not justified. (Gouged walls are beyond ordinary wear, but that doesn't save him.)
This treats the conditions as sufficient. A timely list is necessary, not enough. And we aren't even told whether the tenant broke the window. The principle never says a landlord IS justified.

Tempting, and the most common wrong pick, because Dunn sent no list at all. But the tenant left no forwarding address, so the exception switches off the list requirement. The remaining condition (damage beyond wear) is met. Nothing in the principle condemns Dunn.
Outside the principle's scope. It covers deposit money kept to pay for damage. Unpaid rent isn't damage, so the principle is silent here, whatever the right answer about Sato might be.
Wrong verdict entirely. The principle limits when a landlord may keep money; it never requires keeping any. Returning the full deposit can't violate it.

questions.stimulus: Most of the households that refinanced their mortgages through Graystone Bank last year chose fixed rates, and every one of those households that chose a fixed rate locked in a rate below 6 percent. Hence, at least some of the households that refinanced through Graystone last year locked in a rate below 6 percent.
questions.stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following arguments is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Most members of the Dunmore credit union live in Dunmore, and most of the credit union's members hold savings accounts there. So at least some of the credit union's members who live in Dunmore hold savings accounts there.

Most of the policyholders who renewed with Trelawny Insurance last year chose annual billing, and every policyholder who received a loyalty credit chose annual billing. So at least some of those policyholders received a loyalty credit.

Every tenant in the Wexley building who holds a parking permit owns a car, and most of the tenants in the Wexley building own a car. So at least some of the Wexley building's tenants hold parking permits.
