All of the Haverly Arts Fund's December donors gave online, and most of the fund's online donors are under forty years old. So at least some of the Haverly Arts Fund's December donors are under forty.
At least some members of the Dalton Savings Club earn interest on their deposits, since every club member who keeps a certificate of deposit earns interest, and most of the club's members keep one.
questions.explanation: The argument is valid: most A are B, every B (among A) is C, so some A are C. (E) has that skeleton with its conclusion stated first and its premises in reverse order: every CD-holding member earns interest, most members hold CDs, so some members earn interest. Most students pick (A) because it's valid and also ends with "at least some"; but it combines two "most" premises about one group, a different pattern. (B) echoes the wording but reverses the "every" link, (C) runs the "every" link backward, and (D) runs all-then-most, which is invalid.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: At least some of the Graystone refinancers locked in a rate below 6 percent.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most refinancers chose fixed rates; every fixed-rate refinancer locked in below 6 percent.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Most A are B; all B (among A) are C; so some A are C.

breakdown.analysis: Valid, and deliberately modest: it could have concluded "most," but it only says "at least some." Most A are B; every B is C; so some A are C. Now the hard part: two traps are valid or nearly so, and the right answer is scrambled. Strip each choice to its skeleton and check three things: 1. Is there a "most" premise about the main group? 2. Is there an "every" premise that runs FROM that subgroup TO the new property? 3. Is the conclusion "some" of the main group? Don't stop at "it's valid." A valid argument with a different structure is still wrong. And don't be thrown when the conclusion comes first with "since."

choices.note: Tempting, and the most common wrong pick, because it's valid and ends with "at least some." But its skeleton is most A are B, most A are C, so some B are C. That's two overlapping "most" claims, with no "every" link at all. Valid isn't the same as parallel.

Tempting, because it follows the stimulus's wording and order almost exactly. But the "every" link is reversed: every credit recipient chose annual billing (C → B), not every annual-billing renewer got a credit (B → C). The annual-billing majority could all lack credits. Invalid.
The "every" link points the wrong way for this conclusion: permit → car, and most own cars, so some hold permits? The car owners could all lack permits. Invalid.
All-then-most: every December donor gave online; most online donors are under forty. The December donors could all be in the over-forty minority. Invalid, and the quantifiers are in the wrong slots.

CORRECT. Reorder it: most members keep a CD (most A are B); every member with a CD earns interest (all B are C); so at least some members earn interest (some A are C). Conclusion first, premises reversed, same skeleton and the same modest "at least some."

questions.stimulus: Development director: A gift to our spring appeal counts double only if the donor's employer matches it, and employers match a gift only if the donor files a matching request within 90 days of giving. Most of our spring donors gave more than they did last year. Arturo's gift counted double, so he will be invited to our donor dinner.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the development director's conclusion to be properly drawn?
choices: Every donor who will be invited to the donor dinner filed a matching request within 90 days of giving to the spring appeal.
Every donor who gave more to the spring appeal than he or she gave last year will be invited to the donor dinner.
No one who filed a matching request within 90 days of giving to the spring appeal will go uninvited to the donor dinner.
Most of the donors whose gifts to the spring appeal counted double will be invited to the donor dinner.
Every donor whose employer matched his or her gift within 30 days of receiving the matching request will be invited to the donor dinner.
questions.explanation: Counted double → matched → filed a request within 90 days, so Arturo filed in time. The conclusion needs filing in time to lead to an invitation, and (C) says so with a double negative: anyone who filed in time is invited. Most students pick (E), which reaches the dinner but only for gifts matched within 30 days of the request; we never learn how quickly Arturo's employer acted. (A) reverses the needed link, (B) bridges through the decoy about larger gifts, which we never learn applies to Arturo, and (D) is only "most."

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Arturo will be invited to the donor dinner.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Counts double → employer matched → request filed within 90 days; Arturo's gift counted double; (most donors gave more than last year).

breakdown.analysis: Follow the chain forward: Arturo's gift counted double → employer matched → he filed within 90 days. Great. Now: what does any of that have to do with the dinner? Nothing. The dinner appears only in the conclusion. So we need a bridge from the last link to the new term: filed within 90 days → invited. The answer may hide it in negative form: "no one who filed... will go uninvited." Two negatives make a positive. It's like "no one who RSVPed will be turned away" = "everyone who RSVPed gets in." The line about bigger gifts is a decoy; nothing says Arturo gave more.

choices.note: This reverses the needed bridge. It says invited → filed in time. We need filed in time → invited. Knowing every guest filed doesn't put Arturo on the list.
Bridges through the decoy. We never learn whether Arturo gave more than last year; "most" donors did, and he could be in the rest. The argument never applies this concept to him.

CORRECT. "No one who filed in time will go uninvited" = filed within 90 days → invited. Arturo's gift counted double → matched → filed within 90 days → invited. The double negative hides a perfect bridge.
Right starting point, too weak. "Most" double-counted donors are invited, so Arturo could be one of the exceptions.

Tempting, and the most common wrong pick, because it finally reaches the dinner from the matching chain. But it's too narrow: it covers only matches made within 30 days of the request. We know Arturo's employer matched his gift, not how quickly, so he might fall outside this rule.

questions.stimulus: Advice columnist: Petra has asked whether she should lend her brother $5,000 toward a used car. She should not. She could afford to lose the money, it is true. But her brother has never repaid a loan from anyone, and Petra admits that she would resent him if he failed to repay her.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the advice columnist's reasoning?
choices: No one should lend money that he or she cannot afford to lose to a relative who has failed to repay a loan from someone else.
One should lend money to a relative only if the relative has a record of repaying loans or one would not resent the relative for failing to repay.
One should lend money to a relative only if one could afford to lose that money without suffering serious hardship as a result.
A person should not lend money to a friend who has failed to repay loans from other friends, even if the person can afford to lose it.
If one can afford to lose the money and the relative has always repaid past loans, one should lend the relative the money requested.
questions.explanation: The columnist says no because the brother has never repaid a loan and Petra would resent him, despite her being able to afford the loss. (B)'s contrapositive gives exactly that: no repayment record AND she would resent him → don't lend. Most students pick (A), which sounds like the classic rule; but it applies only to money one cannot afford to lose, and Petra can. (C) states a necessary condition Petra meets, (D) covers friends rather than relatives, and (E) tells you when to lend, with a condition the brother fails.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Petra should not lend her brother the money.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Her brother has never repaid a loan from anyone; she would resent him if he didn't repay; (concession: she could afford to lose the money).

breakdown.analysis: The verdict is "don't lend," and it rests on two facts: no repayment record, and she'd resent him. The affordability point is conceded and set aside. So the right principle has to produce "don't lend" from those two facts, and must NOT depend on her being unable to afford it. It may be hidden as an "only if" with an "or": lend → (record OR no resentment). Contrapositive: no record AND resentment → don't lend. Bingo. Watch for traps that need the conceded fact to go the other way, or that apply to a different kind of person.

choices.note: Tempting, and the most common wrong pick, because it's the familiar "don't lend what you can't afford to lose" rule plus a bad-borrower clause. But it applies only to money one CANNOT afford to lose, and the columnist concedes Petra can. The principle never reaches her case.

CORRECT. Lend → (repayment record OR no resentment). Contrapositive: no record AND resentment → don't lend. The brother has never repaid anyone, and Petra admits she'd resent him. Both triggers are met, the verdict is "don't lend," and affordability plays no role, just as the columnist says.
Affordability is a necessary condition here, and Petra meets it. Meeting a necessary condition gives no verdict, and if anything this points toward lending being acceptable.
Wrong group. It's about lending to a friend, and Petra's borrower is her brother. The scope doesn't cover this case, however close it sounds.
This tells you when you SHOULD lend. The brother has never repaid anyone, so the condition fails, and failing a sufficient condition tells you nothing. It can't justify "don't lend."

questions.stimulus: At Penhallow Trust, a person other than the renter of a safe-deposit box can open the box only if that person is named on the box's access card or presents a court order, and no one under eighteen is ever named on an access card. Most boxes are opened by their renters. Last week someone under eighteen opened box 114, which Delphine Ruiz rents. So whoever opened box 114 last week presented a court order.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Anyone who opens a safe-deposit box at Penhallow Trust by presenting a court order is someone other than the renter of that box.
Most of the people under eighteen who open safe-deposit boxes at Penhallow Trust are not the renters of those boxes.
No one who is named on the access card for a safe-deposit box at Penhallow Trust has ever needed to present a court order there.
The renter of a safe-deposit box at Penhallow Trust is always among the people named on that box's access card.
Whoever opened box 114 last week was not one of the people named on that box's access card.
questions.explanation: The rule constrains only non-renters, so the argument needs the under-eighteen opener not to be Delphine. (D) gets there indirectly: renters are always named on the card, no one named is under eighteen, so no renter is under eighteen, and the opener is not the renter. Not the renter and not named → court order. Most students pick (E), but the premises already establish that (under eighteen → not named); the open question is whether the opener was the renter. (A) reverses the direction, (B) is only "most," and (C) is irrelevant.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Whoever opened box 114 presented a court order.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Non-renter opens → named on card OR court order; no one named is under 18; an under-18 person opened box 114, which Delphine rents; (most boxes are opened by renters).

breakdown.analysis: Chain for non-renters: open → named OR court order. Under 18 → not named. So an under-18 NON-RENTER who opens must have a court order. But wait: who says the opener wasn't the renter? The rule doesn't touch renters at all. If Delphine is 16 and opened her own box, no court order was needed. So we need: the opener isn't the renter. The answer may get there sideways, by making renters impossible to be under 18. It's like a club rule: "guests need a pass or an escort." Knowing the visitor has no pass proves escort only if the visitor isn't a member.

choices.note: Wrong direction. It says court order → non-renter. We need non-renter first, so we can then apply the rule and get the court order. This assumes the conclusion's situation instead of proving it.
"Most" is too weak. The under-18 opener of box 114 could be in the minority who are renters, like Delphine herself. It also leans on the decoy about who usually opens boxes.
Irrelevant. Whether named people ever needed court orders tells us nothing about this opener, who can't be named anyway.

CORRECT. Renter → named on the card. No one named is under 18, so no renter is under 18. The opener was under 18, so the opener wasn't Delphine. Non-renter + not named → court order. A hidden, two-step bridge.

Tempting, and the most common wrong pick, because "not named" is half of what forces the court order. But the premises already give it: under 18 → never named. Restating it adds nothing. The real gap is whether the opener was the renter, and this doesn't touch that.

questions.stimulus: Principle: A charity should identify a donor publicly only if the donor has consented, with one exception: a charity should list in its annual report every donor whose gifts in a year exceed 10 percent of its annual budget, whether or not the donor consents.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: Because Ines agreed to be named, the Corrie Fund was obligated to list her among the donors acknowledged in its annual report for that year.
The Tarn Foundation listed Mr. Osei, whose gifts that year exceeded a fifth of its budget, in its annual report without his consent; it should not have done so.
Because Grace's gifts were under 10 percent of the Beck Shelter's budget, the shelter was required to leave her out of its annual report, even though she had asked to be listed.
The Lowry Trust honored an anonymous donor's request by leaving her out of its annual report, though her gifts exceeded 10 percent of its budget; the trust acted properly.
The Wren Society named Mr. Hollis in its newsletter without his consent; even though his gifts exceeded 10 percent of its budget, it should not have done so.
questions.explanation: Public identification requires consent; the one exception requires listing large donors in the annual report. Hollis was named without consent in a newsletter, which the exception doesn't cover, so the Society should not have named him (E). Most students pick (B) or (D) because the large gift triggers the exception; but the exception requires listing Osei, so (B) gets the verdict backward, and it requires listing the Lowry donor, so (D) is wrong too. (A) treats consent as sufficient, and (C) turns a permission into a requirement: the principle never forbids naming a small donor who consents.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Identify a donor publicly → donor consented; EXCEPT: gifts over 10% of the budget → should be listed in the annual report, consent or not.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Find the verdict the rule actually forces: consent is necessary for any public naming outside the annual-report exception, and big donors must appear in the annual report.

breakdown.analysis: Two rules, and a scope limit. 1. Name publicly → consent (necessary, not sufficient). 2. Exception: gifts > 10% → must be in the annual report. The exception covers one place only, the annual report. Outside it, the consent rule still governs everyone, big donors included. So check each choice: where was the donor named, did they consent, how big was the gift, and what verdict is claimed? It's like "no photos without permission, except the official team photo includes everyone." A player who refused permission still goes in the team photo, but you can't put him on a poster.

choices.note: Consent is necessary for naming, not a trigger that requires it. Agreeing to be named doesn't obligate the charity to name her, and we don't know her gift size.

Tempting, because it's naming without consent. But Osei's gifts exceeded a fifth of the budget, which is over 10%, so the exception applies: the foundation should list him in the annual report, consent or not. The verdict is backward.

Tempting, because Grace falls below the 10 percent line, so the exception doesn't force the shelter to list her. But nothing in the principle requires leaving her out: she consented, so naming her is allowed. The principle never turns falling below the line into a ban.
Tempting, since honoring anonymity sounds right. But her gifts exceeded 10%, so the exception says she should be listed in the annual report whether or not she consents. The trust didn't conform.

CORRECT. A newsletter isn't the annual report, so the exception doesn't reach it. Outside the exception, naming requires consent, which Hollis didn't give. So the Society should not have named him there, despite the size of his gifts. The trap is assuming the exception covers all public naming.

sections.title: Skill Builder: Hard Explain & Weaken II

questions.stimulus: Wildlife biologists in the Aspley Valley fitted snowshoe hares with bright orange radio collars in order to track their movements, expecting that the collars would make the hares easier for predators to spot. Yet over the following winter, the collared hares were killed by predators at a markedly lower rate than were the uncollared hares living in the same areas.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Most of the predators that hunt hares in the Aspley Valley locate their prey mainly by scent rather than by sight, even in daylight.
Several of the collared hares slipped out of their collars during the winter and could no longer be tracked.
Only hares large and healthy enough to carry a collar were collared, and such hares escape predators more often than others.
The number of predators in the Aspley Valley was lower that winter than it had been in most recent winters.
Trapping the hares and fitting them with collars caused them considerable stress, which can leave a hare weakened for several days afterward.
questions.explanation: The collared hares were not a random sample: if only large, healthy hares got collars, and such hares escape predators more often, the collared group would die at a lower rate even if the collars made them a bit easier to see. That is (C). (A) is the trap: it shows why the collars might not hurt, but it gives no reason the collared hares did better than the uncollared ones. (D) affects both groups alike, and (E) deepens the puzzle.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Bright collars should make hares easier for predators to spot, but collared hares were killed at a lower rate than uncollared hares in the same areas.

breakdown.analysis: Why would wearing a bright orange target make you safer? It wouldn’t, unless the collared hares were different to begin with. Ask who got collared. It’s like noticing that marathon runners wearing heavy GPS watches finish faster than runners without them: maybe the serious runners are the ones who buy the watches. We need an answer that shows the collared group was a stronger group from the start. Watch for the trap that only removes the collars’ downside: “no harm” isn’t the same as “better.”

choices.note: Tempting. If predators hunt by scent, the orange color doesn’t matter, so the collars wouldn’t hurt. But that only gets the two groups to equal. It doesn’t explain why the collared hares died less often. Explaining away the expected harm isn’t explaining the benefit.
Lost collars affect how many hares could be tracked, not why the tracked hares survived better. Irrelevant.

CORRECT. The biologists picked the strongest hares to collar. Strong hares escape predators more often, so the collared group would show a lower death rate even if the collars made them slightly more visible. Both facts fit.
Fewer predators would lower the death rate for every hare, collared or not. It doesn’t explain a difference between the groups.
Stress that weakens the collared hares should make them easier prey, not harder. This deepens the puzzle.

questions.stimulus: When the water off the Sennick coast is warm, the plankton that the coast’s anchovies feed on grows poorly, and the total number of anchovies in Sennick waters typically falls. Yet in warm years, the Sennick fishing fleet usually lands more anchovies than it does in cool years, even though the fleet has the same number of boats in both.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Many of the larger fish that prey on anchovies also leave Sennick waters when the water there is warm, returning only once it cools.
Anchovies landed by the Sennick fleet in warm years are, on average, smaller than those landed in cool years.
The plankton on which Sennick anchovies feed recovers within a few months once the water cools again.
Fishing fleets from neighboring coasts, which use similar boats and gear, also land more anchovies in warm years than in cool years.
In warm years, Sennick anchovies crowd into the few patches of cooler water near shore, where the fleet easily finds large schools.
questions.explanation: Fewer fish in the sea can still mean more fish in the nets if the remaining fish are easier to catch. (E) says warm water packs the anchovies into a few near-shore patches where the fleet finds them easily, so catches rise while the population falls. (A) is the trap: fewer predators sounds like more anchovies, but the stimulus already says the number of anchovies falls in warm years, and (A) says nothing about how easily they are caught. (D) just repeats the puzzle on another coast.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: In warm years there are fewer anchovies in Sennick waters, but the same-sized fleet lands more of them.

breakdown.analysis: How do you catch more of something when there’s less of it? You get better at finding it. The catch depends on the population and on how easy the fish are to find. It’s like a smaller crowd at a concert being easier to count if everyone is squeezed into the front rows. We need an answer that makes warm-year anchovies easier to catch. Notice the count/catch gap: the number in the sea and the number landed are different things.

choices.note: Tempting. Fewer predators sounds like more anchovies. But the stimulus already says the anchovy population falls in warm years, and this choice gives no reason the fleet would catch more of a smaller population.
Smaller fish would, if anything, make warm-year landings look worse. Doesn’t explain larger catches.
What happens after the water cools doesn’t explain the warm-year catch. Irrelevant.
This just shows the same puzzle on other coasts. Restating a paradox doesn’t resolve it.
CORRECT. Warm water squeezes the anchovies into a few near-shore patches. There are fewer of them overall, but they’re packed where the boats can find big schools fast, so landings go up.

questions.stimulus: Zoologist: In the Ressa forest, groups of ring-tailed lemurs that include several adult males are attacked by fossas, the lemurs’ chief predator, much less often than are groups that include only one adult male. Evidently, the presence of several adult males in a group deters fossas from attacking it.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the zoologist’s argument?
choices: Groups with several males tend to be far larger overall, and fossas seldom attack large groups of any makeup.
Adult male ring-tailed lemurs frequently fight one another during the breeding season, and these fights sometimes cause serious injuries to both males.
Some lemur groups that include several adult males are nonetheless attacked by fossas from time to time, occasionally losing young.
Groups with several adult males and groups with only one adult male live in the same parts of the Ressa forest.
Fossas sometimes kill adult male lemurs, even though males are larger than other group members.
questions.explanation: The zoologist credits the adult males themselves for the fewer attacks. (A) offers another cause that travels with them: groups with several males are larger overall, and fossas avoid large groups whatever their makeup, so group size, not the males, may be what deters the predator. (B) sounds damaging, but fighting among males says nothing about whether their presence deters fossas. (C) is already allowed by the argument, which says such groups are attacked less often, not never.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Having several adult males in a group deters fossas from attacking it.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Groups with several adult males are attacked much less often than groups with only one.

breakdown.analysis: Is it the males, or something that comes with them? Groups with more adults are usually bigger groups. It’s like noticing that houses with two cars get burgled less and crediting the cars, when the real reason is that someone is usually home. We need an answer that offers another feature of multi-male groups that would explain the fewer attacks.

choices.note: CORRECT. Multi-male groups are bigger, and fossas avoid big groups no matter who is in them. So the fewer attacks may come from group size, not from the males doing any deterring.
Tempting, because it sounds like a cost of having several males. But fighting during the breeding season doesn’t tell us anything about whether the males deter fossas. Wrong question.
The argument says these groups are attacked less often, not never. A few attacks are already expected. So?
This rules out a different explanation (that multi-male groups live in safer places). It helps the argument.

Tempting at a glance: if fossas can kill adult males, how scary can the males be? But the claim is about how often groups get attacked, not whether every attack fails. A deterrent can work most of the time and still lose sometimes. Doesn’t weaken.

questions.stimulus: Glassmakers at the Halbeck works add a small amount of a certain metal compound to their molten glass. On its own, this compound gives glass a distinct purple tint. Yet the Halbeck glassmakers add it precisely because it makes their finished glass look more nearly colorless than it otherwise would.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: The compound is added in amounts far too small to give the finished glass a strongly purple color that anyone would notice.
The other ingredients used at the Halbeck works contain no substances that would give the glass any color.
Some other glassworks use entirely different compounds in order to make the glass they produce colorless.
Iron traces in the sand used at the Halbeck works give glass a greenish tint, which a faint purple tint offsets.
A faint tint in glass is usually invisible to viewers unless the glass is very thick or seen edge-on.
questions.explanation: A purple additive can make glass look clearer only if it cancels some other color. (D) supplies that color: iron in the sand tints the glass green, and a faint purple offsets the green, leaving the glass closer to colorless. (A) is the trap: a tiny dose explains why the glass isn’t strongly purple, but a little purple is still more color, not less.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The compound tints glass purple, but adding it makes the Halbeck glass look more colorless.

breakdown.analysis: How does adding color take color away? Only if there’s already a color in the glass for it to cancel. Think of a hairdresser using a purple toner to remove yellow brassiness from blond hair. We need an answer that names an existing tint the purple cancels. The trap will explain why the purple isn’t strong, which only explains half.

choices.note: Tempting. A tiny amount explains why the glass doesn’t turn strongly purple. But a faint purple tint is still a tint. It doesn’t explain why the glass ends up more colorless than without it.
This deepens the puzzle. If nothing else in the glass has a color, a purple additive can only add color, so the glass should look less colorless, not more.
Other works using other compounds tells us nothing about how this one works. Irrelevant.
CORRECT. Iron in the sand tints the glass green, and a faint purple cancels the green. The compound adds a little purple and removes more green, so the glass looks closer to colorless.

Another one-sided answer, like (A). It explains why people might not notice the purple. But not noticing an added tint still leaves the glass no clearer than before. It doesn’t explain why the glass looks more colorless with the compound than without it.

questions.stimulus: Graylock jays hide food in autumn and retrieve it during the winter. Jays that hide their food in many small, scattered caches later recover a smaller percentage of the food they hid than do jays that hide their food in a few large caches. Yet jays that use many scattered caches are more likely to survive the winter than are jays that use a few large ones.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Remembering the locations of many scattered caches is more demanding for a jay than remembering the locations of a few large caches.
Jays that use scattered caches typically hide several times as much food in all as other jays do.
Squirrels and other animals that raid jays’ caches find large caches far more easily than they find small, scattered ones.
During mild winters, Graylock jays of both kinds eat insects as well as the food they retrieve from their caches.
A few Graylock jays hide some of their food in scattered caches and the rest in a few large ones.
questions.explanation: The stimulus compares percentages recovered, but survival depends on how much food a jay actually gets back. If scattered cachers hide several times as much food, a smaller percentage of a much larger store can still be more food, which is (B). (C) is the trap: it seems to favor scattered caches, but raids are already reflected in the recovery figures, and if raiders hit large caches harder, large cachers should recover the smaller share, which contradicts the stimulus. (A) explains only why scattered cachers recover a smaller share.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Scattered cachers recover a smaller percentage of their food, but they survive the winter more often than jays with a few large caches.

breakdown.analysis: A smaller percentage of what? The stimulus never says the two kinds of jays hide the same amount. Rate versus amount: 40 percent of 1,000 seeds beats 80 percent of 300. We need an answer saying scattered cachers end up with more food even though they recover a smaller share. Most students pick (C) because it sounds like a point for scattered caches. But the recovery percentages already include losses to thieves, and (C) would predict that large cachers recover less, the opposite of what we’re told.

choices.note: Explains one side only. Harder memory work explains why scattered cachers recover a smaller share, but not why they survive better. It makes the puzzle sharper.
CORRECT. Scattered cachers hide several times as much food. A smaller percentage of a much bigger store can still be more food in total, and food is what gets a jay through winter.

Tempting, and the main trap. It sounds like a reason scattered caching pays off. But the percentages the jays recover already reflect what thieves took. If thieves raided large caches more, large cachers would recover the smaller share, which contradicts the stimulus.
Both kinds of jays eat insects in mild winters. Something true of both groups can’t explain a difference between them.
A few mixed cachers don’t tell us why one strategy beats the other. Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Astronomer: The moon Ivren always keeps the same hemisphere facing forward as it orbits its planet, so that hemisphere sweeps up loose debris much as a car’s windshield sweeps up insects. Ivren’s forward hemisphere has about three times as many impact craters as its rear hemisphere. Clearly, the forward hemisphere has been struck by far more debris over Ivren’s history than the rear hemisphere has.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the astronomer’s argument?
choices: The largest impact crater on Ivren, a basin hundreds of kilometers across, lies in its rear hemisphere rather than its forward one.
Debris generally strikes Ivren’s forward hemisphere at higher speeds than it strikes the rear hemisphere.
Several other moons that keep one hemisphere facing forward also have noticeably more craters on that hemisphere than on the other.
Much of Ivren’s rear hemisphere is covered by smooth ice plains that welled up from the interior long after Ivren formed.
Ivren’s rear hemisphere, too, has been struck by a substantial amount of debris over the course of its history.
questions.explanation: The astronomer reads today’s crater counts as a record of every strike in Ivren’s history. That works only if craters, once made, stay visible. (D) says much of the rear hemisphere was resurfaced by ice long after Ivren formed, which would erase old craters there, so the rear could have been hit just as often and simply lost the evidence. (A) is the trap: one large crater on the rear sounds like a heavy blow to the argument, but the argument is about how many strikes, and one big crater is one strike.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Ivren’s forward hemisphere has been struck by far more debris over its history than its rear hemisphere.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The forward hemisphere sweeps up debris; it now has about three times as many craters as the rear hemisphere.

breakdown.analysis: Do craters last forever? The argument treats the craters we see today as a complete tally of every hit. But if something wiped out craters on one side, the count would be lopsided even with equal hits. It’s like judging which classroom gets more graffiti by counting what’s on the walls today, when one room was repainted last summer. We need an answer that shows the rear hemisphere lost its record. Notice the right answer never mentions craters at all, which is why it’s easy to skip.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. A huge crater on the rear sounds like evidence of heavy hitting there. But the claim is about how many strikes each side took. The biggest crater is still just one strike. Size isn’t number.
Faster hits on the forward side fit the astronomer’s windshield picture. It gives no reason to doubt that the forward side was hit more often. If anything, it helps.
This makes the forward-sweeping pattern look general, which supports the astronomer.

CORRECT. Fresh ice welled up over much of the rear hemisphere long after Ivren formed, burying the craters that were there. The rear could have taken as many hits as the front; it just lost the evidence.
The astronomer already allows that the rear was hit. The claim is that the forward side was hit far more. Saying the rear took a lot of hits doesn’t touch the comparison. Conceded point.

questions.stimulus: Over the past twenty-five years, the number of known asteroids whose orbits bring them near Earth has increased more than tenfold. Over the same period, however, astronomers’ estimate of the likelihood that a large asteroid will strike Earth within the next century has fallen substantially.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Most of the large near-Earth asteroids that astronomers once could only infer have since been found, and none is headed for Earth.
Most of the near-Earth asteroids discovered in the past twenty-five years are too small to do serious damage if they struck Earth.
Telescopes now used to search for asteroids can detect objects far fainter than those that could be detected twenty-five years ago.
An asteroid’s orbit can be altered unpredictably when the asteroid passes close to a large planet such as Jupiter or Saturn.
Estimates of how much damage a large asteroid strike would cause have risen sharply over the past twenty-five years.
questions.explanation: A risk estimate built partly on asteroids nobody has found yet must allow that any of them might be headed our way. Once those asteroids are found and tracked, the uncertainty disappears; if none is on a collision course, the estimate falls even as the count of known asteroids soars. That is (A). (B) is the trap: small discoveries explain why finding more asteroids didn’t raise the risk, but not why the risk went down.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: We know of ten times as many near-Earth asteroids, but the estimated chance of a large one hitting Earth has fallen.

breakdown.analysis: Does finding more asteroids mean there are more asteroids? No. They were there all along. The count of known asteroids measures what we’ve found, not what’s out there. Before they were found, astronomers had to assume the unseen ones might be dangerous. It’s like a doctor who is more worried about a lump before the biopsy than after it comes back benign. We need an answer where discovery removed a feared danger. Most students pick (B) because it shrinks the importance of the new discoveries. But that only gets you to “risk unchanged,” not “risk fell.”

choices.note: CORRECT. The big asteroids that astronomers could only assume were out there have now been found, and none is headed for Earth. Uncertainty that used to count as risk is gone, so the estimate falls while the count of known asteroids climbs.
Tempting, and the main trap. If the new finds are small, they don’t add much risk. But that explains only why the risk didn’t go up. It gives no reason the estimate went down.
Better telescopes explain why so many more asteroids were found. That’s the side of the puzzle that needed no explaining. Doesn’t touch the falling risk.
If orbits can shift, astronomers should be less sure an asteroid will miss us. That pushes the risk estimate up, if anything.
Bigger damage estimates are about how bad a hit would be, not how likely one is. Wrong measure.

questions.stimulus: Fisheries officer: Five years ago, Skerrin Island began requiring fishers to return to the sea any female sea bream carrying eggs. Since then, the total weight of sea bream landed at Skerrin Island each year has risen by about 30 percent. Clearly, the rule has increased the number of sea bream in the waters around the island.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the fisheries officer’s argument?
choices: Some of the egg-carrying female sea bream that fishers return to the sea die from the stress of having been caught.
Before the rule took effect, the annual sea bream catch at Skerrin Island had been falling steadily for several years in a row.
Fishers on the neighboring islands, who sell at the same markets, are not required to return female sea bream carrying eggs to the sea.
Sea bream bring a higher price per kilogram at Skerrin Island than do most other fish landed there.
The number of boats fishing for bream out of Skerrin Island has grown by about half in five years.
questions.explanation: The officer treats a bigger total catch as proof of more fish. But a total catch depends on how hard the fleet fishes. If the number of boats grew by about half while the catch grew only 30 percent, each boat is landing less than before, which suggests the bream population may have shrunk. That is (E). (A) is the trap: some returned females dying shows the rule is imperfect, not that it had no effect, and it does nothing to explain away the bigger catch.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The egg-carrying rule has increased the number of sea bream around Skerrin Island.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Since the rule began, the total weight of bream landed each year has risen about 30 percent.

breakdown.analysis: Is a bigger catch the same as more fish? Not if more people are fishing. Total catch = fish per boat × number of boats. It’s like saying a lake has more fish because the town’s anglers caught more this year, when twice as many anglers showed up. We need an answer that explains the bigger catch without more fish. Do the math on (E): 50 percent more boats, 30 percent more fish, so each boat catches about 13 percent less.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. It sounds like the rule doesn’t work. But “some” returned females dying still leaves the rest alive to spawn. And it doesn’t explain the bigger catch at all. A partial flaw in the mechanism isn’t an alternative explanation.
A falling catch before the rule and a rising one after it fits the officer’s story. If anything, it helps.
We aren’t told what happened on the neighboring islands, so this comparison gives us nothing. Irrelevant.
Price might explain why fishers want bream, but it doesn’t tell us how many bream are in the water.

CORRECT. Half again as many boats, but only 30 percent more fish landed. Each boat is catching less than before, which points to the same or fewer bream, not more. The bigger total comes from more fishing.

questions.stimulus: Over the past decade, the average weight of scallop meat landed per trip by boats fishing out of Wexcombe Harbor has nearly doubled. Yet surveys conducted by marine biologists over the same period indicate that the number of scallops on the beds fished by Wexcombe Harbor boats has not increased.
questions.stem: Each of the following, if true, helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above EXCEPT:
choices: Wexcombe Harbor boats now tow larger dredges than they did a decade ago, covering more of the beds on each trip.
Several boats that once fished out of Wexcombe Harbor have left the fishery, so the remaining boats now compete with fewer rivals.
The marine biologists’ surveys have sampled the same locations on the beds at the same time of year throughout the decade.
The scallops on the beds fished by Wexcombe Harbor boats are, on average, considerably larger than they were a decade ago.
Wexcombe Harbor boats now make fewer trips each year, but each trip lasts several days longer than trips did a decade ago.
questions.explanation: Four choices give a way for each trip to bring in more scallop meat without more scallops: bigger dredges (A), less competition (B), bigger scallops (D) and longer trips (E). (C) only shows the surveys were done consistently, which makes the finding of no increase more trustworthy and so deepens the puzzle. (D) is the trap: it seems beside the point because the surveys counted scallops, but the catch is measured by weight, and larger scallops yield more meat per scallop.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Scallop meat landed per trip has nearly doubled, but the number of scallops on the beds hasn’t increased.

breakdown.analysis: EXCEPT question: four answers explain, one doesn’t. Catch per trip can rise without more scallops in three ways: each trip catches more of them (gear, competition, trip length), or each scallop has more meat. Watch the units: the catch is weight per trip, the survey is a count. Most students cross off (D) as irrelevant to the number of scallops. That’s backwards. It’s the weight-versus-count answer, and it explains plenty.

choices.note: Bigger dredges sweep more of the beds per trip, so each trip brings in more without more scallops. Explains, so not the answer.
Fewer rival boats means each remaining boat gets a bigger share of the same scallops. Explains.
CORRECT. Consistent survey methods make the “no increase” finding more reliable. That shores up one side of the puzzle instead of reconciling the two. It explains nothing about the bigger catches.

Tempting to cross off, and the main trap. The survey counted scallops, but the catch is measured by weight. Larger scallops mean more meat per scallop, so the same number can yield much more meat. Explains.
Longer trips catch more per trip even with fewer trips per year. Explains.

questions.stimulus: Town engineer: Rock salt melts ice on roads effectively at temperatures above about −10°C but works poorly in colder weather, whereas calcium chloride remains effective at much lower temperatures. Last winter our town switched from rock salt to calcium chloride, and ice-related traffic accidents on town roads fell by a third compared with the winter before. So the switch prevented many accidents.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the town engineer’s argument?
choices: Calcium chloride, like rock salt, can damage the bodies of cars and the surfaces of concrete roads and bridges over time.
Last winter, temperatures in the town fell below −10°C on far fewer days than they had the winter before.
Calcium chloride costs the town considerably more per ton than the rock salt it replaced.
Some of last winter’s ice-related accidents occurred on roads that had already been treated with calcium chloride.
Neighboring towns that kept using rock salt saw little change in their number of ice-related accidents last winter.
questions.explanation: By the engineer’s own premise, calcium chloride beats rock salt only on days colder than about −10°C. If last winter had far fewer such days, the switch had little chance to make a difference, and the milder weather itself could explain the drop in accidents, which is (B). (D) is the trap: accidents on treated roads sound like failure, but the engineer claimed only that accidents fell, not that they stopped. (E) actually supports the engineer.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Switching from rock salt to calcium chloride prevented many accidents.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Calcium chloride works in colder weather than rock salt; after the switch, ice-related accidents fell by a third.

breakdown.analysis: When is calcium chloride actually better? Only on the really cold days, below about −10°C. So the switch can only have prevented accidents on those days. What if last winter barely had any? Then the switch had nothing to do, and the drop must come from something else, like gentler weather. It’s like crediting your new snow tires for a safe winter in which it hardly snowed. We need an answer that shows the cold days, where the switch matters, were rare last winter.

choices.note: Damage to cars and roads is a cost, but the argument is about preventing accidents, not about cost or wear. Wrong dimension.
CORRECT. Calcium chloride only outperforms salt below −10°C. If last winter had far fewer such days, the switch had little room to help, and the milder winter itself explains the drop in accidents.
Cost is a reason to question the switch as a budget choice, not a reason to doubt it prevented accidents. Wrong dimension.
Tempting, and the main trap. It sounds like calcium chloride failed. But the engineer said accidents fell by a third, not that they disappeared. Some accidents on treated roads were already expected.
If towns that kept salt saw no improvement, that suggests the switch made the difference here. This strengthens the argument.

questions.stimulus: Since the sewage treatment plant serving Delby Harbor was upgraded three years ago, average bacteria levels in the harbor’s water have fallen by 70 percent. Yet in each of the three years since the upgrade, the harbor’s clam beds have been closed to harvesting because of bacterial contamination on more days than in any year before it.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Heavy rains still sometimes wash bacteria from farm fields into Delby Harbor, temporarily raising bacteria levels in the water over the beds.
The upgraded plant releases its treated water at a point farther from the clam beds than the old plant did.
Clams take in bacteria from the water as they feed and can retain those bacteria for some time afterward.
Demand for Delby Harbor clams has grown since the upgrade, and more people now harvest clams there each season.
Since the upgrade, the beds have been tested weekly rather than monthly, and any failed test closes them for a set period.
questions.explanation: Closure days depend not only on how dirty the water is but on how often anyone checks. If inspectors now test four times as often and every failed test triggers a fixed closure, brief spikes that monthly testing used to miss now get caught, so closures can rise even as average contamination falls. That is (E). (A) is the trap: rain-driven spikes explain why closures still happen, but those spikes happened before the upgrade too, so they don’t explain why closures increased.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Average bacteria levels in the harbor fell 70 percent after the upgrade, but the clam beds have been closed for contamination on more days each year than before.

breakdown.analysis: What decides whether a bed closes? Not the average. A failed test. So ask: how often are the beds tested? Average levels can drop while short spikes still occur, and the more often you test, the more spikes you catch. It’s like a town that adds speed cameras: speeding falls, but tickets go up because now someone is watching. We need an answer that raises the number of failed tests without dirtier water. Most students pick (A) because it explains how contamination still happens. But rainstorms aren’t new, so they can’t explain an increase.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. Rain-driven spikes explain why the beds still close at all. But the rains washed in bacteria before the upgrade too. Nothing here explains why closures went up while the water got cleaner.
Releasing treated water farther from the beds should mean fewer closures. Deepens the puzzle.
Clams holding on to bacteria is true before and after the upgrade. A constant can’t explain a change.
More harvesters doesn’t affect whether the beds are contaminated or how often they’re closed. Irrelevant.

CORRECT. Four times as many tests means four times as many chances to catch a brief spike, and each failed test closes the beds for a set period. Cleaner water on average, more closures on the calendar.

questions.stimulus: Amateur astronomer: Members of our club have watched the Orsa meteor shower from the same dark hilltop every year for twenty years. Over that time, the average number of meteors per hour reported by each member has fallen by half. Since the sky over the hilltop is no brighter now than it was twenty years ago, the Orsa shower itself must have grown weaker.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the amateur astronomer’s argument?
choices: Few new members have joined in twenty years, and the eye’s sensitivity to faint light at night declines markedly with age.
The number of club members who attend the yearly viewing on the hilltop has fallen by more than half over the past twenty years.
The Orsa shower is produced by dust left along the orbit of a comet that last passed near the Sun several centuries ago.
Meteor counts made by eye are generally less precise than counts made with cameras, which the club has never used for its counts.
The Orsa shower peaks on about the same night every year, and the club always observes on that night.
questions.explanation: The astronomer rules out a brighter sky but assumes nothing else about the observing has changed. If the club is mostly the same people, now twenty years older, and night vision for faint light declines with age, members would see fewer of the faint meteors even if the shower were as strong as ever. That is (A). (B) is the trap: fewer members would shrink the club’s total count, but the figure cited is the average per member, which a smaller turnout doesn’t lower.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Orsa meteor shower has grown weaker.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Each member’s average count per hour has halved over twenty years; same site; the sky is no brighter.

breakdown.analysis: The astronomer checked the sky. Did anyone check the eyes? A meteor count measures the shower and the observers together. Rule out the sky, and the observers are still there. It’s like a bird-watching group concluding the songbirds have vanished when its members, now in their seventies, can no longer hear high notes. We need an answer that shows the observers changed. Most students jump at (B) because fewer watchers means fewer meteors spotted. But the number in the stimulus is per member, so the size of the turnout cancels out.

choices.note: CORRECT. The club is mostly the same people, now twenty years older, and the ability to see faint light at night fades with age. Members could miss more of the faint meteors while the shower stays as strong as ever.

Tempting, and the main trap. Fewer people watching would cut the club’s total count. But the argument uses the average per member, and a smaller turnout doesn’t change how many meteors each person sees. Count versus rate.
Where the shower’s dust comes from doesn’t tell us whether the observers’ counts reflect a real change. Doesn’t weaken.

Sounds damaging: the counts are imprecise. But the club has counted by eye the whole time. An imprecise method used the same way every year scatters the numbers; it doesn’t produce a steady fall by half. It attacks the evidence’s precision, not the comparison.
This rules out one way the counts could have drifted (watching on the wrong night). It makes the comparison fairer, which helps the argument.

questions.stimulus: Twelve years ago, the nation of Ardeth banned the manufacture and sale of PBX, a flame retardant that was once widely added to foam cushions and mattresses. People absorb PBX mainly from household dust. Yet the average level of PBX in the blood of Ardeth’s residents is higher now than it was when the ban took effect.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Many homes in Ardeth still contain cushions and mattresses that were made, and treated with PBX, before the ban took effect.
Several other nations banned PBX at about the same time that Ardeth did, and their residents’ PBX levels have fallen.
Foam cushions made since the ban contain a different flame retardant, one that people also absorb from household dust and that lingers in the body.
Aging PBX foam sheds more of the chemical into household dust as it crumbles, and much of that foam is still in use.
Researchers measuring PBX in blood today use the same methods that were used when the ban took effect.
questions.explanation: Banning new PBX doesn’t remove the PBX already in homes, and the puzzle is not just that levels failed to fall but that they rose. (D) explains the rise: old foam sheds more PBX into dust as it ages, so exposure from the remaining foam is growing. (A) is the trap: old furniture still in homes explains why exposure continues, but continuing exposure explains only why levels haven’t dropped, not why they are higher.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: PBX was banned twelve years ago, but average blood levels of PBX are higher now than when the ban began.

breakdown.analysis: Read the puzzle exactly: levels didn’t just stay up, they went up. So pointing out that old PBX is still around isn’t enough. We need exposure that is growing. Think of a leaky roof: you stopped adding water to the attic, but the stains on the ceiling keep spreading because the soaked beams are rotting. We need an answer where the PBX already in homes gets into dust faster over time. Most students pick (A) because it names the obvious source. But a steady source keeps levels steady; it doesn’t raise them.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. Old cushions in homes explain why people are still exposed. But steady exposure would keep blood levels about where they were. The stimulus says levels rose, and this gives no reason for that.
What other nations did doesn’t affect blood levels in Ardeth. Irrelevant.
A different retardant would show up as that chemical, not as PBX. Irrelevant to PBX levels.
CORRECT. Old foam sheds more PBX into dust as it breaks down, and much of it is still in use. The ban stopped new PBX, but exposure from the old foam keeps growing, so blood levels can rise.
Consistent methods rule out a measuring quirk. That makes the rise more real, which deepens the puzzle.

questions.stimulus: Entomologist: Colonies of desert harvester ants that forage only in the cool early morning gather less seed per day than colonies that forage throughout the day. Yet in drought years, morning-only colonies survive at the same rate as all-day colonies do. So the amount of seed a colony gathers has little effect on whether it survives a drought.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the entomologist’s argument?
choices: Harvester ant colonies that have stored more seed are more likely than other colonies to survive an unusually cold winter.
Morning-only colonies and all-day colonies are found side by side throughout the same desert regions.
Midday heat kills many foragers, so all-day colonies spend much of their extra seed raising replacement workers.
In years without drought, all-day colonies produce more new queens, and thus more daughter colonies, than morning-only colonies do.
Droughts severe enough to threaten harvester ant colonies have become more common in recent decades.
questions.explanation: The entomologist infers that seed doesn’t matter because colonies that gather more seed survive no better. (C) shows the comparison is lopsided: the all-day colonies pay for their extra seed with dead workers and spend much of it replacing them, so the two kinds of colony may end up with similar usable stores. Equal survival is then just what we’d expect even if seed matters a lot. (A) is the trap: it suggests seed helps colonies survive, but cold winters are a different threat from drought.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The amount of seed a colony gathers has little effect on whether it survives a drought.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: All-day colonies gather more seed than morning-only colonies, yet both survive droughts at the same rate.

breakdown.analysis: More seed gathered, same survival. Does that show seed doesn’t matter? Only if the all-day colonies get to keep their extra seed with no offsetting cost. What if foraging in the heat costs them something that eats up the gain? It’s like concluding money doesn’t affect savings because people with second jobs save no more than others, when the second job’s commute eats the extra pay. We need an answer showing a hidden cost of all-day foraging that cancels the extra seed. Most students go for (A) because it says seed helps colonies survive. But the argument is about drought, not winter.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. It says stored seed helps a colony survive. But the conclusion is about droughts, and a cold winter is a different danger. Seed could matter for one and not the other.
Living in the same regions makes the two groups more comparable, which helps the argument.
CORRECT. Midday foragers die in the heat, and all-day colonies spend much of their extra seed raising replacements. The extra seed is used up, so equal survival doesn’t show that seed is unimportant.
More queens in good years is about reproduction, not about surviving droughts. Wrong outcome.
Droughts being more common doesn’t tell us whether seed affects survival when they happen. Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Of the planets that the Arkady survey has detected orbiting other stars, most orbit their stars more closely than Mercury orbits the Sun. Yet the survey’s own scientists, relying on these same detections, estimate that most planets orbiting such stars lie farther from their stars than Mercury lies from the Sun.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Many astronomers believe that planets often form far from their stars and then gradually move inward over many millions of years.
The survey sees only planets whose orbits appear nearly edge-on from Earth, and the wider an orbit, the rarer that alignment is.
Most of the planets that the survey has detected are considerably larger and more massive than Earth is.
Every planet the survey has reported was later confirmed by follow-up observations made with other, wholly independent telescopes.
Planets orbiting close to their stars are no easier for the survey to detect than equally large planets orbiting farther out.
questions.explanation: The scientists can reason from a lopsided sample to the true population if they know how it is lopsided. (B) never says “bias,” but its consequence is one: the survey sees a planet only when its orbit is nearly edge-on to Earth, and wide orbits rarely line up that way, so each distant planet detected stands for many that went unseen. (A) is the trap: inward migration would explain why so many detected planets are close in, but it pushes against the scientists’ estimate rather than reconciling it. (D) and (E) make the detections look like a fair sample, which deepens the puzzle.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Most planets the survey found orbit closer than Mercury, but the survey’s scientists estimate that most planets orbit farther out.

breakdown.analysis: How can your own data show mostly close planets and you conclude most are far? Only if your method misses far planets much more often, and you know by how much. It’s like a fishing net with big holes: you catch mostly large fish, but you wouldn’t conclude the lake is mostly large fish. We need an answer showing that the survey sees distant planets less often than it sees close ones. The right answer doesn’t say that outright; it gives a geometric fact you have to follow: a planet must line up edge-on to be seen, and wide orbits rarely do. Most students pick (A) because it explains why so many detected planets are close. But that supports the survey’s raw numbers, not the scientists’ opposite estimate.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. If planets drift inward, many really would end up close to their stars. That explains the detections, but it cuts against the scientists’ estimate that most planets are far out. One side only, and the wrong one.

CORRECT. The survey can see a planet only when its orbit is lined up nearly edge-on to us. Wide orbits rarely line up that way, so far-out planets are seen far less often than they occur. Each one found stands for many missed, and the scientists can correct for that.
Size is a different bias. It tells us nothing about distance from the star. Irrelevant.
This shows the detections are real, which shores up the side that says most planets are close in. It deepens the puzzle instead of resolving it.
This deepens the puzzle. If close and distant planets are equally easy to detect, the detections should be a fair sample, and the scientists’ estimate looks even stranger.

questions.stimulus: Water utility spokesperson: Three years ago we began adding orthophosphate to the city’s water; the compound forms a coating inside old lead pipes that keeps lead from dissolving into the water. Since then, lead levels in tap-water samples collected from homes have averaged 60 percent lower than in the three preceding years. Clearly, the orthophosphate is what reduced the lead in residents’ tap water.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the spokesperson’s argument?
choices: Orthophosphate takes several weeks after it is first added to the water to form a complete coating inside lead pipes.
Lead levels in samples from some homes with very old pipes are still well above the level that is considered safe.
Many other cities with old lead pipes also add orthophosphate to their water supplies, for the very same reason.
Some homes in the city are served entirely by newer copper or plastic pipes that contain no lead at all.
Three years ago the utility moved its sample collection from first thing in the morning, after water has sat in household pipes all night, to mid-afternoon.
questions.explanation: The spokesperson compares samples from two periods but assumes they were collected the same way. (E) changes the timing, and the consequence matters: water drawn first thing in the morning has stood in lead pipes all night, while mid-afternoon water has been flowing through them recently and has had little time to pick up lead. So the samples could show 60 percent less lead even if the water residents drink had not improved. (A) is the trap: a delay of a few weeks sounds like a problem, but it is trivial against a three-year average.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Orthophosphate is what reduced the lead in residents’ tap water.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Orthophosphate coats lead pipes; since it was added, lead in tap-water samples has averaged 60 percent lower than in the prior three years.

breakdown.analysis: Did the water change, or did the measuring change? A before/after comparison only works if the samples were taken the same way. The stimulus tells you lead dissolves into water in the pipes, and dissolving takes time. Water that sat in the pipes overnight has had hours to pick up lead; water drawn after a day of use has not. It’s like a diet that “works” because you started weighing yourself before breakfast instead of after dinner. We need an answer that changes how or when the samples were taken. The right answer only mentions the clock, so you have to see what the new time does to the water. Most students pick (A) because a delay sounds like the compound didn’t work. But a few weeks barely dents a three-year average.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. A slow start sounds like trouble. But a few weeks out of three years barely affects the average, and the compound still works after it forms. This doesn’t give another reason for the drop.
“Still above safe” in some homes is compatible with a big drop overall. The claim is that lead fell, not that the problem is solved.
Other cities using orthophosphate tells us nothing about what caused this city’s drop. Irrelevant.
Lead-free homes were lead-free in both periods. A constant can’t explain the change.

CORRECT. Water that has sat in the pipes all night has had hours to pick up lead; by mid-afternoon the household has been running water, so samples come from water that spent little time in the lead pipes. The 60 percent drop could come from the new timing, not from orthophosphate.

sections.title: Skill Builder: Hard Evaluate & Strengthen II

questions.stimulus: Two months ago, the mobile carrier Vantel cut the monthly price of its unlimited data plan by 20 percent. Since then, the number of customers enrolled in that plan has risen by 31,000. Vantel's marketing director concludes that the price cut has drawn tens of thousands of new subscribers to Vantel from other carriers.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the marketing director's conclusion?
choices: Do customers enrolled in Vantel's unlimited data plan use more data each month than customers enrolled in Vantel's other plans?
Were most of the customers who enrolled in the unlimited plan after the price cut already subscribers to another Vantel plan?
Before the price cut, did Vantel's unlimited data plan have more customers enrolled in it than any of Vantel's other plans?
Will Vantel earn more total revenue from the unlimited plan at the new price than it earned at the old price?
Had some Vantel customers complained before the price cut that the unlimited data plan was too expensive?
questions.explanation: Enrollment in one plan rose by 31,000, but the conclusion is about new subscribers coming from other carriers. (B) checks where the enrollees came from: if most were existing Vantel customers who changed plans, the conclusion fails; if they weren't, it gains support. (E) is the tempting answer because complaints about price seem to explain why a cut would attract people, but it matters in one direction at most and says nothing about whether the enrollees were new to Vantel. (C) asks which plan was most popular before the cut, which bears on neither direction, and (D) is about revenue, not where subscribers came from.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The price cut drew tens of thousands of new subscribers to Vantel from other carriers.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Vantel cut the unlimited plan's price 20 percent; enrollment in that plan has since risen by 31,000.

breakdown.analysis: Enrollment in a plan isn't the same as subscribers to the company. Who are these 31,000 people? If they were already Vantel customers who moved up from cheaper Vantel plans, Vantel gained zero new subscribers. It's like a restaurant cutting the price of its steak, selling more steaks, and concluding it found new diners, when its regulars just switched from the chicken. We need a question whose answer tells us whether the enrollees came from inside or outside Vantel. Watch for (E): it sounds like a reason the cut would work, but a yes doesn't tell us where the enrollees came from, and a no doesn't hurt the argument.

choices.note: Irrelevant. How much data people use on the plan has nothing to do with whether they came from another carrier.

CORRECT. Yes: most enrollees were already Vantel customers, so the jump reflects plan-switching and the conclusion falls apart. No: most came from outside the existing customer base, and the conclusion looks much better. Two answers, two directions.
Irrelevant. Which plan was most popular before the cut tells us nothing about where the 31,000 new enrollees came from. Either answer leaves the argument where it was.
Wrong dimension. Revenue tells you whether the price cut was a good business decision, not whether it drew subscribers from other carriers.

Tempting. Complaints about price make a cut sound like it would attract people. But even if some customers complained, those complainers were Vantel customers, which if anything hints at plan-switching. And a no tells you nothing. It doesn't separate new subscribers from old ones.

questions.stimulus: Plant engineer: Last spring our machine shop replaced its old cutting coolant with a new synthetic coolant. Since then, our drill bits have lasted, on average, about 40 percent longer before needing to be replaced. So the new coolant must be reducing the wear on our drill bits.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Is the new synthetic coolant advertised by its manufacturer as a way to reduce wear on cutting tools?
Does the new coolant also reduce wear on the saw blades and milling cutters that the shop uses?
Do drill bits used at other machine shops in the region typically last longer than the bits used at this shop?
Did the shop begin drilling mostly softer metals at about the time it switched to the new coolant?
Did the shop's machinists notice any difference in how the drill bits performed after the coolant was changed?
questions.explanation: The engineer infers that the coolant caused the bits to last longer just because the improvement followed the switch. (D) tests an alternative cause: if the shop started drilling softer metal at the same time, that could explain the longer bit life; if not, the coolant explanation is stronger. (A) is the trap: a manufacturer's claim might add a little support if yes, but a no wouldn't weaken the argument, and an advertisement isn't evidence about this shop. (B) and (E) matter one way at most, and (C) compares this shop with other shops, which can't tell us why bit life changed here.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new coolant is reducing wear on the drill bits.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The shop switched coolants last spring; since then the bits have lasted about 40 percent longer.

breakdown.analysis: Before and after. So what else changed last spring? Bits wear out faster on hard metal than on soft metal, so a change in what the shop drills could do the whole job. It's like crediting a new brand of tires for lasting longer the year you stopped driving on gravel roads. We need a question that tests another change happening at the same time. Watch for (A): an ad saying the coolant reduces wear sounds supportive, but ads aren't evidence about this shop, and a no wouldn't hurt the argument.

choices.note: Tempting. A manufacturer's claim feels like backup. But advertising claims aren't evidence about this shop, and if the answer is no, the argument is untouched. One-directional at best.

Matters one way at most. A yes would fit the idea that the coolant protects tools, but a no wouldn't show it does nothing for drill bits, since different tools wear in different ways. And it can't rule out the rival explanation that the work itself changed.

Irrelevant comparison. How this shop's bits compare with other shops' bits says nothing about why this shop's bits started lasting longer after the switch. The argument is about a change over time here, not a ranking against other shops.

CORRECT. Yes: softer metal could explain the longer bit life, and the coolant may deserve no credit. No: that rival explanation is gone and the coolant becomes the likeliest cause. The answer pushes the argument either way.

Sounds relevant but changes nothing. We already know the bits last 40 percent longer. Whether machinists noticed doesn't tell us why, and it doesn't touch the possibility that something else changed last spring.

questions.stimulus: Ferrow Cookware advertises on a popular cooking podcast, whose listeners are told they can get 15 percent off their first Ferrow order by entering the code SIMMER at checkout. The code is not mentioned in any of Ferrow's other advertising. Over the past six months, 2,400 orders were placed using that code. Clearly, the podcast advertisements brought Ferrow about 2,400 orders during that period.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions most helps in evaluating the argument?
choices: Has the code SIMMER been posted on popular coupon websites where anyone can find it?
Does Ferrow also advertise its cookware in several magazines that are devoted mainly to recipes?
Would Ferrow have earned more from those 2,400 orders if it had not offered customers the discount?
Do listeners of the cooking podcast cook at home more often than most other people do?
Is the discount offered with the code SIMMER available only on a customer's first order from Ferrow?
questions.explanation: The argument counts every SIMMER order as an order the podcast produced, which assumes only podcast listeners used the code. (A) tests that: if the code is on coupon sites that non-listeners visit, many of the 2,400 orders may owe nothing to the podcast; if not, the count looks reliable. (B) is the trap, since other advertising seems like a rival source of orders, but the stimulus says the code appears in none of Ferrow's other ads, so magazine readers wouldn't have it. (E) is already answered by the stimulus.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The podcast ads brought Ferrow about 2,400 orders in six months.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Podcast listeners are offered the code SIMMER; no other Ferrow ad mentions it; 2,400 orders used the code.

breakdown.analysis: The argument treats the code as a perfect tracker: every SIMMER order came from a listener. But codes travel. Once a discount code lands on a coupon website, anyone checking out can find it. It's like counting every person who says the password as a club member, when the password is written on the door. We need a question that checks whether non-listeners could have used the code. Watch for (B): other advertising sounds like a rival source, but the stimulus says the code appears in none of Ferrow's other ads.

choices.note: CORRECT. Yes: people who never heard the podcast could have used the code, so the 2,400 figure overstates what the ads did. No: the code is still a fair tracker of podcast listeners. Two answers, two directions.

Tempting. More advertising seems like another source of orders. But the code isn't in Ferrow's other ads, so magazine readers wouldn't have it. Whether Ferrow advertises in magazines doesn't touch the 2,400 code orders.
Profit is a different question. The argument is about how many orders the ads brought in, not whether the discount was a good deal for Ferrow.
So? Listeners cooking a lot might make them good customers, but it doesn't tell us whether the code orders came from listeners.
The stimulus already says the discount is for a first order. A question you can answer from the stimulus can't help evaluate it.

questions.stimulus: Telecommunications executive: Customers of ours who have chosen to receive their monthly bills by e-mail rather than on paper call our customer-service line 40 percent less often than our other customers do. So if we required all of our customers to switch to e-mailed bills, we could substantially reduce the number of calls to our customer-service line.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Would requiring all customers to switch to e-mailed bills substantially reduce the amount the company spends on printing and postage?
Do the customers who call the customer-service line most often tend to be those with the most complicated service plans?
Did the customers who chose e-mailed bills call customer service less often even before they chose them?
Have some of the customers who switched to e-mailed bills later asked the company to send them paper bills again?
Do customers who receive their bills by e-mail also tend to pay those bills online?
questions.explanation: The e-mail customers chose that option, so they may differ from other customers in ways that already made them call less. (C) tests that selection effect through time order: if they called less even before switching, the bill format isn't doing the work and forcing everyone to switch won't cut calls much; if they called just as often before, the format looks like the cause. (A) is the dominant trap: cost savings are a real benefit of the plan, but the conclusion is about calls, not costs. (B) matters in one direction at most, since we aren't told who has complicated plans.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Requiring all customers to switch to e-mailed bills would substantially reduce calls to customer service.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Customers who chose e-mailed bills call customer service 40 percent less often than other customers.

breakdown.analysis: The key word is "chosen." People who opt into e-mailed bills may be the kind of customers who rarely need help anyway: comfortable online, simple accounts, few problems. If so, the e-mail bill didn't make them call less; they were already low-callers.
