It's like noticing that people who choose the stairs are fitter and concluding that removing the elevator will make everyone fit. We need a question that checks whether the gap existed before the switch. Most students pick (A) because cost savings sound like the point of the plan. They aren't the point of this argument: the conclusion is about call volume.

choices.note: Tempting. Saving on printing and postage is an obvious benefit of the plan, so it feels relevant. But the conclusion is about the number of calls. Whether the plan saves money doesn't tell us whether it reduces calls.
This only matters if we know that paper-bill customers have the complicated plans, and we don't. On its own, either answer leaves the argument where it was.

CORRECT. Yes: the e-mail customers were low-callers before they switched, so choosing e-mail reflects who they are and forcing others to switch won't change much. No: their calls dropped after the switch, which points to the bill format as the cause. The answer pushes the argument in opposite directions.
So? A few customers switching back doesn't tell us whether e-mailed bills reduce calls. Under the plan, everyone would be required to switch anyway.
This describes the e-mail group a bit more, but either answer leaves open whether the bill format is what reduces calls. It doesn't test the causal claim.

questions.stimulus: Marketing consultant: In May, Pellard Coffee put up a large billboard on Route 14 advertising its shop at the Exit 12 interchange. This summer, sales at that shop were 20 percent higher than they were last summer, while sales at Pellard's other shops were unchanged. So the billboard drew new customers to the Exit 12 shop.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the marketing consultant's argument?
choices: Billboards along highways generally draw more attention from drivers than billboards along city streets do.
The billboard cost Pellard less to put up than the additional profit that the Exit 12 shop earned this summer.
Pellard had never before used billboards to advertise any of its shops, on Route 14 or elsewhere.
Traffic on Route 14 near Exit 12 was no heavier this summer than it was last summer.
Some customers at the Exit 12 shop say they stop there because they already know and like Pellard's coffee.
questions.explanation: The other shops rule out a chain-wide boom, but something local to Exit 12 could still explain the jump. (D) rules out the most obvious local alternative: if Route 14 traffic didn't increase, the extra sales weren't simply more cars passing by, and the billboard is left as the likeliest cause. (B) is the dominant trap: it supports a different conclusion, that the billboard paid for itself, and simply takes the extra sales as given. (A) is a general claim about highway billboards that rules out nothing, and (E) if anything weakens.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The billboard drew new customers to the Exit 12 shop.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The billboard went up in May; Exit 12 sales rose 20 percent over last summer; Pellard's other shops were flat.

breakdown.analysis: The comparison with other shops is a good start: it rules out something happening to Pellard as a whole. But what about something happening at Exit 12? More cars on that stretch of road, say from a detour or a new development, would bring more customers with or without a billboard. It's like crediting your new sign for a busier lemonade stand on the day the street fair moved to your block. We need an answer that knocks out a local alternative. Most students pick (B) because extra profit sounds like proof the billboard worked. But it's about whether the billboard was worth the money, not about what caused the extra sales.

choices.note: Out of scope. A general comparison between highway and city billboards doesn't tell us whether this billboard caused this shop's sales jump. It sounds relevant because it praises highway billboards, but it rules out nothing.

Tempting. Extra profit that covers the billboard's cost sounds like proof the billboard worked. But it supports a different claim: that the billboard was a good investment. It takes the extra sales as given and does nothing to show the billboard, rather than something else at Exit 12, caused them.
So? The billboard being Pellard's first doesn't tell us whether it caused the sales increase.

CORRECT. A local increase in traffic is the leading rival explanation for a jump at a single highway shop. If traffic was flat, more passing cars can't explain the 20 percent rise, which leaves the billboard as the best explanation.
If anything this weakens: some customers come for reasons that have nothing to do with the billboard. And "some" is too few to matter either way.

questions.stimulus: Utility analyst: Of the 600 households that our utility flagged last year for unusually high electricity use, 70 percent heat their water with electric water heaters. Thus, electric water heaters are a major reason that some households in our service area use far more electricity than others do.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Did any of the flagged households replace an old electric water heater with a new one during the past year?
Have the electric water heaters sold in the utility's service area become more energy-efficient over the past decade?
Would the flagged households save money on their energy bills by switching to water heaters that run on natural gas?
Was the proportion of flagged households with electric water heaters higher last year than it was in earlier years?
What proportion of all households in the utility's service area heat their water with electric water heaters?
questions.explanation: Seventy percent of high users have electric water heaters, but that means something only if it's higher than the rate among households generally. (E) asks for that base rate: if about 70 percent of all households have electric water heaters, the flagged group is typical and the argument collapses; if far fewer do, electric water heaters are overrepresented among high users and the argument gains support. (D) is the dominant trap: it sounds like a comparison, but it compares the flagged group with itself in earlier years, the wrong time frame and the wrong group, rather than with all households. (B) shifts to a different time frame and (C) to a different conclusion about saving money.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Electric water heaters are a major reason some households use far more electricity than others.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 70 percent of the 600 households flagged for unusually high use have electric water heaters.

breakdown.analysis: Seventy percent sounds like a lot. Compared with what? If 70 percent of every household in the area has an electric water heater, then high users are exactly as likely as anyone else to have one, and the statistic shows nothing. It's like noting that 90 percent of speeding drivers own phones. We need the base rate: how common are electric water heaters overall? Most students pick (D) because it looks like a comparison. But it compares the flagged group with its own past, not with the households that weren't flagged.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Whether some households swapped old heaters for new ones doesn't tell us whether electric water heaters are more common among high users than among everyone else.

Wrong time frame. Whether newer models are more efficient doesn't tell us whether electric water heaters are more common among high users than among everyone else, which is the comparison the argument skips.

This bears on a different conclusion: what the households should do. Savings from switching wouldn't show that electric water heaters are why these households use so much electricity, since without the base rate we can't tell.

Tempting. It sounds like a comparison, and comparisons are what this argument lacks. But it compares the flagged group with itself over time. Whether that share rose or fell, we still don't know how common electric water heaters are among households that weren't flagged.

CORRECT. This is the base rate. Around 70 percent: high users are just like everyone else, and water heaters explain nothing. Much lower: electric water heaters are overrepresented among high users, which supports the analyst. Opposite answers, opposite effects.

questions.stimulus: Network engineer: Within weeks after we released a new version of our phone app, one that automatically plays video previews, complaints about slow data speeds from our customers in Kelsing tripled. So the app's video previews must be generating so much data traffic that the cell towers serving Kelsing are frequently overloaded.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the network engineer's argument?
choices: Since the app's release, traffic through the Kelsing towers has hit their full capacity far more often than before.
The new version of the app uses so much of a phone's processing power that it slows down everything else running on that phone.
Earlier versions of the company's app did not play video previews unless a user chose to play them.
Complaints from Kelsing customers about dropped calls did not increase after the new version of the app was released.
The company plans to add equipment to the Kelsing towers next year in order to increase their capacity.
questions.explanation: The engineer names a specific mechanism: the previews create so much traffic that the Kelsing towers overload. (A) confirms the unstated middle step, showing that the towers have in fact been hitting full capacity far more often since the release. (B) is the dominant trap: it ties the app to slowness, but through a different mechanism, the app bogging down the phones themselves, which competes with the tower-overload story rather than supporting it. (C) restates what "new version" already implies, and (D) if anything weakens.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The app's video previews are overloading the Kelsing towers.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Speed complaints in Kelsing tripled within weeks of the release of the new app version, which plays video previews automatically.

breakdown.analysis: Timing is all we have. The app came out, complaints rose. But the conclusion isn't just "the app caused slow speeds"; it's a specific story: traffic overloads the towers. Is there any evidence the towers are actually overloaded? It's like blaming a traffic jam on a new stadium without checking whether the roads near it are actually full. We need an answer that confirms the overload step. Most students pick (B) because it connects the app to slow performance. But it blames the phones, not the towers, so it's a rival explanation, not support.

choices.note: CORRECT. This confirms the mechanism the engineer relies on. Combined with the timing, it shows the towers are actually overloaded, and overloaded since the app arrived, which is exactly what the traffic story predicts.

Tempting, because it ties the app to slowness. But it points to a different cause: the app bogging down the phones themselves. That's a rival to the tower-overload story, not support for it. If anything it weakens the engineer's argument.
This just spells out what "new version … that automatically plays video previews" already tells us. It adds no evidence about the towers.
If anything this weakens. Overloaded towers could also cause dropped calls, so no rise in dropped calls is a mild point against overload.
Irrelevant. A plan to add capacity next year tells us nothing about what is causing the slowdowns now.

questions.stimulus: Quality manager: In March our plant added a night shift. In the months since then, the number of defective parts our inspectors find each month has roughly doubled. Since the day-shift crew and its procedures have not changed, the night-shift crew must be producing defective parts at a much higher rate than the day-shift crew does.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Are the workers on the night shift, on average, less experienced than the workers on the day shift?
How does the plant's monthly output of parts since March compare with its monthly output before March?
Do other manufacturing plants that run night shifts find more defective parts each month than this plant does?
Do night-shift workers at other manufacturing plants tend to have higher accident rates than day-shift workers do?
Would hiring additional inspectors to work during the night shift substantially increase the plant's labor costs?
questions.explanation: The manager moves from a count (defects doubled) to a rate (the night crew makes defects at a much higher rate). (B) supplies the missing denominator: if total output roughly doubled when the night shift started, the night crew is producing defects at about the same rate as the day crew; if output rose only slightly, the night crew's defect rate must be high. (A) is the dominant trap: less experience would fit the manager's story, but a no wouldn't undercut it, and either way it doesn't tell us the night crew's actual rate. (C) compares this plant with other plants, which bears on neither crew's rate here.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The night crew produces defective parts at a much higher rate than the day crew.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A night shift was added in March; monthly defects found have roughly doubled; the day shift hasn't changed.

breakdown.analysis: Doubled compared with what? A second shift usually means more parts. If the plant now makes twice as many parts, twice as many defects is exactly what you'd expect from two crews with the same defect rate. It's like saying your second bakery must be sloppier because the company now throws out twice as many burnt loaves, when it also bakes twice as many. This is the classic count-versus-rate slip; know it. We need the output numbers. Most students pick (A) because inexperience sounds like a reason for errors. But it only matters one way, and it can't tell us the rate.

choices.note: Tempting. Inexperienced workers might make more mistakes, so a yes seems to back the manager. But a no doesn't hurt him much, and either way we still don't know whether the night crew's defect rate is actually higher. That depends on how many parts it makes.

CORRECT. This gives the denominator. Output roughly doubled: defects grew in step with production, so the night crew's rate looks like the day crew's and the conclusion fails. Output barely rose: the extra defects come from a small amount of night production, so the night rate must be high.
Irrelevant comparison. Other plants differ in size and output, so their defect counts tell us nothing about whether this plant's night crew has a higher defect rate than its day crew.
Accident rates at other plants are a different measure at different plants. They don't tell us about defective parts here.
Labor costs are irrelevant to whether the night crew's defect rate is higher.

questions.stimulus: Plant manager: Last year we replaced the dim fluorescent lamps above our inspection line with bright LED fixtures. Since then, our inspectors have caught 95 percent of defective parts before shipment, up from 85 percent the year before. So the brighter lighting has made it easier for our inspectors to spot defects.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the plant manager's argument?
choices: Inspectors at the plant say they prefer working under the new LED fixtures to working under the old fluorescent lamps.
The LED fixtures use considerably less electricity than the fluorescent lamps that they replaced over the inspection line.
Several inspectors have complained that the LED fixtures cause glare on parts that have polished surfaces.
The plant's inspectors have, on average, more years of experience than the inspectors at most other plants do.
The inspection line has run at the same speed since the lighting change as it did before.
questions.explanation: Better detection followed the new lighting, but inspectors could also be catching more simply because they have more time per part. (E) rules out that alternative: the line speed is unchanged, so the improvement isn't explained by slower inspection, and the lighting becomes the better explanation. (A) is the dominant trap: inspectors preferring the new lights sounds supportive, but it supports only a side claim about comfort, not that the light improved detection, and it rules out no rival cause. (B) supports a different conclusion about energy savings.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The brighter lighting made it easier for inspectors to spot defects.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: LED fixtures replaced fluorescent lamps last year; inspectors' catch rate rose from 85 to 95 percent.

breakdown.analysis: Before and after again. What else could raise the catch rate? Slow the line and inspectors get more time with each part, so they catch more no matter how bright the room is. It's like crediting new glasses for your better proofreading in the same week your deadline was pushed back. We need an answer that rules out a change in inspection conditions. Most students pick (A) because happy inspectors sound like a point for the lighting. But liking the light isn't seeing better, and it leaves the time-per-part explanation untouched.

choices.note: Tempting. Inspectors liking the new light sounds like a point for the lighting. But preferring the light isn't the same as seeing defects better, and it does nothing to rule out other reasons the catch rate rose, such as more time per part.
This supports a different conclusion: that the LEDs save energy. It says nothing about spotting defects.
If anything this weakens: glare would make some defects harder to see.
Experience is a fixed feature of the inspectors, not a change. It doesn't explain why the catch rate rose last year, and it doesn't connect the rise to lighting.

CORRECT. More inspection time per part is a natural rival explanation for a higher catch rate. If the line speed didn't change, inspectors aren't getting extra time, which leaves the new lighting as the best explanation.

questions.stimulus: Operations director: Fifteen years ago we bought a batch of stamping presses from Wendle Industries, which still makes that same model. Over the past five years, the Wendle presses we still operate have needed fewer repairs than any of our other presses. Clearly, Wendle presses are exceptionally durable, so when we replace our oldest presses, we should buy from Wendle.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Does Wendle offer a longer warranty on its presses than the other manufacturers the company has bought presses from?
How many of the presses that the company bought from Wendle fifteen years ago have since been taken out of service?
Were the presses bought from Wendle fifteen years ago delivered and installed on the schedule that Wendle had promised?
Do the company's mechanics find Wendle presses easier to repair than presses made by other manufacturers?
Have the costs of repairing the company's other presses risen over the past five years?
questions.explanation: The evidence covers only the Wendle presses "we still operate," a group that has survived fifteen years. (B) targets that selection effect: if many of the batch broke down and were retired, the survivors are the sturdiest few and say little about Wendle presses in general; if nearly all are still running, the low repair count reflects the whole batch and the argument is strong. (A) is the dominant trap because a long warranty sounds like evidence of durability, but it matters in one direction at most and says nothing about the presses that were retired. (D) concerns ease of repair, not how often repairs are needed.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Wendle presses are exceptionally durable, so the company should buy Wendle when it replaces its oldest presses.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The Wendle presses still in operation needed fewer repairs over five years than any other presses; Wendle still makes that model.

breakdown.analysis: Notice the quiet phrase: the Wendle presses "we still operate." What happened to the rest of the batch? If half of them died and were scrapped, the ones left standing are the toughest of the lot, and of course they need few repairs. It's like judging a car brand by the 30-year-old models still on the road, forgetting all the ones in the junkyard. This is survivorship bias, a selection effect worth knowing. We need to know how much of the batch survived. Most students pick (A) because a warranty sounds like a durability signal. But it's a promise, not a record, and a no wouldn't hurt the argument.

choices.note: Tempting. A long warranty sounds like a sign of a durable product, and it bears on the decision to buy again. But it matters one way at most: a yes is only a maker's promise, and a no doesn't show the presses are fragile. It doesn't touch the real problem, which is that only the surviving presses were counted.

CORRECT. Many taken out of service: the survivors are a hand-picked group of the sturdiest presses, and their low repair count says little about Wendle presses in general. Few or none: the whole batch has held up, and the durability claim stands. Opposite answers, opposite effects.
Delivery schedules are about Wendle's reliability as a supplier, not the durability of its presses.
Ease of repair is a different dimension from how often repairs are needed. Either answer leaves the durability claim untouched.
So? Rising repair costs for other presses don't tell us whether Wendle presses need fewer repairs, and the argument is about how many repairs, not their cost.

questions.stimulus: Utility spokesperson: Two years ago we began offering a discounted rate for electricity used between 11 p.m. and 6 a.m. About a third of our customers enrolled, and since then overnight demand on our system has risen 18 percent, almost entirely because enrolled customers are using more electricity overnight. Clearly, the discount has led those customers to shift some of their electricity use from daytime to overnight hours.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the utility spokesperson's argument?
choices: Since enrolling, customers on the discounted rate have paid less per kilowatt-hour, on average, than customers who did not enroll.
Many customers who enrolled in the discounted rate have since bought electric cars, which they charge overnight at home.
Customers who enrolled in the discounted rate had higher electricity bills, on average, than other customers before enrolling.
The utility's discounted overnight rate is lower than the overnight rate that any other utility in the region offers.
The enrolled customers' total monthly electricity use is about the same as it was before they enrolled.
questions.explanation: The premises establish that enrolled customers use more electricity overnight; the conclusion says they shifted use from daytime, which also requires their daytime use to have fallen. (E) supplies that missing piece indirectly: if their total use is unchanged while their overnight use rose, their daytime use must have dropped by about the same amount, which is what a shift means. (A) is the dominant trap: a lower average price per kilowatt-hour shows enrollees are using more cheap overnight power, but that happens whether the use was shifted or added, so it doesn't support a shift. (B) weakens by offering new overnight demand rather than shifted demand.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The discount led enrolled customers to shift some of their use from daytime to overnight.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A third of customers enrolled in an overnight discount; overnight demand rose 18 percent, almost entirely from enrolled customers using more overnight.

breakdown.analysis: More overnight use isn't the same as shifted use. "Shift" means it moved: less during the day, more at night. The premises only show the night half. Maybe enrolled customers just added new overnight use, like running a pool pump or charging a car, while their daytime use stayed put. It's like a gym saying its discount moved members to off-peak hours because off-peak visits rose, without checking whether peak visits fell. We need evidence that daytime use dropped. The right answer does it with arithmetic: same total, more at night, so less during the day. Most students pick (A) because it shows the discount is working for enrollees. But a lower average price comes from more overnight use, shifted or not, so it can't tell the two stories apart.

choices.note: Tempting. It shows the discount is doing something for enrolled customers. But a lower average price per kilowatt-hour follows from using more power overnight, whether that use was moved from the daytime or simply added. It supports a side claim, that enrollees benefit, not the claim that they shifted their use.
This weakens. Charging new electric cars is added overnight use, not use moved from the daytime. It offers an explanation for the overnight rise that isn't a shift.
So? Who enrolled tells us nothing about whether their daytime use went down.
This might explain why people enrolled, but it doesn't show that they moved use out of daytime hours.

CORRECT. Total unchanged plus overnight up means daytime down by about the same amount. That is exactly what "shift" requires, and it rules out the idea that the extra overnight use was simply new demand.

questions.stimulus: Advertising consultant: In each of the twelve product categories we studied, from laundry detergent to breakfast cereal, the brand with the largest advertising budget also had the largest share of sales. Moreover, in nearly every category, brands' advertising budgets and their shares of sales tended to rise and fall together from year to year. This shows that large advertising budgets enable brands to win market share.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions most helps in evaluating the argument?
choices: Do consumers report that advertisements influence which brands of detergent and cereal they choose to buy?
Were the advertisements for the brands with the largest budgets produced by the largest advertising agencies?
Do companies commonly set each brand's advertising budget at a fixed percentage of that brand's sales revenue?
Do brands in the twelve categories studied spend more on advertising than brands in most other product categories do?
Are the profit margins on laundry detergent higher than the profit margins on breakfast cereal?
questions.explanation: Budgets and sales shares move together, and the consultant reads the correlation as advertising driving share. (C) tests the reverse direction: if companies set ad budgets as a fixed share of sales, then rising sales produce bigger budgets, which explains the correlation without advertising winning anything; if they don't, that reverse explanation is gone and the consultant's reading gains ground. (A) is the dominant trap: consumer reports sound like direct evidence, but self-reports about influence are weak and a no wouldn't refute the argument, so it matters in one direction at most. (D) compares spending across categories, which has no bearing on the direction of the link within them.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Large advertising budgets enable brands to win market share.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: In all twelve categories the biggest advertiser had the biggest share; budgets and shares rose and fell together in nearly every category.

breakdown.analysis: Correlation, yes. But which way does the arrow point? Big ad budgets could produce big sales, or big sales could produce big ad budgets. If a company simply spends, say, 5 percent of each brand's revenue on advertising, the bestseller will always have the biggest budget, and budgets will rise and fall with sales, whether or not the ads do anything. It's like noting that cities with the most firefighters have the most fires: the staffing follows the fires. We need a question that tests the reverse direction. It's hidden here as a budgeting question, which is why it's easy to skip. Most students pick (A) because consumer opinion sounds like direct evidence. But people are poor judges of what influences them, and a no wouldn't sink the argument.

choices.note: Tempting. It sounds like direct evidence about whether ads work. But consumers' reports about what influences them are unreliable, and a no wouldn't show that advertising has no effect. At most it nudges the argument one way. It also doesn't address the real issue: which way the correlation runs.
Irrelevant. Which agency made the ads doesn't explain the link between budgets and sales shares.

CORRECT. Yes: budgets are set from sales, so big sales cause big budgets, and the correlation is explained without ads winning any share. No: that reverse explanation is out, and the consultant's causal reading looks much stronger. Opposite answers, opposite effects.
Irrelevant comparison. How much these categories spend compared with other categories says nothing about which way the link between budgets and shares runs within a category.
Comparing profit margins across categories has nothing to do with whether advertising wins market share within a category.

questions.stimulus: Advertising executive: A week after the Kestry Cup sailing race was televised, a research firm asked a panel of 2,000 consumers to list luxury watch brands. Panelists who had watched the entire broadcast, during which Varenne aired six commercials, were twice as likely as other panelists to name Varenne. So Varenne's commercials made viewers more aware of the brand.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the advertising executive's argument?
choices: When surveyed a month before the race, panelists who later watched the whole broadcast named Varenne no more often than other panelists did.
Varenne was the only maker of luxury watches that aired any commercials during the broadcast of the Kestry Cup race.
Many people who watch televised sailing races have incomes high enough to allow them to buy luxury watches.
Varenne has aired commercials during televised sailing races in each of the past several years.
The research firm also asked the panelists to list the brands of sailing equipment that they could name.
questions.explanation: Viewers and non-viewers weren't randomly assigned: people who sit through a whole sailing broadcast may have known Varenne already. (A) rules out that selection effect: a month before the race, the future viewers named Varenne no more often than anyone else, so the gap appeared after the broadcast, which points to the commercials. (B) is the dominant trap: it seems to isolate Varenne's ads, but whether other watch brands advertised has no bearing on whether viewers' greater awareness of Varenne predates the race. (C) and (D) point toward pre-existing awareness and so weaken.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Varenne's commercials made viewers more aware of the brand.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A week after the broadcast, panelists who watched all of it (and saw six Varenne ads) were twice as likely as others to name Varenne.

breakdown.analysis: Who watches an entire televised sailing race? Probably people who already move in the world of yachts and luxury goods, people who might have known Varenne long before the race. If so, the gap was there all along and the ads did nothing. It's like finding that people who stay for a whole golf telecast can name more golf brands and crediting the commercials. We need an answer that shows the viewers weren't already more aware. The right answer is a before-and-after check on the same people. Most students pick (B) because it seems to make Varenne's ads stand out. But it does nothing about the real problem: who chose to watch.

choices.note: CORRECT. Before the race, the future viewers knew Varenne no better than anyone else. A week after it, they were twice as likely to name it. That rules out pre-existing awareness and leaves the broadcast, and its six Varenne ads, as the best explanation.

Tempting. It seems to isolate Varenne's ads as the only watch message viewers saw. But the problem with the argument is that viewers might have known Varenne before the race. Whether other watchmakers advertised doesn't touch that.
This points the wrong way. If sailing viewers are the kind of people who buy luxury watches, they may have known Varenne already, which weakens the argument.
This also weakens. If Varenne has advertised during sailing races for years, regular viewers may have learned the brand long before this broadcast.
Irrelevant. What else the firm asked doesn't tell us whether the ads raised awareness of Varenne.

questions.stimulus: Utility analyst: Two years ago we identified the 500 Tessford households whose electricity use that year had been the highest, and last year we mailed each of them monthly reports comparing its use with that of similar nearby homes. Last year those households used 9 percent less electricity than the year before, while use by other Tessford households fell by only 1 percent. So the reports prompted their recipients to conserve.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Are the households that received the reports larger, on average, than the other households in Tessford?
Did Tessford households as a whole use more electricity last year than households in neighboring districts did?
Did the utility spend more to print and mail the reports than it lost from selling less electricity to their recipients?
Did use also fall sharply last year at households elsewhere that were their districts' heaviest users two years ago but got no reports?
Did some of the households that received the reports find the comparisons with their neighbors unwelcome?
questions.explanation: The recipients were chosen because their use was the highest in one year, and households picked for an extreme year tend to drift back toward normal the next year regardless. The stated comparison group, all other Tessford households, doesn't control for that. (D) asks about the right comparison group: if other districts' top users also cut use sharply without reports, the 9 percent drop is largely the drift and the argument fails; if their use held steady, the reports look responsible. (A) is the dominant trap: larger households would explain why recipients use more, but not why their use fell. (B) compares Tessford as a whole with other districts, which doesn't bear on the drop.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The reports prompted recipients to conserve.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Reports went to the 500 households with the highest use two years ago; last year their use fell 9 percent; other Tessford households fell only 1 percent.

breakdown.analysis: How were the recipients picked? For having their highest-ever-looking year. Some of them hit the top because of a one-time spike: a broken heater, a houseful of guests, a brutal winter on their side of town. The next year, many of them would come back down on their own. This is called regression to the mean; know it. It's like giving a pep talk to the students with the worst test scores and crediting the talk when their next scores rise. Comparing them with all other Tessford households doesn't help, because those households weren't selected for an extreme year. We need a comparison with households selected the same way but given no reports. Most students pick (A) because it points out a difference between the groups. But size explains a high level of use, not a drop.

choices.note: Tempting. It points to a real difference between recipients and everyone else, and that feels like a confounder. But bigger households explain why use is high, not why it fell 9 percent in one year. Either answer leaves the drop unexplained.
Irrelevant comparison. Whether Tessford uses more than its neighbors overall tells us nothing about why the 500 recipients' use fell. Either answer leaves the drop unexplained.
Whether the program pays off for the utility is a different question from whether the reports caused the drop.

CORRECT. These households were selected the same way but got no reports. Yes, their use also fell sharply: the 9 percent drop is mostly heavy-use years returning to normal, and the reports get little credit. No, their use held steady: the selection effect can't explain the drop, and the reports look responsible.
So? Some recipients disliking the reports doesn't tell us whether the reports caused the drop. A no tells us nothing either.

questions.stimulus: Maintenance supervisor: At our plant, the machines nearest the loading dock suffer bearing failures nearly three times as often as our other machines do. Forklifts carrying heavy loads pass close to those machines all day long. So vibration from the forklifts is most likely what is causing the excess bearing failures.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the maintenance supervisor's argument?
choices: Fitting the machines near the dock with heavier-duty bearings would cost the plant far less than permanently rerouting all of its forklift traffic away from them.
The loading dock's doors stay open for much of the day, letting dust and cold air into the area around the nearby machines.
Among the machines near the loading dock, those mounted on vibration-absorbing pads have bearing failures no more often than the plant's other machines.
Bearing failures across the plant as a whole have become somewhat more frequent over the past three years.
The plant's forklift drivers report that the floor near the loading dock is the smoothest floor in the entire plant.
questions.explanation: The supervisor blames forklift vibration, but anything else special about the dock area (dust, cold, older machines) could explain the failures. (C) confirms the vibration mechanism: dock machines that are shielded from vibration fail no more often than machines elsewhere, so the extra failures go away exactly when vibration is blocked, which rival causes such as dust or cold would not predict. (A) is the dominant trap: it links forklifts and bearings, but it supports a conclusion about which remedy is cheaper, not about what causes the failures. (B) offers rival causes and so weakens, (D) is a plant-wide trend that says nothing about the dock machines, and (E) if anything cuts against vibration.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Vibration from the forklifts is most likely causing the excess bearing failures near the dock.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Machines near the dock have nearly three times the bearing failures of other machines; heavily loaded forklifts pass them all day.

breakdown.analysis: Location is doing all the work. The dock-side machines fail more, and forklifts are near them. But lots of things are different near a loading dock: dust, cold drafts, maybe older machines. Which one is the culprit? It's like blaming the subway for the cracks in a building near the station when the building is also the oldest on the block. The strongest support would isolate vibration: same location, vibration blocked, and the extra failures disappear. That's what the right answer gives us, phrased in a way that looks like a side detail. Most students pick (A) because it mentions both forklifts and bearings. But it's about the cost of fixes, not the cause.

choices.note: Tempting, because it talks about forklifts and bearings together. But it supports a different conclusion: which fix is cheaper. It says nothing about whether vibration is what causes the failures.
This weakens. Dust and cold air are rival explanations for the failures near the dock.

CORRECT. These machines sit in the same spot, with the same dust, drafts and forklift traffic, but the vibration is absorbed, and their excess failures vanish. That isolates vibration as the cause and cuts against the rival explanations.
Wrong time frame and wrong group. A plant-wide trend tells us nothing about why the machines near the dock fail more often than the others, or whether vibration is the reason.
Sounds relevant, since it's about the forklifts' path. But a smooth floor, if anything, means less jolting there, so it doesn't help the vibration story. It certainly doesn't strengthen it.

passages.title: The Fenmore Street terminus
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
When the Northern and Coastal Railway opened its Fenmore Street terminus in Cardell in 1868, visitors approaching from the city saw only a hotel: five storeys of carved sandstone, with a clock tower and a pointed arcade at street level. The train shed behind it, a single span of wrought iron and glass nearly eighty meters wide, could not be seen from the street at all. By the early twentieth century, critics had made the building an emblem of Victorian bad faith. The hotel’s architect, Edwin Saltash, had in their view been ashamed of the most original structure of his age and had hidden it behind a costume borrowed from the cathedrals.

The architectural historian Ines Rowle has argued that this charge holds the building to a standard its designers did not share. The demand that a building display its structure, she observes, became a commonplace of criticism only in the early twentieth century; to a Victorian engineer, a train shed was equipment, no more meant to be seen from the street than a boiler. Rowle points out that the hotel and the shed were commissioned separately, designed by different offices, and paid for from different accounts, and that the contracts for the two scarcely mention each other. She concludes that the hotel concealed nothing, since no one involved thought the shed was the sort of thing a façade might express.

Rowle’s documentary evidence is persuasive as far as it goes, and it disposes of the caricature of Saltash as an architect embarrassed by iron. But her conclusion is too sweeping. Saltash’s correspondence shows that he worried a great deal about the junction between the two structures. He redrew the hotel’s rear wall four times so that its arches would align with the bays of the shed, and in one letter he describes the concourse, where travelers pass from the stone building into the iron one, as “the hinge on which the whole design turns.” An architect who regarded the shed as mere equipment would hardly have labored so over the place where travelers first see it.

What Saltash seems to have intended was not concealment but sequence. The street front announces the station to the city in a language the city could read, while the shed is withheld until the traveler has entered, so that its scale arrives as a revelation rather than as a fact visible from a distance. The concourse, on this reading, is where the design reaches its climax, not where it gives up. Whether this was the wisest way to design a terminus is a fair question, and later critics may reasonably prefer stations that state their engineering openly. But they should not mistake a staged disclosure for a disguise.

passages.title: The Pellworth wage increase
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
Standard accounts of the labor market hold that a firm has no reason to pay more than the wage at which it can hire all the workers it wants. Yet firms sometimes do exactly that, and economists have long debated why. One answer, known as efficiency-wage theory, holds that a wage above the market rate can pay for itself: workers who would lose an unusually good job if dismissed have reason to work harder and to stay longer, so the firm recovers in productivity and reduced turnover what it spends in wages.

The economist Halvard Brune has made the Pellworth Tinplate Works the theory’s showcase. In 1909 Pellworth raised its daily wage by more than half, to a level no other mill in the district approached, and within two years its output per worker rose by nearly forty percent. Pellworth’s directors made no secret of their hope that the raise would pay for itself, and Brune attributes the gain to the wage: men who knew that dozens of applicants waited at the gate every morning, he argues, had every reason not to give the foremen cause to dismiss them.

The historian Ada Kielland has objected that Brune’s figures prove less than he supposes. In 1910 Pellworth installed continuous rolling machinery that its competitors did not acquire until years later, and Kielland argues that the new machines, not any change in the workers’ diligence, account for the rise in output; mills that installed the same machinery in later years, she notes, saw comparable gains without raising wages. She concludes that the episode offers no support for efficiency-wage theory at all, and that the raise is better explained as an attempt to forestall a union then organizing in the district.

Kielland’s point about the machinery is decisive against Brune’s reading of the output figures; no comparison of output before and after 1910 can separate the effect of the wage from that of the machines. But her conclusion overreaches, because output was not the only thing the wage could have affected. Pellworth’s payroll records show that the share of its workers who left within a year fell from nearly half to under a tenth after the raise, and that this decline began in 1909, before the machines arrived. Since each departing worker had to be replaced and trained at considerable cost, the fall in turnover may well have recovered much of what the raise cost. The episode thus supports a narrower version of the theory than Brune’s: the higher wage may have paid for itself by keeping workers, whatever its effect on how hard they worked. Whether the threat of a union also played a part is a separate question, and nothing in the payroll records rules it out.

passages.title: The rule of lenity
passages.subject: law
passages.text:
Under the rule of lenity, when a criminal statute is ambiguous, a court is to adopt the reading more favorable to the defendant. The rule is usually defended on the ground of fair notice: no one should be punished for conduct that the law did not clearly forbid when it was committed, and a statute that admits two readings has not clearly forbidden what only the harsher reading covers. Courts have applied some version of the rule for centuries, and it is often described as among the oldest canons of statutory construction.

The legal scholar Teodor Vasko has argued that this defense cannot survive scrutiny. Few people read criminal statutes before acting, he notes, and fewer still read the appellate opinions that settle what those statutes mean, so the notice the rule is said to protect is largely a fiction. Worse, the rule rewards precisely those defendants who studied a statute closely enough to find a gap in it; a rule meant to protect the unwary, he argues, ends up protecting chiefly the wary. Vasko concludes that lenity should be abandoned and that ambiguous criminal statutes should be read, like any others, in whatever way best serves the legislature’s evident purpose.

Vasko’s criticism of the fair-notice rationale is largely sound. But it does not reach the rule itself, because fair notice was never the rule’s only support, nor its strongest. The rule also reflects the principle that defining crimes is the business of the legislature rather than the courts. When a court resolves an ambiguity in a criminal statute by asking which reading best serves the statute’s purpose, it decides for itself whether conduct the legislature did not clearly address shall be punished—a choice that, in a system reserving the power to criminalize to elected lawmakers, courts ought not to make. Lenity places the burden of clarity on the body that has the power to supply it: a legislature that dislikes a lenient reading can amend the statute, whereas a defendant convicted under a harsh one has no comparable remedy.

This rationale does, however, carry an implication that lenity’s defenders have been slow to accept. Many courts now invoke the rule only as a last resort, after every other interpretive tool—text, structure, history, and purpose—has failed to resolve the ambiguity. If the point of lenity is to keep courts from settling questions of criminal liability that the legislature left open, then consulting a statute’s purpose first defeats that point, since inferring a purpose in order to settle such a question is just the kind of judicial choice the rule exists to prevent. Properly understood, the rule belongs earlier in a court’s analysis than such courts place it, not at the end.

passages.title: Benefit of clergy
passages.subject: law
passages.text:
For centuries English law made nearly every felony, from murder to the theft of goods worth more than a few pence, punishable by death. Yet many of those convicted of felony were never hanged, and one reason was a privilege known as benefit of clergy. Originally the privilege allowed a cleric accused of felony to be handed over to the church’s courts, which could not impose death. Because clerics were among the few who could read, the royal courts came to accept the ability to read a verse of scripture as proof of clerical status, and by the fifteenth century almost any man who could read could claim the privilege. The passage usually set was the opening verse of the fifty-first psalm, which came to be known as the neck verse.

Earlier legal historians treated the privilege as an embarrassment, a medieval anomaly that let literate criminals escape the gallows on a technicality. The historian Ruth Danbury has argued instead that by the sixteenth century it had become a deliberate instrument of mitigation. Parliament, she notes, withdrew the privilege from the gravest offenses while leaving it available for lesser ones, and a statute of 1489 provided that a layman could claim it only once, branding him on the thumb so that a second claim could be detected. The result, Danbury argues, was a graded system within a law that otherwise knew a single penalty: first offenders convicted of lesser felonies were spared, while repeat and grave offenders were not.

Danbury’s account of how the privilege functioned is convincing, but her account of its purpose claims too much. The statutes she cites were passed piecemeal, over more than two centuries, by legislators responding to particular crimes; none of them describes the privilege as a scheme of graded punishment, and several were plainly aimed at closing what their framers regarded as abuses. That the privilege came to work as a system of mitigation does not show that anyone designed it as one. It is better understood as an institution that acquired a function no one set out to give it, one that judges and juries learned to exploit because Parliament had trimmed the privilege, for reasons of its own, into a usable shape.

Nor should the mitigation it provided be overstated. So long as the reading test survived, the privilege favored those who could read, and an illiterate laborer could be hanged for a theft for which a literate defendant would be branded and released. Only when Parliament abolished the reading test in 1706 did the privilege become available to eligible offenders regardless of their schooling, and even then it remained unavailable for the many offenses that Parliament had by that time declared to be without benefit of clergy.

passages.title: Condensates and cellular function
passages.subject: natural-science
passages.text:
Cell biologists have long known that some of the cell’s internal compartments, such as the nucleolus, have no membrane around them. Over the past two decades many researchers have come to regard such structures as condensates: droplets that form when certain proteins and RNA molecules, once they exceed a threshold concentration, separate from the surrounding fluid much as oil separates from water. Proponents of this view hold that condensation is a general mechanism by which cells organize their chemistry. By gathering an enzyme and its substrates into a small volume, a condensate can speed a reaction, and by dissolving when conditions change, it can switch a process off within seconds.

The biochemist Lena Hartig has warned that much of the evidence for this view is weaker than it appears. Many of the proteins said to form condensates have been shown to do so only in a test tube, at concentrations far above any found in a living cell, or in cells engineered to produce the protein in unnatural abundance. Droplets that appear only under such conditions, she notes, may tell us more about the experiment than about the cell. That a protein can form droplets under such conditions, Hartig argues, shows only that it is capable of condensing, not that it condenses in the cell or that condensing does anything there. She suspects that many reported condensates are artifacts of the methods used to detect them.

Hartig’s objection identifies a real gap, but it does not show that the gap cannot be closed. The decisive test is genetic: alter a protein so that it no longer condenses while leaving intact the regions that bind its partners, then ask whether the cell loses the capacity attributed to the condensate. Experiments of this kind on Tolva, a yeast protein that helps cells recover from sudden heat, have been instructive. A variant of Tolva that bound its usual partners normally but could not condense left cells unable to recover from heat shock, while a variant that condensed normally but bound its partners weakly did nearly as well as the unaltered protein. Similar experiments on several other proteins, however, have found that cells tolerate the loss of condensation with no detectable defect.

The proper conclusion is narrower than either side’s. Hartig was right to insist that a capacity observed in a test tube is not yet a function observed in a cell, and proponents who treat the one as evidence of the other have moved too quickly. But condensation is not, as a rule, an artifact of the laboratory either. Whether a particular condensate does anything is a question about that protein, to be answered by experiments of the kind performed on Tolva, and the answer is sometimes yes.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The Fenmore Street terminus shows that its architect was ashamed of the iron shed, which he hid behind a hotel in a style borrowed from the cathedrals.
Saltash was not ashamed of the shed, nor did he see it as mere equipment; his hotel was meant to delay the view of it, not conceal it.
Because the hotel and the shed at Fenmore Street were commissioned and designed separately, the hotel cannot properly be said to have concealed anything at all.
Stations that display their engineering openly are better designed than the Fenmore Street terminus, though its architect cannot fairly be accused of bad faith.
Saltash’s letters show that he redrew the rear wall of the Fenmore Street hotel several times so that its arches would align with the bays of the shed.
questions.explanation: The author agrees with Rowle that Saltash was not 'embarrassed by iron' but rejects her claim that the shed was mere equipment, concluding that Saltash intended 'not concealment but sequence' (fourth paragraph). B states both halves. A is the critics' charge, C is Rowle's conclusion, which the author calls 'too sweeping', and E is supporting evidence. D drops the author's qualification: the author says only that critics 'may reasonably prefer' open stations and calls the question of wisdom 'a fair question', without taking a side.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall position on the hidden train shed.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first sentences of the third paragraph and the whole fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Three views. The critics: Saltash hid the shed out of shame. Rowle: the hotel hid nothing, because nobody thought of the shed as something to express. The author: Rowle is right that he wasn't ashamed, wrong that the shed was mere equipment; the design stages a reveal. We need an answer with the author's own view: not a disguise, not equipment, a sequence.

choices.note: This is the critics' view from the first paragraph. Both Rowle and the author reject it.
CORRECT. It keeps the concession (not embarrassment), the rejection of Rowle (not mere equipment), and the author's thesis (delay, not concealment).

Tempting, because the author does think the hotel wasn't a disguise. But this is Rowle's reasoning, and the author calls her conclusion 'too sweeping'. The author thinks the shed mattered a great deal to Saltash.
Too strong. The author says later critics 'may reasonably prefer' open stations and calls the wisdom of the design 'a fair question'. That's not the author saying open stations are better.
True (third paragraph), but it's one piece of evidence, not the point of the passage.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Rowle points out that the hotel and the shed at Fenmore Street
choices: were designed so that the arches of the hotel’s rear wall would line up exactly with the bays of the shed
were both regarded by those who designed them as equipment rather than as works of architecture
were built at different times, the shed having been completed some years before the hotel
were condemned by critics who believed that each was dishonest in its own particular way
were paid for separately, under contracts that scarcely refer to one another
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says Rowle points out that the two were 'paid for from different accounts' and that 'the contracts for the two scarcely mention each other', which E paraphrases. A is real, but it comes from Saltash's correspondence, which the author uses against Rowle. B misreads Rowle: she calls only the shed equipment. C and D are never stated.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what Rowle cites about how the two structures were commissioned.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The third sentence of the second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Rowle's evidence: commissioned separately, different offices, different accounts, contracts that barely mention each other. Watch for evidence from the third paragraph. That's the author's, not Rowle's.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's in the passage. But it comes from Saltash's letters, which the author offers against Rowle. Wrong speaker.
Rowle calls the shed equipment, like a boiler. She never says the hotel was equipment.
Nothing about construction dates. Different accounts isn't different times.
The critics attacked the building as a whole for hiding the shed. Nobody says each part was dishonest.
CORRECT. 'Paid for from different accounts' and contracts that 'scarcely mention each other', in synonyms.

questions.stem: In describing the concourse as “the hinge on which the whole design turns” (fourth sentence of the third paragraph), Saltash most probably meant that
choices: the transition from hotel to shed was central to how he conceived the terminus
the concourse was the structural element that physically joined the iron shed to the masonry of the hotel
the success of the design depended on travelers being able to see the great shed from the street
the hotel could be redesigned freely so long as the concourse itself was left unchanged
the concourse was the only part of the terminus for which he and the shed’s designers were jointly responsible
questions.explanation: The author quotes the phrase to show that Saltash cared about 'the place where travelers first see' the shed (third paragraph), and the fourth paragraph calls the concourse the design's 'climax'. A captures this figurative sense. B is the literal, dictionary sense of 'hinge': the passage says nothing about a structural joint. C reverses the design, which keeps the shed hidden from the street. D and E are unsupported.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Decide what 'hinge' means here: literal or figurative.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The fourth and fifth sentences of the third paragraph, and the third sentence of the fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: A hinge is the point everything turns on. The author uses the quote to prove that Saltash cared about where travelers move from stone into iron and first see the shed. So the phrase means: that transition is the key to the whole design. Watch for the literal sense, a physical connector.

choices.note: CORRECT. The transition from stone to iron is what the design turns on, which is why the author later calls the concourse its 'climax'.

Tempting: a hinge is literally a joint. But the passage never discusses how the two structures are physically connected. The author uses the quote to show what Saltash cared about, not how the building was engineered.
Opposite. The shed 'could not be seen from the street at all', and the author says the design withholds it until the traveler enters.
Saltash redrew the rear wall four times to make it match the shed. That's the reverse of 'the rest can change freely'.
Rowle says the two were designed by different offices; nothing says the concourse was shared work, let alone the only shared part.

questions.stem: The author mentions that Saltash redrew the hotel’s rear wall four times (third paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: support Rowle’s claim that the hotel and the shed were designed by two different offices
show that Saltash cared more about the hotel’s appearance from the street than about the shed
suggest that Saltash, despite Rowle’s documentary evidence, was in fact embarrassed by the shed
challenge part of Rowle’s conclusion by showing that Saltash attended closely to the hotel’s relation to the shed
illustrate how hard it was to align a masonry building with an iron structure of so large a span
questions.explanation: The detail follows 'But her conclusion is too sweeping' and supports the claim that Saltash 'worried a great deal about the junction between the two structures'; an architect who saw the shed as mere equipment 'would hardly have labored so' (third paragraph). D states that purpose. A gets the direction wrong: the detail is used against Rowle. C revives the critics' view, which the author says Rowle's evidence 'disposes of'. B and E describe purposes the passage never pursues.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find why the author brings up the four redrawings.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second through fifth sentences of the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Look at what comes right before it: 'But her conclusion is too sweeping.' Then: Saltash worried about the junction, redrew the wall four times, called the concourse a hinge. Then: someone who thought the shed was mere equipment wouldn't do that. So the detail is evidence against one part of Rowle's view.

choices.note: Wrong direction. The detail appears in the paragraph that pushes back on Rowle, and it says nothing about separate offices.
Opposite. The rear wall faces the shed, not the street. Redrawing it shows concern for the shed.
Tempting if you think hiding means shame. But the author says Rowle's evidence 'disposes of the caricature of Saltash as an architect embarrassed by iron.'
CORRECT. It's evidence against Rowle's claim that nobody involved treated the shed as more than equipment, while the author keeps her other point.
Sounds plausible, but the author never discusses engineering difficulty. The point is what Saltash cared about, not how hard the job was.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Rowle holds that
choices: Saltash withheld the shed from view so that travelers would grasp its scale only after they had entered
the demand that a building display its structure is an unreasonable standard by which to judge any building of any period
the critics who condemned the terminus judged it by a principle that gained wide acceptance only after it was built
Saltash’s own correspondence shows that he regarded the iron shed as mere equipment rather than as a true work of architecture
the hotel’s street front was meant to express the engineering of the shed in a language that the people of the city could read
questions.explanation: Rowle argues that the critics' charge 'holds the building to a standard its designers did not share', since the demand that a building display its structure 'became a commonplace of criticism only in the early twentieth century' (second paragraph); the terminus opened in 1868. C paraphrases this. A is the trap: it is the author's own account of Saltash's intention (fourth paragraph), not Rowle's. B overstates her claim, which is about anachronism, not about the standard being unreasonable in general. D cites the wrong evidence: Saltash's letters are the author's evidence against Rowle. E garbles the fourth paragraph.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick out the view that belongs to Rowle, not to the author or the critics.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second paragraph, and compare the third and fourth.

breakdown.analysis: Hard because several answers are things the passage says, just not things Rowle says. Rowle's moves: 1. the standard that a building 'display its structure' came later (early twentieth century); 2. a shed was equipment to a Victorian; 3. the two were commissioned separately; 4. so the hotel concealed nothing. Ask of each choice: who said this?

choices.note: Tempting. It's the most memorable idea in the passage, but it belongs to the author, who uses it partly against Rowle. Rowle thinks nobody involved saw the shed as something to show at all.
Too strong. Rowle says the standard wasn't shared in 1868. That's a claim about timing, not a claim that the standard is unreasonable for every building.
CORRECT. The standard 'became a commonplace of criticism only in the early twentieth century', after the 1868 building, and it was one 'its designers did not share'.
Wrong evidence. Rowle relies on commissions, accounts and contracts. Saltash's letters are what the author uses to show he did care about the shed.
The 'language the city could read' line is the author's, and it describes the street front announcing the station, not expressing the shed.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, the author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements about a railway terminus whose train shed was plainly visible from the street?
choices: Its design would be preferable to that of the Fenmore Street terminus, since it would state its engineering openly.
Its designers would probably have shared the standard that Rowle says became a commonplace only in the early twentieth century.
It would show that its architect, unlike Saltash, regarded the train shed as something more than mere equipment.
It would almost certainly have been commissioned and paid for as a single project rather than as two separate ones.
It could not produce the particular effect that Saltash sought by keeping the shed out of sight until travelers entered.
questions.explanation: Two steps. First, the author says Saltash's design withholds the shed 'so that its scale arrives as a revelation rather than as a fact visible from a distance' (fourth paragraph). Second, a shed plainly visible from the street is exactly such a fact. So that design cannot produce Saltash's effect: E. A is the trap: the author grants only that critics 'may reasonably prefer' open stations and calls the question 'fair', never endorsing the preference. C wrongly implies Saltash saw the shed as mere equipment, which the author denies. B and D go beyond anything the passage supports.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply the author's account of Saltash's design to a different, hypothetical station.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second through fourth sentences of the fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Step 1: what was Saltash's effect? The shed is hidden until you enter, so its scale hits you as a revelation instead of being 'a fact visible from a distance'. Step 2: in a station with the shed visible from the street, the shed is exactly that kind of fact. So that station gives up the reveal. Watch for answers that turn the author's 'fair question' into a verdict.

choices.note: Tempting, because the author mentions this preference. But the author says only that critics 'may reasonably prefer' such stations. Granting that a preference is reasonable isn't holding it. The author takes no side.
We have no idea when or where this hypothetical station was built, so we can't say what standard its designers held.
This treats Saltash as someone who saw the shed as equipment. The author argues the opposite: Saltash labored over where travelers first see it.
Separate commissioning is Rowle's evidence about Fenmore Street. Nothing links a visible shed to a single contract.
CORRECT. Saltash's effect depends on the shed staying hidden until the traveler enters. A shed visible from the street can't deliver that reveal.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The rise in output per worker at the Pellworth Tinplate Works after 1909 shows that a wage well above the market rate can make workers more diligent.
The Pellworth wage increase is better explained as an attempt to forestall a union than as an application of efficiency-wage reasoning.
The Pellworth evidence cannot show that the raise made workers more productive, but it suggests the raise paid for itself through lower turnover.
The Pellworth episode confirms efficiency-wage theory, since the higher wage both reduced turnover and raised output per worker at the mill.
Because Pellworth installed new machinery shortly after raising its wages, the episode can shed no light on whether a high wage can pay for itself.
questions.explanation: The author accepts Kielland's point that output figures can't separate wage from machines, but says her conclusion 'overreaches': the turnover decline, which began before the machines, supports 'a narrower version of the theory' (fourth paragraph). C states that. A is Brune's view, B and E are Kielland's, and D drops the author's qualification by claiming the output gain for the wage and calling the theory confirmed.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's conclusion about what the Pellworth case shows.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The fourth paragraph, especially its second and fifth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Three views. Brune: the wage made men work harder, so output rose. Kielland: no, the machines did it; the episode supports nothing; it was about a union. Author: Kielland is right about output, wrong that it supports nothing, because turnover fell before the machines. So: narrower support, through turnover. The answer needs both the concession and the narrower support.

choices.note: This is Brune's reading, and the author calls Kielland's objection to it 'decisive'.
Kielland's explanation. The author calls the union question 'separate' and says only that the records don't rule it out. That's not endorsing it.
CORRECT. The concession (output can't show the wage worked) plus the author's claim (turnover gives narrower support).
Too strong. The author never credits the output rise to the wage, and 'may have paid for itself' isn't 'confirms'.
Tempting, because the machinery point really is decisive against Brune. But this is Kielland's overreach: the author says the turnover data, which predate the machines, do bear on the question.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the continuous rolling machinery installed at Pellworth
choices: was not acquired by Pellworth’s competitors until some years after Pellworth had installed it
was installed in the same year in which Pellworth raised its daily wage by more than half
accounts, in Brune’s view, for only a small part of the rise in Pellworth’s output per worker
contributed, in the author’s view, to the fall in the share of workers who left within a year
was purchased in the hope that it would eventually allow the mill to reduce its wages again
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says Pellworth installed the machinery in 1910 and 'its competitors did not acquire [it] until years later', which A paraphrases. B is the near-miss: the raise came in 1909 and the machines in 1910, a gap the author's argument depends on. C invents a view for Brune, who never discusses the machines. D reverses the author's point that the turnover decline began 'before the machines arrived'. E is unsupported.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says about the machinery.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second sentence of the third paragraph, and the third sentence of the fourth.

breakdown.analysis: Facts: installed in 1910; competitors got it years later; mills that got it later saw similar gains without raising wages. The raise came in 1909. Keep the dates straight; one answer blurs them.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'Its competitors did not acquire [it] until years later.'
Tempting, because the dates are close. But the raise was in 1909 and the machines came in 1910, and the author's whole turnover argument depends on that one-year gap.
Brune isn't said to discuss the machinery at all. That's Kielland's objection to him.
Opposite. The author stresses that the turnover decline began in 1909, 'before the machines arrived', precisely so it can't be credited to them.
Nothing about why the machinery was bought, and nothing about cutting wages again.

questions.stem: The author mentions that the decline in turnover at Pellworth began in 1909 (third sentence of the fourth paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: show that Brune was right after all to credit the higher wage with the rise in output per worker
indicate that this change, unlike the rise in output, cannot be credited to the factor Kielland cites against Brune
establish that the threat of a union played no part in Pellworth’s decision to raise its daily wage
suggest that the new machinery had less effect on Pellworth’s output than Kielland claims that it had
show that the share of workers leaving within a year fell faster than output per worker rose
questions.explanation: Kielland's objection is that the 1910 machines confound the output figures. By noting that the turnover decline began in 1909, 'before the machines arrived', the author shows that this change escapes her objection, which is what B says in abstract terms. A is the trap: the author says no comparison of output 'can separate the effect of the wage from that of the machines.' C contradicts the last sentence of the passage, and D and E make claims the author never makes.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find why the date of the turnover decline matters to the argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first three sentences of the fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Why care whether turnover fell in 1909 or 1911? Because Kielland's objection is about timing: the machines came in 1910 and muddy everything after. A change that started in 1909 can't be the machines. We need an answer that says the timing shields the turnover evidence from Kielland's objection.

choices.note: Tempting, because the 1909 date helps the wage theory. But it helps the turnover version, not Brune's output claim. The author says output before and after 1910 can't be untangled.
CORRECT. 'The factor Kielland cites' is the machinery. The output rise can't be separated from it; the 1909 turnover decline can.
The author says the opposite: 'nothing in the payroll records rules it out.'
The author never measures how much the machines did. Kielland's point is accepted as 'decisive' about output.
The passage gives no basis for comparing the two rates, and that isn't why the date is mentioned.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?
choices: A theory is outlined; a case offered in support of it is described; an objection to that use of the case is presented; the objection is rejected and the original reading of the case is reaffirmed.
Two rival explanations of a puzzling practice are outlined; a case that appears to support one of them is described; that explanation is then qualified in light of further evidence.
A theory is outlined; a case offered in support of it is described; an objection to the theory is presented; the theory is abandoned in favor of a historical explanation of the case.
A puzzling practice is described; a case offered in support of a theory explaining it is examined; the case is shown to support a rival explanation, though the theory is not wholly rejected.
A theory is outlined; a case offered in support of it is described; an objection to that use of the case is presented; the objection is partly accepted, and narrower support is drawn from the case.
questions.explanation: First paragraph: efficiency-wage theory. Second: Brune's Pellworth case. Third: Kielland's objection. Fourth: the author accepts the machinery point but finds narrower support in the turnover data. E matches every step. A gets the last step wrong (the objection is accepted, not rejected). B invents a second explanation in the first paragraph, C has the theory abandoned, and D has the case supporting the union explanation, which the author never endorses.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match each paragraph to a step and find the choice that gets every step right.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first sentence of each paragraph, and the second and fifth sentences of the fourth.

breakdown.analysis: Organization answers die on one wrong word. P1: a theory. P2: Brune's case for it. P3: Kielland's objection (machines; no support). P4: objection right about output, wrong overall; narrower support from turnover. Check the last step closely: partly accepted, not rejected and not fully accepted.

choices.note: Close, but the last step is backwards. The author calls Kielland's point 'decisive' against Brune's reading, so Brune's reading isn't reaffirmed.
The first paragraph gives one explanation, efficiency-wage theory, not two rival ones. The union idea only shows up in the third paragraph.
The theory isn't abandoned. The author keeps a narrower version of it.
The author never says the case supports the union explanation, only that the records don't rule it out.
CORRECT. Every step fits, including the key one: the objection is 'decisive' about output but 'overreaches' as a conclusion, and the case gives narrower support.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Kielland maintains that
choices: nothing in Pellworth’s payroll records rules out the possibility that fear of a union influenced the raise
the Pellworth episode supports only a narrower version of efficiency-wage theory than the one Brune defends
Brune’s figures for the rise in Pellworth’s output per worker after the raise of 1909 are inaccurate
the gains in output Pellworth achieved were later matched elsewhere by mills whose wages did not rise
the fall in the share of Pellworth’s workers who left within a year was caused by the new machinery
questions.explanation: The third paragraph reports that, according to Kielland, 'mills that installed the same machinery in later years... saw comparable gains without raising wages', which D restates.
