A is the author's remark in the last sentence, not Kielland's, and B is the author's own conclusion, which Kielland's 'no support... at all' contradicts. C changes 'prove less than he supposes' into 'inaccurate': she disputes what the figures show, not the figures. E is never claimed by anyone.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the claim that the passage attributes to Kielland herself.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The third paragraph, and compare the fourth.

breakdown.analysis: Kielland's claims: 1. Brune's figures prove less than he thinks; 2. the machines explain the output rise; 3. mills that got the machines later saw similar gains without raises; 4. the episode gives no support at all; 5. the raise was about a union. The fourth paragraph is the author talking. Watch for claims about unions and narrower versions that come from the author.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's about the union, which is Kielland's topic. But this sentence is the author's, in the last line of the passage. Kielland goes further: she says the union is the better explanation.
This is the author's conclusion. Kielland says the episode offers 'no support for efficiency-wage theory at all.'
A qualifier swap. 'Prove less than he supposes' is about what the numbers show, not whether they're right. She accepts the output rise and explains it differently.
CORRECT. Her comparison case: mills that installed the machinery later saw 'comparable gains without raising wages.'
No one says this, and the author points out that turnover began falling before the machines arrived.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that the author regards the claim that Pellworth’s higher wage made its workers more diligent as
choices: neither established nor refuted by the evidence from Pellworth that the passage describes
refuted by the evidence that the new machinery accounts for the rise in Pellworth’s output
supported by the fall in the share of Pellworth’s workers who left within a year
less plausible than the claim that the raise was meant to forestall a union
established for the period before 1910, though not for the years after the machines arrived
questions.explanation: Two steps. The author says no comparison of output 'can separate the effect of the wage from that of the machines' (fourth paragraph), so the output data don't establish greater diligence; and the author's narrower version holds that the wage may have paid for itself 'whatever its effect on how hard they worked', leaving diligence open rather than denying it. Together these give A. B is the trap: it turns 'can't separate' into 'refuted'. C confuses staying with working harder, D ranks two explanations the author never ranks, and E relies on output data before 1910 that the passage never gives.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out how the author rates Brune's diligence claim: proven, disproven, or open.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first and fifth sentences of the fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: First: is diligence proven? No. The output rise can't be separated from the machines. Second: is it disproven? Also no. The author's narrower version works 'whatever its effect on how hard they worked.' So it's open. This is the classic 'unsupported' versus 'false' trap: don't confuse 'no evidence for' with 'evidence against'.

choices.note: CORRECT. Not established (the output figures are confounded) and not refuted (the author leaves the effect on effort open).

Tempting, because Kielland says the machines explain the rise and the author calls her point 'decisive'. But decisive against Brune's reading means the evidence can't separate the two causes. That leaves the diligence claim unproven, not disproven.
Staying longer isn't working harder. The turnover data support the retention mechanism, which the author keeps separate from effort.
The author calls the union question 'separate' and doesn't compare its plausibility with anything.
The passage gives output only as a two-year rise. There's no pre-1910 output figure that could establish anything for that period alone.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Because the fair notice the rule of lenity is said to protect is largely a fiction, courts should read ambiguous criminal statutes in whatever way best serves their purpose.
The rule of lenity is justified because no one should be punished for conduct that the law did not clearly forbid at the time the conduct occurred.
The rule of lenity is better supported by the principle that the legislature should define crimes than by the principle of fair notice.
Though its usual justification is weak, the rule of lenity is warranted on other grounds, which imply that courts should apply it earlier in their analysis.
Courts should resort to the rule of lenity only after the text, structure, history, and purpose of a criminal statute have all failed to resolve its ambiguity.
questions.explanation: The author grants that Vasko's attack on fair notice is 'largely sound', defends lenity on separation-of-powers grounds (third paragraph), and concludes that the rule 'belongs earlier in a court's analysis' (fourth paragraph). D captures all three. A is Vasko's conclusion, B is the rationale the author calls weak, and E is the current practice the author criticizes. C is the strongest trap: it is true to the third paragraph but drops the fourth paragraph's conclusion, which the rest of the passage builds toward.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall conclusion about the rule of lenity.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first two sentences of the third paragraph and the last sentence of the passage.

breakdown.analysis: Layers: the usual defense (fair notice); Vasko (fair notice is fiction, so scrap the rule); the author (Vasko is right about notice, wrong about the rule, because lenity rests on legislative supremacy, and that rationale means courts should apply it earlier). The main point needs the concession, the new ground and the payoff in the last paragraph.

choices.note: Vasko's argument. The author says his criticism 'does not reach the rule itself.'
The fair-notice defense, which the author calls weak: Vasko's criticism of it is 'largely sound.'

Tempting, because the author does believe this. But it stops at the third paragraph. The passage goes on to draw the conclusion that matters most: courts should use the rule earlier. A main point that leaves out where the argument ends up is incomplete.
CORRECT. Weak usual justification, a better one, and its implication for when courts apply the rule.
This is what 'many courts now' do, and the author argues against it: the rule 'belongs earlier... not at the end.'

questions.stem: According to the passage, Vasko argues that the rule of lenity
choices: places the burden of clarity on the legislature, which alone has the power to supply that clarity
should be invoked only after all of the other tools of interpretation have failed to resolve an ambiguity
tends to benefit defendants who examined a statute closely enough to discover an ambiguity in it
is among the oldest canons of statutory construction and for that reason ought to be retained by courts
leaves defendants who are convicted under harsh readings of criminal statutes without any adequate legal remedy
questions.explanation: Vasko says the rule 'rewards precisely those defendants who studied a statute closely enough to find a gap in it' (second paragraph), which C paraphrases. A and E come from the author's defense of lenity in the third paragraph, B describes what many courts do, and D twists the first paragraph's description into an argument nobody makes; Vasko wants the rule abandoned.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what Vasko says about the rule.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Vasko's points: 1. people don't read statutes, so notice is a fiction; 2. the rule rewards the defendants who studied the statute; 3. so abandon the rule and read for purpose. Everything else belongs to someone else.

choices.note: The author's argument from the third paragraph. Vasko wants the rule gone.
That's what 'many courts now' do (fourth paragraph), not a claim of Vasko's.
CORRECT. 'Rewards precisely those defendants who studied a statute closely enough to find a gap in it.'
The first paragraph mentions the rule's age, but nobody argues it should be kept for that reason, and Vasko wants it abandoned.
The author's point in the third paragraph, offered in favor of lenity.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which one of the following is true of a legislature that dislikes a court’s lenient reading of a criminal statute?
choices: It has no remedy comparable to the one that is available to a defendant who has been convicted under a harsh reading.
It is in a position to correct the result, which a defendant convicted under a harsh reading is not.
It must accept the reading, since appellate opinions settle what criminal statutes mean.
It can ask the court to reconsider the statute in light of the legislature’s evident purpose.
It has failed, in Vasko’s view, to give fair notice of the conduct that the statute forbids.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says 'a legislature that dislikes a lenient reading can amend the statute, whereas a defendant convicted under a harsh one has no comparable remedy.' B states this asymmetry. A reverses it. C borrows the phrase about appellate opinions from Vasko's argument and draws a conclusion the passage contradicts. D and E are unsupported.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says about a legislature unhappy with a lenient reading.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last sentence of the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The author's asymmetry: the legislature can amend; the convicted defendant has no comparable remedy. That's why the burden of clarity goes to the legislature. Watch for the reversal.

choices.note: Tempting if you read fast, because it uses the passage's own words. But it flips who lacks the remedy. It's the defendant who has 'no comparable remedy.'
CORRECT. The legislature 'can amend the statute'; the defendant 'has no comparable remedy.'
Appellate opinions come up in Vasko's point about what people read. The author says the legislature can simply amend the statute.
Nothing about asking a court to reconsider. The passage's remedy is amendment.
Vasko's argument is that fair notice is a fiction, not that legislatures fail to give it.

questions.stem: The author’s attitude toward Vasko’s argument as a whole is most accurately described as
choices: acceptance of its conclusion about the rule, combined with serious doubts about the reasoning by which Vasko actually arrives at it
rejection of it as a whole, on the ground that fair notice is a far more substantial protection than Vasko allows
acceptance of it, subject only to the reservation that lenity should still be retained by courts as a last resort
agreement with its view that courts err in consulting a statute’s purpose, but rejection of its proposal to abandon the rule
agreement with its assessment of the usual rationale for lenity, but rejection of the conclusion it draws about the rule
questions.explanation: The author calls Vasko's criticism of fair notice 'largely sound' but says it 'does not reach the rule itself' (third paragraph), rejecting his call to abandon lenity. E fits. A reverses which part is accepted. B contradicts the author's agreement on fair notice. C mistakes current court practice, which the author criticizes, for a reservation. D is the trap: the author does think courts err in consulting purpose first, but Vasko holds the opposite; he wants statutes read for purpose.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how the author responds to Vasko: which parts are accepted and which rejected.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second paragraph and the first two sentences of the third.

breakdown.analysis: Vasko's argument has two parts: the premise (fair notice is a fiction) and the conclusion (abandon lenity, read for purpose). The author accepts the premise, 'largely sound', and rejects the conclusion, which 'does not reach the rule itself.' Watch for an answer that pins the author's own view on Vasko.

choices.note: Backwards. The author accepts Vasko's reasoning about fair notice and rejects his conclusion.
The author agrees fair notice is weak ('largely sound'). The objection to Vasko rests on a different rationale.
The last-resort practice is what the author criticizes in the fourth paragraph, and Vasko wants the rule gone entirely.

Tempting, because the author really does think consulting purpose first is a mistake. But that's the author's view, not Vasko's. Vasko wants ambiguous statutes read for 'the legislature's evident purpose.' So the author can't be agreeing with him on that.
CORRECT. Agrees the usual rationale fails; rejects the conclusion that lenity must go.

questions.stem: The primary function of the fourth paragraph is to
choices: draw from the rationale defended in the third paragraph a conclusion about where the rule belongs in a court’s analysis
concede that the rationale defended in the third paragraph is open to an objection that its defenders have overlooked
provide further support for Vasko’s claim that the notice the rule is said to protect is largely a fiction
show that courts have abandoned the rule of lenity in practice while continuing to endorse it in principle
reconcile Vasko’s proposal with the principle that defining crimes is the business of the legislature
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph opens with an 'implication' of the third paragraph's rationale: if lenity keeps courts from settling questions the legislature left open, consulting purpose first defeats it, so the rule 'belongs earlier.' A says this. B is the trap: 'however' and 'slow to accept' sound like a concession, but the implication is an unwelcome consequence for current practice, not a flaw in the rationale. C, D, and E misdescribe the paragraph.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Decide what the last paragraph does in relation to the rest of the passage.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The fourth paragraph, read against the third.

breakdown.analysis: Don't let 'however' fool you. The paragraph says the rationale does 'carry an implication' its defenders don't like: the rule should come earlier, before purpose. The author isn't admitting a weakness. The author is following the argument to a conclusion that courts resist.

choices.note: CORRECT. It draws out what the legislative-supremacy rationale implies about when to apply the rule.
Tempting, because of 'however' and 'slow to accept.' But what defenders are slow to accept is a consequence for practice, not an objection to the rationale. The author endorses the implication.
Fair notice isn't discussed in the fourth paragraph at all.
Too strong. Many courts still use the rule; they just use it last.
The author rejects Vasko's proposal. Reading for purpose is exactly what the fourth paragraph says defeats the rule's point.

questions.stem: Suppose that a criminal statute’s text, structure, and history leave its meaning ambiguous, but its evident purpose clearly favors the harsher of two readings. Based on the passage, the author would most likely hold that a court should
choices: adopt the harsher reading, since the rule of lenity properly applies only after every other interpretive tool has failed
adopt the harsher reading, since few defendants actually read criminal statutes before they decide how to act
adopt the more lenient reading, leaving it to the legislature to amend the statute if it wishes
adopt the more lenient reading only if the defendant can show reliance on that reading
decline to apply the statute until the legislature has said which reading it intended
questions.explanation: Two steps. First, the author's rationale: courts should not decide whether conduct 'the legislature did not clearly address shall be punished', and the legislature 'can amend the statute' (third paragraph). Second, the implication: 'consulting a statute's purpose first defeats that point', so lenity comes before purpose (fourth paragraph). So the court applies lenity despite the purpose: C. A is the trap: it describes what 'many courts now' do, the practice the author rejects. B is Vasko's reasoning, D assumes the fair-notice rationale, and E is a remedy the passage never mentions.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply the author's view to a case where purpose points one way and lenity the other.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The fourth and fifth sentences of the third paragraph and the third and fourth sentences of the fourth.

breakdown.analysis: Step 1: why does the author keep lenity? So courts don't decide questions of criminal liability the legislature left open; the legislature can fix a lenient reading. Step 2: so the rule should come before purpose, not after. Text, structure and history are all ambiguous here, and only purpose favors the harsh reading. Under the author's view, purpose doesn't get to settle it.

choices.note: Tempting. This is exactly how 'many courts now' work, and it would win under their method. But the author argues the rule belongs earlier than that, precisely so purpose doesn't decide.
Vasko's reasoning. The author agrees notice is weak but doesn't rest the outcome on it.
CORRECT. Lenity before purpose, with the burden of clarity on the legislature, which can amend.
Reliance is a fair-notice idea, and the author doesn't rest lenity on fair notice. Nothing requires the defendant to show anything.
The passage offers no option of refusing to apply a statute. The author's rule gives an answer: the lenient reading.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Benefit of clergy was an anomaly that let literate criminals escape the gallows on a mere technicality until Parliament abolished the reading test in 1706.
By the sixteenth century Parliament had deliberately made benefit of clergy into a graded system that spared first offenders convicted of lesser felonies.
Benefit of clergy began as a protection for clerics but was extended, by means of a reading test, to almost any man who could read.
Although Danbury misjudges the purpose of benefit of clergy, the privilege extended its mercy equally to all felons once the reading test was abolished.
Benefit of clergy came to spare some felons from death, though not by design, and for a long time its mercy was unevenly distributed.
questions.explanation: The author accepts Danbury's account of 'how the privilege functioned' but denies that it was designed for mitigation (third paragraph), then adds that its mitigation should not 'be overstated' because it favored readers until 1706 (fourth paragraph). E combines these. B is Danbury's view, A the earlier historians', and C is first-paragraph background. D overstates: even after 1706 the privilege 'remained unavailable' for many offenses.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall position on benefit of clergy.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first and third sentences of the third paragraph and the first sentence of the fourth.

breakdown.analysis: Three views. Earlier historians: an embarrassing loophole. Danbury: by the 1500s, a deliberate tool of mitigation. Author: right about how it worked, wrong about the design; and the mercy was lopsided. The main point needs function yes, design no, and the limit on the mercy.

choices.note: The earlier historians' view, which the passage moves past. The author grants that the privilege did work as mitigation.
Tempting, because the author accepts half of it. But 'deliberately' is exactly what the author denies: no one 'designed it as one.'
Accurate background from the first paragraph, not the point.
Too strong. After 1706 it 'remained unavailable for the many offenses' Parliament had excluded, so not 'all felons'.
CORRECT. It worked as mitigation, it wasn't designed for that, and its mercy was uneven.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the ability to read a verse of scripture
choices: was first required of those claiming the privilege by the statute of 1489 that limited laymen to a single claim
came to be accepted by the royal courts as proof that a person claiming the privilege was a cleric
was, according to Danbury, a test that Parliament devised to separate lesser offenders from grave ones
ceased to matter after 1706, because the privilege was then open to every offender whatever the crime
was a skill that clerics alone possessed until well into the fifteenth century
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says the royal courts 'came to accept the ability to read a verse of scripture as proof of clerical status', which B restates. D is the near-miss: after 1706 reading no longer mattered for eligible offenders, but the privilege 'remained unavailable' for many offenses. E overstates 'among the few who could read.' A and C attach the reading test to the wrong statute or the wrong person.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says about the reading test.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The fourth sentence of the first paragraph and the last sentence of the passage.

breakdown.analysis: The reading test: courts accepted reading as proof of being a cleric, so by the 1400s almost any reading man could claim; it was abolished in 1706. Check qualifiers: 'among the few', 'eligible offenders'.

choices.note: The test is described in the first paragraph, well before the 1489 statute, which concerned branding and a single claim.
CORRECT. 'Came to accept the ability to read a verse of scripture as proof of clerical status.'
Danbury's graded system comes from Parliament withdrawing the privilege for grave offenses and the one-claim rule, not from the reading test.
Tempting, because reading did stop mattering in 1706. But 'every offender whatever the crime' is too broad: the privilege 'remained unavailable for the many offenses' Parliament had excluded.
Too strong. Clerics were 'among the few' who could read, not the only ones.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the statute of 1489
choices: withdrew the privilege from the gravest offenses while leaving it available for lesser ones
described the privilege as one part of a scheme of graded punishment for felonies
required every person who claimed the privilege to be branded on the thumb
made it possible to detect a layman’s second claim to the privilege
was, according to the author, aimed at closing what its framers regarded as an abuse
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the 1489 statute 'provided that a layman could claim it only once, branding him on the thumb so that a second claim could be detected.' D restates this. C drops that qualifier: the branding applied to laymen, not 'every person.' A describes other parliamentary action, not this statute. B contradicts the author ('none of them describes the privilege as a scheme'). E applies to 'several' unnamed statutes, not specifically to this one.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find exactly what the passage attributes to the 1489 statute.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The third sentence of the second paragraph, and the second sentence of the third.

breakdown.analysis: Only one sentence is about this statute: laymen get one claim and are branded so a second claim can be caught. Everything else in that sentence and the next paragraph concerns other statutes or Parliament in general. Watch the qualifier 'layman'.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's in the same sentence. But it's something Parliament did, not something the 1489 statute is said to have done.
The author says 'none of them describes the privilege as a scheme of graded punishment.' That's Danbury's interpretation, not the statute's own words.
Tempting, because the branding is right there. But it applied to a 'layman', not 'every person'. Clerics weren't held to one claim.
CORRECT. Branding laymen 'so that a second claim could be detected.'
The author says 'several' of the statutes targeted abuses but never says which. We can't pin it on 1489.

questions.stem: In saying that Parliament had “trimmed the privilege, for reasons of its own, into a usable shape” (last sentence of the third paragraph), the author most likely means that
choices: the limits Parliament placed on the privilege, whatever their aim, left it in a form suited to distinguishing among offenders
Parliament deliberately reshaped the privilege so that judges and juries could use it to grade punishments for felonies
Parliament restricted the privilege until it was so rarely available that it no longer mattered much in actual practice
Parliament simplified the procedure by which an accused felon could claim the privilege before the royal courts
Parliament extended the privilege to defendants who could not read so that it could be applied more widely
questions.explanation: 'Trimmed' refers to Parliament's restrictions (withdrawing the privilege from grave offenses, the one-claim rule), and 'for reasons of its own' means those restrictions had aims other than mitigation, yet they left a tool that judges and juries 'learned to exploit.' A fits. B is the trap: it is Danbury's claim that the restrictions were deliberately designed for grading, which the author rejects. C contradicts 'usable', and D and E misread 'trimmed'; E describes the 1706 change, which widened the privilege.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Interpret the phrase in light of the author's argument against Danbury.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The third and fourth sentences of the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Two pieces: 'trimmed' = cut back (restrictions); 'for reasons of its own' = not for the reason Danbury says. Put together: Parliament's cuts, whatever they were for, left the privilege shaped so it could sort offenders. The trap will add the intent the author takes out.

choices.note: CORRECT. Restrictions with other aims that nonetheless produced a sorting tool.
Tempting, because it describes the result accurately. But 'deliberately... so that judges and juries could' is Danbury's purpose claim, and 'for reasons of its own' is there to deny it.
'Usable' means it still worked. Judges and juries used it.
'Trimmed' means cut back, not made procedurally simpler; nothing is said about procedure.
Trimming narrows. Extending the privilege to people who couldn't read describes 1706, and it widened the privilege.

questions.stem: The author’s statement that several of the statutes “were plainly aimed at closing what their framers regarded as abuses” (second sentence of the third paragraph) functions primarily to
choices: lend support to the earlier legal historians’ view that the privilege was an embarrassing medieval anomaly
show that the privilege did not in fact operate as a means of sparing some felons from death
suggest that those who shaped the privilege were not pursuing the aim Danbury attributes to them
explain why judges and juries eventually came to use the privilege as a way of distinguishing among offenders
indicate that Parliament’s ultimate goal was to abolish the privilege for every offense
questions.explanation: The third paragraph accepts Danbury's account of how the privilege functioned but disputes her account of its 'purpose.' Noting that several statutes aimed at closing abuses, together with the piecemeal passage and the absence of any statement of a graded scheme, shows that the legislators were not building a system of mitigation. That is C. A is the trap: 'abuses' echoes the earlier historians' 'embarrassment', but the author doesn't revive their view. B contradicts the author's acceptance of the functional account. D is the job of the fourth sentence, and E overreaches.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what role this statement plays in the author's argument against Danbury.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first through third sentences of the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The author splits Danbury's view: function (accepted) and purpose (rejected). Everything in the second sentence is evidence about purpose: piecemeal, reacting to particular crimes, no talk of a scheme, aimed at abuses. Legislators trying to plug abuses weren't designing a mercy system.

choices.note: Tempting, because 'abuses' sounds like 'embarrassment'. But the author isn't siding with the earlier historians. The point is about what the legislators intended, and it's aimed at Danbury.
The author says Danbury's account of 'how the privilege functioned is convincing.' It did spare felons.
CORRECT. Evidence that the statutes' framers had other aims, which undercuts Danbury's claim of deliberate design.
That's the job of the last sentence of the paragraph, about judges and juries exploiting the trimmed privilege.
Closing abuses isn't aiming at total abolition. The passage says nothing about such a goal.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship of the fourth paragraph to the third paragraph?
choices: The fourth paragraph provides further evidence for the third paragraph’s claim that the privilege was never designed by anyone as a means of mitigation.
The third paragraph accepts one part of an account and rejects another, and the fourth qualifies the part that the third accepts.
The fourth paragraph withdraws a concession made in the third paragraph and concludes that the privilege did not in fact mitigate punishment.
The third paragraph criticizes Danbury’s account, and the fourth paragraph defends the earlier historians’ view of the privilege against that same criticism.
The fourth paragraph describes a later development that confirms the account of the privilege’s original purpose that is rejected in the third paragraph.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph accepts Danbury's account of how the privilege functioned and rejects her account of its purpose. The fourth ('Nor should the mitigation it provided be overstated') limits the accepted part: the mitigation favored readers until 1706 and never covered excluded offenses. B describes this abstractly. A is the trap: 'Nor' suggests continued argument against design, but the fourth paragraph is about who received mercy, not about intent. C is too strong, since the privilege still spared some. D and E misidentify whose view is involved.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out how the last paragraph relates to the one before it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first sentence of the third paragraph and the whole fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Third paragraph: Danbury's function claim, yes; her purpose claim, no. Fourth paragraph: the mitigation was real but uneven, favoring readers. Which half does that touch? The function half, the one the author accepted. So the fourth paragraph trims a claim the third paragraph granted. The abstract wording of the right answer is the hard part here.

choices.note: Tempting, because 'Nor' sounds like piling on. But the fourth paragraph says nothing about what anyone intended. It's about who benefited, which is a limit on the function, not evidence about design.
CORRECT. Function accepted, purpose rejected; then the accepted function is qualified ('Nor should the mitigation it provided be overstated').
Too strong. Saying the mitigation shouldn't be overstated limits it; it doesn't deny it. A literate defendant was still 'branded and released.'
The earlier historians don't come back. The fourth paragraph is the author's own qualification.
The abolition of the reading test in 1706 doesn't show deliberate design, and the paragraph doesn't present it that way.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Many reported condensates are probably artifacts of the methods used to detect them, since proteins often form droplets only under highly unnatural conditions.
Condensation is a general mechanism by which cells organize their chemistry, as the genetic experiments performed on Tolva have confirmed.
Experiments on the yeast protein Tolva have shown that Hartig’s objection to the evidence offered for condensates is mistaken.
Although a protein’s ability to condense is no evidence that condensing serves a function in the cell, experiments can show that it sometimes does.
Condensates speed reactions by gathering enzymes and their substrates into a small volume, and they can switch processes off by dissolving.
questions.explanation: The author says the proper conclusion is 'narrower than either side's': Hartig is right that a test-tube capacity 'is not yet a function observed in a cell', but whether a condensate functions can be 'answered by experiments of the kind performed on Tolva, and the answer is sometimes yes' (fourth paragraph). D states this. A is Hartig's suspicion, which the author rejects 'as a rule.' B drops the author's qualification and turns one case into a general principle. C is too strong: Hartig's objection 'identifies a real gap.' E is first-paragraph background.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's conclusion about the condensate debate.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first sentence of the third paragraph and the whole fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Proponents: condensation is a general way cells organize. Hartig: most evidence is test-tube stuff; many condensates are artifacts. Author: Hartig's gap is real, but experiments can close it case by case, and sometimes the answer is yes. The answer must keep both the concession to Hartig and the case-by-case 'sometimes'.

choices.note: Hartig's suspicion. The author says condensation is 'not, as a rule, an artifact of the laboratory.'
Tempting, because Tolva is a success story for the proponents. But the author rejects the general claim, and other proteins showed 'no detectable defect.' One case doesn't make a general mechanism.
Too strong. The author says Hartig's objection 'identifies a real gap' and that she 'was right to insist' on it. Tolva shows the gap can be closed, not that she was wrong.
CORRECT. Capacity isn't evidence of function (Hartig's point), but the right experiment can show function in particular cases (Tolva).
Background from the first paragraph: the proponents' claim about what condensates can do.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the variant of Tolva that could not condense
choices: did nearly as well as the unaltered protein at helping cells recover from sudden heat
bound the proteins that Tolva usually binds as well as the unaltered protein did
was produced in cells engineered to make the protein in unnatural abundance
formed droplets in a test tube only at concentrations far above those in a living cell
was one of several altered proteins whose loss of condensation cells tolerated without defect
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says the variant 'bound its usual partners normally but could not condense', which B restates. A is the trap: 'did nearly as well' describes the other variant, the one that condensed normally but bound weakly. C and D come from Hartig's description of weak evidence in the second paragraph, and E describes the 'other proteins', whose results differed from Tolva's.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says about the non-condensing Tolva variant.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The fourth sentence of the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Two variants, easy to swap. Variant 1: binds normally, can't condense, so cells can't recover from heat. Variant 2: condenses normally, binds weakly, does nearly as well as normal. The question asks about variant 1.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's in the same sentence. But this describes the other variant. The non-condensing one 'left cells unable to recover from heat shock.'
CORRECT. It 'bound its usual partners normally.' That's the control that makes the experiment decisive.
Overproduction is Hartig's complaint about weak evidence, not something said about this variant.
Test-tube concentrations are also from Hartig's paragraph. This variant couldn't condense at all.
Opposite. Cells with this variant had a clear defect. The no-defect results were for other proteins.

questions.stem: The primary function of the second paragraph is to
choices: describe the experiments by which proponents established that condensates serve functions in cells
offer an alternative explanation of how cells form the compartments described in the first paragraph
present a challenge to the evidence offered for the view described in the first paragraph
show that the view described in the first paragraph is false for most proteins said to condense
explain why the nucleolus and similar structures lack a membrane around them
questions.explanation: The second paragraph presents Hartig's warning that 'much of the evidence for this view is weaker than it appears.' C says this. D is too strong: Hartig says the evidence shows only capacity, and she only 'suspects' many condensates are artifacts. A describes the third paragraph's test, and B and E misdescribe what Hartig does.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Decide what the second paragraph does in the passage.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first sentence of the second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: First paragraph: the condensate view. Second paragraph: Hartig says the evidence for it is weak, since test tubes and overproduction show capacity, not function. That's a challenge to the evidence, not a disproof.

choices.note: Those experiments come in the third paragraph, and the author, not the proponents, proposes them.
Hartig doesn't propose a different way compartments form. She questions the evidence for this one.
CORRECT. Hartig argues the evidence is 'weaker than it appears.'
Too strong. She argues the evidence proves less than claimed and 'suspects' artifacts. She doesn't show the view is false.
The first paragraph mentions the missing membrane, but no one explains it.

questions.stem: The author mentions that a variant of Tolva that condensed normally but bound its partners weakly did nearly as well as the unaltered protein (third paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: show that Tolva’s ability to bind its usual partners plays no role at all in helping cells recover from sudden heat
give an example of a protein whose loss of the ability to condense cells tolerate with no detectable defect
show that Hartig is mistaken to suspect that many reported condensates are laboratory artifacts
illustrate how a condensate speeds a reaction by gathering an enzyme and its substrates together
suggest that Tolva’s role in recovery from heat depends more on condensing than on how tightly it binds
questions.explanation: Paired with the non-condensing variant, which bound normally but failed, the weak-binding variant that still condensed did 'nearly as well', so recovery tracks condensation more than binding strength. That is E. A is the trap: 'nearly as well' with weak (not absent) binding doesn't show binding plays no role. B describes the other proteins, C is too broad for one protein, and D describes a mechanism the experiment never examined.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find why the author reports the second Tolva variant.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The fourth sentence of the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Put the two variants side by side. Normal binding with no condensing: failure. Weak binding with normal condensing: nearly normal. So condensing matters more than binding strength. Watch for the overstatement: weak binding isn't zero binding, and 'nearly as well' isn't 'just as well'.

choices.note: Tempting, because binding strength barely mattered. But the variant still bound its partners, just weakly, and did only 'nearly' as well. That doesn't show binding plays 'no role.'
This variant didn't lose condensation; it 'condensed normally.' The no-defect cases were other proteins.
Too broad. One protein can't show that 'many' reported condensates aren't artifacts, and the author agrees Hartig's gap is real.
The passage never tests how Tolva works chemically. That mechanism is the proponents' general claim from the first paragraph.
CORRECT. The contrast between the two variants points to condensing, not tight binding, as what recovery depends on.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly supports which one of the following about the several other proteins mentioned in the last sentence of the third paragraph?
choices: They do not form condensates in living cells, and the droplets reported for them were artifacts of detection methods.
The experiments performed on them establish that their condensing has no effect of any kind on the cells containing them.
They were studied only in cells engineered to produce them in far greater quantities than normal cells do.
The experiments performed on them provided no evidence that the cell depends on their ability to condense.
They bind their usual partners more weakly than Tolva binds the partners it usually binds.
questions.explanation: The genetic test asks whether 'the cell loses the capacity attributed to the condensate' when condensation is removed (third paragraph). For these proteins, cells tolerated the loss 'with no detectable defect', so the test gave no evidence of dependence: D. A is the trap: these experiments removed condensation, which presupposes that the proteins condense, and the author says condensation is 'not, as a rule, an artifact.' B overstates 'no detectable defect' as 'no effect of any kind.' C and E have no support.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Infer what the negative results for the other proteins show, and what they don't.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second and last sentences of the third paragraph and the fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Step 1: the test logic. Take away condensing; if the cell loses something, condensing does a job. Step 2: for these proteins, the cell lost nothing detectable. So there's no evidence the cell needs their condensing. Don't go further: no detected defect isn't proof of no effect, and it says nothing about whether the droplets are artifacts.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like a win for Hartig. But the experiments took condensation away from proteins that had it, and the author denies condensates are generally artifacts. Not doing anything isn't the same as not existing.
Too strong. The passage says 'no detectable defect.' A defect the experiment didn't detect is still possible.
Overproduction is Hartig's complaint about other evidence. Nothing says these experiments used it.
CORRECT. The genetic test looks for a lost capacity; none turned up, so the test gave no evidence of dependence.
Binding strength is reported only for the Tolva variants. Nothing compares these proteins with Tolva.

passages.title: Promises to the dead
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
Most accounts of promising hold that a promise binds because it gives the person to whom it is made an assurance on which he or she may rely, and that the obligation ends if that person releases the promisor. Taken together, these claims raise a puzzle about promises made to people who have since died. A dead promisee can neither rely on anything nor release anyone. Yet a person who has promised a dying parent to keep the family farm, or to see that a manuscript is burned unread, does not ordinarily feel released by the death, and someone who breaks such a promise is generally thought to have done wrong, even if no one else ever learns of the breach.

The philosopher Edda Haske has offered the most influential attempt to vindicate this ordinary judgment. Haske argues that some of a person’s interests outlast the person. We have interests in how our reputations fare, in whether projects we began are completed, and in whether our wishes about our property are respected, and these interests can be set back after we die even though we will never learn of the setback. A promise to the dead remains binding, on Haske’s view, because breaking it defeats one of these surviving interests.

Haske’s account has the merit of explaining why such promises carry any weight at all, and why their weight does not depend on anyone’s learning that they were broken, but it explains too much. If the obligation derives from the dead person’s surviving interests, then the promise itself contributes nothing to it. A stranger who happened to learn of the dead person’s wish that the manuscript be burned would be under the same obligation as the friend who swore to burn it, provided the stranger could act at no greater cost. Yet no one thinks that a stranger who declines to act has broken faith with anyone. Haske’s view thus makes the promise merely the occasion on which the promisor learned of an obligation that existed independently of it.

A better account would locate the obligation in the exchange that took place while both parties were alive. In accepting the promise, the promisee relied on it, and often forwent other arrangements, such as asking someone else or adding a provision to a will, that might have secured the same end. Death does not undo that reliance; it only removes any chance of compensating the promisee for its betrayal. On this account, the promisee’s inability to release the promisor is not an embarrassment for the theory of promising but a consequence of it: the only person who could have waived the obligation is the one whose reliance created it, and that person is gone.

passages.title: Aligned spins in the Teskar family
passages.subject: natural-science
passages.text:
When a collision shatters a large asteroid, the fragments continue to orbit the Sun on similar paths, and astronomers call such a group a family. Because a shattering collision flings fragments outward in every direction and sets each one tumbling, the spin axes of a family’s members have generally been expected to point every which way. It was therefore a surprise when measurements of how the brightness of ten large members of the Teskar family varied as they rotated revealed that the four members spinning in the same direction as their orbital motion had spin axes that were nearly parallel and rotation periods that were nearly identical. The six members spinning in the opposite direction showed no such alignment; their periods instead clustered near the extremes, either very fast or very slow.

The astronomer Ulla Brandvik proposed that the alignment was inherited: if the parent body broke apart gently, its fragments might have retained much of its original spin. But the Teskar family is thought to be some two billion years old, and over that span collisions among small bodies should have scrambled any spin the fragments inherited. Nor can inheritance explain why only the members spinning in one direction are aligned, since all ten fragments emerged from the same breakup.

A more successful account, developed by Pieter Hallen, appeals to an effect of sunlight. A rotating asteroid absorbs sunlight and reradiates the energy as heat, and because its surface is warmest some hours after local noon, the heat leaves the body unevenly, exerting a tiny recoil. Over hundreds of millions of years this torque can change both how fast an asteroid spins and how its axis is tilted. Acting alone, the torque would push spin axes toward extreme tilts rather than toward any common direction. Hallen showed, however, that as the torque slowly alters an asteroid’s spin, the slow wobble of its axis can come to match a periodic swing in the orientation of its orbit caused by the gravity of the giant planets. An asteroid caught in this resonance has its axis held at one particular orientation, so asteroids caught in it come to share that orientation. Only asteroids spinning in the same direction as their orbital motion can be caught; the others are driven instead toward the fast and slow extremes.

Hallen’s account makes predictions that the inheritance hypothesis does not. Because the thermal torque acts more strongly on small bodies than on large ones, the family’s smaller members should, if anything, be aligned more fully than the ten large members studied so far. And families too young for the torque to have acted should show no alignment at all. Observations of several young families have borne out the second prediction; the first awaits instruments capable of measuring much fainter asteroids.

passages.title: Seaward and landward in Mavuro
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
Speakers of Mavuro, a language of the fishing villages along the coast of Ambra Island, have no words that locate objects to a person’s left or right. A Mavuro speaker says that a cup stands seaward of a plate, or that a door is on the landward side of a room, even indoors. In the 1990s the linguist Ruth Abernell asked whether this habit of speech affects how speakers remember spatial arrangements. She showed participants a row of three toy animals on one table, turned them around to face a second table, and asked them to set out the same row again. Mavuro speakers tended to rebuild the row so that the animal that had been seaward remained seaward, reversing its left-to-right order, while speakers of the island’s official language, which has words for left and right, tended to preserve the left-to-right order. Abernell concluded that a language’s habitual frame of reference shapes how its speakers encode space even when they are silent.

Abernell’s critics replied that her two groups differed in more than language. The Mavuro speakers lived where the sea is nearly always visible and were tested outdoors; the speakers of the official language lived in the island’s inland capital and were tested in an office. People who spend their days oriented to a single prominent landmark, the critics argued, will come to remember arrays by reference to it whatever language they speak; the Mavuro way of talking is a symptom of that orientation, not its cause.

The objection is a fair one against Abernell’s study, which could not separate language from setting. It does not follow, however, that language plays no role, and a later study by Tomas Iver suggests otherwise. Iver tested children in the village of Pelloc whose families had moved there from inland. Some of these households had adopted Mavuro at home; others continued to speak the official language. The children all attended the same school and played on the same shore, yet those raised in Mavuro-speaking homes rebuilt the rows seaward, while the others preserved left and right. Iver’s result does not settle the matter, since a family’s choice of home language may go along with other habits, such as whether its members fish, that also direct attention to the sea. But it changes what the critics must show: they now need to name some feature of these households, other than language, that differs along with it.

Both sides of this dispute have assumed that language and surroundings are rival explanations, so that whatever is credited to one must be subtracted from the other. Iver’s findings suggest a different picture, in which a language is one of the means by which a community teaches its children which features of their surroundings to keep track of.

passages.title: Sunset provisions
passages.subject: law
passages.text:
Passage A

Sunset provisions, which cause a statute to expire on a set date unless the legislature reenacts it, are usually defended as a way of forcing legislators to ask whether a law has done what it was meant to do, rather than leaving it in force by default. The record of such provisions is disappointing, for three reasons.

First, renewal rarely involves review. A legislature facing dozens of expiring provisions in a single session tends to extend them together, often in one bill passed in the last days before the deadline, and few legislators examine any particular law in the process. Indeed, the more laws carry sunset dates, the less attention each renewal can receive. Second, a sunset date gives the interests that benefit from a law a recurring occasion to press their case. Because those interests are organized and the general public is not, the renewal debate, when there is one, more often becomes an occasion to enlarge the law than to scrutinize it, and a law meant to be temporary emerges from each renewal broader than before.

Third, the people who must comply with a law cannot plan around a rule that may vanish. Businesses deciding whether to invest and agencies deciding whether to hire must discount for the chance that the law will lapse, and they bear that cost even for laws whose renewal is never in doubt.

Review of whether laws work is worth having. But legislators can obtain it by requiring agencies to report on a law’s effects and by holding hearings on those reports, without staking the law’s survival on a vote that may never receive real attention.

Passage B

Legislative inertia ordinarily favors whatever is already law. A statute stays in force until a majority agrees to repeal it, so a law that has outlived its rationale can survive for decades if those who benefit from it can keep such a majority from forming. Opponents of a law, by contrast, gain nothing from delay; every session in which they fail to agree is a session in which the law continues. A sunset provision reverses this default for the laws to which it is attached: the law lapses unless a majority affirmatively wants to keep it.

The reversal matters most for measures adopted quickly under pressure, such as emergency powers or experimental programs, where legislators acted on predictions they had no way to check. If the predictions fail, the law should not need a fresh coalition to end it. Critics observe that renewal votes are often perfunctory. Perhaps so; but even a perfunctory vote must be taken, and the requirement guarantees any legislator who has doubts about the law a moment at which the law’s defenders, not its opponents, must assemble a majority.

Reporting requirements, which critics of sunset provisions often recommend instead, offer no such moment. They produce documents that no one is obliged to read, let alone act on.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Promises made to people who have since died do not bind the promisor, since a dead promisee can neither rely on a promise nor release anyone from it.
Haske is right that some interests outlast the person who has them, but such interests can ground obligations only for those who have made a promise.
The puzzle about promises to the dead shows that the standard account of promising, which ties a promise’s force to reliance, must be abandoned.
Haske’s explanation of why promises to the dead still bind leaves the promise no role; the obligation is better traced to the promisee’s reliance while alive.
Because some of a person’s interests survive death, breaking a promise to the dead wrongs the promisee in the same way as breaking a promise to the living.
questions.explanation: The author grants Haske’s account a merit but says it ‘explains too much’ because ‘the promise itself contributes nothing’ (third paragraph), then offers ‘a better account’ that locates the obligation in the promisee’s reliance (fourth paragraph): D. C is the main trap: the author says the puzzle is ‘not an embarrassment for the theory of promising but a consequence of it,’ so the theory is kept, not abandoned. A is the conclusion the puzzle seems to force, which the author rejects, and E is Haske’s view without the author’s objection.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author’s overall position on promises to the dead.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph (‘it explains too much’) and fourth paragraph (‘A better account would locate the obligation…’).

breakdown.analysis: Three things happen: a puzzle (promises bind through reliance and end on release, but the dead can do neither), Haske’s fix (surviving interests), and the author’s verdict (Haske proves too much; reliance while alive is the better answer). So is the author against Haske? Partly. Against the standard view? No, the last paragraph rescues it. We need an answer with both halves: Haske’s account fails for a specific reason, and reliance does the job instead.

choices.note: The puzzle seems to push toward this, but the whole passage defends the ordinary judgment that such promises still bind. Opposite of the author’s view.

Half right. The author never denies that interests outlast the person, but nothing in the passage says those interests bind only promisors. The author’s point is that the obligation comes from the promise, not from the interests.

Tempting, because the puzzle does put pressure on the standard account. But the last paragraph says the dead promisee’s inability to release is ‘not an embarrassment for the theory of promising but a consequence of it.’ The author saves the theory.
CORRECT. Haske’s view ‘makes the promise merely the occasion’ for an obligation that exists anyway, and the author’s ‘better account’ grounds the obligation in reliance during the exchange.
This is Haske’s position, and even Haske doesn’t say ‘in the same way.’ The author argues against grounding the obligation in surviving interests.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Haske holds that
choices: a promise to the dead binds only if the promisee forwent other ways of securing the promised end
a person’s interests can be set back by events of which that person never learns
a stranger who learns of a dead person’s wishes is under no obligation to carry them out
the only interests that survive a person’s death are those concerning that person’s reputation
the obligation created by a promise ends when the promisee can no longer release the promisor
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says Haske holds that surviving interests ‘can be set back after we die even though we will never learn of the setback,’ which B paraphrases. A is the author’s own reliance account from the fourth paragraph, and it turns ‘often forwent’ into a requirement. C contradicts what the author says follows from Haske’s view, D lists one of three examples as the only one, and E is the lapse view Haske is trying to answer.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim the passage attributes to Haske.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Haske’s view in one line: some interests outlast us (reputation, unfinished projects, wishes about property), they can be set back after we die even though we never learn of it, and breaking a promise to the dead defeats one of them. Watch for the wrong party: the fourth paragraph is the author’s view, not Haske’s.

choices.note: Wrong party. Reliance and forgone arrangements are the author’s account in the last paragraph, and even there ‘often forwent’ is not a requirement.
CORRECT. ‘These interests can be set back after we die even though we will never learn of the setback.’
The opposite. The author argues that Haske’s view implies the stranger WOULD be under the same obligation as the promisor.
Too narrow. Reputation is one of three examples, along with unfinished projects and wishes about property.
This is the lapse view that Haske is trying to refute. Haske thinks the obligation survives.

questions.stem: In saying that the promisee’s inability to release the promisor is “not an embarrassment for the theory of promising but a consequence of it” (last sentence of the passage), the author most likely means that
choices: the standard theory of promising must be given up, since it cannot explain why a dead promisee is unable to release anyone
Haske’s account, once properly understood, already explains why only the promisee can waive a promise
the inability to release the promisor is a minor difficulty that any theory of promising can safely set aside
a dead promisee’s inability to release the promisor shows that the promisee’s surviving interests cannot be waived
a feature that seemed to count against the theory in fact follows from a correct version of it
questions.explanation: The first paragraph presents the inability to release as the source of the puzzle; the last paragraph shows that on a reliance account only the promisee could waive the obligation, so the inability follows from the theory: E. B is the main trap: the explanation the author praises is the author’s own reliance account, not Haske’s, which the author criticizes. A reverses the author’s claim, C misreads ‘not an embarrassment’ as ‘not important,’ and D brings in Haske’s surviving interests.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain what the author means by calling the inability to release ‘a consequence’ of the theory rather than ‘an embarrassment.’

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First paragraph (the two claims and the puzzle) and the last sentence of the fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Back in the first paragraph, the fact that a dead person can’t release anyone looked like trouble for the theory: if release ends a promise and reliance grounds it, what happens when the promisee dies? The author flips it. If reliance created the obligation, only the person who relied could waive it; that person is gone, so no one can. The awkward fact is now a prediction of the theory. We need an answer that says ‘what looked like a problem for the theory actually follows from it.’

choices.note: Opposite. ‘Not an embarrassment’ is the author saying the theory survives.

Tempting, because Haske is the other account in play and the sentence is about explaining the puzzle. But the account doing the explaining here is the author’s ‘better account,’ built on reliance. The author thinks Haske’s view ‘explains too much.’
This reads ‘not an embarrassment’ as ‘not a big deal.’ The author doesn’t set the point aside; the author says it follows from the theory.
Mixes in Haske. The last paragraph is about reliance, not surviving interests, and says nothing about waiving interests.
CORRECT. The feature that generated the puzzle turns out to be implied by the reliance version of the theory.

questions.stem: According to the account the author favors, the death of a promisee
choices: eliminates any opportunity to make amends to the promisee if the promise is broken
undoes the promisee’s reliance on the promise but leaves the promisor’s obligation fully in place
transfers to those who inherit the promisee’s property the power to waive the promisor’s obligation
ends the obligation in those cases in which the promisee forwent no other arrangements
makes the obligation depend on whether the promisee’s surviving interests are defeated
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says death ‘only removes any chance of compensating the promisee for its betrayal,’ which A restates. D is the main trap: the passage says the promisee ‘often forwent’ other arrangements, but the reliance it treats as the source of the obligation occurs whenever the promise is accepted, so the account gives no case in which the obligation ends at death. B contradicts ‘Death does not undo that reliance,’ C adds heirs the passage never mentions, and E is Haske’s view.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the author’s reliance account says death does.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, third sentence.

breakdown.analysis: The key sentence: ‘Death does not undo that reliance; it only removes any chance of compensating the promisee for its betrayal.’ So death leaves the reliance (and the obligation) in place and takes away only the chance to make it up to the person. Read the quantifier in the second sentence: the promisee relied on the promise, and OFTEN forwent other arrangements. ‘Often’ is not ‘always,’ and nothing makes the obligation depend on it.

choices.note: CORRECT. ‘It only removes any chance of compensating the promisee for its betrayal.’ Making amends = compensating.
Half wrong. The passage says death does NOT undo the reliance.
Plausible in real life, but heirs never appear in the passage. The author says the only person who could have waived the obligation is gone.

Tempting, because forgone arrangements are in the account. But the author says the promisee ‘often’ forwent them; the obligation rests on reliance, which happens whenever the promise is accepted. The passage never says the obligation ends when nothing was forgone.
This is Haske’s view, not the author’s.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?
choices: Two widely held claims about promising are stated; a philosopher’s argument against both claims is summarized; the author defends one of the claims against that argument.
A puzzle is stated; two rival solutions to it are described; the author argues that both solutions fail for the same reason; a restatement of the puzzle is proposed.
A puzzle arising from two widely held claims is posed; a solution is proposed and then objected to; an alternative treats a source of the puzzle as an implication.
A puzzle arising from two widely held claims is posed; a proposed solution is described and defended against an objection; the solution is then extended to a further class of cases.
A common judgment is called into question; a philosopher’s defense of that judgment is described; the author concludes that the judgment cannot be defended and should be given up.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph derives a puzzle from two claims about promising, the second gives Haske’s solution, the third objects that it ‘explains too much,’ and the fourth offers a reliance account on which the inability to release is ‘a consequence’ of the theory: C. D is the main trap: its first two steps match, but the author raises the objection against Haske rather than defending Haske from it, and nothing is extended. A misdescribes Haske as attacking the two claims, B invents a second solution, and E has the author abandon a judgment the author defends.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match each paragraph to a step in the answer.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Whole passage: paragraph 1 (puzzle), 2 (Haske), 3 (objection), 4 (author’s alternative).

breakdown.analysis: Map it first: 1. Two claims (promises bind through reliance; release ends them) plus dead promisees = puzzle. 2. Haske’s solution: surviving interests. 3. Objection: it explains too much (the stranger). 4. The author’s alternative: reliance during the exchange, which makes the inability to release a consequence. Organization answers are long chains; one wrong link kills the answer, so check every step.

choices.note: Haske doesn’t argue against the two claims; Haske tries to defend the ordinary judgment the puzzle threatens.
There is only one proposed solution (Haske’s), and the author ends with a new account, not a restatement of the puzzle.
CORRECT. Every link matches, including the last: the inability to release, which generated the puzzle, becomes a consequence of the author’s account.

Tempting, because the first two links are perfect. But the objection in the third paragraph is the author’s objection TO Haske, not a defense of Haske, and the last paragraph replaces the solution rather than extending it.
The author defends the common judgment that promises to the dead bind; only Haske’s defense of it is rejected.

questions.stem: The author discusses a stranger who learns of a dead person’s wish (third paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: illustrate the claim that a person’s interests can be defeated even by those who never made that person any promise at all
argue that people who have made no promise are never under any obligation concerning the wishes of the dead
show that Haske’s account cannot explain why breaking a promise to the dead is generally and rightly thought to be wrong
suggest that a promisor’s obligation to a dead promisee is weaker than Haske’s account implies
bring out an implication of Haske’s view that conflicts with a judgment the author takes to be widely shared
questions.explanation: The stranger shows what follows from Haske’s view (the stranger would have ‘the same obligation as the friend’) and then sets it against a common judgment (‘no one thinks that a stranger who declines to act has broken faith’): E. C is the main trap: the author grants that Haske’s account explains ‘why such promises carry any weight at all,’ so the complaint is that it explains too much, not that it fails to explain the wrong. A is a premise of Haske’s view rather than the point of the example, B overstates the author’s claim, and D is never suggested.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the stranger example is in the passage.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, especially its first and fourth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Ask what the stranger is doing to Haske. Haske’s view: the obligation comes from the dead person’s interests. Then anyone who knows of those interests, like the stranger, is equally bound. But nobody thinks the stranger broke faith. So Haske’s view produces an obligation where we see none: it ‘explains too much.’ Notice what the author does NOT say: that Haske fails to explain why breaking the promise is wrong. The author explicitly credits Haske with explaining that. We need an answer that says ‘draws out a consequence of Haske’s view that clashes with common opinion.’

choices.note: The stranger example does involve someone who made no promise, but its job isn’t to illustrate Haske’s claim about interests; it’s to show that the claim proves too much.
Too strong. The author says only that we don’t think the stranger ‘has broken faith with anyone.’ ‘Never under any obligation’ goes far beyond that.

Tempting, because the example does attack Haske. But the author says Haske’s account ‘has the merit of explaining why such promises carry any weight at all.’ The complaint is overreach: the account explains the promisor’s obligation and also gives one to the stranger.
Nothing in the passage says the obligation is weaker than Haske thinks. The author’s point is about where the obligation comes from and who has it.
CORRECT. Haske’s view implies the stranger is as bound as the friend; ‘no one thinks’ the stranger has broken faith. Implication vs. shared judgment.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Haske is mistaken in holding that some of a person’s interests can be set back after that person has died.
That a dead promisee cannot release the promisor does not by itself show that the promisor’s obligation has lapsed.
A promise made to a dying person is more binding than a promise made to someone who is in good health.
A stranger who learns of a dead person’s wishes is obligated to carry them out if doing so would cost nothing.
Promises to the dead that concern property are more binding than promises that concern a person’s reputation.
questions.explanation: On the author’s account the obligation rests on reliance that death ‘does not undo,’ and the inability to release is ‘a consequence’ of the theory rather than a sign that the obligation is gone, so B follows. A is the main trap: the author attacks Haske’s claim that surviving interests ground the obligation, never the claim that such interests exist. D is what the author says Haske’s view implies and then rejects, and C and E compare kinds of promises the passage never ranks.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the author’s views support.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph (what the author grants and denies about Haske) and fourth paragraph (reliance and release).

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase, so sort the choices by what the author actually commits to. The author thinks promises to the dead still bind, grounds that in reliance, and says the dead promisee’s inability to release is a consequence of the theory, not a reason to think the obligation lapsed. What the author never does is deny that interests can survive death. The objection is that interests are the wrong SOURCE of the obligation. ‘Wrong source’ is not ‘doesn’t exist.’

choices.note: Tempting, because the author is arguing against Haske. But the author never disputes that interests can be set back after death; the complaint is that if they ground the obligation, the promise does no work. Attacking how a claim is used isn’t denying the claim.

CORRECT. In the first paragraph the inability to release seems to imply lapse; the author’s account keeps the obligation alive while admitting no one can release it. So the inability alone doesn’t show lapse.
The passage never compares promises to the dying with promises to the healthy. The dying parent is just an example.
This is what Haske’s view implies, according to the author, and the author uses it against Haske: ‘no one thinks’ the stranger has broken faith.
Property and reputation are both listed as surviving interests in Haske’s view. Nothing ranks them.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: argue that collisions among small asteroids are much rarer than astronomers have generally assumed
explain how the heat radiated by a rotating asteroid can alter its rate of spin over long periods
describe a surprising feature of an asteroid family and show why one explanation of it is preferable to another
present two explanations of a puzzling observation and argue that neither can be assessed until fainter asteroids are measured
challenge the view that an asteroid family forms when a collision shatters a single large parent body
questions.explanation: The passage reports the unexpected alignment (first paragraph), rejects Brandvik’s inheritance explanation (second), presents Hallen’s ‘more successful account’ (third), and notes its predictions (fourth): C. D is the main trap: only one of Hallen’s two predictions awaits fainter asteroids, the other has been borne out, and the author has already preferred Hallen’s account. B describes only part of the third paragraph, and A and E contradict assumptions the passage relies on.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find why the author wrote the whole passage.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First sentence of the third paragraph (‘A more successful account’) and the passage as a whole.

breakdown.analysis: Map it: 1. surprise (aligned spins where randomness was expected); 2. Brandvik’s explanation and why it fails; 3. Hallen’s explanation and how it works; 4. Hallen’s predictions. The author clearly ranks the two (‘more successful’). We need an answer that covers the puzzle AND the preference for one explanation.

choices.note: The passage relies on collisions scrambling spins over two billion years; it never says collisions are rarer than thought.
This is one step inside Hallen’s explanation (part of the third paragraph), not the point of the passage.
CORRECT. Surprising feature (aligned prograde spins) plus one explanation (Hallen’s) favored over another (Brandvik’s).

Tempting, because the last sentence mentions fainter asteroids. But only one prediction is waiting on them; the other ‘has been borne out,’ and the author already calls Hallen’s account ‘more successful.’
The first sentence takes this view for granted. The passage builds on it.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the six members of the Teskar family that were studied and that spin opposite to their orbital motion
choices: have rotation periods that tend toward either very fast or very slow
have spin axes that are nearly parallel to one another
were caught in a resonance caused by the giant planets
are on average smaller than the four members that are aligned
broke away from the parent body later than the other four did
questions.explanation: The last sentence of the first paragraph says the six members spinning the other way ‘showed no such alignment; their periods instead clustered near the extremes, either very fast or very slow’: A. B is the trap: it describes the four members spinning in the same direction as their orbits. C contradicts the third paragraph (only same-direction spinners can be caught), and D and E are never stated.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says about the six opposite-spinning members.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Last sentence of the first paragraph; last sentence of the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Two groups, two descriptions. Same-direction spinners (four): axes nearly parallel, periods nearly identical. Opposite spinners (six): no alignment, periods at the fast or slow extremes. Don’t mix the groups.

choices.note: CORRECT. ‘Their periods instead clustered near the extremes, either very fast or very slow.’
Wrong group. That describes the four same-direction spinners.
Wrong group again. The third paragraph says only same-direction spinners can be caught in the resonance.
The passage compares small and large bodies only in general (the torque acts more strongly on small ones). It never compares the sizes of these two groups.
All ten ‘emerged from the same breakup’; nothing about timing.

questions.stem: According to the passage, if the thermal torque described in the third paragraph were the only influence on an asteroid’s spin, it would tend to
choices: scramble the spin axes of a family’s members so that they point in every direction
slow the rotation of every asteroid until the asteroid ceased to spin at all
bring the axes of a family’s members into a single shared orientation
push spin axes toward extreme tilts rather than a common direction
act more strongly on large asteroids than on small asteroids
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says ‘Acting alone, the torque would push spin axes toward extreme tilts rather than toward any common direction’: D. C is the main trap: the shared orientation comes from the resonance with the giant planets’ effect on the orbit, which the torque only makes possible. A is what collisions do (second paragraph), B is never stated, and E reverses the fourth paragraph.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the torque does on its own, without the resonance.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, fourth sentence.

breakdown.analysis: The third paragraph has two pieces: the torque (from uneven heat loss) and the resonance (from the giant planets). The stem isolates the torque: ‘acting alone.’ The passage answers that directly. The alignment needs both pieces, so an answer that gives the torque credit for alignment has merged them.

choices.note: That’s what collisions do over two billion years (second paragraph), not the torque.
The torque changes spin rate in either direction; the opposite spinners end up very fast or very slow. ‘Ceased to spin’ is never said.

Tempting, because the third paragraph ends with shared orientation. But that comes from capture in the resonance. Acting alone, the torque pushes axes ‘toward extreme tilts rather than toward any common direction.’
CORRECT. Near-quote of the fourth sentence of the third paragraph.
Reversed. The fourth paragraph says the torque ‘acts more strongly on small bodies than on large ones.’

questions.stem: The author mentions that the Teskar family is thought to be some two billion years old (second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: explain why the thermal torque has had enough time to bring some of the family’s members into alignment
