indicate that the family is older than the young families in which no alignment has been observed
support the suggestion that the family’s parent body broke apart gently rather than violently
suggest that the family’s members have been struck so often that their spins cannot be measured reliably
cast doubt on the idea that the members’ present spins could have been inherited from their parent body
questions.explanation: The age appears in the sentence beginning ‘But,’ which answers Brandvik: over two billion years collisions ‘should have scrambled any spin the fragments inherited,’ so E. A is the main trap: the age is consistent with the torque having time to act, but the sentence uses it against inheritance and says nothing about the torque, which is introduced only in the next paragraph. B is true but not why the age is mentioned, C is Brandvik’s supposition that the age undercuts, and D overstates the point about collisions.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the family’s age is mentioned where it is.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, second sentence (‘But the Teskar family is thought to be some two billion years old…’).

breakdown.analysis: Function questions are about the job a detail does in its own sentence. This sentence starts with ‘But,’ right after Brandvik’s inheritance idea. Two billion years of collisions should have scrambled any inherited spin. So the age is evidence against Brandvik. Don’t let what you know from later paragraphs (the torque needs a long time) replace what this sentence is doing.

choices.note: Tempting, because a long age does give the torque time to work. But this sentence is a ‘But’ aimed at Brandvik, and the torque hasn’t even been introduced yet. True implication, wrong job.
True that the fourth paragraph mentions young families, but the age is cited here to answer Brandvik, not to compare families.
A gentle breakup is Brandvik’s supposition; the age is used to undercut her explanation, not support it.
Too far. The passage says collisions should have scrambled the spins, not that the spins can’t be measured. The spins were measured.
CORRECT. Two billion years of collisions should have scrambled any inherited spin, so inheritance can’t explain today’s alignment.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?
choices: An observation is reported; two explanations of it are presented; the author argues that the explanations are compatible and that each accounts for part of the observation; a test of their combination is proposed.

An observation at odds with an expectation is reported; one explanation is rejected on two grounds; a second, which accounts for the observation’s features, is presented; its predictions and their testing are noted.
An expectation is stated; an observation that confirms it is reported; an explanation of the observation is offered; that explanation is then qualified in light of observations of younger families.

An observation at odds with an expectation is reported; one explanation is rejected on two grounds; a second explanation is presented; observations of young families are said to have conclusively confirmed it.
An observation at odds with an expectation is reported; two explanations are presented; the author declines to choose between them; observations that might decide between them are described.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph reports alignment where randomness was expected; the second rejects Brandvik’s inheritance explanation on two grounds (the family’s age and the one-direction pattern); the third presents Hallen’s account, which explains both the alignment and the extreme periods; the fourth gives two predictions, one borne out and one untested: B. D is the main trap: it matches until the last step, but young families confirm only one prediction, and the other ‘awaits instruments,’ so nothing is conclusive. E ignores the author’s preference, A invents a combination, and C has the observation confirm the expectation.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match each paragraph to a step in the answer.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Whole passage; especially the second paragraph (‘But…’, ‘Nor…’) and the fourth (‘borne out the second prediction; the first awaits…’).

breakdown.analysis: Map it: 1. Expected random spins, found aligned ones (observation vs. expectation). 2. Brandvik: inheritance. Rejected twice: ‘But…’ (age) and ‘Nor…’ (only one direction aligned). 3. Hallen: torque plus resonance explains alignment AND the opposite spinners’ extreme periods. 4. Two predictions: one confirmed, one waiting. Several answers share the first steps; the last step is where they split. Watch for ‘conclusively.’

choices.note: The author doesn’t combine the explanations; Brandvik’s is rejected.
CORRECT. Every link fits, including the last one: predictions, one borne out and one still awaiting testing.
The observation contradicted the expectation (‘It was therefore a surprise’), it didn’t confirm it.
Tempting, because the first three links are right. But observations of young families bore out only one prediction, and the other ‘awaits instruments.’ ‘Conclusively confirmed’ is too strong.
The author does choose: Hallen’s is ‘a more successful account.’

questions.stem: The passage states which one of the following about the resonance described in the third paragraph?
choices: Whether an asteroid is caught in it depends partly on a change in the asteroid’s spin produced by another effect.
It results from the uneven way in which a rotating asteroid reradiates, as heat, the energy of the sunlight it has absorbed.
It can catch asteroids spinning in either direction, though it holds only some of those it catches at a fixed orientation.
It pushes the axes of the asteroids caught in it toward extreme tilts over hundreds of millions of years.
It has acted on every member of the Teskar family, though with different results for different members.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says that ‘as the torque slowly alters an asteroid’s spin, the slow wobble of its axis can come to match’ the swing in its orbit; capture depends on a spin change produced by the thermal torque, a separate effect: A. B is the main trap: uneven reradiation produces the torque, while the resonance involves a swing in the orbit ‘caused by the gravity of the giant planets.’ C contradicts ‘Only asteroids spinning in the same direction … can be caught,’ D describes the torque acting alone, and E is contradicted by the same sentence as C.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says about the resonance (not the torque).

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, fifth through last sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Keep the two mechanisms apart. Torque: from heat leaving the surface unevenly; changes spin rate and tilt. Resonance: the axis’s wobble matches a swing in the orbit caused by the giant planets; once caught, the axis is held. The link between them: the torque changes the spin until the wobble matches. So the torque is what brings an asteroid into the resonance. The right answer may describe that link in abstract words (‘another effect’).

choices.note: CORRECT. The torque ‘slowly alters an asteroid’s spin’ until the wobble matches; that’s a spin change from another effect, and it’s what lets the asteroid be caught.
Tempting, because uneven reradiation is right there in the same paragraph. But that’s the source of the torque. The resonance comes from the giant planets’ effect on the orbit. Wrong mechanism.
Contradicted: ‘Only asteroids spinning in the same direction as their orbital motion can be caught.’
That’s what the torque does acting alone. The resonance holds axes ‘at one particular orientation.’
Only same-direction spinners can be caught, so the opposite spinners weren’t; they were ‘driven instead toward the fast and slow extremes’ by the torque.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly supports which one of the following about Hallen’s account?
choices: It implies that a family’s smaller members are caught in the resonance before any of its larger members are.
It implies that some of the spin inherited from a parent body contributes to the alignment of a family’s members.
It implies that families too young to show alignment were formed by gentler collisions than older families were.
It implies that alignment among a family’s members that spin with their orbits tends to grow as the family ages.
It implies that a family’s members that spin against their orbits will eventually come into alignment as well.
questions.explanation: On Hallen’s account the torque works ‘over hundreds of millions of years’ to bring same-direction spinners into the resonance, and ‘families too young for the torque to have acted should show no alignment,’ so alignment builds up with age: D. A is the main trap: the passage says only that smaller members should ‘if anything, be aligned more fully’; ‘before any’ larger member is a much stronger claim. B is Brandvik’s rejected idea, C mixes in her gentle breakup, and E contradicts the claim that only same-direction spinners can be caught.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what Hallen’s account commits to.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph (the torque works over hundreds of millions of years) and fourth paragraph (the two predictions).

breakdown.analysis: Combine two pieces. Alignment comes from capture, and capture happens only after the torque has slowly changed the spin. And young families should show no alignment. So the older the family, the more time for capture, the more alignment: a trend with age. Now check strength. The size prediction is hedged (‘if anything,’ ‘more fully’). Any answer that turns that hedge into a strict ordering is too strong.

choices.note: Tempting, because it echoes the size prediction. But the passage says only that smaller members should ‘if anything, be aligned more fully.’ ‘Before any of its larger members’ is a strict ordering for every pair of members. Right idea, wrong strength.
That’s Brandvik’s inheritance idea, which the author rejects. Hallen’s account doesn’t rely on it.
Gentle breakup is Brandvik’s idea, and Hallen explains the lack of alignment in young families by time, not by the kind of collision.
CORRECT. Alignment requires the slow torque to bring members into the resonance, and families too young for the torque show none; so alignment tends to increase with age.
Contradicted. Only same-direction spinners can be caught; the others are driven toward fast or slow extremes instead.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Iver’s study has shown that the language people speak, rather than the surroundings in which they live, determines how they remember spatial arrangements.
Abernell’s critics were wrong to claim that her study failed to separate the influence of language on spatial memory from the influence of setting.
Mavuro speakers remember arrays by reference to the sea because the sea is almost always visible to them, and their way of speaking merely reflects this.
Since a family’s home language may vary with its other habits, no study can determine whether language affects how people remember spatial arrangements.
Though a fair objection undercuts Abernell’s study, later evidence suggests that language does affect spatial memory, perhaps as one way communities direct attention.
questions.explanation: The author calls the critics’ objection ‘a fair one against Abernell’s study’ but says Iver’s study suggests language plays a role, then proposes that language is one means by which a community teaches attention to surroundings (third and fourth paragraphs): E. A is the main trap: it treats Iver as having settled the matter, though the author says his result ‘does not settle the matter,’ and its ‘rather than’ is the either-or framing the last paragraph rejects. B contradicts the author’s concession, C is the critics’ view, and D overstates the author’s caution.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author’s overall position on the Mavuro dispute.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph (‘The objection is a fair one… It does not follow, however…’) and fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Three parties: Abernell (language shapes spatial memory), the critics (it’s the surroundings; language is a symptom), the author. The author grants the critics’ point against Abernell’s study, uses Iver to say language does matter after all, and then says the either-or framing is wrong. So the main point has a concession, a claim, and a hedge (‘suggests’). Watch for answers that drop the hedge.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sides with language as the author does. But the author says Iver’s result ‘does not settle the matter,’ and the last paragraph rejects treating language and surroundings as rivals, which is exactly what ‘rather than’ does. Too strong, and the wrong framing.
The author says the opposite: the objection ‘is a fair one against Abernell’s study, which could not separate language from setting.’
This is the critics’ position from the second paragraph, which the author argues does not follow.
Too strong. The author says Iver’s result doesn’t settle it, not that no study can. The author even says what the critics now need to show, which implies further evidence could decide the matter.

CORRECT. Concession (a fair objection to Abernell’s study), claim (language does affect spatial memory), and the last paragraph’s picture (language as a way of directing attention), with the author’s hedge intact.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Abernell’s critics objected that
choices: the Mavuro speakers in her study were tested indoors, where they could not see the sea
the toy animals she used were too familiar to the Mavuro speakers to test their memory fairly
her two groups differed both in their daily surroundings and in where they were tested
some of the speakers of the official language had been raised in households that spoke Mavuro
the way Mavuro speakers talk about space is a result of how they remember spatial arrangements
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the critics pointed out that the Mavuro speakers lived where the sea is nearly always visible and were tested outdoors, while the other group lived in the capital and was tested in an office: C. E is the main trap: the critics say the Mavuro way of talking is a symptom of speakers’ orientation to a landmark, which also explains their memory; they don’t say talk is caused by memory. A reverses where the Mavuro speakers were tested, and B and D are never mentioned.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the critics said was wrong with Abernell’s study.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The critics’ objection: the two groups differed in more than language. Mavuro speakers: sea visible, tested outdoors. Official-language speakers: inland capital, tested in an office. And their causal story: orientation to a landmark → both the way of remembering and the way of talking. Language is ‘a symptom,’ not a cause.

choices.note: Reversed. The Mavuro speakers were tested outdoors; the other group was tested in an office.
Nothing in the passage questions the toy animals.
CORRECT. Different surroundings (sea visible vs. inland capital) and different test settings (outdoors vs. office).
Household language is Iver’s variable in the third paragraph, not part of the critics’ objection.

Tempting, because the critics do say Mavuro talk is caused by something nonlinguistic. But that something is orientation to a prominent landmark, which in turn explains how speakers remember arrays. Memory and talk are both effects; neither causes the other.

questions.stem: The author’s attitude toward the objection raised by Abernell’s critics can best be described as
choices: dismissive, on the grounds that it rests on a misunderstanding of how Abernell conducted her tasks
accepting of it as a criticism of one study but unpersuaded that it supports the critics’ wider conclusion
persuaded by it that the Mavuro way of speaking is a product of the surroundings in which speakers live
unsure whether it applies to Abernell’s study, since the passage does not fully describe that study
sympathetic to it at first but convinced by Iver’s study that it was mistaken in every respect
questions.explanation: The author says ‘The objection is a fair one against Abernell’s study’ but ‘It does not follow, however, that language plays no role’ (third paragraph): B. E is the main trap: Iver’s study is used against the critics’ broader claim, not against the objection to Abernell’s study, which the author never withdraws. A and D contradict ‘a fair one,’ and C is the critics’ conclusion the author rejects.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how the author regards the critics’ objection.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, first two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Two claims in the critics’ package: (1) Abernell’s study confounded language and setting; (2) so language is just a symptom. The author accepts (1) (‘a fair one’) and rejects the move to (2) (‘It does not follow’). Attitude answers are usually mixed like this; traps overshoot in one direction.

choices.note: The author calls the objection ‘a fair one.’ Not dismissive at all.
CORRECT. Fair against Abernell’s study; but ‘it does not follow… that language plays no role.’
That’s the critics’ conclusion, which the author says doesn’t follow.
The author shows no doubt about the objection’s fit; the author says the study ‘could not separate language from setting.’

Tempting, because Iver’s study does push back on the critics. But it pushes back on their wider claim that language plays no role. The author never says the objection to Abernell’s study was wrong. ‘Every respect’ is the overshoot.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the children in Iver’s study who preserved left-to-right order
choices: belonged to households whose members did not fish
had moved to Pelloc more recently than the others
attended a school apart from the Mavuro-raised children
shared their everyday surroundings with children who rebuilt the rows seaward
were raised in households that had given up the official language
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says all the children ‘attended the same school and played on the same shore,’ yet those from Mavuro-speaking homes rebuilt the rows seaward while ‘the others preserved left and right’: D. A is the main trap: the author raises fishing only as a habit that ‘may go along with’ home language, and never says which households fish. C contradicts ‘the same school,’ E reverses the households, and B is never stated.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says about the Iver children who kept left and right.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, third through fifth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Who are these children? All of Iver’s children came from families that moved to Pelloc from inland. Some households switched to Mavuro; others kept the official language. The official-language children kept left and right. And all the children shared a school and a shore. That shared setting is the whole point of the study. The right answer may describe it in roundabout words.

choices.note: Tempting, because fishing comes up right after the study. But the author says only that home language ‘may go along with’ habits such as fishing. The passage never says which households fish. Possible isn’t stated.
All the families moved from inland; nothing says when, or that one group came later.
Contradicted: ‘The children all attended the same school.’
CORRECT. Same school, same shore; the children who rebuilt seaward were their schoolmates and playmates.
Reversed. These children came from households that ‘continued to speak the official language.’

questions.stem: The author’s remark that the critics “now need to name some feature of these households, other than language, that differs along with it” (last sentence of the third paragraph) serves primarily to
choices: specify what the critics would have to establish to reconcile Iver’s result with their own position
concede that Iver’s result is most likely explained by differences in the households’ working habits
suggest that the critics have already identified the household feature responsible for Iver’s result
argue that no feature of a household other than its language could affect how children remember arrays
show that Iver’s study suffers from the same flaw that undermined Abernell’s earlier study
questions.explanation: Iver’s result is a problem for the critics, and the sentence tells them what would answer it: a household feature other than language that varies with language and could explain the difference: A. B is the main trap: the preceding sentence says home language ‘may go along with’ other habits, a possibility, not the most likely explanation. E is tempting too, but Abernell’s flaw was a difference in setting, which Iver’s design removed; C and D are never claimed.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what job the ‘name some feature’ sentence does.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, last two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Read the two sentences together. First: Iver’s result ‘does not settle the matter,’ because home language might travel with other habits like fishing. Second: ‘But it changes what the critics must show.’ The critics used to be able to point at different surroundings. Now the surroundings are shared, so they’d need a household difference besides language. The sentence states the critics’ new burden. It does not say that such a feature exists or is likely.

choices.note: CORRECT. The critics’ position survives Iver only if some non-language household feature explains the difference; the sentence names that requirement.

Tempting, because fishing is named as a possibility. But the author says only that home language ‘may go along with’ such habits. ‘Most likely explained by’ turns a possibility into a verdict, and the next sentence treats the question as open.
If the critics had already named such a feature, they wouldn’t ‘now need to’ name it.
Too strong. The author admits other habits might matter; that’s why the result ‘does not settle the matter.’
Tempting, but Abernell’s flaw was that her groups lived and were tested in different settings. Iver’s children shared a school and shore. Any remaining weakness is a different one.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the function of the last paragraph?
choices: It summarizes the evidence that has led the author to side with Abernell’s critics against Abernell herself.
It proposes that the dispute be resolved by testing children raised in the island’s inland capital.
It concludes that language and surroundings are rival explanations, of which Iver has shown language to be the correct one.
It identifies a flaw in Iver’s study that both Abernell and her critics failed to take into account.
It questions a supposition common to both sides of the dispute and sketches an alternative picture.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says ‘Both sides of this dispute have assumed that language and surroundings are rival explanations’ and then offers ‘a different picture’ in which language is a means of teaching attention to surroundings: E. C is the main trap: it reuses the paragraph’s own phrase ‘rival explanations,’ but as the author’s conclusion, when the paragraph rejects that framing. A, B, and D describe moves the paragraph never makes.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what the last paragraph does in the passage.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Two sentences: 1. Both sides assumed language and surroundings are rivals (credit one, subtract from the other). 2. Iver’s findings suggest a different picture: language is one way a community teaches attention to its surroundings. So the paragraph names a shared assumption and offers an alternative. Watch for an answer that uses the paragraph’s words but flips their role.

choices.note: The author doesn’t side with the critics; the third paragraph says their conclusion doesn’t follow.
No new test is proposed, and the inland capital belongs to Abernell’s study.

Tempting, because ‘rival explanations’ is a direct quote. But the paragraph attributes that framing to both sides and then rejects it. The author doesn’t pick a winner between rivals; the author denies they’re rivals.
The possible weakness in Iver’s study (habits like fishing) is raised in the third paragraph, not the fourth.
CORRECT. The shared supposition is that language and surroundings are rivals; the different picture is language as a means of teaching attention to surroundings.

questions.stem: Which one of the following studies would be most analogous in design to Iver’s study as described in the passage?
choices: testing musicians from two countries on melody recall, where one country’s language uses pitch to distinguish words and the other’s does not
testing children on melody recall before and after they learn a language that uses pitch to distinguish words
testing children from one town on melody recall, where some homes use a language in which pitch distinguishes words and the others do not
testing adults who speak a language that uses pitch to distinguish words on melody recall, once at home and once in a laboratory
testing children from one town on melody recall, where some take music lessons and some do not, though all speak the same language at home
questions.explanation: Iver held the surroundings fixed (one village, one school, one shore) and compared children whose home languages differed: C does the same with one town and different home languages. E is the main trap: it matches the single-town setting but varies music lessons rather than language, so it mirrors the confound the author worries about rather than Iver’s design. A copies Abernell’s design (two places, two languages), and B and D vary time or test setting instead of home language.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a study with the same design as Iver’s.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, third through fifth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Strip Iver’s study to its skeleton: same place and shared surroundings; groups that differ in home language; compare how they remember something. Then check each choice for all three parts. Analogy traps usually match two parts and swap the third.

choices.note: This is Abernell’s design: two groups in two places with two languages. It can’t separate language from setting, which is exactly the flaw Iver avoided.
A before-and-after design on the same children. Iver compared different children at the same time.
CORRECT. One town (shared surroundings), home language differs, memory compared. Same skeleton as Iver.
This varies the test setting while holding language fixed, the reverse of Iver’s design.

Tempting, because it matches the one-town setting and compares children. But what varies is music lessons, not language. That’s like comparing fishing and non-fishing households: the confound the author worries about, not Iver’s variable.

questions.stem: Both passages are primarily concerned with
choices: whether legislatures that renew many expiring laws in a single bill examine any of those laws
whether making a statute’s survival depend on reenactment is a worthwhile legislative practice
whether reporting requirements can serve as an adequate substitute for sunset provisions
how sunset provisions affect the plans of businesses and agencies that must comply with the law
why laws adopted quickly under pressure are especially likely to outlive their original purpose
questions.explanation: Passage A argues that the record of sunset provisions ‘is disappointing,’ and passage B defends them as reversing legislative inertia, so both are about whether requiring reenactment is worthwhile: B. C is the main trap: both passages mention reporting requirements, but each does so only in its final paragraph, as a side comparison. A and D come only from passage A, and E distorts a remark in passage B.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the question both passages are mainly about.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First paragraph of each passage; last paragraph of each for the reporting requirements.

breakdown.analysis: A: sunset provisions don’t deliver the review they promise; get review another way. B: sunset provisions flip the default so defenders must win a vote; reporting does no such thing. Same practice, opposite verdicts. For ‘both… primarily concerned,’ the answer must be central to each, not merely mentioned in each.

choices.note: Only passage A makes this point, and it’s one of A’s three reasons. B mentions perfunctory votes, but not bulk renewal.
CORRECT. A says sunset provisions disappoint; B says they serve a real purpose. Both are about whether the practice is worth having.
Tempting, because both passages mention reporting requirements. But each raises them only at the end, as a side comparison. ‘Primarily concerned with’ needs the main topic.
Only passage A, and only its third reason.

Passage B says sunset provisions matter most for such laws because legislators couldn’t check their predictions. It never says these laws are more likely to outlive their purpose, and passage A doesn’t discuss them.

questions.stem: According to passage A, the uncertainty that sunset provisions create
choices: falls most heavily on the organized interests that benefit from the laws in question
can be avoided by holding renewal votes well before a law is scheduled to expire
is the chief reason that legislatures renew expiring laws in a single bill
imposes costs even in the case of laws whose renewal is never in doubt
affects agencies deciding whether to hire but not businesses deciding whether to invest
questions.explanation: The third paragraph of passage A says those who must comply ‘bear that cost even for laws whose renewal is never in doubt’: D. A is the trap: organized interests appear in passage A’s second reason as the ones who benefit at renewal, not as the ones who bear the cost of uncertainty. B and C are never stated, and E contradicts the passage, which names both businesses and agencies.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what passage A says about the uncertainty sunset provisions cause.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph of passage A.

breakdown.analysis: Passage A’s third reason: those who must comply can’t plan around a rule that may vanish; businesses and agencies discount for the chance of lapse; and they pay that cost ‘even for laws whose renewal is never in doubt.’ The last clause is the detail most answers will play with.

choices.note: Tempting, because organized interests are a big part of passage A. But they show up in the second reason, as the people who gain at renewal time. The cost of uncertainty falls on those who must comply.
Passage A never discusses when renewal votes are held as a cure for uncertainty.
Passage A gives no reason for bulk renewal beyond the number of expiring provisions; uncertainty isn’t linked to it.
CORRECT. ‘They bear that cost even for laws whose renewal is never in doubt.’
Contradicted: both businesses deciding whether to invest and agencies deciding whether to hire are named.

questions.stem: In passage B, the author’s discussion of the observation that renewal votes are often perfunctory serves primarily to
choices: grant a criticism of sunset provisions while denying that it shows the provisions lack value
dispute the evidence on which critics rely in claiming that renewal votes are seldom substantive
show that perfunctory renewal votes occur more often for emergency measures than for other laws
suggest that a legislator who objects to a law will usually be able to prevent the law’s renewal
argue that renewal votes would receive more attention if fewer laws carried sunset dates
questions.explanation: Passage B answers the critics with ‘Perhaps so; but even a perfunctory vote must be taken,’ granting the point and then saying the required vote still makes the law’s defenders assemble a majority: A. D is the main trap: passage B says the requirement gives a doubting legislator ‘a moment’ at which defenders must assemble a majority, not that the legislator can usually block renewal. B contradicts ‘Perhaps so,’ C is never claimed, and E is passage A’s point, not passage B’s.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what passage B does with the critics’ point about perfunctory votes.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph of passage B, last two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Concede-and-rebut: ‘Critics observe… Perhaps so; but…’ The author doesn’t fight the fact. The author says the fact doesn’t matter much, because even a perfunctory vote forces the law’s defenders to win a majority. Note the strength of the rebuttal: it gives doubters ‘a moment,’ not a veto.

choices.note: CORRECT. ‘Perhaps so’ grants the criticism; ‘but even a perfunctory vote must be taken’ denies that it makes the requirement worthless.
The author doesn’t dispute the evidence; ‘Perhaps so’ accepts it.
Emergency measures come up in the sentence before, but nothing compares how perfunctory their renewal votes are.

Tempting, because the passage does say the requirement helps a doubting legislator. But what it guarantees is ‘a moment at which the law’s defenders… must assemble a majority.’ The defenders may well assemble it. A moment isn’t a veto.
This echoes passage A (‘the more laws carry sunset dates, the less attention each renewal can receive’). Passage B never says it.

questions.stem: Passage B states which one of the following?
choices: Laws adopted quickly under pressure are more likely than other laws to lose their original rationale.
Sunset provisions should be attached to every law whose beneficiaries are well organized.
Reporting requirements are of use only when they are combined with a sunset provision.
Most laws to which sunset provisions are attached are renewed without any real debate taking place.
Without a sunset provision, the burden of assembling a majority falls on a law’s opponents.
questions.explanation: Passage B says ‘A statute stays in force until a majority agrees to repeal it’ and that a sunset provision ‘reverses this default’; so without one, the law’s opponents must assemble the majority: E. A is the main trap: passage B says sunset provisions matter most for laws adopted under pressure because legislators ‘acted on predictions they had no way to check,’ which is about uncertainty, not about how often such laws lose their rationale. B, C, and D overstate or invent claims.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find something passage B actually says.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First paragraph of passage B (the default); second paragraph (laws adopted under pressure).

breakdown.analysis: Passage B’s core idea: normally a law lives until a majority repeals it, so the burden is on opponents. A sunset provision flips that: the law dies unless a majority keeps it, so the burden is on defenders. The right answer may restate the normal case rather than the sunset case. Watch for answers that turn ‘matters most for’ into a factual comparison.

choices.note: Tempting, because passage B singles out laws adopted under pressure. But the reason given is that legislators acted on predictions they couldn’t check. Uncertain isn’t the same as more likely to fail. The passage never compares how often such laws lose their rationale.
Passage B mentions beneficiaries who block repeal, but never recommends sunset provisions for every such law.
Passage B says reporting requirements ‘offer no such moment,’ not that they’re useful only in combination.
Passage B concedes renewal votes are ‘often perfunctory.’ ‘Often’ isn’t ‘most,’ and perfunctory isn’t ‘without any debate.’
CORRECT. ‘A statute stays in force until a majority agrees to repeal it’: without a sunset date, the opponents carry the burden.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the two passages?
choices: Passage A describes a legislative practice without evaluating it, while passage B evaluates that practice and recommends its wider use.
Passage B responds in turn to each of the objections raised in passage A and concludes that none of those objections succeeds.
Passage B defends a practice that passage A criticizes, answering some but not all of passage A’s considerations.
Passage A proposes an alternative to a practice, and passage B argues that the alternative has the same defects as the practice.
Passage B presents a general principle about legislative inertia, and passage A applies that principle to one kind of statute.
questions.explanation: Passage B defends sunset provisions, answers passage A’s point about perfunctory renewal and its preference for reporting requirements, but says nothing about lobbying at renewal or the cost of uncertainty: C. B is the main trap: passage B does reply to some of passage A’s objections, but not to all of them, and it never says that all of them fail. A misdescribes passage A, D gives passage B the wrong complaint about reporting, and E reverses which passage is general.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how passage B relates to passage A.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A’s three reasons and last paragraph; passage B’s second and third paragraphs.

breakdown.analysis: Make a checklist of A’s points: 1. renewal is perfunctory; 2. organized interests use renewal to expand laws; 3. uncertainty costs; 4. use reporting instead. Now check B: it answers 1 (‘Perhaps so; but…’) and 4 (‘Reporting requirements… offer no such moment’). It says nothing about 2 or 3. So B is a defense that covers part of A’s case.

choices.note: Passage A clearly evaluates: ‘The record of such provisions is disappointing.’ And passage B doesn’t recommend wider use.

Tempting, because passage B does answer passage A’s points about perfunctory votes and reporting. But it ignores lobbying and uncertainty, and never says all the objections fail. ‘Each’ is too strong.
CORRECT. Opposite verdicts on the same practice; B answers points 1 and 4 of A’s case but not 2 and 3.
Passage B criticizes reporting for a different reason (no one must act on the reports), not for the defects passage A finds in sunset provisions.
Backwards. Passage B gives the general point about inertia, but passage A doesn’t apply it; A argues against the practice B defends.

questions.stem: Which one of the following pairs of titles most accurately describes the content of passage A and passage B, respectively?
choices: “Sunset Provisions and the Cost of Uncertainty” and “The Case Against Legislative Reporting Requirements”
“Why Expiring Laws Seldom Deliver the Review They Promise” and “Expiring Laws and the Burden of Inertia”
“The Hidden Benefits of Renewing Laws in Bulk” and “Emergency Powers and the Need for Expiration Dates”
“Lobbying and the Renewal of Expiring Laws” and “Why Renewal Votes Are Seldom Perfunctory”
“Why Expiring Laws Seldom Deliver the Review They Promise” and “How Organized Interests Exploit Sunset Provisions”
questions.explanation: Passage A argues that sunset provisions rarely produce real review, and passage B argues that they shift the burden created by legislative inertia: B. E is the main trap: its first title fits passage A, but its second describes passage A’s own second reason, which passage B never discusses. A’s titles each fit only one paragraph, C contradicts passage A and narrows passage B to an example, and D’s second title contradicts passage B’s concession.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the pair of titles that fits each passage’s main content, in order.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Each passage as a whole, especially passage A’s first paragraph and passage B’s first paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Summarize each passage in a phrase first. A: sunset provisions are supposed to force review, and they don’t. B: sunset provisions flip the default so a law’s defenders, not its opponents, must win the vote. Then check BOTH titles in each pair. A pair with one perfect title is still wrong if the other belongs to the wrong passage.

choices.note: Each title covers a single paragraph: the first is passage A’s third reason, the second is passage B’s last two sentences.
CORRECT. A: the review sunset provisions promise rarely happens. B: their value lies in reversing the inertia that favors existing law.
Passage A criticizes bulk renewal, and emergency powers are only one example in passage B.
The first title is one of passage A’s reasons, and the second contradicts passage B, which concedes votes are ‘often perfunctory.’
Tempting, because the first title is exactly right. But exploitation by organized interests is passage A’s second reason. Passage B never mentions it.

questions.stem: The attitude of the author of passage A toward the aim of having legislators reconsider whether existing laws have worked can best be described as
choices: dismissive, since the author regards reconsideration as chiefly an opportunity for organized interests
skeptical that legislators are capable of judging whether a law has accomplished its aims
indifferent, since the author is concerned solely with the costs that expiring laws impose
approving of the aim but doubtful that sunset provisions reliably achieve it
enthusiastic, since the author holds that such review matters more than the stability of the law
questions.explanation: Passage A’s last paragraph says ‘Review of whether laws work is worth having’ and recommends reports and hearings as a better route, after three reasons why sunset provisions fail to produce it: D. A is the main trap: passage A says organized interests exploit sunset renewal debates, not reconsideration as such. B misreads passage A’s point about volume as one about ability, C ignores the last paragraph, and E reverses passage A’s concern for those who must plan around the law.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe the attitude of passage A’s author toward the goal of reviewing laws (not toward sunset provisions).

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, first paragraph and last paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Separate the goal from the tool. The tool (sunset provisions) gets three criticisms. The goal (review) gets an endorsement: ‘Review of whether laws work is worth having,’ plus a better way to get it. So: yes to the end, no to this means. Traps will transfer the author’s criticism of the tool to the goal.

choices.note: Tempting, because passage A does say organized interests use renewal debates to enlarge laws. But that’s a complaint about the renewal vote a sunset date forces, not about reconsideration itself, which the author calls ‘worth having.’
Passage A says few legislators examine each law because there are too many at once. That’s about time and volume, not ability.
The last paragraph shows the author cares about review and proposes a way to get it.
CORRECT. ‘Review… is worth having’ (approves the aim); the three reasons and the alternative show doubt about sunset provisions as the means.
The author never ranks review above stability; the third reason treats the instability sunset provisions create as a real cost.

passages.title: Concealment in The Pellow Letters
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
For much of the twentieth century, critics treated the epistolary novel, a novel told entirely through letters written by its characters, as the eighteenth century’s great experiment in psychological intimacy. Because each letter is composed in the midst of events, before its writer knows how they will turn out, the form was thought to give readers unmediated access to a mind at a given moment. On this account Hester Lyall’s The Pellow Letters (1794), whose heroine, Anne Pellow, writes almost daily to a cousin, ranks among the most intimate novels of its period, and its occasional inconsistencies—Anne describes the same quarrel quite differently in two letters written a week apart—were attributed to haste on Lyall’s part.

The critic Tomas Rennick has challenged this account. A letter, Rennick observes, is never written to no one; it is written to a particular reader whom its writer wishes to please, persuade, or deceive. The letters of epistolary fiction are therefore not windows but performances, and the form’s true subject is the distance between what characters feel and what they choose to tell. Anne’s two accounts of the quarrel, on this view, involve no lapse: the first is addressed to her cousin, the second to the suitor whose good opinion she hopes to keep.

Rennick’s reading is a genuine advance, and it explains much that the older view could only excuse. But it does not, as he claims, overturn the idea that the form grants access to private thought; it relocates that access. A reader of The Pellow Letters sees what no correspondent in the novel sees: every letter, to every recipient. Anne’s cousin never reads the letter to the suitor, and the suitor never reads the letter to the cousin. Only the reader can lay the two side by side, and the discrepancy between them discloses Anne’s feelings more reliably than any confession could. The intimacy the older critics sensed was real; they simply located it in the individual letter, when it lies in an arrangement of letters that only a reader can survey.

This revision matters because it accounts for an episode that Rennick passes over. In the novel’s final third, Anne learns that her guardian has been secretly opening and copying her letters, and thereafter she writes guardedly and conventionally to everyone. If the letters had been nothing but performances all along, the discovery would change little; Anne would simply have one more audience to manage. Yet the novel treats the discovery as a catastrophe, and readers feel it as one. What is lost is not Anne’s sincerity in any single letter but the reader’s privileged position: once each letter is written for every possible reader, the discrepancies that revealed her disappear.

passages.title: Looking time and infant expectation
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
Since the 1980s, much of what developmental psychologists believe about the minds of infants has rested on a single measure: how long an infant looks at something. In a typical study, an infant watches two events. In one, a ball rolls behind a screen and stops against a wall; in the other, the ball appears to pass through the wall. Infants as young as four months generally look longer at the impossible event, and researchers have taken the difference to show that the infants expected the ball to stop and were surprised when it did not. On this interpretation, the knowledge that solid objects cannot pass through one another is present long before infants can act on it.

The psychologist Marit Selby has argued that the step from looking to expecting is too quick. Infants look longer at whatever is perceptually novel, she points out, and the impossible events used in such studies have rarely been matched to the possible ones in their purely visual properties. If the ball in the impossible event comes to rest farther to the right, say, an infant may be responding to an unfamiliar arrangement of shapes rather than to a violation of physical law. When Selby’s laboratory repeated several classic studies using events matched for position, color, and duration of motion, the difference in looking time shrank by about half, though it did not disappear.

Selby’s critics reply that the remaining difference is precisely what matters: if half the effect survives careful matching, then something beyond novelty is at work. The reply is fair as far as it goes, but it concedes more than its proponents seem to notice. A measure whose results can be halved by controls once thought unnecessary is a measure whose earlier results cannot be taken at face value, and the many studies that were never repeated with matched events support their conclusions less firmly than was believed.

Recent work by Paolo Venn, a former student of Selby’s, suggests a way forward. Rather than recording only how long infants looked, Venn tracked where they looked in the moments before the ball reached the wall. Infants who went on to look longer at the impossible event had, in the preceding second, shifted their gaze more often to the near side of the wall, where the ball should stop, than to the far side. Such anticipatory looking cannot be explained by the novelty of an outcome the infant has not yet seen. If the finding holds up, the original conclusion about infants’ grasp of solidity may well survive. What will not survive is the assumption that a difference in looking time could, by itself, have established it.

passages.title: The Varnay franchise petitions
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
Between 1838 and 1846 the parliament of the Duchy of Varnay received more than nine hundred petitions asking that the vote be extended to men who rented rather than owned their homes. Together the petitions bore some 310,000 signatures, at a time when the duchy’s adult male population was perhaps 1.1 million. For most of the twentieth century, historians treated these figures as a rough measure of popular feeling: if nearly three in ten adult men had signed, the campaign for a wider franchise was plainly a mass movement, and the parliament’s refusal to act on it until 1867 amounted to defiance of the popular will by a chamber elected by property owners alone.

In an influential 1994 study, the historian Agnes Hollin challenged this reading. Petitions, she showed, were seldom signed spontaneously. Most were carried from house to house, and to markets and taverns, by paid canvassers or by agents of local reform associations, and in some districts signatures were collected at public meetings where the petition was first read aloud and approved by acclamation. A signature, Hollin argued, recorded not a settled conviction but a moment of social pressure—the reluctance to be seen refusing a neighbor or an employer—and the petitions therefore measured the organizing capacity of the associations rather than the opinions of the population.

Hollin’s evidence about how signatures were gathered is persuasive, and it rightly discourages anyone from reading the totals as a kind of poll. But her conclusion does not follow as directly as she supposes. Organizing capacity is not independent of opinion: canvassers paid by the signature had every reason to work wherever signatures came most easily, so that the associations’ efforts would have followed sympathy wherever it was found. Moreover, the records of the Brenmark Association, which kept accounts of each canvasser’s daily takings, show that a canvasser in the weaving towns of the north routinely collected four or five times as many signatures in a day as one working the farming parishes of the south. Pressure can explain why a given man signed; it cannot easily explain why the same pressure, applied by the same association, yielded so much more in one region than in another.

The petitions, then, are poor evidence of how many of Varnay’s men favored reform, but they may be good evidence of where support for reform was concentrated. That is a more modest claim than the one Hollin’s predecessors made, and it does nothing to vindicate their charge that the parliament defied the popular will. It does, however, restore the petitions to a use that Hollin’s account had seemed to rule out: as evidence, however indirect, of what the people of Varnay actually thought.

passages.title: Funding research by lottery
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
Passage A

Most public research funding is allocated by peer review: panels of scientists score proposals, and those ranked highest are funded until the money runs out. When agencies could fund a third or more of the proposals they received, this system worked tolerably well. Many now fund fewer than one in seven, and the line between funded and unfunded proposals falls deep within a large group that reviewers regard as excellent.

Within that group, the evidence that panels can tell better proposals from worse is weak. When the same proposals have been scored independently by two panels, the panels have agreed reasonably well about which proposals were weak but scarcely better than chance about how to order the strong ones. Yet it is precisely that ordering which now decides who is funded. The weeks of work that scientists devote to polishing each proposal, time taken from research itself, are thus spent largely on a contest whose outcome is close to random already.

A better system would admit the randomness openly. Panels would do what they do well, separating fundable proposals from unfundable ones, and grants would then be awarded by lot among the fundable. Such a system would be no less fair than the present one, since the present ordering is unreliable, and it would be more honest. It would also relieve reviewers of an impossible task, that of ranking proposals they cannot reliably distinguish, and free applicants from an arms race of presentation. Most important, a lottery cannot be swayed by a reviewer’s preference for familiar approaches or for applicants from prestigious institutions, biases that, unlike merit, panels apply with great consistency.

Passage B

Advocates of funding research by lottery rest their case on the unreliability of peer review among strong proposals, and on that point they are largely right. It does not follow, however, that a lottery would cost nothing. A ranking that is unreliable for any single proposal can still be informative on average: if panels place truly stronger proposals in the upper half of the fundable group even modestly more often than chance, then funding by rank will, across thousands of grants, support somewhat better science than funding by lot.

There is also the matter of how applicants would respond. Under a lottery, a proposal that barely clears the threshold has the same chance as an outstanding one, and applicants who understand this will have reason to submit many adequate proposals rather than a few excellent ones. The volume of applications, already burdensome to reviewers, could rise sharply, and the threshold, now the only point at which merit would count, would have to bear the full weight of selection.

None of this argues for leaving the present system as it is. Agencies might reasonably use a lottery to break ties among proposals that panels cannot separate, while continuing to rank wherever rankings carry information. That is a narrower reform than its advocates propose, but it is one whose costs can be measured.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Rennick has shown that the letters in epistolary novels are performances shaped for particular readers rather than faithful records of what their writers actually think and feel at the time.
The inconsistencies in The Pellow Letters, long attributed to Lyall’s haste, are deliberate devices that distinguish Anne’s feelings for her cousin from her feelings for her suitor.
Rennick’s reading explains the discrepancies that the older critics attributed to haste, but its chief failing is that it cannot account for the guardian episode late in the novel.
Although Rennick is right that epistolary letters are shaped for their recipients, the form still discloses private thought, through the reader’s view of all the letters together.
The older critics correctly located the intimacy of the epistolary novel but were wrong to attribute Anne’s inconsistent accounts of the quarrel to haste on Lyall’s part.
questions.explanation: The author calls Rennick’s reading ‘a genuine advance’ but says it ‘relocates’ rather than overturns the form’s access to private thought, which lies in ‘an arrangement of letters that only a reader can survey’ (third paragraph); D states that position with its concession. A is the most tempting trap: it is Rennick’s claim without the author’s qualification. E fails on one word: the older critics sensed real intimacy but, the author says, located it in the wrong place. C states a supporting point from the fourth paragraph as if it were the author’s chief objection, and B misstates Rennick’s explanation of a single discrepancy.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author’s overall position on the epistolary form and on Rennick’s challenge.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph (‘a genuine advance … it relocates that access’) and the last sentence of the passage.

breakdown.analysis: Three views: the older critics (each letter is a window into the mind), Rennick (letters are performances, not windows), and the author (Rennick is right about the letters, but the access survives in the reader’s view of all of them together). The author takes Rennick’s premise and rejects his conclusion that the access is gone. We need both halves: letters are shaped for recipients, yet the form still reveals private thought.

choices.note: Tempting, because the author praises Rennick and agrees the letters are shaped for their readers. But the author says Rennick does not ‘overturn the idea that the form grants access to private thought.’ This is Rennick’s view with the author’s reservation dropped.

Too narrow, and off. Rennick explains the quarrel discrepancy by the two recipients, but the passage never says it distinguishes Anne’s feelings for one person from her feelings for another, and one discrepancy isn’t the main point.

Half right. The author does say Rennick ‘passes over’ the guardian episode. But the episode is offered in the fourth paragraph as support for the author’s revision; the author’s central objection is that Rennick wrongly thinks access to private thought has been overturned, and this choice never says what the author thinks the form does disclose.
CORRECT. The concession (Rennick is right that letters are performances) plus the author’s claim (access is relocated to the reader’s survey of all the letters).

Close, and that’s the danger: the author does say the intimacy the older critics sensed ‘was real’ and that the inconsistencies were not haste. But the author says they ‘located it in the individual letter, when it lies in an arrangement of letters.’ ‘Correctly located’ is exactly what the author denies. One word sinks it.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the critics who regarded the epistolary novel as an experiment in psychological intimacy explained the inconsistencies in Anne’s accounts of the quarrel as
choices: a sign that Lyall wished to show how Anne’s feelings had changed over the course of a week
the product of haste on Lyall’s part rather than of any design
a consequence of the different readers to whom Anne addressed her two letters
evidence that Anne already suspected her letters were being read by her guardian
a reflection of the conventions that governed letters written to suitors in the 1790s
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says the novel’s inconsistencies ‘were attributed to haste on Lyall’s part’ by the critics who saw the form as intimate, so B is correct. C is the trap: it is Rennick’s explanation from the second paragraph, offered against those critics. A, D and E are never attributed to anyone in the passage.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find how the older critics explained the two different accounts of the quarrel.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First paragraph, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Two groups explain the discrepancy differently. The older critics blame the author (haste). Rennick credits Anne (she writes for two different readers). The stem asks about the older critics, so keep the two straight.

choices.note: Nobody in the passage says this. The letters are a week apart, but no one explains the discrepancy as a change of feeling.
CORRECT. ‘Attributed to haste on Lyall’s part.’ Haste means no design, which is exactly why Rennick says his reading explains what the older view ‘could only excuse.’
Tempting, because it’s the explanation the passage spends the most time on. But it’s Rennick’s, and he offers it against the older critics. Wrong party.
The guardian comes up only in the final third of the novel, and nobody uses him to explain the quarrel letters.
Conventions of 1790s courtship letters are never mentioned. Outside information.

questions.stem: In saying that Rennick’s reading ‘relocates that access’ (second sentence of the third paragraph), the author most likely means that
choices: Rennick himself places the form’s access to private thought in the reader’s comparison of letters rather than in any single letter
the private thought that critics attributed to Lyall’s characters should instead be attributed to Lyall herself
Rennick’s reading shifts critical attention from the novel’s early letters to those written after the guardian’s intrusion
Rennick’s reading implies that the reader, rather than Anne, is the true subject of The Pellow Letters
once Rennick’s point is granted, the form’s disclosure of private thought must be sought somewhere other than where earlier critics sought it
questions.explanation: The author says Rennick’s reading does not ‘overturn the idea that the form grants access to private thought; it relocates that access’: granting Rennick’s point, the access lies not in the individual letter, where the older critics found it, but in the arrangement only a reader surveys. E says that. A is the trap: it gives the author’s own relocation to Rennick, who, the author says, ‘claims’ to overturn the idea altogether. B, C and D invent shifts the passage never describes.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out what the author means by saying Rennick’s reading ‘relocates’ the access to private thought.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, first two sentences and last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Read the whole sentence: Rennick’s reading ‘does not, as he claims, overturn the idea that the form grants access to private thought; it relocates that access.’ So Rennick thinks he has abolished the access; the author says his point, properly understood, just moves it. Moves it where? The last sentence tells you: from the individual letter (the older critics’ spot) to the arrangement of letters only the reader sees. Watch whose view is whose: the relocation is the author’s conclusion, not Rennick’s.

choices.note: Tempting, because this is exactly where the access ends up. But it’s the author who puts it there. Rennick, ‘as he claims,’ thinks he has overturned the idea of access altogether. Wrong person.
Lyall’s own private thought never comes up. The access is to the characters’ feelings, Anne’s in particular.
The guardian episode is in the fourth paragraph and is something Rennick ‘passes over.’ Nothing is shifted to late letters.
The reader gets a privileged position, but nowhere does the author say the reader becomes the novel’s subject. Anne’s feelings are still what is disclosed.
CORRECT. Granting that letters are performances, the access is no longer in the single letter (where the older critics found it) but in the reader’s survey of all the letters.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which one of the following is a claim made by Rennick?
choices: What the older critics took for a lapse reflects a difference between the people Anne was writing to.
The discrepancy between Anne’s two accounts of the quarrel discloses feelings that neither of the two accounts states outright.
The reader of an epistolary novel sees what none of the correspondents within the novel can ever see.
Anne’s letters become guarded and conventional after she learns of her guardian’s intrusion.
The older critics rightly sensed intimacy in the form but were wrong about where it lies.
questions.explanation: In the second paragraph, ‘on this view’ (Rennick’s), Anne’s two accounts ‘involve no lapse’ because one is addressed to her cousin and the other to her suitor. A restates that from the older critics’ side: what they called haste is really a difference of recipient. B is the dominant trap: it concerns the same discrepancy, but the claim that the discrepancy ‘discloses Anne’s feelings’ is the author’s reply to Rennick in the third paragraph; Rennick holds that the letters are performances and claims to overturn the idea of access. C and E are also the author’s claims, and D is the author’s description of an episode Rennick ‘passes over.’

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the one claim the passage attributes to Rennick rather than to the author.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph (Rennick) versus third and fourth paragraphs (the author).

breakdown.analysis: This is a ‘whose view is it?’ question. Rennick gets the second paragraph only: letters are performances, and the two accounts of the quarrel differ because they go to different readers, so they ‘involve no lapse.’ The third paragraph turns to the author (‘But it does not, as he claims…’), and everything there about what the discrepancy reveals is the author’s answer to Rennick. The right answer won’t quote the second paragraph; it says the same thing from the other side: the ‘lapse’ the older critics saw is a difference of addressee.

choices.note: CORRECT. The older critics blamed haste (a lapse in craft); Rennick says the two accounts ‘involve no lapse’ because the first goes to the cousin and the second to the suitor. Same claim, stated as a correction of the older view.

Tempting, because it’s about the very same two letters and sounds like Rennick’s ‘distance between what characters feel and what they choose to tell.’ But the idea that the discrepancy discloses Anne’s feelings comes after ‘But it does not, as he claims…’: it is the author’s reply. Rennick thinks the letters are performances and claims to overturn the idea that the form gives access to private thought.
The author’s claim (third paragraph), the heart of the author’s revision of Rennick.
This is the author’s description of the novel’s final third, an episode Rennick ‘passes over.’
The author’s verdict in the last sentence of the third paragraph. Rennick denies the access altogether.

questions.stem: The author discusses Anne’s discovery that her guardian has been opening her letters (fourth paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: show that Anne’s letters had been entirely sincere until the guardian’s intrusion compelled her to begin writing for an audience
illustrate the older critics’ view that the epistolary novel gives readers access to its heroine’s mind
cite an episode that the author’s account explains but that a view the author considers incomplete cannot
suggest that Lyall intended the novel’s final third as a warning to her readers against the dangers of private correspondence
concede that Rennick’s reading adequately accounts for the change in the tone of Anne’s letters late in the novel
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says the author’s revision ‘accounts for an episode that Rennick passes over’: if the letters were only performances, the discovery ‘would change little,’ yet the novel treats it as a catastrophe. So the episode is evidence that the author’s account explains and Rennick’s does not, which C describes abstractly. A is the dominant trap: it reads the loss as a loss of sincerity, but the author says explicitly that ‘what is lost is not Anne’s sincerity in any single letter.’ B credits the older critics, whom the author has already corrected; D invents Lyall’s intention; E reverses the point about Rennick.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out why the author brings up the guardian episode.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, first sentence and last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: The first sentence tells you the job: ‘This revision matters because it accounts for an episode that Rennick passes over.’ The middle shows Rennick’s view can’t explain it (one more audience would change little), and the last sentence explains it the author’s way (the reader’s privileged position is lost). So the episode is a test case that the author’s view passes and Rennick’s fails. The answer may describe Rennick’s view abstractly, as ‘a view the author regards as incomplete.’

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like the obvious story: she was honest, then she had to perform. But the author rules this out in so many words: ‘What is lost is not Anne’s sincerity in any single letter.’ And the author accepts that her letters were always written for someone.
The older critics placed the access in the individual letter, and the author has corrected them. The episode supports the author’s revised view, not theirs.
CORRECT. The author’s account explains why the discovery is a catastrophe; Rennick’s view (a ‘genuine advance’ that misses something, hence incomplete) predicts it would ‘change little.’
Nothing about Lyall’s intentions or a warning. The author is arguing about how the form works.
Opposite. Rennick ‘passes over’ this episode, and on his view it ‘would change little.’ No concession here.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?
choices: A traditional interpretation is described; a challenge to it is presented; the challenge is rejected; and the traditional interpretation is confirmed by an episode in a novel.
A traditional view is described; a critic’s objection to it is presented; the objection is partly accepted and the traditional view revised; and an episode is cited that the revision explains.
Two interpretations of a novel are presented; each is shown to rest on a misreading of the novel’s ending; and a third interpretation is proposed in their place.
A claim about a literary form is stated; evidence for it is drawn from a single novel; the claim is extended to the form as a whole; and an objection to the extension is answered.
A literary form is defined; its origins in the eighteenth century are traced; a critic’s account of its decline is summarized; and that account is qualified.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 gives the older view, paragraph 2 Rennick’s objection, paragraph 3 accepts the objection in part (‘a genuine advance’) while revising the older view (the access is ‘relocated’), and paragraph 4 cites the guardian episode that the revision ‘accounts for.’ That is B. A is the trap: the author does not reject Rennick’s challenge, and the older view is revised, not confirmed. C, D and E each include a step the passage lacks.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match the sequence of the four paragraphs.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The opening sentence of each paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraph by paragraph: 1. the older critics’ view; 2. Rennick’s challenge; 3. ‘a genuine advance … but’ — partly accept, partly revise; 4. an episode that the revised account explains. Organization answers die on one wrong element, so check each step, especially the verb for paragraph 3.

choices.note: Tempting, because the author does end up keeping the idea of access to private thought. But the challenge isn’t ‘rejected’ (it’s ‘a genuine advance’), and the traditional view isn’t ‘confirmed’: the author says the older critics put the intimacy in the wrong place. One wrong verb kills it.
CORRECT. Every step matches: older view, Rennick’s objection, partial acceptance with revision, and the guardian episode as something the revision explains.
There aren’t two interpretations of a novel shown to misread its ending, and no third interpretation replaces both.
The passage doesn’t argue from one novel to the whole form, and there’s no answered objection to such an extension.
No history of the form’s origins, and no account of its decline. Invented frame.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, the author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements about an epistolary novel consisting entirely of letters written by one character to a single correspondent?
choices: It would give readers more direct access to its letter writer’s private thoughts than The Pellow Letters gives, since the writer would have only one reader to please.
Its letters, unlike those in The Pellow Letters, could not properly be read as performances shaped for a particular recipient.
Any inconsistencies among its letters would have to be explained as the result of carelessness on the part of its author.
It would be more likely than The Pellow Letters to be treated by critics as an experiment in psychological intimacy.
It would lack the means by which, on the author’s account, The Pellow Letters discloses feelings that its heroine never states.
questions.explanation: For the author, the form discloses private thought because the reader ‘sees what no correspondent in the novel sees: every letter, to every recipient,’ and can compare letters addressed to different people (third paragraph). If every letter goes to one correspondent, that correspondent sees everything the reader sees, so the means the author identifies is missing: E. A is the dominant trap: it sounds like the older critics’ intuition, but the author accepts that each letter is shaped for its reader, so having one reader doesn’t make the letters windows, and it removes the comparison the author relies on. B contradicts the author’s acceptance of Rennick’s point, C overstates, and D is unsupported.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply the author’s account of how epistolary novels disclose feelings to a novel with only one recipient.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph (especially ‘every letter, to every recipient’) and the last sentence of the fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: What, for the author, does the disclosing? Not any single letter. It’s the reader’s comparison of letters to different recipients, which no character can make. Now remove the different recipients: one writer, one correspondent. The correspondent reads every letter the reader reads, so the reader has no privileged comparison. The guardian episode makes the same point: once every letter may be read by anyone, the discrepancies vanish. We need an answer that says this novel lacks that mechanism.

choices.note: Tempting, because one audience sounds simpler and more candid. But the author agrees with Rennick that every letter is shaped for its reader, so one reader doesn’t make the letters more direct. And the author’s source of access, comparing letters to different people, would be gone. So less access on the author’s account, not more.
Opposite. The author accepts that letters are ‘written to a particular reader’ and shaped for that reader. One recipient is still a recipient.
Too strong. Nothing forces ‘carelessness’; the letters could shift as feelings or circumstances change. ‘Would have to’ goes far beyond the passage.
The passage says nothing about how critics would classify such a novel. Unsupported prediction.
CORRECT. The author’s mechanism needs letters to different recipients that only the reader sees together. With a single correspondent, there is nothing the reader sees that the recipient doesn’t.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Although infants’ grasp of solidity may yet be demonstrated, differences in how long infants look at events cannot by themselves show what infants expect.
Selby’s experiments have shown that the longer looking observed in classic studies reflects the perceptual novelty of impossible events rather than infants’ expectations.
Although perceptual novelty explains part of the difference in looking time, the part that survives careful matching shows that infants expect solid objects to stop at barriers.
Venn’s measurements of anticipatory looking have established that infants as young as four months know that solid objects cannot pass through one another.
Developmental psychologists should abandon looking-time measures in favor of procedures that record where infants look before an event is completed.
questions.explanation: The passage ends by saying the conclusion about solidity ‘may well survive’ if Venn’s finding holds up, but ‘what will not survive is the assumption that a difference in looking time could, by itself, have established it’; A states both halves. D is the dominant trap: it drops the author’s qualification (‘If the finding holds up … may well survive’) and turns a promising result into an established one. C is the critics’ reply, which the author finds ‘fair as far as it goes’ but which claims that the surviving looking-time difference shows what infants expect, the very inference the last sentence rejects. B overstates Selby, and E recommends abandoning a measure the author never rejects.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author’s overall conclusion about what looking-time studies can show.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph and the last two sentences of the fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The author’s verdict is in the last two sentences: the conclusion about solidity might survive (thanks to Venn), but looking time alone could never have proved it. Note the hedges: ‘If the finding holds up,’ ‘may well survive.’ A main-point answer must keep them. Don’t let the author’s optimism about Venn turn into certainty.

choices.note: CORRECT. It keeps the hedge (‘may yet be demonstrated’) and the claim the author is sure of (looking time alone can’t show what infants expect).

Too strong. Matching shrank the difference ‘by about half, though it did not disappear,’ so Selby hasn’t shown that novelty explains all of it. The author treats her point as a reason for doubt, not a refutation.

Tempting, because the author calls this reply ‘fair as far as it goes.’ But it is Selby’s critics’ position, and the author’s closing sentence denies exactly what it asserts: a looking-time difference could not, ‘by itself,’ have established what infants expect. Wrong viewpoint.

Tempting, because Venn’s work is the passage’s hopeful ending and the infants did look ahead. But the author says ‘If the finding holds up’ and ‘may well survive.’ ‘Have established’ drops the qualification. The trap is the right idea at the wrong strength.
Too strong. Venn still measured looking time too; he added anticipatory looking. The author never recommends abandoning the measure.

questions.stem: According to the passage, when Selby’s laboratory repeated classic studies using matched events, the difference in looking time between the possible and impossible events
choices: disappeared among the youngest infants but persisted among older ones
reversed, so that the infants looked longer at the possible events
decreased by roughly half but did not disappear entirely
remained about as large as it had been in the original studies
depended chiefly on how long the ball remained in motion
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the difference ‘shrank by about half, though it did not disappear,’ which C restates. A is the most tempting wrong answer because it also has the effect partly surviving, but the passage never breaks the results down by age. B, D and E are not stated; duration of motion was one of the things the events were matched for.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what happened to the looking-time difference in Selby’s matched studies.
