setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: One sentence answers this: ‘shrank by about half, though it did not disappear.’ Look for both pieces: smaller, but still there.

choices.note: Tempting, since part of the effect did survive. But the passage never splits the infants by age. Made-up detail.
Nothing reversed. Infants still looked longer at the impossible events, just by less.
CORRECT. ‘Shrank by about half, though it did not disappear.’
Opposite. It shrank by about half.
Duration of motion was something the events were matched on, so it can’t be what the difference depended on.

questions.stem: The passage states that the infants in Venn’s study who went on to look longer at the impossible event
choices: had shifted their gaze to the near side of the wall more often than did the infants who did not go on to look longer
looked longer at unfamiliar arrangements of shapes than at familiar ones throughout the course of the study
had seen the ball pass through the wall in an earlier session before they took part in Venn’s study
had looked toward the spot where the ball ought to halt more than past it, before the outcome could be seen
showed no anticipatory looking once the events had been matched for position, color, and duration
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says these infants had, ‘in the preceding second, shifted their gaze more often to the near side of the wall, where the ball should stop, than to the far side,’ an outcome ‘the infant has not yet seen.’ D restates this in other words: more looking at the stopping point than beyond it, before the outcome was visible. A is the dominant trap: it reuses ‘shifted their gaze to the near side … more often,’ but changes the comparison from near side versus far side (within these infants) to these infants versus other infants, a comparison the passage never reports. B borrows Selby’s novelty idea, C contradicts the point that the outcome had not been seen, and E is never stated.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what Venn observed about the infants who later looked longer at the impossible event.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, third sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Read the comparison exactly. Venn’s finding compares two places these infants looked: the near side of the wall (where the ball should stop) versus the far side, in the second before the ball arrived. It doesn’t compare these infants with any other group. The right answer will say the same thing in different words (‘the spot where the ball ought to halt’ for ‘near side,’ ‘past it’ for ‘far side’); a trap will keep the passage’s words but swap what is being compared.

choices.note: Tempting, because it repeats the passage’s phrasing almost word for word. But look at what’s compared. The passage says these infants looked at the near side more often than at the far side. It never compares them with the infants who didn’t look longer. Same words, different comparison.
Novelty of shapes is Selby’s explanation of looking time in general, not something Venn reported about these infants.
Opposite of the passage’s point. Anticipatory looking matters because it happens before the infant has seen the outcome.

CORRECT. ‘The spot where the ball ought to halt’ is the near side ‘where the ball should stop’; ‘past it’ is the far side; ‘before the outcome could be seen’ is the preceding second, before the ball reached the wall.
Never stated. Venn’s study isn’t described as varying matched and unmatched events at all.

questions.stem: The author mentions the possibility that the ball ‘comes to rest farther to the right’ (third sentence of the second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: describe a flaw that Selby discovered in the design of the experiments she herself had conducted only a few years earlier
illustrate how a possible and an impossible event might differ in a way unrelated to physical law
explain why infants younger than four months are unable to follow an object as it moves behind a screen
identify the specific difference between events that accounted for the entire effect found in the classic studies
show that the impossible events are generally more complex visually than the possible events with which they are paired
questions.explanation: The sentence is introduced with ‘say’: it is a hypothetical example of how unmatched events could differ visually, so that an infant ‘may be responding to an unfamiliar arrangement of shapes rather than to a violation of physical law.’ That is B. D is the trap: it treats the illustration as an identified cause and gives it the ‘entire’ effect, though matching removed only about half. A, C and E are unsupported.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out why the ‘farther to the right’ example appears.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, second and third sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The second sentence makes Selby’s general point: impossible and possible events weren’t matched visually. The third gives an example (‘say’) of what an unmatched difference might look like. It’s an illustration of a possibility, not a finding.

choices.note: Selby is criticizing other researchers’ classic studies, not her own earlier work.
CORRECT. The ball’s final position is a visual difference unrelated to physics, and it’s offered as an example (‘say’) of how the two events could differ.
Age limits on tracking objects never come up. Infants as young as four months are said to look longer, nothing more.
Tempting, because the example is about exactly this kind of difference. But it’s hypothetical (‘say’), and matching cut the effect only by about half, so nothing accounts for ‘the entire effect.’
‘More complex’ isn’t the point; just different. And ‘generally’ overgeneralizes a single hypothetical.

questions.stem: The primary function of the third paragraph is to
choices: present new evidence that casts doubt on Selby’s finding that looking-time differences shrink when events are matched
defend the classic interpretation of looking-time studies against the objection described in the second paragraph
describe a method of measurement that avoids the difficulty identified in the second paragraph
explain why Selby’s critics deny that perceptual novelty has any effect on how long infants look at an event
evaluate a response to Selby’s findings and draw out an implication that the response’s proponents overlook
questions.explanation: The third paragraph states the critics’ reply, judges it ‘fair as far as it goes,’ and then argues that it ‘concedes more than its proponents seem to notice’: the earlier results cannot be taken at face value. E describes that. B is the trap: the paragraph reports a defense of the classic interpretation, but the author’s own move is to show the defense has a cost. C describes the fourth paragraph, and A and D are unsupported.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what the third paragraph does in the passage.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, all three sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Sentence 1: the critics’ reply. Sentence 2: the author’s verdict (fair, but concedes more than they notice). Sentence 3: what it concedes. So the paragraph reports a reply and then turns it back on the people who made it.

choices.note: No new evidence appears, and nobody disputes that the difference shrank.
Tempting, because the critics’ reply is a defense. But the paragraph isn’t mainly the defense; it’s the author’s evaluation of it, and the author concludes the reply weakens many earlier studies.
That’s the fourth paragraph (Venn’s anticipatory looking).
The critics don’t deny novelty matters; they argue that something ‘beyond novelty’ is also at work.
CORRECT. The response is evaluated (‘fair as far as it goes’) and the overlooked implication drawn out (earlier results can’t be taken at face value).

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the passage?
choices: At least some researchers once regarded it as unnecessary to match possible and impossible events in their visual properties.
Selby’s critics now openly acknowledge that the results of the earlier looking-time studies cannot simply be taken at face value.
Infants younger than four months do not look longer at impossible events than they do at possible ones.
Most developmental psychologists now doubt that infants know that solid objects cannot pass through one another.
Anticipatory looking has been observed only in infants who had previously watched the impossible event.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph refers to ‘controls once thought unnecessary,’ meaning the matching for position, color and duration that Selby introduced, and the second paragraph says such events ‘have rarely been matched.’ So at least some researchers once thought such matching unnecessary: A. B is the dominant trap: the author says the critics’ reply ‘concedes more than its proponents seem to notice,’ so the implication about earlier results is the author’s, not something the critics acknowledge. C misreads ‘as young as four months,’ D is unsupported, and E contradicts the point that anticipatory looking precedes an outcome ‘the infant has not yet seen.’

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the passage best supports.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, second sentence; third paragraph, second and third sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase. Watch for answers that hand the author’s conclusions to someone else. The third paragraph has a quiet fact in it: matching was a control ‘once thought unnecessary.’ Thought so by whom? By the researchers who ran the unmatched studies. That modest claim is safe. Compare the critics: the author says their reply concedes more than they ‘seem to notice.’ People who haven’t noticed a concession haven’t acknowledged it.

choices.note: CORRECT. ‘Controls once thought unnecessary’ plus ‘rarely been matched’ means at least some researchers thought matching wasn’t needed. ‘At least some’ keeps it safe.

Tempting, because their reply does logically imply this, according to the author. But the author says they don’t ‘seem to notice’ it. An implication the author draws isn’t an acknowledgment by the critics. Wrong party.
‘As young as four months’ tells you the youngest age tested, not that younger infants fail. We don’t know.
Nothing says most psychologists now doubt this. The author even says the conclusion ‘may well survive.’
Opposite. Anticipatory looking matters because it comes before the infant has seen the outcome.

questions.stem: The author’s attitude toward the reply made by Selby’s critics (first sentence of the third paragraph) can best be described as
choices: dismissive, on the grounds that the difference remaining after the matching is too small to be meaningful
approving without reservation, since the reply shows that something beyond perceptual novelty is at work
doubtful that as much as half of the original difference in fact survived the matching of the events
accepting of the reply’s reasoning while holding that it implies a weakness in much earlier research
noncommittal, since the author nowhere takes a position on what the remaining difference in looking time shows
questions.explanation: The author calls the reply ‘fair as far as it goes’ (acceptance) but says it ‘concedes more than its proponents seem to notice’: the many unmatched studies ‘support their conclusions less firmly than was believed’ (third paragraph). D captures both. B is the dominant trap: ‘fair’ sounds like endorsement, but the ‘but’ adds a serious reservation. A and C contradict the author’s acceptance of the reply’s reasoning, and E ignores the clear evaluation.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pin down how the author evaluates the critics’ reply.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, second and third sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Two signals: ‘fair as far as it goes’ (yes, the leftover half shows something beyond novelty) and ‘but it concedes more than its proponents seem to notice’ (the reply admits that matching can halve results, which undermines every study never redone with matched events). So: accepts the reasoning, adds a sting. Attitude answers are usually mixed like this; watch for the answer that keeps only the positive half.

choices.note: The author accepts the reply’s point about the remaining difference and never calls it too small.
Tempting, because ‘fair’ is a positive word. But ‘as far as it goes’ and the ‘but’ that follows add a reservation. ‘Without reservation’ drops it.
The author reports that the difference shrank by about half as fact and never doubts it.
CORRECT. Accepts the reasoning (‘fair as far as it goes’) and draws the cost: the unmatched studies support their conclusions less firmly than believed.
The author does take a position: the reply is fair, and it has an unwelcome implication.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Hollin has shown that the franchise petitions measured the organizing capacity of the reform associations rather than the opinions of Varnay’s population.
Because support for reform was concentrated in the northern weaving towns, the parliament’s refusal to act before 1867 defied at least the will of the north.
Although the petitions cannot show how widely reform was supported, they can still serve as evidence of how support for reform was distributed.
Although many petitions were signed under social pressure, they remain good evidence of how many of Varnay’s men favored a wider franchise.
Historians should stop relying on petition totals and should rely instead on the daily accounts that canvassers kept of the signatures they collected.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph concludes that the petitions ‘are poor evidence of how many of Varnay’s men favored reform, but they may be good evidence of where support for reform was concentrated’; C states this. A is the dominant trap: the author calls Hollin’s evidence ‘persuasive,’ but A is Hollin’s conclusion, which the author says ‘does not follow as directly as she supposes.’ D drops the author’s distinction between how many and where. B turns the author’s tentative regional claim into a fact and uses it to revive the charge of defiance, which the author says the claim ‘does nothing to vindicate.’ E overstates the role of the Brenmark records.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author’s overall conclusion about what the petitions can show.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, first two sentences, and the fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Three views. Earlier historians: the totals measure popular feeling, so parliament defied the people. Hollin: signatures measure pressure and organization, not opinion. The author: Hollin is right about the totals, but the regional pattern still tells us where support was. The key distinction is how many (no) versus where (yes). A main point has to keep that split.

choices.note: Tempting, because the author praises Hollin’s evidence and accepts her point about the totals. But this is Hollin’s conclusion, and the author says it ‘does not follow as directly as she supposes.’ It’s the opposing view the author is answering.

Tempting, because it sounds like the author’s regional point applied with care. But the author says only that the petitions ‘may be’ good evidence of where support was concentrated, and says outright that this claim ‘does nothing to vindicate their charge that the parliament defied the popular will.’ It revives the earlier historians’ charge in a smaller form.
CORRECT. Poor evidence of how many, possibly good evidence of where. That is the author’s ‘more modest claim.’
This drops the author’s distinction. The author says the petitions are ‘poor evidence of how many of Varnay’s men favored reform.’
Too strong. The Brenmark records are one piece of evidence, and the author proposes a new use for the petitions rather than abandoning them.

questions.stem: According to the passage, in some districts signatures on the franchise petitions were collected
choices: only from men who owned rather than rented their homes
by officials acting on behalf of the parliament
at polling places during parliamentary elections
by canvassers paid by the number of households they visited
at public meetings after the petition had been read aloud and approved
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says that ‘in some districts signatures were collected at public meetings where the petition was first read aloud and approved by acclamation,’ which E restates. D is the most tempting wrong answer: canvassers were paid ‘by the signature,’ not by households visited. A, B and C are not stated, and A conflicts with the petitions’ purpose.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find how signatures were gathered in some districts.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, third sentence.

breakdown.analysis: The third sentence of the second paragraph names three methods: house-to-house and market canvassing by paid canvassers, agents of associations, and, ‘in some districts,’ public meetings where the petition was read aloud and approved first. The stem’s ‘in some districts’ points straight at the meetings.

choices.note: Nothing says so, and the petitions were asking for the vote for renters, so limiting signers to owners makes no sense here.
No parliamentary officials are mentioned; the collectors were canvassers and association agents.
Polling places never come up.
Tempting, because paid canvassers are real in the passage. But the third paragraph says they were paid ‘by the signature,’ not by the households they visited.
CORRECT. ‘Public meetings where the petition was first read aloud and approved by acclamation.’

questions.stem: The passage indicates that the historians who wrote before Hollin
choices: believed that most of the petitions’ signatures had been obtained through social pressure
judged support for reform by the share of adult men who had signed
held that the parliament extended the franchise in 1867 because of the petitions it had received
relied chiefly on the surviving account books of reform associations such as the Brenmark Association
regarded the petitions as more representative of opinion in the north than of opinion in the south
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says these historians took the figures ‘as a rough measure of popular feeling’: ‘if nearly three in ten adult men had signed, the campaign … was plainly a mass movement.’ B paraphrases that. C is the trap: the passage mentions 1867 only as the year the parliament finally acted, and says nothing about why it acted. A is Hollin’s view, and D and E are the author’s evidence and argument.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says about the earlier historians.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First paragraph, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: The earlier historians did a simple calculation: 310,000 signatures out of about 1.1 million men is nearly three in ten, so a mass movement. That’s judging support by the proportion who signed. Everything about pressure, organization and regions comes later from other people.

choices.note: That’s Hollin’s argument, made against these historians.
CORRECT. ‘Nearly three in ten adult men had signed’ was their basis for calling the campaign a mass movement.

Tempting, because the passage mentions 1867 and the earlier historians care about the parliament’s response. But it says only that the parliament refused to act ‘until 1867.’ Why it acted then is never said. Plausible outside story.
The Brenmark records are the author’s evidence, in the third paragraph.
The north–south comparison is the author’s, and even the author draws it from canvassers’ daily rates, not from the earlier historians.

questions.stem: The author’s remark that canvassers were ‘paid by the signature’ (third sentence of the third paragraph) serves primarily to
choices: support Hollin’s claim that a signature recorded a moment of social pressure rather than a settled conviction
suggest that many of the signatures on the franchise petitions were obtained by fraudulent means
explain why the petition totals overstate the level of support for reform in the southern farming parishes
indicate one way in which the reform associations’ organizing efforts would have followed popular opinion
show that the Brenmark Association was more successful than the other reform associations
questions.explanation: The remark supports the claim that ‘organizing capacity is not independent of opinion’: canvassers paid per signature would work where signatures came easily, so the associations’ efforts ‘would have followed sympathy.’ That is D. A is the dominant trap: payment sounds like pressure, but the author uses the point against Hollin’s conclusion, not for it. B and E are unsupported, and C gets the direction of the regional comparison wrong.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out what the ‘paid by the signature’ point does in the author’s argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, second and third sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Sentence 2: Hollin’s conclusion doesn’t follow. Sentence 3: ‘Organizing capacity is not independent of opinion,’ and then the reason: canvassers paid per signature go where signatures come easily, i.e., where people are sympathetic. So the payment detail shows how organization would track opinion, which undercuts Hollin’s ‘organization rather than opinion.’

choices.note: Tempting, because paid canvassing sounds like the very pressure Hollin describes. But the author uses it in the ‘But her conclusion does not follow’ part of the paragraph: payment drew canvassers toward sympathetic places, linking organization to opinion. It works against Hollin’s conclusion.
Fraud is never suggested.
The passage never says the totals overstate support in the farming parishes; the farming parishes are where canvassers did worse.
CORRECT. Paid per signature, canvassers went where signatures came easily, so the associations’ efforts followed sympathy.
No comparison between associations. The Brenmark Association appears only as the source of the daily records.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the records of the Brenmark Association show that
choices: a canvasser working the southern farming parishes typically gathered in a day only a fraction of what a canvasser in the northern weaving towns gathered
the weaving towns of the north routinely yielded four or five times as many of the association’s signatures as the farming parishes of the south
the association paid its canvassers more for each signature gathered in the north than for each one gathered in the south
the association employed more canvassers in the northern weaving towns than it did in the southern farming parishes
canvassers who moved from the northern towns to the southern parishes collected fewer signatures after they moved
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says the records show that ‘a canvasser in the weaving towns of the north routinely collected four or five times as many signatures in a day as one working the farming parishes of the south.’ A states the same rate from the other side: a southern canvasser’s daily take was a fraction (roughly a quarter to a fifth) of a northern canvasser’s. B is the dominant trap: it keeps the passage’s words (‘routinely,’ ‘four or five times as many’) but turns a daily rate per canvasser into a regional total, which also depends on how many canvassers worked each region and for how long, figures the passage never gives. C, D and E are not stated.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the Brenmark records showed.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, fourth sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Read the numbers carefully: ‘a canvasser … collected four or five times as many signatures in a day as one working the farming parishes.’ That’s a rate: signatures per canvasser per day. Flip it and you get the same fact: a southern canvasser got a quarter to a fifth as many per day. It says nothing about regional totals, because a total is rate times canvasser-days, and we aren’t told how many canvassers worked each region. A rate isn’t a total. The trap here even keeps the passage’s exact numbers to make the swap harder to see.

choices.note: CORRECT. ‘Four or five times as many’ for the north is the same as ‘only a fraction’ for the south, per canvasser, per day. It’s the passage’s fact stated from the other side.

Tempting, because it borrows ‘routinely’ and ‘four or five times as many’ straight from the passage. But it swaps a daily rate per canvasser for a regional total. If the association sent ten canvassers south for every one it sent north, the south could supply more signatures overall. Rate vs. total.
Pay rates by region are never mentioned. Canvassers are said to be paid by the signature, nothing more.
The number of canvassers in each region is exactly what the passage doesn’t give.
The passage compares canvassers in different regions, not the same canvassers before and after a move. ‘The same association’ isn’t ‘the same canvassers.’

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?
choices: A historical event is described; two explanations of it are compared; and both explanations are rejected in favor of a third.
A traditional interpretation is presented; a challenge to it is described; and the traditional interpretation is defended against the challenge.
A traditional reading of some evidence is described; a challenge to it is presented and partly accepted; and a narrower use of the evidence is proposed.
A body of evidence is described; a historian’s method of analyzing that evidence is summarized; and the method is then applied to a newly discovered set of records.
A historian’s thesis is stated; evidence supporting it is presented; and the thesis is then used to explain the outcome of a later parliamentary vote on the franchise.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 gives the earlier historians’ reading of the petitions, paragraph 2 Hollin’s challenge, paragraph 3 accepts her evidence but disputes her conclusion, and paragraph 4 proposes the ‘more modest claim’ that the petitions show where support was concentrated. That is C. B is the trap: the author does not defend the traditional reading, saying the new claim ‘does nothing to vindicate’ it. A, D and E describe steps the passage lacks.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match the sequence of the four paragraphs.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first sentence of each paragraph, and the first sentence of the fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: 1. Earlier historians: totals measure feeling. 2. Hollin: no, totals measure organization. 3. The author: Hollin’s evidence is persuasive, but her conclusion goes too far. 4. The author’s modest use: where, not how many. Check every step.

choices.note: The passage centers on how to read a body of evidence, not on competing explanations of an event, and Hollin’s view is partly accepted, not rejected.
Tempting, because the author does push back on Hollin. But the author doesn’t return to the traditional reading; the new claim ‘does nothing to vindicate’ it.
CORRECT. Traditional reading, Hollin’s challenge, partial acceptance, and a narrower use of the petitions (where support was concentrated).
Hollin’s method isn’t applied to new records; the Brenmark records are used against her conclusion.
No thesis explains the 1867 vote; the passage never says why the parliament finally acted.

questions.stem: Both passages are primarily concerned with answering which one of the following questions?
choices: Why have peer-review panels become less able to distinguish strong research proposals from weak ones?
Should research grants be awarded by lot among the proposals that reviewers judge worthy of funding?
Can peer-review panels reliably separate proposals worth funding from those that should not be funded at all?
Would awarding grants by lot reduce the effort that applicants devote to polishing each of their proposals?
Would replacing the ranking of proposals with a lottery cause the number of grant applications to rise?
questions.explanation: Passage A argues that grants should be awarded by lot among fundable proposals; passage B argues that such a lottery has costs and should be confined to breaking ties. Both address B. E is the dominant trap: it is a central point of passage B’s second paragraph, but passage A never considers how a lottery would affect the number of applications. C is something both passages assume rather than argue, D is a side benefit mentioned in passage A, and A misstates both passages, which say panels separate weak from strong proposals reasonably well.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the question both passages are mainly trying to answer.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, third paragraph; passage B, first and third paragraphs.

breakdown.analysis: A says: award grants by lot among the fundable. B says: a full lottery has costs; use it only to break ties. Same proposal, different verdicts. So the shared question is ‘should grants be awarded by lot among fundable proposals?’ For a ‘both passages’ question, test every choice against both passages; the trap is usually one passage’s pet issue.

choices.note: Neither passage says panels have become worse at telling strong from weak. A says they do that part ‘reasonably well’; the trouble is ordering the strong ones, and the funding rate has fallen.
CORRECT. A says yes; B says only in part (as a tiebreaker). Both are answering this question.

Both passages take this for granted rather than argue it. Passage A says panels agree ‘reasonably well’ about which proposals are weak and would leave that job to them; passage B keeps the threshold too. A shared assumption isn’t the question either passage is mainly answering.

Right idea, wrong scope. Passage A lists freeing applicants from ‘an arms race of presentation’ as one benefit of a lottery, and passage B’s worry about ‘many adequate proposals’ brushes against it. But it’s a side effect in each, not the question either passage is built to answer.
Tempting, because passage B makes a lot of it. But passage A never discusses the volume of applications. One passage’s concern, not both.

questions.stem: According to passage A, when the same proposals have been scored independently by two panels, the panels
choices: have agreed scarcely better than chance about which proposals deserved to be funded at all
have disagreed most often about proposals submitted by applicants from prestigious institutions
have agreed reasonably well about which proposals were strong but scarcely better than chance about how to order the weak ones
have agreed about how to order strong proposals only when they used the same scoring criteria
have been more consistent in picking out the proposals that fall short than in deciding which strong proposal should come first
questions.explanation: Passage A’s second paragraph says the panels ‘agreed reasonably well about which proposals were weak but scarcely better than chance about how to order the strong ones.’ E says the same in other words: more consistency in spotting proposals that fall short than in ranking the strong ones. C is the dominant trap: it reuses the passage’s phrases (‘agreed reasonably well,’ ‘scarcely better than chance’) but swaps ‘weak’ and ‘strong.’ A moves the near-chance agreement to the basic fundable/unfundable judgment, and B and D are never stated.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what passage A says about two panels scoring the same proposals.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, second paragraph, second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: The sentence has two halves: good agreement on which proposals are weak, near-chance agreement on how to order the strong ones. Passage A’s whole proposal depends on that split (keep the panels for the threshold, use a lottery above it). The right answer restates the split in new words; the trap keeps the passage’s exact phrases and quietly swaps which group goes with which.

choices.note: The near-chance agreement was about ordering the strong proposals. On which proposals are weak, the panels agreed ‘reasonably well,’ which is why passage A trusts them with the threshold.
Bias toward prestigious institutions is mentioned later, but not as something the two-panel comparisons showed.

Tempting, because both of its phrases come straight from the passage. But it swaps the groups: the panels agreed on which proposals were weak and failed to agree on how to order the strong ones. Familiar words, reversed relationship.
Scoring criteria never come up.
CORRECT. ‘Proposals that fall short’ are the weak ones they agreed on; ‘which strong proposal should come first’ is the ordering they couldn’t agree on.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, according to passage B, would be sufficient for funding by rank to support better research overall than funding by lot?
choices: two panels scoring the same strong proposals agree on their order even modestly more often than chance would predict
applicants respond to the funding system by submitting only a few excellent, carefully prepared proposals rather than many merely adequate ones
reviewers are relieved of the task of separating fundable proposals from unfundable ones
panels’ rankings, though often mistaken about particular proposals, favor the better proposal slightly more often than a coin toss would
funding agencies continue to receive roughly the same number of applications each year as they receive under the present system
questions.explanation: Passage B’s first paragraph argues that a ranking ‘unreliable for any single proposal can still be informative on average’: if panels put truly stronger proposals higher even modestly more often than chance, ranking will, across thousands of grants, fund somewhat better science than a lottery. D restates that condition in other words: often wrong case by case, but slightly better than a coin toss. A is the dominant trap: it reuses ‘even modestly more often than chance’ but attaches it to agreement between two panels, passage A’s evidence, rather than to accuracy; two panels can agree on an order that doesn’t track which proposals are truly stronger. B and E concern passage B’s separate worry about applicants, and C describes nothing passage B proposes.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what passage B says would be enough for ranking to beat a lottery.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, first paragraph, second and third sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Passage B’s condition is about accuracy, and the bar is low: the ranking has to put the truly stronger proposal higher a bit more often than chance, even though it’s ‘unreliable for any single proposal.’ So the answer will sound weak and unimpressive (‘often mistaken,’ ‘slightly more often than a coin toss’), and that’s the point. Agreement between panels is a different thing: two panels can share the same blind spot and agree while both being wrong.

choices.note: Tempting, because it borrows passage B’s exact qualifier, ‘even modestly more often than chance.’ But passage B attaches that qualifier to placing ‘truly stronger proposals’ higher, which is accuracy. Panels agreeing with each other is passage A’s evidence, and agreement doesn’t guarantee accuracy: two panels with the same bias would agree and still be wrong.
That’s from passage B’s second paragraph, about how applicants would behave under a lottery, not the condition for ranking to win.
Passage B never proposes this. In fact both passages keep the panels at the threshold.

CORRECT. ‘Often mistaken about particular proposals’ is ‘unreliable for any single proposal’; ‘slightly more often than a coin toss’ is ‘even modestly more often than chance.’ Passage B says that’s enough, across many grants.
Also from the applicant-behavior worry. Holding the number of applications steady isn’t the condition passage B gives for ranking to produce better science.

questions.stem: The attitude of the author of passage B toward passage A’s characterization of the competition among strong proposals as ‘a contest whose outcome is close to random already’ (end of the second paragraph of passage A) can best be described as
choices: acceptance of it as a description of individual funding decisions, together with a denial that it shows ranking to be worthless
rejection of it, on the grounds that panels place stronger proposals in the upper half of the fundable group more often than chance
acceptance of it, together with agreement that a lottery would therefore cost nothing in the quality of the research funded
skepticism, since the studies in which proposals were scored by two panels examined only weak proposals
indifference, since passage B’s case against a full lottery rests entirely on how applicants would respond to it
questions.explanation: Passage B says the lottery advocates are ‘largely right’ about the unreliability of peer review among strong proposals, but adds that ‘a ranking that is unreliable for any single proposal can still be informative on average,’ so a lottery would not ‘cost nothing.’ A captures both. B is the dominant trap: passage B states its claim about the upper half only as a condition (‘if panels place…’), not as a fact, and it concedes the unreliability. C ignores passage B’s denial that a lottery is costless, D misdescribes the panel studies, and E ignores passage B’s first paragraph.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pin down how passage B’s author regards passage A’s claim that the ranking of strong proposals is close to random.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, second paragraph; passage B, first paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Passage B opens with a concession: on the unreliability point the advocates are ‘largely right.’ Then the turn: unreliable for any single proposal is not the same as useless on average. So B accepts A’s description case by case, and denies what A draws from it (that ranking adds nothing). Watch the ‘if’ in B’s next sentence: B never asserts that panels beat chance; it says what follows if they do.

choices.note: CORRECT. Accepts the claim for single decisions (‘largely right,’ ‘unreliable for any single proposal’) but denies that ranking is therefore worthless (‘informative on average’).

Tempting, because passage B does talk about panels beating chance. But it puts that as a condition (‘if panels place …’), not as a finding, and it opens by calling the advocates ‘largely right.’ It never rejects A’s description.
Half right. B accepts the unreliability, but says outright: ‘It does not follow … that a lottery would cost nothing.’
Passage A says the panels agreed on the weak proposals and not on ordering the strong ones, so the studies covered both. And passage B raises no doubts about them.
Passage B’s first paragraph is a direct response to this claim, so the author is hardly indifferent. Applicant behavior is a second, separate point.

questions.stem: Which one of the following pairs of titles would be most appropriate for passage A and passage B, respectively?
choices: “Peer Review Under Strain” / “In Defense of Peer Review as It Now Stands”
“The Hidden Costs of Writing Grant Proposals” / “Bias on the Funding Panel”
“Admitting Chance into Research Funding” / “A Lottery for Ties, Not for All”
“Why Peer Reviewers Disagree with One Another” / “Why Applicants Multiply”
“The Case for Randomness in Science Funding” / “The Case Against Randomness in Science Funding”
questions.explanation: Passage A argues for openly awarding grants by lot among fundable proposals; passage B concludes that a lottery should be used ‘to break ties among proposals that panels cannot separate’ but not in its full form. C fits both. E is the dominant trap: it casts passage B as opposed to randomness, but passage B endorses a lottery for ties. A misreads B, which says ‘none of this argues for leaving the present system as it is’; B and D each name a single detail.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the titles that capture each passage’s overall point.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, third paragraph; passage B, third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Passage A: let chance decide among the fundable. Passage B: don’t go that far; use chance only for ties. A title for B has to keep B’s partial yes. ‘Against’ is too strong for B, and ‘defense of the status quo’ contradicts its last paragraph.

choices.note: Passage B says flatly, ‘None of this argues for leaving the present system as it is.’ It doesn’t defend peer review as it stands.
Each title names one detail: the effort of polishing proposals in A, and reviewer bias, which is also from A, not B.
CORRECT. A admits chance into funding; B limits the lottery to ties.
Each names a sub-point (unreliable ordering in A, more applications in B) rather than the passage’s argument.
Tempting, because it fits A perfectly and B does argue against A’s proposal. But B accepts randomness for breaking ties. ‘The case against randomness’ drops B’s qualification.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the two passages?
choices: Passage A defends an existing practice against criticism; passage B argues that the criticism is better founded than passage A allows.
Passage A presents evidence for a claim about peer review; passage B reinterprets that evidence so that it supports the opposite claim.
Passage A advocates a reform; passage B disputes the central premise of that advocacy and argues for a more limited version of the reform.
Passage A reports the results of a trial of a new method of funding; passage B questions whether those results can be generalized.
Passage A advocates a reform; passage B grants a central premise of that advocacy but argues for a more limited version of the reform.
questions.explanation: Passage A proposes a lottery among fundable proposals; passage B concedes that advocates are ‘largely right’ about the unreliability of ranking but recommends a lottery only ‘to break ties.’ E describes this. C is the dominant trap: it matches B’s narrower proposal, but says B disputes A’s central premise, when B explicitly grants it and challenges only the inference that a lottery costs nothing. A reverses passage A’s stance, B misdescribes passage B’s use of the evidence, and D invents a trial.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how passage B relates to passage A.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, third paragraph; passage B, first sentence and third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Passage A: proposal (lottery among the fundable), based on a premise (ordering of strong proposals is unreliable). Passage B: concedes the premise (‘largely right’), points to costs, and ends with a smaller version (lottery for ties). The answer needs all three of those moves. Two choices get the ending right, so the premise is what separates them: did B grant it or dispute it?

choices.note: Passage A attacks the existing practice; it doesn’t defend it.
Passage B doesn’t reinterpret A’s evidence; it accepts it (‘largely right’) and disputes what follows from it.

Tempting, because its second half matches B’s closing proposal exactly, and B’s ‘informative on average’ can look like a challenge to A. But B opens by saying the advocates are ‘largely right’ about the unreliability of ranking among strong proposals. B grants the premise and disputes what A infers from it. One verb is wrong.
Nobody reports a trial. Passage A argues from scoring studies and from principle.
CORRECT. The premise granted (‘largely right’ about unreliability) and the narrower reform (a lottery for ties).

questions.stem: The authors of the passages would be most likely to disagree over whether
choices: peer-review panels can reliably separate proposals that should not be funded from those that might be
the order in which panels rank the strong proposals is actually reliable for any individual proposal
the present method of allocating public research funding ought to be changed in at least some respect
a lottery among all fundable proposals would cost something in the quality of research funded
a lottery would lead applicants to submit more proposals than they submit under the present system
questions.explanation: Passage A holds that the ordering of strong proposals is ‘close to random already,’ so a lottery among the fundable gives up nothing and removes bias; passage B says ‘it does not follow … that a lottery would cost nothing’ and that ranking ‘will … support somewhat better science’ if it beats chance even modestly. They split on D. B is the dominant trap: both authors agree that the ranking is unreliable for individual proposals. A and C are points of agreement, and E is raised only by passage B.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a point on which one author would say yes and the other no.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, second and third paragraphs; passage B, first paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one author must say yes and the other no. List what they share first: the ranking of strong proposals is unreliable case by case; panels can handle the threshold; the system should change. Then find the split: A thinks a full lottery loses nothing (the ordering is near-random anyway, and a lottery removes bias). B says a lottery would not ‘cost nothing,’ because a weakly informative ranking still beats chance across thousands of grants.

choices.note: Both agree. Passage A says panels do this well; passage B keeps the threshold and gives it more weight.

Tempting, because it’s the central issue in both passages. But they agree on it: A says agreement is ‘scarcely better than chance,’ and B says the ranking is ‘unreliable for any single proposal.’ Same answer from both, so no disagreement.
Both say yes. A wants a full lottery; B says ‘None of this argues for leaving the present system as it is.’
CORRECT. A: no cost (the ordering is near-random, and a lottery removes bias). B: some cost (‘it does not follow … that a lottery would cost nothing’).
Only passage B raises this. Passage A never addresses how many proposals applicants would submit, so we can’t say it disagrees.
